Section 00-01: Identification Codes

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) 

A 17-digit combination of numbers and letters form the vehicle 
identification number (VIN). The VIN is located in the center area of the 
Vehicle Rating Label. Refer to Vehicle Rating Label in this section for the 
label locations. 

By looking at the 17-digit VIN, a variety of information about the 
vehicle can be determined. The first three digits identify the manufacturer 
and the vehicle make and type. The fourth digit determines the type of brake 
system (air or hydraulic) and the gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) class for 
trucks (completed vehicles). For incomplete vehicles, the fourth digit 
determines the brake system only. Digits five, six and seven identify the 
model or line, series, chassis and cab type. The eighth digit points out the 
particular engine and type (gas or diesel) found in the vehicle. Digit nine is 
the VIN check digit. Digit 10 identifies the model year of a Ford-completed 
vehicle, or the model year of the incomplete vehicle, if sold by Ford as an 
incomplete vehicle. Digit 11 determines the assembly plant. Digits 12 through 
17 make up the sequential serial and warranty number. Digit 12 uses the letter 
A until the production or sequence of 99,999 units (digits 13 through 17) is 
reached. Letter A then becomes B for the next production sequence of vehicles. 

Refer to the code portion of this section for specific definitions of 
the numbers and letters of the vehicle identification number (VIN).

[FIGURE: DY0069B.gif]

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Rating Label 

The following illustration shows a typical Vehicle Rating Label. On 
cowl and windshield vehicles, the Rating Label is mounted on the right side of 
the cowl top panel under the hood. On incomplete vehicles, the rating label is 
attached to a booklet (incomplete vehicle manual) and secured to a suitable 
interior location. On all other vehicles, the rating label is mounted on the 
rear face of the left front door. 

The vehicle data appears on the Vehicle Rating Label on the two lines 
following the identification number. The code set (two numbers or a number and 
letter) above COLOR identify the exterior paint color (two sets of codes 
designate a two-tone). The first three digits under WB designate the wheelbase 
in inches. The letter and three digits under TYPE/GVW designate the truck 
model within a series and the gross vehicle weight rating. The letters or 
numeral under BODY designate the interior trim, seat and body type. The 
transmission installed in the vehicle is identified under TRANS by two 
letters, or a number and one letter. (If so equipped, a number is also stamped 
before the transmission code to identify the auxiliary transmission.) A letter 
and a number or two numbers or two letters under AXLE identify the rear axle 
ratio (when required, a letter is also stamped after the rear axle code to 
identify the front axle). 

A two-digit number is stamped above DSO to identify the district that 
ordered the vehicle. If the vehicle is built to special order (Domestic 
Special Order, Foreign Special Order, Limited Production Option or other 
special order), the complete order number will also appear above DSO. The 
vehicle model year appears in the lower right corner area of the decal under 
DSO. The charts that follow list the various vehicle data codes.

Supplemental Data Plate 

The original data plate can get damaged or become difficult to read. A 
supplemental data plate is installed on all vehicles. The supplemental metal 
data plate is installed on the body B-pillar below the striker pin on F-Cab 
and on the dash panel above the ashtray on F-Cowl and B-Series vehicles. A 
blank field is provided for the dealer to stamp with in-service data or any 
other desired information.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Build Date Stamp Location

The vehicle build date stamp is a four-digit number representing month 
and day of manufacture. On F- and B-Series vehicles, the vehicle build date is 
stamped on the front surface of the radiator support on the passenger side of 
the vehicle. 

For a build date of January 24, for example, the vehicle build date 
stamp reads 0124; for a build date of October 21, the vehicle date stamp reads 
1021.

Yellow ink is normally used for the date stamp. When the marking 
surface is painted the body color, the date stamp will be marked in red ink. 
Units from the Ontario Truck Plant (Code C) will be marked with silver ink.

1999 F800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) 

The official vehicle identification number (VIN) for title and 
registration purposes is stamped on a metal tab that is fastened to the 
instrument panel close to the windshield glass on the left hand side of the 
vehicle. It is visible from the outside.

The vehicle identification number (VIN) is a 17-character alphanumeric 
vehicle identification number. This number is used for warranty identification 
of the vehicle and indicates the following:

World manufacturer identification

Gross vehicle weight and brake type

Vehicle type

Body type

Engine type

Check digit

Model year

Assembly year

Consecutive unit number

The last six digits of the vehicle identification number indicate the 
consecutive unit number of each unit built.

 Typical Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) 

[FIGURE: DY0278A.gif]

Item

Description

1

World Manufacturer Identifier

2

Brake System/GVWR Class for Complete Trucks (Brake System Only for
Incomplete Trucks)

3

Line, Body Type

4

Engine Type

5

Check Digit

6

Vehicle Model Year

7

Assembly Plant

8

Constant A until sequence of 99,999 is reached, then changes to a constant
B and so on

9

Production Sequence Number

1999 F and B-Series

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Noise 

Noise, defined as any unpleasant sound, can be described in a variety 
of ways, such as tapping, whistling, buzzing, humming, clunking or booming. 

All noises can be associated with a probable cause. Based on 
experience, these descriptions will assist in isolating the condition and 
correcting it. 

Generally recognizable concern areas are engine, driveline, wind and 
road surface noises. 

Other less obvious areas that should be considered as noise concern 
sources are any of the conditions that cause the vibrations described in this 
section. 

A gear driven mechanism, especially a drive axle, will produce a 
certain amount of noise. 

Some noise is acceptable and can be audible at certain speeds or under 
various driving conditions: for example, tire noise on a newly paved blacktop 
road or brake pedal noise associated with hydro-boost brake units. 

Such noise is in no way detrimental to the operation of the vehicle and 
must be considered normal.

================================================================================
PAGE 2207
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Vibration 

Vibration, technically, is a high-frequency trembling, shaking or 
grounding condition, felt or heard, that is constant or variable in level and 
occurs during a portion of the total operating speed range. The types of 
vibrations that can be felt in the vehicle can be divided into three groups: 

Vibrations of various unbalanced rotating parts of the vehicle. 

Body and frame vibrations excited by powertrain, wind or road inputs. 

Tip-in moans or resonance vibrations from stressed engine or exhaust 
system mounts or driveline flexing modes. 

These vehicle vibrations can also be subdivided into those that occur 
at low speeds and those that are most noticeable at higher speeds. Since the 
dividing line between low and higher speed vibrations is not clear, there will 
be vibrations that overlap the two ranges. 

 Low-Speed Vibrations — Typical (Less Than 72 km/h [45 mph]) 

Exhaust vibration 

Engine harshness 

Driveline vibration due to improper driveline angles

Improper installation of engine and transmission rear support 
insulators (voided areas of insulators must be positioned at 12 o'clock and 6 
o'clock). Most noticeable at idle and low speeds.

Air conditioner compressor or drive belt vibrations 

Take-off shudder (clutch or driveline concerns) 

Brake roughness or harshness 

Driveline roughness 

Clutch torsion vibration 

Driveline slip-yoke or U-joints, automatic transmission clutch slippage

 High-Speed Vibrations — Typical (Above 72 km/h [45 mph]) 

Axle and companion flange runout or imbalance 

Driveshaft imbalance or improper angles

Excessive tire-wheel and drum assembly imbalance 

Tire roughness due to high nonuniformity (force variation) or 
out-of-balance condition

Rear axle pinion gear pitch line runout 

Excessive tire and wheel runout 

Worn suspension components 

Front end accessory vibrations 

Exhaust vibration (greatly reduced in exhaust systems decoupled by a 
flexible coupling and mounted with blade and block hangers)

================================================================================
PAGE 2208
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 00-04: Noise, Vibration and Harshness

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Harshness 

Harshness is the term commonly used to describe the ride quality of the 
vehicle. Hard ride or harshness is usually caused by the tires or suspension 
system, namely: 

Overinflated tire installed on the vehicle 

Worn suspension components 

Suspension components installed with preload on pivot points, bearings 
and bushings 

Units equipped with tires not specified by the manufacturer (different 
brand tires often give different ride qualities to vehicle) 

Bent or bound-up shock absorbers 

Heavy-duty components installed on vehicle 

Improper installation of cab mounts (groundings) 

Improper installation of engine and transmission rear support 
insulators (voided areas of insulators must be positioned at 12 o'clock and 6 
o'clock). Most noticeable at idle and low speeds.

Other vehicle ride motions can be summarized as follows: 

Vehicle bounce — the vertical motion of a vehicle on its 
suspension system, front and rear in phase. A low frequency "float," an 
intermediate frequency "kick." 

Vehicle pitch — the out-of-phase vertical motion of the front and 
rear of the vehicle. A flat ride is considered the opposite of a pitch ride. 

Vehicle roll — the side-to-side rotation of the vehicle body 
about the front and rear axles.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Weight Distribution 

Weight properly distributed to front and rear axles gives the best ride 
and steerability, and eliminates premature failures due to overloaded axles, 
springs, tires, etc. 

Payload distribution has a definite bearing on vehicle performance. 
Even if the total vehicle is not loaded beyond the recommended maximum gross 
vehicle weight, this does not mean that individual components cannot be 
overloaded. 

Overloading can be due to the improper positioning of heavy materials 
so that the load is centered over one rear tire or so far forward in the body 
that the front axle and tires are overloaded. 

Unloaded or diminishing load type operations also affect the ride 
characteristics of a vehicle. Road vibrations and shock, for example, are not 
dampened in a light vehicle to the extent that they are under heavily loaded 
conditions.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Noise, Vibration and Harshness

 Inspection and Verification 

The noise, vibration and harshness (NVH) section is designed to give a 
working knowledge of the process of diagnosing noise and vibration situations. 
It is divided into several portions, each based on the description of a 
condition. If a condition occurs at high speed, for example, the most likely 
place to start is under High Speed Shake. The Vehicle Vibration Road Test 
portion will tell how to sort the conditions into categories and how to tell a 
vibration from a shake.

A gear-driven unit will produce a certain amount of noise. Some noise 
is acceptable and can be audible at certain speeds or under various driving 
conditions. The slight noise is in no way detrimental and must be considered 
normal. 

NVH usually occur in four areas: tires, engine accessories, suspension 
and drivetrain. It is important, therefore, that an NVH concern be isolated 
into its specific area as soon as possible. The easiest and quickest way to do 
this is to perform a road test. 

Make a visual inspection as part of the preliminary diagnostic routine, 
writing down anything that does not look right. Note tire pressures, but do 
not adjust them yet. Note leaking fluids, loose nuts or bolts, or bright spots 
where components might be rubbing against each other. Check cargo area for 
unusual loads. 

Do not service or make any adjustments until a road test and a thorough 
visual inspection of the vehicle have been performed. Do not change tire 
pressure or vehicle load. Adjusting tire pressures or vehicle load, or making 
some other adjustment, can reduce the condition's intensity to a point where 
it cannot be identified clearly. It can also inject a new condition into the 
system, preventing proper diagnosis. 

Make notes throughout diagnosis. It will help cover all bases when 
starting to compile data. Use a road test form that includes space for 
comments. Write down even the smallest bit of information, as it can turn out 
to be most important. 

Road test the vehicle, and define the condition by reproducing it 
several times during the road test. 

Perform the vehicle vibration road test as soon as the condition is 
reproduced. This will identify the proper section of the diagnostic procedure. 
Run through the test more than once to make sure a usable result is being 
obtained. Remember, the road test might not tell where the concern is, but it 
will tell where it is not.

 Vehicle Vibration Road Test 

24-80 km/h (15-50 mph): With light acceleration, a moaning noise is 
heard, and possibly a vibration is felt in the floorpan. It is usually worse 
at a particular engine speed and at a particular throttle setting during 
acceleration at that speed. It can also produce a moaning sound, depending on 
what component is causing it. 

High speed shake: With slow acceleration and deceleration, a shake is 
sometimes noticed in the steering wheel/steering column tube, seats, floorpan, 
trim panels, or front end sheet metal. It is a low frequency vibration (around 
9-15 cycles per second). It might or might not be increased by applying brakes 
lightly. 

High speed vibration: A vibration is felt in the floorpan or seats with 
no visible shake, but with an accompanying sound or rumble, buzz, hum, drone 
or booming noise. Coast with clutch depressed or transmission control selector 
lever in NEUTRAL and engine idling. If vibration is still evident, it can be 
related to wheels, tires, front disc brake rotors, front or rear brake drums, 
wheel hubs or wheel bearings. 

0-high speed: A vibration is felt whenever the engine reaches a 
particular rpm. It will disappear in NEUTRAL coast. The vibration can be 
duplicated by operating the engine at the problem rpm while the vehicle is 
parked. It can be caused by any component, from the accessory drive belt to 
the clutch or torque converter, which turns at engine speed when the vehicle 
is stopped. 

 Noise Diagnosis Procedure 

 Non-Axle Noises 

There are some noise conditions that can sound like axle noise and have 
to be considered while performing road test diagnosis. The most common 
conditions are noise from the transmission, exhaust system and tires. 
Therefore, be sure that none of these non-axle noise conditions are the cause 
of the noise concern before proceeding with an axle teardown and diagnosis.

 Noise Conditions 

If noise is produced as part of a vibration condition, correcting the 
vibration will eliminate the noise. If the noise is related to a specific 
component or system, refer to the appropriate service manual section for 
further diagnosis.

 Vibration Conditions 

Engine or accessory vibration, all speeds — refer to Pinpoint 
Tests B and D in this section.

High-speed shake, 80 km/h (50 mph) and up:

Refer to Section 04-04 for tire conditions contributing to high-speed 
shake.

Refer to rotor and drum runout checks contained in Section 06-00 .

Tip-In Moan — refer to Pinpoint Test C in this section.

Vibration, technically, is a high-frequency trembling, shaking or 
grounding condition, felt or heard, that is constant or variable in level and 
occurs during a portion of the total operating speed range. The types of 
vibrations that can be felt in the vehicle can be divided into three groups:

Vibrations of various unbalanced rotating parts of the vehicle.

Body and frame vibrations excited by powertrain, wind or road inputs.

Tip-in moans or resonance vibrations from stressed engine or exhaust 
system mounts or driveline flexing modes.

These vehicle vibrations can also be subdivided into those that occur 
at low speeds and those that are most noticeable at higher speeds. Since the 
dividing line between low and higher speed vibrations is not clear, there will 
be vibrations that overlap the two ranges.

 Leakage Conditions 

Most rear axle lubricant leakage conditions can be corrected without a 
teardown. However, it is important to clean up the leaking area enough to 
identify the exact source.

A plugged axle vent will cause excessive seal lip wear due to internal 
pressure buildup. When a leak occurs, check the vent located near the top of 
the differential housing. Make sure the vent hose is not kinked. Remove the 
vent hose from the vent nipple and make sure the hose is clear of dirt or 
other foreign materials. While hose is removed, pass a length of mechanics' 
wire or small diameter Allen wrench in and out of the vent nipple to clean it 
of any dirt or foreign materials. Install vent hose. If vent cannot be 
cleared, it must be replaced.

Make sure axle lubricant is within specified limits.

ADJUSTMENTS

Driveline 

For additional driveline adjustment procedures, refer to Section 05-00 . 

 Slip-Spline Coupling Binding 

If, while driving the vehicle, particularly during acceleration or 
deceleration, a ringing or grinding noise in the driveline is noted, or if the 
driveshaft center support bearing has been damaged, the driveshaft slip-spline 
coupling is a likely source. 

These noise conditions can be caused by the coupling shaft dust shield 
contacting the center support bearing insulator or bracket, as the result of a 
tight or binding slip-spline (between coupling shaft and driveshaft). When 
this condition exists, the coupling shaft, if pulled rearward into the center 
support bearing when the vehicle is being driven, causes the resultant noise 
or insulator damage. 

If this condition is verified, perform the following procedure:

Disconnect driveshaft universal joint from rear axle pinion flange. 

Push and pull driveshaft forward and rearward to work driveshaft to 
coupling shaft slip joint. 

If the slip joint has loosened up with the slipping action and is 
functioning satisfactorily, no replacement of the driveshaft or coupling shaft 
is necessary. Replace only damaged parts, such as the center support 
insulator. 

If after working the slip joint back and forth several times there 
still is excessive tightness or binding, the entire coupling shaft assembly 
(including the center support) should be replaced. 

Verify proper slip-spline action with the new coupling shaft and 
proceed with repairs. 

 NOTE: Check driveshaft for proper yoke phasing (90-degree phase angle shown). 

[FIGURE: E3745C.gif]

 Driveline Support Plate Position 

An adjustable driveline support plate is used on some applications. 
Although it can be mounted in any one of several positions, only one position 
is correct for a specific application. The correct position can be determined 
from the support plate part number shown on the Truck Specification List 
attached to each vehicle. 

The numerical digit in the adjustable support plate part number suffix 
indicates the hole set to be used. 

For example, support plate 4831 is bolted to crossmember (or bracket 
4691, some installations) through support plate hole set number 1. The hole 
sets are identified by the numbers stamped into the bracket 4691 or support 
plate 4831.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Body Sealer Types and Application

Since many sealers are used in the assembly of the vehicle, the 
following all-purpose sealers have been selected for service use. The method 
and points of application are shown in each applicable group.

 Liquid Butyl Sealer 

Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B (Black) or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G162-A does not run, is fast drying and remains 
semi-elastic. The sealer can be used for seam sealing in such areas as the 
floorpan, wheelhouse, dash panel, running board, door openings and drip rails. 
It can also be used to seal outside moulding clip holes and for windshield and 
rear window installation.

 Caulking Cord 

Caulking Cord D6AZ-19560-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESB-M4G32-A has a plastic base, is heavy-bodied and is commonly known as 
perma-gum. It is used on spotweld holes, around mounting clips and between two 
surfaces not sealed by a gasket. Apply the sealer with a putty knife.

 Weatherstrip Adhesive 

Weatherstrip Adhesive E8AZ-19552-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M2G14-A is a quick-drying, strong adhesive designed to 
cement weatherstripping to doors, bodies, cowl ventilators and the surrounding 
metal. Windows and windshields that are set in rubber can be effectively 
sealed against leakage by flowing cement into affected areas.

Clean all grease, dirt and old sealer from the surfaces to be cemented 
and apply a medium coat of cement to both surfaces. Immediately press both 
surfaces together.

 Silicone Lubricant 

Silicone Lubricant COAZ-19553-AA or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M13P4-A can be used for lubricating rubber parts exposed to 
weather.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Dust and Water Leaks

The forward motion of the vehicle creates a slight vacuum within the 
body, particularly if a window or ventilator is partially open. Any unsealed 
crevice or small opening in the lower section of the body will permit air to 
be drawn into the body. If dust is present in the air, it will also be drawn 
into the body.

Under certain conditions, water can enter the body at any point where 
dirt or dust can enter. Any consideration of water leakage must take into 
account all points covered under dust leaks.

To determine the exact location of a dust leak, remove the following 
trim from the cab: the cowl trim panel, the kick pads and the floor mats.

Removal of the trim will reveal the location of most leaks. Seal these 
leaks, and road test the vehicle on a dusty road to make sure all leaks are 
sealed. The entrance of dust is usually indicated by a pointed shaft of dust 
or silt at the point of entrance. After the road test, check for indications 
of a dust pattern around the door openings, cowl panel and cowl side panel.

Sometimes leaks can be located by putting bright lights under the 
vehicle, with the above components removed, and checking the interior of the 
body at joints and weld lines. The light will show through where leaks exist.

================================================================================

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Wind Noise

Air entering or exiting the vehicle through small openings in the body 
can result in wind noise. Sources of wind noise are detected by driving the 
vehicle at highway speeds in four different directions. Listen for sources of 
wind noise with all windows closed, radio off, heater and air conditioner 
blower motor turned off and ventilation ducts open. A stethoscope can be used 
to pinpoint the source of the noise.

Most wind noise-producing leaks will occur at the door and window seals 
or at sheet metal joints in the door or the door opening in the body.

Seal all leaks with RTV sealant and foam tape or by repositioning or 
replacing the seals. Road test the vehicle to make sure all leaks have been 
adequately sealed.

An alternate method of verifying corrective actions involves the use of 
Rotunda Combination Engine EAR/Chassis EAR 107-R2102 or equivalent. After 
identifying the leak point through a drive evaluation, obtain a meter reading 
by using the leak detector. A check with the leak detector after repairing the 
leak will verify the effectiveness of the corrective action. A final test 
drive is still advisable to check for additional leaks.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Rattle Elimination

Most rattles are caused by a loose bolt or screw. Foreign objects such 
as nuts, bolts or small pieces of body deadener in the door wells and pillars 
are often the source of rattles. Door wells can be checked by carefully 
striking the underside of the door with a rubber mallet. The impact made by 
the mallet will indicate if loose objects are in the door well.

Tighten all bolts and screws periodically. In the event that tightening 
the bolts and screws located on such assemblies as the doors does not 
eliminate the rattles, the trouble is probably caused by misalignment. If this 
is the case, follow the adjustment and alignment procedures for these 
assemblies.

Rattles and squeaks are sometimes caused by weatherstripping and 
anti-squeak material that has slipped out of position. Apply additional cement 
or other adhesive, and install the material in the proper location to 
eliminate this difficulty.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Paint Damage from Airborne Materials

The following information gives a detailed description of paint damage 
caused by chemical or organic materials. If service is required, identify the 
source of the damage and follow the recommended service procedure.

 Chemical 

The effects of chemical airborne materials can be seen as follows:

dark blotches in the paint where the pigment in the paint surface has 
been attacked

irregular spots that are cracked or etched around the edges and dull in 
the centers

small orange-colored spots caused by iron particles that appear on the 
paint surface

Generally, materials that attack a paint film are either acidic or 
alkaline in nature.

Sulfuric and nitric acids, in general, cause extreme damage to 
automotive paint finishes. Even very small concentrations of the same 
materials can cause chemical spotting damage. Due to evaporation and 
condensation, these acids can create severe etching that can eventually crack 
or lift the paint film after some time in service.

Although some automotive finishes are more resistant than others, none 
are completely immune to these chemicals. The most resistant paints used today 
are the urethanes because their resin system is least likely to react with 
chemicals. Air-dried coatings are more susceptible to attack only when they 
are fresh. The longer the paint dries, the more resistant it becomes.

Metallic colors are more intolerant to chemicals because aluminum flake 
is fairly reactive with either an acid or alkali. The following chart contains 
the most common acid materials found on automotive finishes.

 CHEMICAL SPOTTING DAMAGE OF AUTOMOTIVE FINISHES

 a Caustic refers to any alkaline substance that can be harsh
or corrosive, depending on strength or concentration.

 Organic 

Organic damage is generally easier to identify. Organic damage is 
mostly due to tree sap, bird and insect droppings, dead insects and pollen. 
Tree sap is easily identified by clear raised drops that can be hard or 
sticky. Bee or bug dropping spots can appear brownish or yellow in color, 
about 3.1 mm to 6.3 mm (1/8 to 1/4 inch) in diameter. Dead and decomposing 
insect bodies are readily visible to the eye. Pollen deposits are small yellow 
clusters.

Each of these items is potentially damaging to any currently available 
paint system. Other noticeable traits of organic damage are spots that are 
raised (swelling), micro-crazing (cracked) and pitting due to pollen eating 
into the paint film. The active ingredients in most organic contaminants are 
tannic and formic acids. These acids are found in berries and bodily fluids of 
insects and birds. Organic damage is accelerated by heat. During very hot 
weather conditions, it is important to wash vehicles more often.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Chemical or Organic Damage Repair

Iron dust particles or other industrial fallout can imbed themselves 
into the paint film. After some weathering, tiny dots of rust that feel rough 
to the touch or irregular discoloration begin to appear. This type of paint 
damage is difficult to repair. Use the following procedure to remove these 
particles and contaminants. Refer to the Specifications portion of this 
section for product information necessary for this procedure.

 WARNING: THE TECHNICIAN MUST WEAR PROTECTIVE CLOTHING AND EYE PROTECTION TO 
PREVENT SKIN IRRITATION. 

 CAUTION: Any changes to this procedure will cause an incomplete or 
unsatisfactory repair and can result in possible damage to the painted 
surfaces and trim. 

 CAUTION: The use of any other product or procedure can cause damage to aluminum, 
flexible painted surfaces or other painted surfaces. Follow directions exactly 
and rinse thoroughly after each step. 

 NOTE: This procedure must be performed before any buffing, polishing, color 
sanding or refinishing is attempted. The materials in this procedure are 
alkaline, acidic and neutral. They must be used in the specified order.

 NOTE: This decontamination procedure is designed to remove surface 
contaminants from the paint on vehicles that have been contaminated up to 120 
days. Vehicles that have experienced the condition longer than this period 
might require an additional treatment to remove metal contaminants.

 NOTE: Ford does not recommend the use of oxalic acids or other fallout 
removal products. Use Finish Kare, Inc., products 1119, 883 and 118SC to 
decontaminate the paint surface.

Rinse off dust and debris with cold water. Be sure to start at the 
bottom of vehicle and work up.

Prepare product 1119 by mixing one part product 1119 with four parts 
cold water.

Use clean wash mitt and apply mixture to entire vehicle, starting at 
the bottom and working up to the top surface. Keep car wet with the solution 
for 5 to 10 minutes. Do not allow it to streak down the sides. Rewipe with 
mitt if necessary to avoid streaks.

Rinse vehicle with cold water.

Dry the flat surface of the vehicle hood and roof.

 NOTE: Product 883 is ready to use from the bottle. No mixing is necessary.

Apply product 883 directly to the contaminated surfaces using a clean, 
dry sponge, wash mitt, or soft truck brush. Keep the areas wet with product 
883 for 5 to 7 minutes. Do not allow to dry on vehicle. Wipe down to the body 
line on the sides.

Prepare product 118SC by mixing 0.03 liter (1 oz) with 3.7 liters (1 
gallon) of water.

 NOTE: Do not use the same mitt to apply shampoo that was used to apply 
product 883 or 1119. Always keep these mitts separate.

Shampoo the vehicle with product 118SC mixture using a clean wash mitt. 
Rinse with cold water.

Inspect the paint surface to see if rust particles have been removed. 
If rust particles have been on the vehicle for a long period of time, it may 
be necessary to repeat each of the previous steps. Acid rain discoloration or 
etching will require either buffing, color sanding or refinishing if etching 
is visible.

 Correction of Surface Following Decontamination 

Use the buffing products from only one manufacturer. Do not intermix 
products.

Always follow the manufacturer's product sequence. Use appropriate pads 
with each product as recommended by the manufacturer.

Use a dual action sander with a Velcro®-mount backing plate and 
appropriate foam pad for final polishing swirl removal.

Use an alcohol and water mixture (1:4 ratio) to clean buffed areas to 
verify removal of scratches and swirls before application of final protective 
glaze.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Repainting

 CAUTION: Some state and local governments have specific health and safety 
regulations that recommend the use of special breathing apparatus when using 
finishing materials containing toxic products. 

Before attempting repainting, determine the surface and overall 
condition of the existing paint. Horizontal surfaces usually show the greatest 
surface deterioration.

Carefully inspect the hood and roof panel to determine the overall 
condition of the paint.

Clean the areas being inspected and look carefully for any signs of 
surface deterioration or any other form of film breakdown such as checking, 
cracking or humidity blistering. In particular, note the gloss level. Low 
gloss indicates surface irregularities caused by such defects as checking or 
blistering.

Look for evidence of brittleness, poor adhesion or excessive chipping. 
If in doubt about the condition of the paint, scrape the finish slightly and 
examine further.

If a complete repaint job is necessary, plan a painting sequence, 
primarily for the sake of continuity so as to avoid dry joint overlaps and 
minimize unnecessary work, before beginning to spray.

Spray all locations that are not easily accessible (hood and hood 
edges, drain channels, door jambs). Keep doors slightly ajar to prevent 
sticking and to permit efficient drying. The purpose of this initial spraying 
is to remove dust that otherwise might be blown about and adversely affect the 
exterior finishing operation.

 Respray Sequence 

Once the difficult access areas have been sprayed, begin painting 
vehicle in the following sequence:

Paint the roof panel at the rear corner, along the drip rail to the 
front body pillar, then paint the rail inward toward the roof panel center.

Move to the opposite side of the body. Pick up the wet paint edge by 
applying the paint from the center of the roof panel. Continue outward and 
along the drip rail to the front body pillar and finish the roof panel by 
spraying the rear corner pillar.

Extend the coat application down the rear corner pillar, then paint the 
entire body side, including the door and vertical portion of the hood assembly.

Move across the front cowl and horizontal portion of the hood assembly.

Continue along the vertical portion of the opposite side of the hood 
assembly and along the body side including the door and the rear corner pillar.

Paint the back panel.

 Drying Paint Repair Work 

Following the painting procedure, dry vehicle paint thoroughly to 
ensure the best protection from organic and chemical elements.

 NOTE: If all openings caused by missing window frames, etc., are properly 
masked, it is not necessary to remove plastic parts from the interior of the 
vehicle.

Remove or cover the radiator grille. Cover the turn signal indicator 
lamps, headlamps, any lamps located on the roof panel, air horns and exterior 
mirrors.

Dry the vehicle at approximately 90°C (200°F).

Monitor the temperature of the passenger compartment.

Latch doors in the first catch to avoid distortion of the weatherstrips.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Floorpan Plugs and Grommets

If any plugs are missing or damaged, a dust or water leak can result. 
Such leakage can also occur around grommets used on the dash panel. When dust 
or water leaks are evident, these plugs and grommets must be checked for 
proper installation.

Many plugs and grommets are used in the floorpan and dash panel. The 
floorpan plugs seal the various body bolt access holes.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Drain Holes

Drain holes are located on the underside of each door along the weld 
line of the inner and outer panels. If these holes become clogged with mud or 
road tars, water will collect inside the panels and rust the sheet metal from 
the inside. A sound of sloshing water in a door is an indication of this 
condition.

Check the drain holes regularly. Clean dirt and foreign material from 
the drain holes with a punch or screwdriver.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Trim

The trim on the vehicles requires no special care. Periodic cleaning 
will preserve the beauty and life of the finishes. Wash with clear water or, 
if the parts are very dirty, use Multi-Purpose Cleaner Concentrate 
B8A-19523-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESR-M14P4-A using a 
clean soft cloth or a sponge and water. Rinse and wipe the parts dry. Custom 
Bright Metal Cleaner 8A-19522-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESR-M5B194-B can be used sparingly to remove rust, salt and road chemicals 
from aluminum or stainless steel parts. Do not scour aluminum parts with steel 
wool or polish them with products containing abrasives. A wax will provide 
excellent protection for all bright metal parts.

Remove lower apron attachment. 

Remove the following components from grille opening panel assembly: 
headlamp, parking lamp and turn signal electrical sockets. 

Remove fender to grille opening panel boss nuts. 

Remove grille opening panel assembly from vehicle by removing two 
F-mount bolts from bottom centerline of grille opening panel.

 Installation 

Position grille opening panel assembly to vehicle and secure two 
F-mount bolts to bottom centerline of grille opening panel. 

Attach boss nuts securing fender to grille opening panel. 

Install headlamp, parking lamp and turn signal electrical sockets. 

Install lower apron attachment. 

Install air intake to radiator support. 

Install radiator and coolant recovery bottle to radiator support. 

Install bracket assembly from front fender apron to radiator support. 

Install front bumper. Refer to Section 01-19 .

Section 01-03: Doors

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Doors 

 Removal 

Remove all usable hardware, trim, glass parts and watershield, if so 
equipped. 

Remove the upper and lower hinge access hole cover plates. Mark the 
location of the hinge on the door and body. 

Remove the door-to-lower hinge retaining bolts. 

Support the door, and remove the door-to-upper hinge retaining bolts. 
Slide the door off the hinges. 

If a hinge is to be replaced, remove the hinge-to-pillar bolts and the 
hinge. 

 Installation 

Install the door weatherstrip in proper position. 

If a hinge has been removed, align the hinge with the marks and tighten 
the hinge bolts securely. 

Position the door on the hinges, and install the retaining bolts snugly. 

Install the lock mechanism. Install the glass mechanism, glass, and 
vent window assembly. Make all necessary adjustments as these assemblies are 
installed. Refer to Section 01-14 for lock assembly adjustments and Section 01-11 for glass and window mechanism adjustments. 

Adjust the door and tighten all hinge bolts to 26-34 Nm (19-25 
lb/ft). To provide a good weatherstrip seal, the upper edge of the door must 
be 4.76 mm (3/16 inch) inboard of the upper part of the pillar from the belt 
line to a point near the front of the door. The door margin to the B-pillar is 
3.5-6.5 mm (0.14-0.25 inch).

Install the watershield, if so equipped. Cement the top edge to the 
inside surface of the inner panel. 

Install the hinge access hole cover plates and the door access hole 
cover plate.

Install the door trim and hardware that was removed.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Trim Panels, Door, Front 

 Removal

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Seats and Tracks

The following removal and installation procedures apply generally to 
all F-Series vehicles. If some of the steps do not apply to the particular 
vehicle being serviced, proceed to the next step and refer to the appropriate 
illustration.

typical of all bucket and bench seat assemblies.

components such as seat assemblies and track assemblies. Refer to Seat Track, Manual in the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

PAGE 2264
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 01-10: Seats and Tracks

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Seat, Passenger

 CAUTION: Use care when handling seat and track assembly. Dropping assembly or 
sitting on seat when not secured in vehicle can result in damaged components. 

 Removal 

Remove the seat mount-to-floorpan retaining screw and washer assemblies. 

Remove the seat assembly from the vehicle.

[FIGURE: R10444B.gif]

 Installation 

Apply a bead of Ford Caulking Cord D6AZ-19560-A or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification ESB-M4G32-A around mounting holes approximately 3.1 mm (1/8 
inch) from hole edge. 

Lift the seat assembly into the cab and secure it to the floorpan with 
the retaining screw and washer assemblies. Tighten the screws to 30-40 
Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

================================================================================
PAGE 2265
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 01-10: Seats and Tracks

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Seat Track, Manual 

 CAUTION: Use care when handling seat and track assembly. Dropping assembly or 
sitting on seat when not secured in vehicle can result in damaged components. 

 Removal 

Remove retaining nuts from the rear end of the two seat tracks. 

Remove the seat track-to-floorpan retaining screw and washer assemblies 
(one on each side). Remove safety belt anchor bolts and lift the seat and 
track assembly out of the vehicle. 

Disconnect the seat track latch tie rod from the latches on the seat 
tracks. 

Remove the seat track-to-seat cushion screws (two on each side) and 
remove the tracks from the cushion.

 Seat Track, Manual

safety belt anchor bolts. Tighten to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

tracks. Tighten nuts to 34-46 Nm (25-34 lb-ft).

Window Regulator, Manual 

 Removal 

Remove door trim panel and access cover, if so equipped.

Support the glass in the full up position. 

Remove the center pin from the regulator retaining rivets with a drift 
punch. Drill the head from each rivet using a 6.35-mm (1/4-inch) drill and 
remove the rivet. Be careful not to damage sheet metal holes during drilling. 

Disengage the regulator arm from the glass bracket and remove the 
regulator assembly. 

 Installation 

Position the regulator assembly in the door and insert the arm into the 
glass bracket channel. 

Position regulator assembly to the inner panel and install rivets using 
Rotunda Blind Fastener Installation Tool 107-R0600 or equivalent to attach the 
regulator assembly to the inner panel. If hand tool for installing the pop 
rivets is not available, use a 1/4-inch -20 x 1/2-inch screw and washer 
assembly and a 1/4-inch -20 nut and washer assembly to retain regulator. 
Equivalent metric retainers can also be used. 

Check the operation of the window mechanism and install the door trim 
panel.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Windshield Glass

 Removal 

Remove the windshield wiper arms and blades.

Remove all mouldings, glass stops and retainers.

 Windshield Exterior Moulding 

[FIGURE: N4550C.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

03682

Moulding Assy

2

03132

Moulding Assy

3

03164

Moulding Assy

4

29100

Clip

5

03100

Glass Assy

6

42413

Retainer

Spray Equalizer Cutting Lubricant ECL-784 around windshield urethane 
cutting area. 

 NOTE: On bonded, encapsulated parts, turn blade of cutting knife over so flat 
side is against pinch weld. If blade is not turned over, it can cut or damage 
plastic encapsulation. 

Cut urethane around windshield with utility knife. 

Insert Rotunda Interior Auto Glass Cut-Out Knife Kit 164-R2450 or 
equivalent into urethane at lower center of windshield and continue toward 
driver side. 

Remove the windshield with aid of an assistant. 

 NOTE: If the urethane has cured all the way through, it will be necessary to 
remove enough urethane to leave only a 1.5-mm (1/16-inch) thick layer on the 
sheet metal.

If urethane has not cured all the way through, use care not to smear 
the urethane on component parts and instrument panel.

Check flange sealing area for damaged sheet metal or foreign objects 
that have caused, or will cause, glass breakage. Service sheet metal if 
necessary. 

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Use only urethane for air and water leaks in urethane seal. 

 CAUTION: When replacing urethane installed glass parts, the vehicle should not 
be driven until the urethane has cured (normally a minimum of 24 hours). This 
will prevent the windshield from being jarred out of position. 

 CAUTION: Leave door windows open slightly, and do not slam doors closed until 
urethane has cured. 

 NOTE: Installation of glass with urethane-type seal is performed using 
Windshield and Backlite Seal Urethane Kit EOAZ-19562-A. The kit contains tools 
and materials required for glass installation. Materials listed in this 
procedure are part of the kit.

 NOTE: Repair any damage to sheet metal flange. 

 NOTE: Dress remaining urethane on pinch weld so that it is of uniform level 
and thickness, approximately 1.5 mm (1/16 inch) all around.

Using applicator supplied with kit, apply Urethane Metal Primer 
WSB-M2G234-C to windshield opening flange where bare or painted sheet metal is 
exposed. Allow a minimum of 10 minutes for urethane metal primer surface to 
dry. 

[FIGURE: N11818A.gif]

Install Polyvinyl Chloride (Foam Dam) Tape with self-adhesive back 
around window opening at end of metal flange, and at uppermost side of seal 
plane along cowl. 

[FIGURE: N11819B.gif]

Place the windshield on a low, stable work surface, inside up. 

Clean the windshield.

 NOTE: Wipe off urethane glass cleaner immediately after application because 
cleaner flash-dries. 

Using applicator supplied with kit, wipe the outer 25.4 mm (1 inch) of 
the inside windshield periphery with Urethane Glass Wipe WSB-M5B280-C2. 
Immediately following application, before evaporation occurs, wipe off with a 
lint-free cloth. Repeat application.

[FIGURE: N11820B.gif]

Use glass spacers to properly align windshield glass to body. Glass 
must be centered so that the difference between the side margins is no more 
than 3.0 mm (0.11 inch) along the entire A pillar. Mark alignment points with 
masking tape or crayon on four sides of both glass and opening.

[FIGURE: N11821A.gif]

Remove windshield glass from vehicle and place on work table. 

Thoroughly shake and stir Urethane Glass Primer WSB-M2G314-B to make 
sure pigment mixes uniformly. 

Using a clean brush, apply primer to the outer 25.4 mm (1 inch) of the 
inside of the windshield. Allow at least five minutes drying time.

[FIGURE: N11822B.gif]

Apply an even bead of Urethane Adhesive WSB-M2G316-B around entire 
windshield edge using an air pressure cartridge gun. Air line pressure should 
be approximately 276 kPa (40 psi). The bead should be triangular in shape, 14 
mm (0.55 inch) high, and 8.0 mm (0.33 inch) at base.

[FIGURE: N11823B.gif]

Install the windshield assembly onto the vehicle, taking care to align 
the marks on the glass to the body. This must be done before adhesive skins 
over. Apply enough pressure to seat the windshield with the sealer into the 
opening. 

[FIGURE: N11824B.gif]

Install the retainers, glass stops and mouldings. 

[FIGURE: N11825A.gif]

Install windshield wiper arms and blades.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Back Window Glass

 Removal 

 WARNING: AN ASSISTANT IS NECESSARY WHEN REMOVING OR REPLACING THE GLASS. 

 NOTE: Some F-Series vehicles have vinyl mouldings. It is not necessary to 
remove the mouldings for glass removal. 

From the interior of the vehicle, pull down the weatherstrip. Push the 
back window glass and weatherstrip out of the window opening from inside the 
cab while an assistant grasps the window from outside the cab. 

Remove the weatherstrip from the glass. Clean all sealer from the 
weatherstrip and glass, if either is to be reused. 

Clean all sealer from the back window opening. 

 Installation 

Position the weatherstrip to the back window. 

Install a draw cord all around the weatherstrip in the flange crevice, 
allowing the cord to overlap at the bottom center of the glass. Coat the 
weatherstrip mounting surface with a rubber lubricant meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1B6-A.

[FIGURE: N11271B.gif]

Apply Liquid Butyl Sealer C9AZ-19554-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESB-M4G162-A to the back window opening as shown. 

Position the glass and weatherstrip to the window opening. With the 
assistant applying hand pressure from outside the cab, perform the following 
steps: 

Pull the weatherstrip lip over the window opening flange with the draw 
cord from the inside. 

Pull the weatherstrip over the lower flange, pulling one end of the 
cord at a time. 

Pull the weatherstrip over the side flanges and upper flange. 

Clean the glass and the area around the window to remove all excess 
sealer. 

Test for water leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Window, Vent

 Removal 

Remove the door trim panel retaining screws and remove the door trim 
panel.

Remove the screw retaining the division bar to the door inner panel 
(Section E in the Window Retainer and Run Assembly illustration at the 
beginning of this section). 

Remove the two screws retaining the vent assembly to the leading edge 
of the door. 

Lower the door glass. 

Pull the top weatherstrip part way out of the door window frame in the 
division bar area (Section D in Window Retainer and Run Assembly illustration 
at the beginning of this section). 

Tilt and remove the vent window and division bar assembly from the door. 

Separate the run from the vent window division bar. 

Remove two vent upper pivot-to-vent frame screws. 

Remove the retaining nut and tension spring from the vent window lower 
pivot. 

Separate the vent glass retainer and the pivot stops from the vent 
frame and weatherstrip assembly. 

 Installation 

Position the vent glass retainer assembly with the pivot stops into the 
vent window frame and weatherstrip assembly. 

Install the two upper pivot-to-frame retaining screws. 

Install the pivot tension spring and retaining nut. Adjust spring 
tension so the vent will stay open at highway speeds. 

Position the run assembly in the vent window assembly. 

Position the vent window and division bar assembly into the door and to 
the glass edge. 

Install vent window frame to leading edge of door window frame and 
install two retaining screws. 

Install division bar retaining screw. 

Position the weatherstrip back into the door window frame (division bar 
area). 

Install the retainer bar lower run-to-door inner panel screw (adjust 
the run for proper door window operation). 

Install the door trim panel.

LUBRICATION

Window Regulator

The window glass mechanism should be lubricated whenever the glass 
channel or front door window regulator assembly is removed, or excessive 
effort is required to operate the windows. To lubricate a door window 
regulator, apply an even coating of Multi-Purpose Grease DOAZ-19584-AA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M1C159-A and ESB-M1C93-A to the 
window regulator rollers, shafts and the entire length of the roller guides as 
illustrated.

ADJUSTMENTS

Door Window Glass 

Secure loose door glass by performing the following adjustment 
procedure: 

Lower glass to full down position. 

Using blunt tool, remove door glass run at rear of door frame from top 
of door to bolt. 

Install piece of two-sided Vinyl Foam Tape C6AZ-19627-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESB-M3G77-A, 12.7 mm (1/2 inch) wide x 3.18 mm (1/8 
inch) thick x 355.6 mm (14 inches) long as shim in run retainer. 

Install run and cycle glass up and down to check for smooth operation. 

Lower the glass and check the height of the top edge of the glass. It 
should be nearly flush with the belt line. 

If, after performing the above procedure, glass tilts or comes out of 
glass run approximately two-thirds of the way up, perform the following steps. 

Remove door trim panel and watershield.

Lower glass to full down position. 

Loosen self-tapping screws retaining vent window to door frame. Loosen 
retainer screw for vent window division bar. 

Raise vent window as high into door frame as possible, and tighten vent 
window retaining screws. 

Cycle glass up and down to check for smooth operation. 

Install door trim panel and watershield.

 Lateral/Longitudinal Adjustment 

Loosen the screw at the lower end of the vent window division bar. 

Loosen the lower rear run attaching screws as described in this section. 

Lower the glass half of the way down. 

Tighten all of the attaching screws and check the operation of the 
window mechanism.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Instrument Panel

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable.

Remove the instrument panel pad.

Remove the right and left cowl side trim panels, if so equipped.

Remove the lower trim cover from the steering column opening of the 
instrument panel.

Disconnect the PRNDL from the shift tube, if so equipped.

Remove four screws retaining the steering column seal and seal retainer 
to the dash panel.

Remove two nuts retaining the steering column clamp to the brake pedal 
support, and lower the steering column toward the seat.

Disconnect the speedometer cable from the speedometer.

Remove one screw retaining the left end of the plenum to the dash panel.

Remove one screw retaining the lower center of the plenum to the dash 
panel.

Remove two nuts retaining the evaporator case and plenum to the dash 
panel.

Remove one screw retaining each lower end of the instrument panel to 
the side cowl.

Disconnect the two instrument panel support center braces from the 
lower edge of the instrument panel (one screw each).

Remove one screw retaining the instrument panel to the brake pedal 
support at the steering column opening.

Place a protective cover over the steering column and support the 
instrument panel.

Disconnect the courtesy lamp wires from the right door courtesy lamp 
switch, if so equipped.

Disconnect the antenna lead-in cable from the radio, if so equipped.

Remove one screw retaining the upper right and left corners of the 
instrument panel to the cowl at the windshield lower corners.

Position the instrument panel right end rearward, as necessary, to 
disconnect any wires, cables or vacuum hoses preventing moving the instrument 
panel.

Carefully remove the instrument panel from the vehicle.

 Installation 

Position the instrument panel to the vehicle, connecting any wires, 
cables and hoses that were disconnected to move the instrument panel rearward. 
Install one screw to retain each upper corner of the instrument panel to the 
cowl at the windshield lower corners.

Connect the antenna lead-in cable to the radio, if so equipped.

Connect the courtesy lamp wires to the right door courtesy lamp switch, 
if so equipped.

Install one screw to retain the instrument panel to the brake pedal 
support at the steering column opening.

Connect the two instrument panel support center braces to the lower 
edge of the instrument panel.

Install one screw to retain each lower end of the instrument panel to 
the cowl side panels.

Install two nuts retaining evaporator case and plenum to the dash panel.

Install one screw to retain the lower center of the plenum to the dash 
panel.

Install one screw to retain the left end of the plenum to the dash panel.

Connect the speedometer cable to the speedometer.

Position the steering column clamp to the brake pedal support. Install 
the retaining nuts.

Install the steering column opening seal and seal retainer at the dash 
panel (four screws).

Reconnect the PRNDL to the shift tube, if so equipped.

Install the lower trim cover to the steering column opening of the 
instrument panel.

Install the cowl side trim panels, if so equipped.

Install the instrument panel pad.

Connect battery ground cable.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Lock Cylinder, Door

 Removal 

Roll the window to the UP position. 

Remove the trim panel and pull away the watershield, if so equipped. 

Disconnect the lock actuating rod from the lock control link. 

Slide the lock cylinder retainer away from the lock cylinder. 

Remove the lock cylinder. 

 Installation 

Insert the lock cylinder in the door and connect the lock cylinder. 

Connect the lock actuating rod to the lock control link clip. 

Install the watershield. Cement the top and side edges of the 
watershield to the inner surface of the inner panel. Use Weatherstrip Adhesive 
E8AZ-19552-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESB-M2G14-A.

Install the access hole cover and trim panel.

ADJUSTMENTS

Striker Plate, Door Latch

 CAUTION: Do not cover up a poor door alignment with a latch striker adjustment. 

Use Torx® Drive Bit Set D79P-2100-T or equivalent where 
required to loosen or tighten striker. 

The striker pin can be adjusted laterally and vertically as well as 
fore and aft. The latch striker should not be adjusted to correct door sag. 
The latch striker should be shimmed to get the clearance shown in the 
following illustrations, between the latch striker and the latch. 

To check clearance, perform the following steps: 

Clean the latch jaws and the striker area. 

Apply a thin layer of Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to the latch striker.

[FIGURE: P11691C.gif]

As the door is closed and opened, a measurable pattern will result. 

Move the striker assembly laterally to provide a flush fit with the 
door and body. Do not use more than one shim. 

Position the striker as shown and tighten the striker to 35-45 
Nm (26-33 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: N60771A.gif]

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Wiper and Washer System

 Inspection and Verification 

Verify the customer's original concern by operating the wiper and 
washer systems.

Visually inspect the components of the systems.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Electrical

Binding wiper pivot arms

Damaged wiper motors

Wiper mounting arm and pivot shaft improperly connected to wiper motor

Low washer fluid level

Plugged or damaged washer hoses or washer nozzle jet

Loose or corroded connectors

Check the windshield wiper pivot arms for proper adjustment and proper 
connection to the windshield wiper mounting arm and pivot shaft.

Check washer hoses for proper routing and connections.

Inspect the wiper or washer system wiring harnesses and connectors for 
obvious signs of damage.

If the fault is not visually evident, determine the symptom and proceed 
to the symptom chart.

 Symptom Chart — Wiper And Washer Systems 

Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for the 
connector numbers in the pinpoint tests.

 NOTE: Use Rotunda Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 or equivalent to perform 
pinpoint tests.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Windshield Wiper

 Pivot Arm 

 Removal 

Raise the blade end of the arm off of the windshield and move the slide 
latch away from the pivot shaft. This will unlock the wiper pivot arm from the 
pivot shaft and hold the blade end of the pivot arm off of the glass at the 
same time.

Pull the wiper pivot arm off of the pivot shaft without the aid of any 
tools. 

 Installation 

Make sure the pivot shaft is in PARK position and the blade assembly is 
positioned to the correct dimension. 

Hold the main arm head on to the pivot shaft while raising the blade 
end of the wiper pivot arm. Push the slide latch into the lock under the pivot 
shaft head. 

Lower the blade to the windshield. If the blade does not touch the 
windshield, the slide latch is not completely in place.

[FIGURE: K21797A.gif]

 Mounting Arm and Pivot Shaft 

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable.

Mark hood hinge location and loosen bolts. 

Remove wiper pivot arm and blade assemblies. 

Disconnect washer hose. 

Remove cowl top vent panel and seal. 

Disconnect linkage at motor (one clip). 

Remove three bolts retaining mounting arm and pivot shaft assembly to 
cowl. 

Remove mounting arm and pivot shaft assembly. 

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order. 

Align hood with marks made previously. 

 Wiper Motor 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cables.

Remove wiper pivot arm and blade assemblies. 

Disconnect washer hose. 

Mark hood hinge location and loosen bolts (alligator hood only). 

Remove cowl top vent panel and seal. 

Remove reinforcement. 

Disconnect electrical connector. 

Remove three wiper motor retaining screws. 

Rotate motor assembly and partially remove. 

Disconnect linkage at motor (one clip). 

Remove motor.

 Installation 

Transfer windlatch nut and gasket to new motor (if installing new 
motor). 

Connect mounting arm and pivot shaft to motor assembly. 

Connect electrical connector. Position motor to dash panel and install 
three retaining screws. 

Install reinforcement. 

Install cowl top vent panel and seal. 

Connect washer hose. 

Connect battery ground cable. 

Cycle wiper system and allow system to park. 

Install wiper pivot arm and blade assemblies.

[FIGURE: K2423B.gif]

On vehicles equipped with an alligator hood, align hood with marks and 
tighten bolts.

 Windshield Wiper Motor Installation

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Washer Pump and Reservoir 

 Removal 

Disconnect battery negative cable.

Disconnect electrical connections.

Remove the screws mounting the reservoir and remove the reservoir.

Disconnect hose and drain reservoir.

Using a small-bladed screwdriver, pry out retaining ring. 

[FIGURE: K3034E.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

17407

Windshield Washer Reservoir

2

17664

Windshield Washer Pump 

3

—

Retaining Ring (Part of 17664)

A

—

Dry Lube in this Location

Using pliers to grip one wall around the electrical terminals, pull out 
the motor, seal and impeller assembly. If the impeller and seal come off when 
the motor is pulled, they can be reassembled. Make certain the reservoir pump 
chamber is free of foreign material prior to installing the old assembly in 
the new reservoir.

 Installation 

Before installing the pump assembly, lubricate the outside diameter of 
the pump with a dry lubricant such as powdered graphite. This will ease the 
installation of the washer pump into the reservoir motor cavity. 

Align small projection on the motor end cap with the slot in the 
reservoir and assemble so that the seal seats against the bottom of the motor 
cavity. 

Using a 25.4-mm (1-inch) socket (preferably 12-point) hand-press 
retaining ring securely against motor end plate. 

Connect hose and replace the reservoir assembly in the vehicle by 
following removal procedures in reverse order. 

 CAUTION: Do not make electrical connection prior to filling reservoir. Do not 
operate reservoir pump prior to filling reservoir. 

Fill the reservoir. 

Make electrical connections.

Connect battery negative cable.

 CAUTION: Do not operate pump until fluid is added to the reservoir. 

Operate pump and check for leaks.

ADJUSTMENTS

Park Position 

Remove the pivot arm and blade assemblies from the pivot shafts. Turn 
on the wiper switch, allow the motor to move the pivot shafts three or four 
cycles, and then turn off the wiper switch. This will place the pivot shafts 
in the PARK position. 

Install the pivot arm and blade assemblies on the pivot shafts to 
Dimension X (2.5-3.7 inches). Dimension X is the distance between the 
centerline of the blade saddle and the windshield lower moulding or 
weatherstrip.

Section 01-20: Restraints, Active

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Occupant Restraint System 

 WARNING: BELT ASSEMBLIES MUST BE INSTALLED IN MATCHED SETS AS RECEIVED AND MUST 
NOT BE INTERCHANGED BETWEEN VEHICLE MODELS. IF A COMPONENT PORTION (BUCKLE 
PORTION, RETRACTOR PORTION, ETC.) OF A SAFETY BELT IS NONFUNCTIONAL OR 
DAMAGED, THE ENTIRE ASSEMBLY MUST BE REPLACED. 

The lap and shoulder safety belts are factory-installed in their proper 
locations. If the safety belts are removed for any reason, they must be 
installed as shown in the illustrations in this section. Sealer is placed 
around all safety belt anchor bolt holes in the floorpan. Tighten the anchor 
bolts to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

The restraint system buckle/retractor assembly is serviced separately.

================================================================================
PAGE 2301
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 01-20: Restraints, Active

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Restraints, Active

 Inspection and Verification 

 NOTE: The passenger belt can be tested utilizing a driver only, providing the 
driver has the ability to grasp the right front shoulder belt and extend it 
approximately 660 mm (26 inches) with no compromise to safe driving.

 NOTE: If test is to be performed by driver only, do not extend passenger side 
safety belt fully. False indication of lockup will result.

 NOTE: This method applies to the 8 km/h (5 mph) test only.

The driver will buckle up and proceed to a safe test area. If the 
passenger seat belt must be tested, a passenger can be buckled into the right 
front seat.

After reaching a safe area to perform sudden stops, the driver will 
attain a speed of approximately 8 km/h (5 mph). The driver will inform the 
passenger, if applicable, that he is preparing to make a severe brake 
application. At this time, both driver and rider will grasp their respective 
shoulder safety belts and prepare to lean slightly forward at the moment the 
brake application is made. 

 WARNING: THE DRIVER AND PASSENGER MUST BE PREPARED TO BRACE THEMSELVES IN THE 
EVENT THE SAFETY BELT RETRACTOR DOES NOT LOCK. 

The driver will make a maximum brake application (approximately 9.7 
m/sec. [32 ft./sec.]) without tire skid. (The maximum brake application 
should be on dry concrete or equivalent hard road surface, never on a wet or 
gravel road.) The driver and passenger will lean slightly forward into the 
shoulder safety belt. At this instant, the belts should lock up without 
webbing payout.

If there is a lockup of both shoulder safety belts, the safety belt 
assemblies are functioning properly. Should either or both retractors fail to 
lock up at the 8 km/h (5 mph) speed, repeat the test at a constant 24 km/h (15 
mph). (This test must be performed with a passenger if the right front belt is 
to be tested.) 

 WARNING: IF THE RETRACTOR OF A NEW SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLY HAS BEEN BOLTED INTO A 
DAMAGED OR DISTORTED MOUNTING AREA, THE NEW RETRACTOR CAN BE WARPED AND WILL 
NOT FUNCTION. IF THIS IS THE CASE, REWORK THE SHEET METAL BACK TO ITS ORIGINAL 
SHAPE AND STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY, AND INSTALL ANOTHER NEW COMPLETE SAFETY BELT 
ASSEMBLY. 

If either or both shoulder safety belts do not lock up at the 24 km/h 
(15 mph) test, the vehicle is to be returned for service of the inoperative 
safety belts. Remove the retractor and rework the sheet metal (if required) in 
the retractor's mounting surface back to its original shape and structural 
integrity. Install the retractor assembly and test the safety belt 
assembly(ies) as previously stated.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Safety Belt with Anchor Plate Thread Damage 

 Removal 

Remove the broken or stripped bolt and discard. 

Drill out the internal threads in the safety belt anchorage plate with 
a 27/64-inch drill. 

Rethread the anchor plate with a 1/2-13 tap (safety belt). 

Blow out the chips. 

 Installation

Belts in the Removal and Installation portion of this section. Tighten the 
replacement bolt to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft). Original parts are to be 
replaced with the repair parts indicated in the safety belt parts replacement 
chart at the end of this section. Unless specified in the chart, use original 
parts. 

When repairing a multiple belt and attachment, install nut 382599 to 
the bolt in the tunnel area from the underside of the floorpan. Tighten to 
30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Safety Belt Procedure After a Collision

 WARNING: ALL SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLIES INCLUDING RETRACTORS, BUCKLES, FRONT SAFETY 
BELT BUCKLE SUPPORT ASSEMBLIES (SLIDEBAR), IF SO EQUIPPED, CHILD SAFETY SEAT 
TETHER ATTACHMENTS (IF SO EQUIPPED), AND ATTACHING HARDWARE MUST BE INSPECTED 
AFTER ANY COLLISION. FORD RECOMMENDS THAT ALL SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLIES IN USE 
DURING A COLLISION BE REPLACED UNLESS THE COLLISION WAS MINOR AND A QUALIFIED 
TECHNICIAN FINDS THAT THE BELTS SHOW NO DAMAGE AND CONTINUE TO OPERATE 
PROPERLY. SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLIES NOT IN USE DURING A COLLISION MUST ALSO BE 
INSPECTED AND REPLACED IF EITHER DAMAGE OR IMPROPER OPERATION IS NOTED. 

Safety belt assemblies must be periodically inspected to ensure that 
they have not become damaged and that they remain in proper operating 
condition, particularly if they have been subjected to severe stress.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Functional Test Procedure

 NOTE: The passenger belt can be tested utilizing a driver only, providing the 
driver has the ability to grasp the right front shoulder belt and extend it 
approximately 660 mm (26 inches) with no compromise to safe driving.

 NOTE: If test is to be performed by driver only, do not extend passenger side 
safety belt fully. False indication of lockup will result.

 NOTE: This method applies to the 8 km/h (5 mph) test only.

Driver will buckle up and proceed to a safe test area. If the passenger 
seat belt must be tested, a passenger can be buckled into the right front 
seat. 

After reaching a safe area to perform sudden stops, the driver will 
attain a speed of approximately 8 km/h (5 mph). The driver will inform the 
passenger, if applicable, that he is preparing to make a severe brake 
application. At this time, both driver and rider will grasp their respective 
shoulder safety belts and prepare to lean slightly forward at the moment the 
brake application is made. 

 WARNING: THE DRIVER AND PASSENGER MUST BE PREPARED TO BRACE THEMSELVES IN THE 
EVENT THE SAFETY BELT RETRACTOR DOES NOT LOCK. 

The driver will make a maximum brake application (approximately 9.7 
m/sec. [32 ft./sec.]) without tire skid. (The maximum brake application 
should be on dry concrete or equivalent hard road surface, never on a wet or 
gravel road.) The driver and passenger will lean slightly forward into the 
shoulder safety belt. At this instant, the belts should lock up without 
webbing payout.

If there is a lockup of both shoulder safety belts, the safety belt 
assemblies are functioning properly. Should either or both retractors fail to 
lock up at the 8 km/h (5 mph) speed, repeat the test at a constant 24 km/h (15 
mph). (This test must be performed with a passenger if the right front belt is 
to be tested.) 

 WARNING: IF THE RETRACTOR OF A NEW SAFETY BELT ASSEMBLY HAS BEEN BOLTED INTO A 
DAMAGED OR DISTORTED MOUNTING AREA, THE NEW RETRACTOR CAN BE WARPED AND WILL 
NOT FUNCTION. IF THIS IS THE CASE, REWORK THE SHEET METAL BACK TO ITS ORIGINAL 
SHAPE AND STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY, AND INSTALL ANOTHER NEW COMPLETE SAFETY BELT 
ASSEMBLY. 

If either or both shoulder safety belts do not lock up at the 24 km/h 
(15 mph) test, the vehicle is to be returned for service of the inoperative 
safety belts. Remove the retractor and rework the sheet metal (if required) in 
the retractor's mounting surface back to its original shape and structural 
integrity. Install the retractor assembly and test the safety belt 
assembly(ies) as previously stated.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Safety Belt Webbing 

The following procedures are recommended for the removal of spots and 
stains from belts. It is important that proper cleaning techniques and 
cleaning agents be used to prevent setting the stain or affecting the color 
and flame resistance of the belts. Avoid bleaching or redyeing the webbing as 
this can hinder belt strength and performance. 

 WARNING: DO NOT BLEACH OR REDYE THE WEBBING AS THIS CAN REDUCE BOTH BELT 
EFFECTIVENESS AND OCCUPANT SAFETY. 

The following materials are needed to clean safety belts: 

clean, undyed cotton fabric 

medium hard bristle brush 

Ford Spot and Stain Remover F3AZ-19521-WA or equivalent commercial 
product 

Ford Extra Strength Upholstery Cleaner E8AZ-19523-AA or equivalent 
commercial product in aerosol spray can 

Prior to selecting a cleaning method, perform the following steps.

Remove excess staining material from fabric by scraping or wiping with 
a clean cloth. 

Identify the staining material if possible. 

Clean the fabric as described in the following Methods A, B or C. 

 Spot Cleaning Method A 

For stains from grease, oil, tar, water spotting, crayon and lipstick.

 CAUTION: Use care during application of the spot lifter to avoid contact with 
vinyl trim. 

 NOTE: Using other than recommended cleaners or procedures may affect fabric 
flammability, appearance or durability. 

Spray Extra Strength Upholstery Cleaner E8AZ-19523-AA or equivalent 
commercial product on fabric as directed by instructions on can. 

Allow spot lifter to dry completely until it forms a white powder on 
surface of fabric. 

Brush and vacuum white powder from fabric. 

If soiled spot is not removed from fabric, repeat as necessary. 

Wipe cleaned area with damp cloth to remove any residual cleaner. 

 General Cleaning Method B 

For stains such as grease, oil, tar, adhesive, crayon and lipstick. 

If stain is still visible after spot cleaning procedure (Method A), 
blot soiled area with a clean cotton cloth saturated with Ford Spot and Stain 
Remover F3AZ-19521-WA or equivalent commercial product. 

Rub in a circular motion while continuously exposing clean portion of 
cloth. 

Gradually widen area of application onto edges of belts. 

Repeat as necessary. 

Wipe cleaned area with clean, damp cloth to remove any residual cleaner. 

 General Cleaning Method C 

For stains from dirt, soil, food and beverages. 

 NOTE: Spot cleaning as described in Method A will be sufficient when the 
soiled area is not excessive. In the event of severe soiling or staining, 
clean the entire belt to avoid a ring condition. 

Apply Rosenthal or Bissell or equivalent upholstery cleaner with cloth 
or brush as directed by instructions on container. 

Rub in a circular manner until stain is removed. 

Gradually widen area of application to edges of belts. 

Repeat as necessary. 

Rub cleaned area with a damp cloth to absorb residual cleaner. 

Allow belts to dry at room temperature.
