SERVICE PROCEDURES

Cylinder Heads 

 CAUTION: Do not plane or grind more than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) from original 
cylinder head gasket surface. 

Replace the head if it is cracked.

Remove all burrs or scratches with an oil stone. 

 Cleaning 

 CAUTION: Do not damage the cylinder head gasket surface. 

With the valves installed to protect the valve seats, remove deposits 
from the combustion chambers and valve heads with a scraper and a wire brush. 

Remove valves. 

After the valves are removed, clean the valve guide bores. Use cleaning 
solvent to remove dirt, grease and other deposits from the valves with a fine 
wire brush or buffing wheel. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the cylinder heads for cracks or excessively burned areas in 
the exhaust outlet ports. 

Check the cylinder head for cracks and inspect the gasket surface for 
burrs and nicks. Small imperfections of this type can be dressed down using an 
oil stone. Replace the head if it is cracked. 

The following inspection procedures are for a cylinder head that is to 
be completely overhauled. For individual service operations, use only the 
pertinent inspection procedure. 

 Spark Plug Thread Service 

Damaged spark plug threads in the cylinder head can be serviced using 
Rotunda Taperset Installation Kit 107-R0921 or equivalent.

The procedure involves cutting new threads in the spark plug hole. 
After rethreading operation, tapered sleeve will be installed in the cylinder 
head. The sleeve is threaded on the inside and outside. The outside threads 
into the cylinder head while the inside provides new threads for the spark plug.

The service is permanent and will have no effect on cylinder head or 
spark plug fit.

 CAUTION: The cylinder head must be removed from engine before installing a 
taperset. The service procedure includes a thread cutting process which 
produces metal chips. Performing this procedure while the cylinder head is on 
the cylinder block will cause metal chips to fall into the cylinder. Once in 
the cylinder, these chips can damage the cylinder wall when the engine is 
started. 

 NOTE: The use of power or air driven tools is not approved for the 
installation of tapersets.

Thoroughly clean spark plug counterbore, seat and threads of all dirt 
or other foreign material.

[FIGURE: A23674B.gif]

Start tap into spark plug hole, being careful to keep it properly 
aligned. As tap begins cutting new threads, apply cutting oil to tap.

Continue cutting threads and applying oil until stop ring bottoms 
against spark plug seat.

Remove tap. Remove all metal chips using compressed air.

Coat threads of mandrel with cutting oil. Thread taperset onto mandrel 
until one thread of mandrel extends beyond taperset.

[FIGURE: A23459A.gif]

 NOTE: A properly installed taperset will be flush to 1.0 mm (0.040 inch) 
below spark plug gasket seat.

Thread taperset into tapped spark plug hole using a torque wrench. 
Continue tightening mandrel until torque wrench indicates 61 Nm (45 
lb-ft).

To loosen mandrel for removal, hold mandrel stationary and turn mandrel 
body approximately one-half turn. Remove mandrel.

 Cylinder Head Flatness 

When a cylinder head is removed because of gasket leaks, check the 
flatness of the cylinder head gasket surface for conformance to specification. 
For specifications, refer to the appropriate engine section in Group 03.

 CAUTION: If necessary to refinish the cylinder head gasket surface, do not plane 
or grind off more than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch). 

Check the cylinder head flatness diagonally and across the center.

[FIGURE: A2895D.gif]

 Valve Seat Runout 

Check the valve seat runout with a valve seat runout gauge. Follow the 
instructions of the gauge manufacturer. If the runout exceeds the wear limit, 
the valve seat will need to be reground. For specifications, refer to the 
specification chart in this section.

[FIGURE: DA0873A.gif]

 Valve Stem-to-Valve Guide Clearance 

Check the valve stem-to-valve guide clearance of each valve in its 
respective valve guide with Valve Stem Clearance Tool TOOL-6505-E or 
equivalent. Use a flat-end indicator point. 

Install the tool on the valve stem until it is fully seated, and 
tighten the knurled setscrew firmly. Permit the valve to drop away from its 
seat until the tool contacts the upper surface of the valve guide. 

Position the dial indicator with its flat tip against the center 
portion of the tool's spherical section at approximately 90 degrees to the 
valve stem axis. 

Move the tool back and forth in line with the indicator stem. 

 NOTE: If necessary, use a magnetic base.

Take a reading on the dial indicator without removing the tool from the 
valve guide upper surface. Divide the reading by two, the division factor for 
the tool. If valve stem-to-valve guide clearance exceeds the wear limit, ream 
the valve guide for the next oversize valve stem as described in this section.

[FIGURE: A10707D.gif]

 Valves, Select Fitting 

If the valve stem-to-valve guide clearance exceeds the service 
clearance, ream the valve guide for the next oversize valve stem. Valves with 
oversize stem diameters of 0.38 mm and 0.76 mm (0.015 inch and 0.030 inch) are 
available for service in oversize valve guide diameters of 0.41 mm and 0.81 mm 
(0.016 inch and 0.032 inch).

 CAUTION: Always reface the valve seat after the valve guide has been reamed. 
Refer to Valve Guides, Reaming under Cylinder Head in the Service Procedures 
portion of this section. 

In the case of valve stem-to-valve guide clearance, the service 
clearance is intended as an aid to diagnosing engine noise only, and does not 
constitute a failure or indicate need for service. However, when overhauling 
or reconditioning a cylinder head, the service clearance should be regarded as 
a practical working value, and used as a determinant for installing the next 
oversize valve to ensure extended service life. 

 Valve Guides, Reaming 

If it becomes necessary to ream a valve guide to install a valve with 
an oversize stem, a hand reaming kit is available which contains the following 
reamer and pilot combinations: a 0.38-mm (0.015-inch) OS reamer with a 0.76-mm 
(0.03-inch) OS pilot, and a 0.76-mm (0.03-inch) reamer with a 0.38-mm 
(0.015-inch) OS pilot.

[FIGURE: A21329A.gif]

When replacing a standard size valve with an oversize valve, always use 
the reamer in sequence (smallest oversize first, and then next smallest, etc.) 
so as not to overload the reamers.

 CAUTION: Always reface the valve seat after the valve guide has been reamed, and 
use a suitable scraper to break the sharp corner (inside diameter) at the top 
of the valve guide. 

 NOTE: If oversize valve stems and oversize stem seals are not available, bore 
out original guide and install service bushing. Ream inside diameter for 
specified clearance for standard size valve. Reface valve seat as required. 
Install standard size valve stem oil seal. 

If the valve face runout is excessive and to remove pits and grooves, 
reface the valves to a true 45-degree angle. Remove only enough stock to 
correct the runout or to clean up the pits and grooves. If the edge of the 
valve head is less then 0.794 mm (1/32 inch) thick after grinding, replace the 
valve as the valve will run too hot in the engine.

 CAUTION: The interference angle of the valve and seat must not be lapped out. 
Remove all grooves or score marks from the end of the valve stem, and chamfer 
it as necessary. Do not remove more than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch) from the end of 
the valve stem. 

If the valve or valve seat has been refaced, it will be necessary to 
check the clearance between the rocker arm pad and the valve stem with the 
valve train assembly installed in the engine. 

 Valve Seats, Refacing 

Exhaust valve seats are inserted and intake valve seats are induction 
hardened and cannot be refaced. 

 Valves, Inspection 

The critical inspection points and tolerances of the valve are 
illustrated below. Refer to the specification chart in this section.

Inspect the valve stem for bends, and the end of the stem for grooves 
or scoring. 

Inspect the valve face and the edge of the valve head for pits, grooves 
or scores. 

Inspect the stem for a bend condition and the end of the stem for 
grooves or scores. 

Check the valve head for signs of burning or erosion, warpage and 
cracking. Minor pits, grooves, etc., can be removed. Discard severely damaged 
valves. 

Inspect the valve spring assembly, valve spring retainers, locks and 
sleeves and discard any visually damaged parts. 

 Valves, Refacing 

Minor pits or grooves may be removed. Discard valves that are severely 
damaged, if the face runout cannot be corrected by refinishing, or stem 
clearance exceeds specification. Refer to the appropriate engine section for 
specifications. Discard any excessively worn or damaged valve train parts.

Refer to Engine Service in the Rotunda Tool catalog for a description 
of the various types of valve resurfacing equipment. 

Make sure refacer grinding wheels are properly dressed. Refer to the 
following illustration for typical valve inspection points. Refer to 
specification chart in this section.

[FIGURE: A14139D.gif]

 Valve Spring Tension 

Inspect the valve spring, valve spring retainers, and keys for wear or 
damage. Discard any damaged parts. 

Check the springs for proper pressure at the specified spring lengths 
using Valve/Clutch Spring Tester TOOL-6513-DD or equivalent. Weak valve 
springs cause poor engine performance. Replace any spring not within 
specification. For specifications, refer to the appropriate engine section. 
Manually rotating the valve spring assemblies while installed in the engine 
will not determine condition of valve springs.

[FIGURE: A21330B.gif]

 Valve Spring Squareness 

Check each spring for squareness using a steel square and a flat 
surface. Stand the spring and square on end of the flat surface. Slide the 
spring up to the square. Revolve the spring slowly and observe the space 
between the top coil of the spring and the square. Refer to the following 
illustration.

[FIGURE: A8517A.gif]

Refer to specifications chart in this section for out-of-square limits. 
Follow the same procedure to check squareness of new valve springs before 
installation. Make sure the proper spring (color-coded) is installed.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Valve Rocker Arm/Shaft Assembly 

 Cleaning 

Clean all parts thoroughly. Make sure all oil passages are open. 

Make sure oil passage in the push rod end of the rocker arm is open. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the shaft and the rocker arm bore for nicks, scratches, scores 
or scuffs. Replace any damaged parts. 

Inspect the pad at the valve end of the rocker arm for indications of 
scuffing or abnormal wear. If the pad is grooved, replace the rocker arm. 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to true this surface by grinding. On pedestal-mounted 
rocker arms, check the rocker arm pad, side rails and fulcrum seat for 
excessive wear, cracks, nicks, or burrs. Check the rocker arm bolt for 
stripped or broken threads.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Push Rods 

 Cleaning 

Clean the push rods in a suitable solvent. Blow out the oil passage in 
the push rods with compressed air. 

 Inspection 

Check the ends of the push rods for nicks, grooves, roughness or 
excessive wear. Replace damaged push rods. 

The push rods can be visually checked for straightness while they are 
installed in the engine by rotating them with the valve closed. They also can 
be checked with a dial indicator. 

If the push rod is bent beyond specifications, it must be replaced. Do 
not attempt to straighten push rods.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Intake Manifold 

 Cleaning 

Remove all gasket material from the machined surfaces of the manifold. 
Clean the manifold in a suitable solvent and dry it with compressed air. 

 Inspection 

Inspect the manifold for cracks, damaged gasket surfaces, or other 
problems that can make it unfit for further service. Replace all studs that 
are stripped or otherwise damaged. Clean the EGR exhaust passages. Remove all 
filings and foreign matter that may have entered the manifold as a result of 
service.

Check the baffle plate on the underside of the manifold if so equipped. 
The baffle must be securely fastened.

Exhaust Manifold 

 Cleaning 

Remove all foreign material from all inlet and outlet sealing surfaces

 Inspection 

Inspect the cylinder head joining flanges of the exhaust manifold for 
evidence of exhaust gas leaks. 

Inspect the manifold for cracks, damaged surfaces, or other damage that 
will make them unfit for further service. Warped or cracked exhaust manifolds 
must be replaced.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Flywheel Inspection

 Automatic Transmission 

Inspect the flywheel for cracks or other damage that can make it unfit 
for further service. Inspect the flywheel ring gear for worn, chipped or 
cracked teeth. If the teeth are damaged, replace the ring gear and flywheel 
assembly. 

With the flywheel installed on the crankshaft, check the gear face 
runout.

 Manual Transmission 

Inspect the flywheel for cracks, heat check, or other damage that can 
make it unfit for further service. Machine the friction surface of the 
flywheel if it is scored or worn. If it is necessary to remove more than 1.143 
mm (0.045 inch) of stock from the original thickness, replace the flywheel. 

Inspect the ring gear for worn, chipped or cracked teeth. If the teeth 
are damaged, replace the ring gear. 

With the flywheel installed on the crankshaft, check the flywheel face 
runout. Refer to Diagnosis and Testing in this section.

Flywheel Clutch Surface Machining

Flywheel resurfacing machining requirements:

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling System

 CAUTION: The use of a winter front or other airflow restriction device mounted 
in front of the radiator is not recommended on vehicles equipped with 
chassis-mounted air-to-air aftercooling. Airflow restriction causes high 
exhaust temperatures, power loss, excessive fan usage, and a reduction in fuel 
economy. If a winter front or other airflow restriction device is used, it 
must have a permanent opening directly in line with the center of the fan 
drive. The minimum opening size must be 120 square inches. 

The cooling system consists of the following components:

Coolant, which consists of ethylene glycol antifreeze and water. It 
carries excess heat from engine to radiator, where the excess heat is 
transferred to the surrounding air.

Radiator, which allows excess engine heat to be transferred to the air.

Radiator hoses, which attach radiator to engine.

Water pump, which circulates coolant through system.

Passageways cast into the cylinder block and cylinder heads, which 
allow coolant to circulate and absorb excess heat so that engine parts are not 
damaged by excess heat. Water thermostat, which controls coolant temperature, 
allowing quicker engine warm-up improving fuel economy and reducing pollution.

Water thermostat, which controls coolant temperature, allowing quicker 
engine warm-up improving fuel economy and reducing pollution.

Bypass hose or passageway, which allows coolant to circulate within the 
engine when the water thermostat is closed, preventing hot spots.

Coolant recovery reservoir, which holds surplus coolant. When the 
system is hot and coolant expands, coolant goes into coolant recovery 
reservoir. When the vehicle cools, the system draws coolant back into the 
radiator, eliminating the need for frequent topping-off of the cooling system. 
The coolant recovery reservoir eliminates the loss of coolant through an 
overflow tube.

Pressure-vacuum radiator cap, which allows coolant to escape to coolant 
recovery reservoir when it expands so system pressure does not build, possibly 
bursting a hose or radiator tube. The radiator cap allows coolant to be drawn 
back in from coolant recovery reservoir when system cools, refilling system 
and preventing hoses from collapsing from a partial vacuum in system. 
Pressurizing the cooling system raises the boiling temperature of the coolant, 
allowing more efficient, higher engine temperatures and reducing the risk of 
boiling over when driving at high altitudes.

Engine cooling fan, which draws air through the radiator to help 
cooling at low speeds or when the vehicle is not moving. The system is 
designed so that air forced through the radiator by the forward motion of the 
vehicle is sufficient at driving speeds.

Fan clutch, which decreases engine power needed to drive fan by 
allowing fan to free-wheel when engine is cold or when vehicle motion forces 
air through the radiator. 

Drive belt, which drives the water pump, fan and other accessories off 
of engine crankshaft. Refer to Section 03A-05 , Section 03B-05 , Section 03C-05 
or Section 03D-05 for more information on drive belt.

================================================================================
PAGE 2369
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Coolant 

 Approved Coolant and Concentration 

Whenever engine coolant is added to the radiator, use equal parts of 
water and Ford Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid (low silicate) 
E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford Specification ESE-M97B18-C. Also, add 
Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System Additive FW-15 or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESN-M99B169-A at a strength of 4 ounces per gallon of engine 
coolant being added. If coolant must be added more than once a month, or more 
than one quart at a time must be added, check the cooling system for leaks.

A standard ethylene glycol hydrometer can be used to check the 
protection level of the long-life coolant or Rotunda Battery/Anti-Freeze 
Tester 014-R1060 or equivalent.

When water or coolant is added to the supply tank, operate the engine 
at fast idle for 30 minutes before letting the vehicle stand with the engine 
off for prolonged periods to prevent damage to the cooling system during 
periods of below freezing temperatures. This will allow a uniform mixture 
throughout the cooling system and prevent damage by freezing, when sufficient 
antifreeze is used.

To avoid possible overheating in very hot weather, do not use mixtures 
with more than 50 percent antifreeze except in areas where antifreeze 
protection below -37°C (-35°F) is required. In this case, refer to the 
coolant mixture chart on the Ford Cooling System Fluid container.

For vehicles equipped with other than Ford diesel engines, refer to the 
diesel engine manufacturer operator's manual for cooling system maintenance 
procedures.

 Unsatisfactory Coolant Materials 

 CAUTION: Do not add any radiator sealers containing water-soluble oil to the 
cooling system of diesel engines, as it will make the corrosion resistor 
inoperative. 

Do not use alcohol or methanol antifreeze, or mix them with the 
specified coolant.

Some engine coolant recycling manufacturers have claimed to have the 
ability to recycle engine coolant. Ford Motor Company has not authorized the 
use of recycled engine coolant nor have they sanctioned the use of any 
machines or devices that recycle engine coolant. Recycled coolant is not 
equivalent to the Ford Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid (low 
silicate) E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESE-M97B18-C.

 Coolant Disposal 

The disposal of all used engine coolant must always be done in 
accordance with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations.

Ordinary tap water may be used in an emergency except in areas where 
the water is known to be exceptionally hard or to have a high alkali content. 
The cooling system should be drained and flushed and the proper mixture of 
coolant added as soon as possible. With only water in the system, do not let 
the engine run hot.

 NOTE: For information on the warning and shutdown system, refer to Section 13-09A .

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Coolant Conditioner

 CAUTION: Inadequate concentration of the coolant conditioner can result in major 
corrosive damage to engine cooling system components. Overconcentration can 
cause formation of gels that can cause coolant flow restriction, plugging of 
passages and overheating. 

With Ford diesel engines, always use engine cooling system conditioner 
as specified in the maintenance schedule.

Changing engine coolant filter/conditioner as specified in the 
maintenance schedule will help keep engine coolant properly conditioned.

Engine coolant conditioner provides additional long-term protection 
against cavitation erosion and corrosion beyond that provided by the engine 
coolant solution.

Do not add any radiator sealers containing water-soluble oil to the 
cooling system of diesel engines; it will make the corrosion resistor 
inoperative.

PAGE 2371

1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Oil Cooler

On diesel engine applications, an oil temperature thermostat is located 
in the top of the oil cooler housing. The thermostat modulates oil flow at 
temperatures between 100° and 115°C (212° and 239°F) and fully 
through the oil cooler at temperatures above 115°C (239°F). The 
thermostat also incorporates a pressure relief feature that allows oil to 
bypass the cooler should it ever become plugged.

PAGE 2372
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-03: Engine Cooling

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Block Heater

The engine block heater consists of an electrical heating element 
installed in one or more of the core plug openings in the engine block and an 
electrical cable that plugs into a standard 110-volt AC electrical outlet. It 
is designed to keep the engine coolant warm during cold weather to aid in cold 
weather starting.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Engine Cooling

 Inspection and Verification 

Verify the original concern by operating the engine cooling system to 
duplicate the condition.

Check for leaks at the following points:

all hoses and hose connections

radiator seams, radiator core, and radiator drain petcock

all block core plugs and drain plugs

edges of all other cooling system gaskets

transmission oil cooler

vehicle heating system components

water pump

Examine oil dipstick for evidence of engine oil contaminated coolant.

Check radiator for evidence of oil in coolant (leakage at transmission 
oil cooler).

Radiator Coolant Level Check

Check coolant level in the radiator coolant recovery reservoir at least 
once a month.

With a cold engine, the level must be maintained at or above the FULL 
COLD mark.

At normal engine operating temperature, the coolant level should be at 
the FULL HOT mark. If coolant level in the radiator coolant recovery reservoir 
is less than the above indicated levels, a 50/50 mixture of Ford Premium 
Cooling System Fluid E2FZ-19549-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESE-M97B44-A (In Canada, Motorcraft CXC-8-B) for gasoline engines and 
Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine Cooling System Fluid E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESE-M97B18-C for diesel engines and water should be 
added to the radiator coolant recovery reservoir to the specified levels. Also 
add Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System Additive FW-15 or equivalent meeting 
Ford specification ESN-M99B169-A (for Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 only) at a 
strength of 4 ounces per gallon of engine coolant being added.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Draining, Filling and Bleeding

 CAUTION: Never operate an engine with the cooling system filled solely with 
water, as severe engine corrosion can result. Refer to the Owner Guide 
maintenance schedule for proper cooling system additives. Do not operate 
engine without additive. 

To prevent loss of antifreeze when draining the radiator, attach a hose 
to the radiator drain cock and drain the coolant from the radiator into a 
clean container.

Open the drain cock and remove the radiator or supply tank cap.

Close drain cock.

 CAUTION: Never operate an engine with the cooling system filled solely with 
water. Severe engine corrosion can result. Refer to the owner guide 
maintenance schedule for proper cooling system additives. Do not operate 
engine without additive. 

Always use the specified mixture of water and Premium Cooling System 
Fluid E2FZ-19549-AA (In Canada, Motorcraft CXC-8-B) or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESE-M97B44-A for gasoline engines and Heavy-Duty Diesel Engine 
Cooling System Fluid E6HZ-19549-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESE-M97B18-C for diesel engines. Also add Motorcraft Heavy-Duty Cooling System 
Additive FW-15 or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESN-M99B169-A (for 
Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 only) at a strength of four ounces per gallon of engine 
coolant being added. In areas where protection against freezing is not 
required (hot climates), it is advisable to use a concentration of antifreeze 
to make sure of protection against corrosion. The approved antifreeze agents 
contain corrosion-inhibiting properties.

Refer to the Coolant mixture chart in the Specifications portion of 
this section to establish correct proportions of water and antifreeze to be 
used in cooling system.

Place heater temperature control in maximum HEAT position.

 NOTE: Add required amount of cooling system additive for Cummins B5.9 and 
C8.3 diesel engines only.

Fill supply tank or the radiator to bottom of filler neck with the 
recommended permanent antifreeze mixture. Leave the radiator cap off.

 WARNING: DO NOT STAND IN LINE WITH OR NEAR COOLING FAN WHEN REVVING ENGINE. 

 NOTE: This procedure is for both gasoline and diesel engines. Do not run 
engines above 2500 rpm for this procedure.

Start engine. Vary rpm between idle and 1500 rpm for three minutes.

Increase rpm to maximum (governed) and run engine until the thermostat 
opens (upper radiator hose becomes hot) and an additional ten minutes to allow 
air to escape from the cooling system.

Throttle back to idle and fill the system with coolant to the bottom of 
the filler neck. Install the radiator cap. During subsequent operation of the 
engine, some coolant may be disposed of through the overflow nipple. This is 
normal. After extended operation of the vehicle, when the engine has cooled 
off to ambient temperature, the coolant level should be stabilized at a level 
approximately in line with the mounting tabs of the tank.

If the vehicle is equipped with a coolant recovery reservoir, fill to 
the HOT mark.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Cooling System, Cleaning

 Cooling System Flush Procedure, Radiator Installed 

Slowly fill cooling system with a mixture of clean water and a suitable 
flushing agent (mixed according to manufacturer's recommendations). If cooling 
system is still hot, either fill with hot water or allow system to cool, then 
fill with cold water.

Start engine and allow it to idle until normal operating temperature is 
reached. Run engine for ten minutes, and then switch off.

Drain cooling system, fill, and run engine. Repeat procedure until 
water draining from radiator is clean.

Reverse-flush radiator as follows:

Disconnect radiator top and bottom hoses.

Insert a hose in radiator lower tank, and pack cloth around hose.

Back-flush radiator until clean water flows freely from top connection. 
If difficulty is experienced in back-flushing, remove radiator from vehicle. 
Turn radiator upside down, and then back-flush.

Back-flush cylinder block and cylinder head as follows:

Remove thermostat housing cover, and remove thermostat(s). Refer to 
 Section 03A-03 , Section 03B-03 , Section 03C-03 or Section 03D-03 .

Insert a hose into thermostat housing, and back-flush engine until 
clean water flows freely from radiator bottom hose.

Install thermostat(s) and housing cover. Refer to Section 03A-03 , 
 Section 03B-03 , Section 03C-03 or Section 03D-03 . Connect radiator top and 
bottom hoses. Tighten securely.

After flushing system replace coolant filter.

 Heater Core Back-Flushing 

All engine cooling system flushing and back-flushing procedures must 
include a separate back-flushing of the heater or air conditioning system 
heater core after the back-flushing of the engine cooling system. This will 
prevent engine cooling system particles from clogging the heater core tubes 
and reducing (or eliminating) coolant flow through the heater core. The heater 
core must be back-flushed separately from the engine cooling system for proper 
back-flush water flow direction through the heater core.

Disconnect the heater core outlet heater hose from the water pump 
fitting. Install a female garden hose-end fitting adapter in the end of the 
outlet heater hose. Secure with a hose clamp.

Connect the female garden hose-end of the outlet heater hose to the 
male end of a water supply garden hose.

Disconnect the heater core inlet heater hose from the engine block 
fitting and allow to drain into a suitable container.

Turn the water supply valve on and off several times so the surge 
action will help to dislodge larger stubborn particles from the heater core 
tubes. Allow full water pressure to flow approximately five minutes.

Remove the hose clamp and female garden hose-end adapter from the end 
of the outlet heater hose and connect the outlet heater hose onto the water 
pump fitting.

Connect the inlet heater hose onto the engine block fitting.

Fill the cooling system.

Test the system for proper heater performance with the specified engine 
cooling system conditions.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter System

The function of the starting system is to crank the engine at a speed 
fast enough to permit the engine to start.

The system consists of the following components:

starter motor

flywheel ring gear

starter relay

ignition switch 

battery and interconnecting wiring

neutral switch/vehicle interface module

 WARNING: WHEN SERVICING THE STARTER MOTOR OR PERFORMING OTHER UNDERHOOD WORK IN 
THE VICINITY OF THE STARTER MOTOR, BE AWARE THAT THE HEAVY-GAUGE BATTERY INPUT 
LEAD AT THE STARTER SOLENOID IS ELECTRICALLY HOT AT ALL TIMES.

 28-MT Starter 

[FIGURE: J6443A.gif]

 37-MT Starter

[FIGURE: J6210A.gif]

 Starter Motor 

The starter motors are of the same basic construction and function 
essentially the same. Electrically, the motors consist of an armature, field 
coils and a brush assembly.

The field coils are mounted in the starter frame and are held in 
position by the pole shoes. Current flow through field coils generates 
magnetic fields that are concentrated by the pole shoes.

The armature consists of insulated wire loops connected to the segments 
on the commutator. Battery current supplied to the armature wires through the 
brushes and commutator generates magnetic fields in the armature. The 
repelling action between the magnetism generated in the armature loops and 
field coils forces the armature to rotate. The rotating armature is supported 
on bronze bushings located in the brush end housing, lever housing and drive 
end housing.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Solenoid

The starter solenoid performs two functions. It shifts the starter 
drive pinion into engagement with the engine flywheel and connects the starter 
motor to the positive side of the battery.

The drive pinion is shifted through a lever that is connected to the 
solenoid plunger. The electrical circuit between the starter B- and 
M-terminals is closed by a contact disc that is also attached to the solenoid 
plunger.

Movement of the plunger is the result of a magnetic field generated by 
the pull-in and hold-in windings contained in the solenoid.

When the ignition switch is turned to START, current flows through both 
solenoid windings. This creates a magnetic field strong enough to pull in the 
plunger, shifting the overrunning clutch and drive pinion into mesh with the 
flywheel. As the plunger nears bottom, it strikes the contact disc and forces 
the disc against the starter motor contacts. This completes the battery 
circuit, and the starter motor operates.

When the contact disc closes the contacts, the pull-in winding loses 
its effect due to the voltage being equal at both ends of the winding. The 
hold-in coil continues to hold the plunger in the closed position and reduces 
the current needed by the solenoid. When the ignition switch is released, the 
current to the solenoid stops. The springs within the solenoid open the 
starter motor circuit contacts and shift the clutch and pinion assembly to the 
at-rest position.

[FIGURE: J6403A.gif]

PAGE 2395
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Overrunning Clutch

During engine cranking, the drive pinion is locked to the armature 
shaft through an overrunning clutch. When the engine starts and picks up 
speed, the overrunning clutch allows the pinion to spin freely on the cranking 
motor driveshaft, preventing the engine from driving the cranking motor. This 
protects the armature from excessive speed during the brief period that the 
starter drive pinion gear remains enmeshed and the engine has started.

[FIGURE: J6465A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starter Relay

The starter relay is an electrically operated switch used to connect 
the windings in the starter motor solenoid to the battery. The relay consists 
of a coil, plunger and contact disc. When the coil is connected to battery 
power through the ignition or push-button switch, it becomes an electromagnet. 
The magnetic force draws the plunger into the coil core. A disc connected to 
the plunger contacts the relay terminal, completing the battery-to-solenoid 
circuit. When the key or button is released, the magnetic field in the coil 
collapses and spring pressure returns the plunger and contact disc to the open 
circuit position.

[FIGURE: J6406A.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 2397
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Sequence of Operation

On an automatic transmission-equipped vehicle, shift lever is 
positioned in NEUTRAL (N) to close neutral switch. On a manual 
transmission-equipped vehicle, clutch pedal disengages engine from transmission.

Ignition switch is turned to START position.

Battery voltage is connected to starter relay coil through ignition 
switch. Current flow through relay coil generates magnetic field.

Iron core is drawn into relay coil. Disc connected to core closes 
electrical contacts inside relay.

Electrical contacts and disc complete circuit between relay battery 
feed terminal and starter solenoid S-terminal.

Starter solenoid is energized, creating a magnetic field in solenoid 
pull-in and hold-in windings.

Iron plunger core is drawn into solenoid coil.

Lever connected to drive assembly engages drive pinion gear with 
flywheel ring gear.

When iron plunger core is all the way into the coil, its contact disc 
closes circuit between battery and motor terminals. As current flows to 
starter motor, solenoid pull-in coil is bypassed. Hold-in coil keeps drive 
pinion gear engaged with flywheel.

Current flow through field coils generates magnetic field.

Current flow through brushes and armature wires generates magnetic 
field. Repelling magnetic fields cause armature to rotate.

Starter remains engaged until ignition switch is released from START 
position. Overrunning clutch in drive assembly protects starter motor from 
excessive speeds during brief period before ignition switch is released from 
START position (as engine starts).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starting Aid, Ether

 WARNING: DO NOT SMOKE WHEN INSTALLING, MAINTAINING, TESTING OR TROUBLESHOOTING 
AN ETHER START SYSTEM. MAKE SURE YOU ARE IN A WELL-VENTILATED AREA AWAY FROM 
HEAT, OPEN FLAMES OR SPARKS. WEAR GOGGLES WHEN TESTING TO AVOID EYE INJURY. 
MAKE SURE OPENINGS IN THE VALVE, TUBE OR NOZZLE ARE POINTED AWAY FROM YOU 
WHILE TESTING. 

 CAUTION: Do not use the ether cold start system for purposes other than cold 
starting. When high engine temperatures are expected, such as during warm 
weather or when carrying a heavy load in a mountainous or hilly area, remove 
the cylinder to avoid activation of the cylinder's safety relief valve. The 
safety relief valve is set to activate at approximately 93°C (200°F), 
causing a loss of starting fluid. 

In cold weather starting, the heat of piston compression is dissipated 
into the cold cylinder walls, reducing the chamber's ability to attain 
385°C (725°F) temperature required for diesel fuel combustion.

The reduced 180°C (360°F) ignition temperature of the injected 
ether supplies the external starting aid fuel and heat source for the rapid 
increase in the combustion chamber temperature required for fuel oil combustion.

This system consists of an ether supply cylinder, an actuator valve, a 
temperature-sensitive switch and an atomizer orifice located in the intake 
manifold and the connecting tubing.

The ether cold start system is a fully automatic engine starting fluid 
system designed to spray a controlled amount of starting fluid into the air 
intake system of an engine during and immediately after cranking.

The system's engine temperature sensor (ETS) switch determines when the 
system should function. When needed, the solenoid valve is activated 
automatically during engine cranking. Starting fluid is released from the 
pressurized cylinder, flows through the valve, through the vaporizing fitting, 
through the nylon tubing, and out of an injector nozzle located in the 
engine's air intake system. A reservoir in the valve maintains a flow of 
starting fluid after cranking to prevent the just-started engine from 
faltering or dying.

[FIGURE: J6408A.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 2399
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Starting Aid, Intake Air Heater

The intake air heater system improves cold weather startability and 
reduces white smoke after a cold engine start. The system is activated by an 
electronic controller when engine temperature is below 7°C (45°F). 
Intake air is heated by burning a small amount of diesel fuel in the intake 
manifold. The fuel is ignited by a pair of glow plugs installed in the intake 
manifold.

The system operates in two cycles — pre-heat and post-heat. 
During pre-heat, the wait-to-start light is on while the glow plugs reach 
operating temperature. After the engine starts, the controller maintains the 
post-heat cycle for two to three minutes, depending on engine temperature.

If a system fault occurs, the controller has self-test capabilities. 
Refer to Starting Aid, Intake Air Heater, Inspection and Verification for 
further details on system self test.

[FIGURE: J6409A.gif]

 Controller Inputs 

Engine temperature sensor: installed in engine block; provides engine 
temperature signal. Based on this input, system will activate when engine 
temperature is below 7°C (45°F).

Oil pressure switch: closed by engine oil pressure; provides engine 
running signal. When controller receives engine running signal, it switches to 
post-heat cycle.

Engine cranking: spliced into starter relay circuit; provides engine 
cranking signal. Based on this input, controller will open fuel valve.

 Controller Outputs 

Wait-to-start light: length of time light remains on depends on engine 
temperature. Waiting period allows glow plugs to reach operating temperature. 

Glow plug relay: controller provides battery power to relay coil. When 
relay contacts close, glow plugs are connected to battery power.

Fuel solenoid valve: fuel from injection system enters glow plugs when 
fuel valve opens. Controller opens valve by providing battery power to 
solenoid attached to valve.

 Intake Air Heater System

Valve Assembly, Ether Start 

Refer to illustrations under Ether Reservoir in the Removal and

 Removal 

Remove cylinder and install protective cap on valve inlet. 

Remove valve assembly shield. 

Disconnect union-fitting on ether injection line at valve assembly 
fitting.

Disconnect electrical wiring at valve. 

Remove bolts attaching valve assembly and remove valve assembly from 
mounting bracket. 

 Installation 

Position valve assembly on mounting bracket and install mounting nuts 
and bolts. 

Connect electrical wiring. 

Remove protective cap and install cylinder assembly hand-tight. Tighten 
retaining clamp hand-tight. 

Check system operation. If OK, install valve assembly shield.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Jump-Starting 

The following instructions for starting the vehicle with jumper cables 
contain precautions that should be observed to avoid possible injury or damage 
to the vehicle.

 WARNING: HYDROGEN AND OXYGEN GASES ARE PRODUCED DURING NORMAL BATTERY OPERATION. 
THIS GAS MIXTURE CAN EXPLODE IF FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED TOBACCO ARE BROUGHT 
NEAR THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR USING A BATTERY IN AN ENCLOSED SPACE, 
ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION AND SHIELD YOUR EYES. DO NOT DISCONNECT THE BATTERY 
OF THE VEHICLE TO BE STARTED. DISCONNECTING THE BATTERY COULD DAMAGE THE 
VEHICLE'S ELECTRONIC SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: TO AVOID ANY POSSIBILITY OF INJURY, USE PARTICULAR CARE WHEN CONNECTING 
A BOOSTER BATTERY TO A DISCHARGE BATTERY. 

 CAUTION: Headlamp filament failures can occur when vehicle with a dead battery 
is jump-started with the headlamp switch on. 

 CAUTION: Use only a 12-volt jumper system. A 12-volt starting motor and other 
vehicle components can be damaged beyond repair by connecting it to a 24-volt 
power supply (two 12-volt batteries in series, or a 24-volt motor generator 
set). 

 NOTE: Battery top has warnings. 

To prevent any damage to electrical or lighting components during 
jump-starting, proceed as follows. 

 NOTE: Follow procedure in exact sequence. 

Position vehicles so jumper cables will reach, being careful that 
vehicles do not touch.

Turn all lights off before and during jump-starting. 

Turn on heater blower motor to remove transient voltage. 

Avoid contact with any moving engine parts. 

Make connections in numerical order. Disconnect in reverse order.

Connect ends of one cable to the positive (+) terminal of each 
battery starting with the discharged battery (1 in the following illustration) 
and going to the booster battery (2 in the following illustration).

[FIGURE: J2704C.gif]

 WARNING: MAKING THE FINAL CABLE CONNECTION CAN CAUSE AN ELECTRICAL SPARK NEAR 
THE BATTERY, RESULTING IN AN EXPLOSION. REFER TO WARNING AT THE BEGINNING OF 
THE JUMP-STARTING PROCEDURE. 

Connect one end of other cable to negative (-) terminal of good battery 
(3 in preceding illustration). Connect other end of the same cable to engine 
block on vehicle being started (4 in preceding illustration), NOT TO NEGATIVE 
(-) TERMINAL OF BATTERY.

Make sure jumper cables are not in the way of moving engine parts.

Start engine of vehicle with good battery. Do not crank engine 
continuously for more than 30 seconds at a time. Allow two minutes for starter 
motor to cool between cranking. Run engine at a moderate speed.

Start engine of vehicle with discharged battery. Follow starting 
instructions in the Owner Guide.

Leave all switches off except heater blower motor. Reduce engine speed 
to idle on both vehicles to prevent possible damage to vehicle electrical 
system.

Make sure engines are at idle speed before disconnecting jumper cables. 

Remove cable from engine block first, then other end of negative cable. 

Remove ends of positive cable.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Starting System

Wipe field coils, armature, commutator and armature shaft with a clean 
cloth. Wash springs, shims, thrust washer, trip collar, locking collar, and 
brush end housing assembly in solvent. Dry the parts. 

Examine contacts on starter solenoid assembly and, if necessary, clean 
them with very fine sandpaper or crocus cloth. 

The starter solenoid windings can be tested for internal shorts or open 
circuits with an ohmmeter. Connect instrument across windings and note 
reading. Resistance of pull-in winding should be 0.14-0.16 ohms, while 
resistance of hold-in winding should be 0.65-0.70 ohms. A low reading will 
generally indicate an internal short circuit, while no reading at all 
indicates an open circuit. 

If starter solenoid contacts are badly burned or starter solenoid 
winding is shorted, replace solenoid assembly, then adjust drive travel.

PAGE 2412
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Armature, Starter Motor

Inspect armature for broken or burned insulation and unsoldered 
connections. Inspect commutator surface for grooves, and check for runout. 

If surface of commutator is rough or more than 0.051 mm (0.002 inch) 
out of round, turn it down. Do not undercut the mica. 

Check armature windings with a growler tester.

================================================================================
PAGE 2413
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03-06: Starting System

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bushings

The armature shaft is supported on three sintered bronze bushings 
installed in the drive end housing, lever housing and brush end plate.

These bushings have a dull finish, as compared to the early-type 
machined, cast bronze bushings, which had a shiny finish. 

The bushings can be pressed or tapped out of their housing using a 
suitable puller or driver of the appropriate size. Be sure the housing is well 
supported.

Saturate all bushings, wicks and oil reservoirs with SAE No. 20 oil.

Before pressing the bushing into place, dip it in SAE No. 20 oil. Also, 
soak tangent wicks with SAE No. 20 oil. Insert the wick into place first, and 
then press in the bushing. 

DO NOT DRILL, REAM OR MACHINE sintered bushings in any way. These 
bushings are supplied to size. If drilled or reamed, the ID (inside diameter) 
will be too large; also, the bushing pores will be sealed over. 

It is not necessary to cross-drill a sintered bushing when used with a 
tangent wick. Because the bushing is so highly porous, oil from the wick 
touching the outside bushing surface will bleed through and lubricate the 
shaft. 

The lever housing bushing prevents starter motor armature deflection 
during cranking. As compared to end frame bushings, the clearance between the 
lever housing bushing and shaft is large and the clearance provides a loose 
fit when assembled.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Brush and Brush Holder

Check brushes for free movement in brush holders. Inspect brushes for 
excessive wear. Where brush leads are insulated, make sure insulation is not 
burned or worn. 

The brushes must be well seated to commutator; that is, contacting 
commutator over at least 60 percent of brush contact area. If not, fit brushes 
to commutator with fine sandpaper until desired seating area is obtained. Do 
only one brush at a time. Clean brushes and commutator with compressed air. 
Make sure no abrasive particles from sandpaper are embedded in the contact 
area of brushes. 

New brushes are not ground to fit the commutator; therefore, they must 
be seated as described. 

Mark each brush and brush holder with which it was seated to permit 
assembly in the same position.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Intake Heater Starting Aid System — Electrical

To assist in cold weather starting, the Cummins Encore engine is

base of the air intake.

[FIGURE: DJ0499A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) System

The positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) system performs the following 
functions:

circulates crankcase vapors into the combustion chambers to be burned 
during the combustion cycle

aids in the reduction of emissions levels

helps prevent backfire from traveling into the crankcase

uses a positive crankcase ventilation valve mounted in the valve cover

 CAUTION: Do not remove the PCV system from the engine. Operating engine without 
PCV system will reduce both fuel economy and engine ventilation. This will 
weaken engine performance and shorten life.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) System

The exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) system is designed to:

reintroduce exhaust gas into the combustion cycle

lower combustion temperatures

reduce the formation of oxides of nitrogen

The amount of exhaust gas reintroduced and the timing of the cycle 
varies by calibration. Timing and volume are controlled by engine rpm, engine 
vacuum, exhaust system back pressure, engine coolant temperature and throttle 
position. The EGR valve is vacuum actuated. The vacuum hose routing diagram is 
shown on the Vehicle Emission Control Information (VECI) decal.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheel Alignment, Front

Wheel alignment measurements describe the angular orientation of the 
wheel/tire assembly and the steering axis.

Caster, camber and toe are the three major, measurable alignment 
parameters.

================================================================================
PAGE 2446
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Caster

 NOTE: Keep in mind that if the caster is changed, the toe adjustment must be 
rechecked.

Caster is the amount in degrees that the top of the spindle pin is 
inclined toward the front or rear of the vehicle as viewed from the side of 
the vehicle. The caster angle can range from a positive angle to a negative 
angle.

Positive caster is the tilting of the top of the spindle pin toward the 
rear of the vehicle, while negative or reverse caster is the tilting of the 
spindle pin toward the front of the vehicle.

Positive caster imparts a trailing action to the front wheels, while 
negative or reverse caster causes a leading action. The correct amount of 
caster helps to keep the front wheels in the straight-ahead position. When in 
a turn, caster acts as a lever, assisting the driver to return the front 
wheels to the straight-ahead position.

Caster specifications are based on vehicle design load (no payload) 
which will usually result in a level frame. Because of this, raising (or 
lowering) the rear without changing front ride height will subsequently 
decrease (or increase) the caster angle by the same amount the frame angle 
changes. If the frame is not level when alignment checks are made, this must 
be considered when determining whether the caster setting is correct.

[FIGURE: F9180A.gif]

PAGE 2447
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Camber

Camber is the amount in degrees that the wheel inclines away from the 
vertical at the top, as viewed from the front of the vehicle.

Positive camber is an outward tilt or inclination of the wheel at the 
top.

Negative or reverse camber is an inward tilt of the wheel at the top.

The amount of camber depends on the amount in degrees the spindle pin 
is inclined. An incorrect camber angle causes the side of the tread to wear, 
resulting in abnormal tire wear.

Unequal camber in the front wheels can cause the vehicle to lead to the 
right or left on a level road. The vehicle will lead to the side that has the 
most positive camber.

Spindle pin inclination (angle) is the amount in degrees that the top 
of the spindle pin inclines away from the vertical toward the center of the 
vehicle as viewed from the front of the vehicle.

[FIGURE: F9181A.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

Camber Angle

2

3

Spindle Pin Inclination

4

—

Level of Spring Pad

5

—

Centerline of Tire

Spindle pin inclination working together with the camber angle puts the 
approximate center of the tire tread in contact with the road. Spindle pin 
inclination has the effect of reducing steering effort and improves 
directional stability in the vehicle.

There is no means of adjusting this angle; therefore, it will not 
change unless the front axle has been bent. Corrections or changes to this 
angle are accomplished by replacement of broken, bent or worn parts.

================================================================================
PAGE 2448
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 04-00: Suspension, Service

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Toe

Toe-in is the amount in millimeters (or fractions of an inch) that the 
front wheels are closer together at the front than at the back as viewed from 
the top of the vehicle. With camber on the front wheels, the left front wheel 
tries to steer to the left and right front wheel tries to steer to the right. 
This is due to the wheels wanting to turn in the same direction each wheel 
leans. To overcome this condition, the wheels are given a certain amount of 
toe-in.

No change should be made in toe-in until the other factors of front 
wheel alignment are known to be within specifications.

================================================================================
PAGE 2449

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Load Effect

Truck front end alignment settings change between loaded vehicle and 
unloaded vehicle conditions. The amount of this change will depend on vehicle 
suspension and front axle design, as well as the actual amount of load on the 
front axle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tandem Drive Axle Alignment 

Vehicle alignment (axle alignment) is the process of setting the axles 
of the vehicle into a position to establish true rolling action of the tires 
on the ground.

[FIGURE: F9182A.gif]

Drive axle alignment affects the overall wear rate and wear patterns of 
steering axle tires as well as drive axle tires. Proper drive axle alignment 
should be confirmed before making final front end alignment settings. 

The two primary objectives in setting drive axle alignment are, first, 
that the drive axles be positioned perpendicular to the chassis centerline and 
second, that the two axles be parallel to one another. Most drive axle tandem 
suspensions have provisions for setting alignment.

Although single rear axles are not specifically addressed, the 
procedures in this section are applicable to both single and tandem rear axle 
vehicles. The procedure for aligning the axles with respect to squareness to 
the frame is the same. The portions discussing rear rear drive axle-to-forward 
rear drive axle alignment (parallelism) can be ignored for single rear axle 
vehicles. 

 Axle Alignment Procedure Example 

The tractor should be on a level surface and positioned so that all 
suspension joints are free. This can be done by slowly moving the vehicle 
backward and forward several times in a straight line. Release all brakes and 
chock the front wheels. 

Securely clamp a 9-foot section of angle iron or straight bar stock to 
both frame rails. Use a carpenter's square to ensure a 90-degree 
(perpendicular) relationship between the angle iron and frame rails. Locate 
the angle iron as far forward as practical.

[FIGURE: F45971B.gif]

Using a trammel gauge or other suitable device, measure from the angle 
iron to the center of the rear drive axle on both sides (A 1 and A 2 
 in the illustration). If these measurements differ by more than 
5 mm (3/16 inch), reposition the rear axle so that A 1 = A 2 
. Depending on the particular suspension, this adjustment can be 
made by changing the length of the torque rod(s), turning an eccentric or 
adding or removing shims. 

Similarly measure from rear rear drive axle centers to forward rear 
drive axle centers on both sides (B 1 and B 2 in the 
illustration). If these measurements differ by more than 3 mm (1/8 inch), 
reposition the forward rear drive axle so that B 1 = B 2 
. After repositioning axles, move the vehicle backward and forward several 
times in a straight line to allow suspension joints to return to their neutral 
settings. Recheck measurements to confirm A 1 = A 2 
and B 1 = B 2 with a tolerance of no more than 3 mm 
(1/8 inch).

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Suspension

 Inspection and Verification 

 Tire Wear 

Verify the operator's original concern regarding the tires to duplicate 
the condition.

 NOTE: Tires that show irregularities and definite roughness must be replaced.

Inspect to determine if the following conditions apply.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

condition of wheel or tire and bent or damaged wheel

Loose, damaged or worn front suspension parts

 Tire Wear 

[FIGURE: F8903A.gif]

 Vibration and Roughness 

Vibration, roughness, tramp, shimmy and thump can be caused by 
excessive tire or wheel runout, worn or cupped tires, or wheel and tire 
imbalance.

These conditions can also be caused by rough or undulating road 
surfaces. Driving the vehicle on different types of road surfaces will 
indicate if the road surfaces are actually causing the condition.

Do not immediately suspect the tires when attempting to diagnose a 
vibration concern. Other sources of vibration include:

loose or worn wheel bearings

loose or worn suspension or steering components

brake hub and rotor runout

loose engine or transmission supports

engine driven accessories

This section covers those vibrations related to the tires and wheels.

For diagnostic procedures and service for non-tire related vibrations, 
refer to Section 00-04 .

 Road Test 

A tire vibration diagnostic procedure always begins with a road test. 
The road test and customer interview (if available) will provide much of the 
information needed to find the source of a vibration.

During the road test, drive the vehicle on a road that is smooth and 
free of undulations. If vibration is apparent, note and record the following:

the speed at which the vibration occurs

what type of vibration occurs in each speed range — mechanical 
(such as shake) or audible (such as tire whine)

how the vibration is affected by changes in vehicle speed, engine 
speed, and engine torque

type of vibration sensitivity — torque sensitive, vehicle speed 
sensitive or engine speed sensitive

If the road test indicates the vibration is related to the tires or 
wheels, use the Tire Wear Diagnosis Chart in this section or vibration 
diagnostic procedures in Section 00-04 . If the road test indicates that there 
is tire whine, but no shake or vibration, the noise originates with the 
contact between the tire and the road surface.

A thumping noise usually means that the tire has flat or soft spots 
making a noise as they slap the roadway. Tire whine can be distinguished from 
axle noise because axle noise diminishes or changes according to load or 
speed. Tire noise remains the same over a range of speeds.

To verify that tire noise is not associated with shake or vibration, 
inflate the tires one at a time and check for a change in the sound. The pitch 
or whine will change as the increased pressure changes the tire frequency.

Be sure to deflate tires to their proper pressures after this check is 
completed.

Use the following explanation of terms to help isolate the source of 
the vibration.

 Torque Sensitive 

The condition can be improved or worsened by accelerating, 
decelerating, coasting, maintaining a steady vehicle speed and applying engine 
torque.

 Vehicle Speed Sensitive 

The vibration always occurs at the same vehicle speed and is not 
affected by engine torque, engine speed, or transmission gear selection.

 Engine Speed Sensitive 

The vibration occurs at varying vehicle speeds when a different 
transmission gear is selected. It can sometimes be isolated by increasing or 
decreasing engine speed with the transmission in NEUTRAL, or by stall testing 
with the transmission in gear. If the condition is engine speed sensitive, the 
condition is not related to tires.

 Front End 

 CAUTION: Do not attempt to adjust front wheel alignment without making a 
preliminary inspection of the front end parts, and correcting where necessary. 

Fill all fluids to specification.

Remove any excessive accumulation of mud, dirt or road deposits from 
the chassis and underbody.

Retain all normal loads in the vehicle. Inflate all tires to the 
pressure specified on the Safety Compliance Certification Label (usually 
located on the inside driver door pillar).

Check both front tires and make sure they are the same size, ply 
rating, and load range.

Check for excessive front wheel bearing end play. Adjust or replace the 
front wheel bearings. Refer to appropriate section in Group 04.

Check for worn or damaged spindle pin bushings and loose spindle pin 
lock pins. Refer to Spindle Pin Bushing Wear Check procedure in the Diagnosis 
and Testing portion of this section.

Check for bent steering linkage or excessively worn joints. Refer to 
 Section 11-03 .

Check the steering gear mounting bolts and tighten to the specified 
torque. Refer to Section 11-02A .

Check other suspension components for damage.

Check for aftermarket changes to steering, suspension, wheel and tire 
components (i.e., competition, heavy-duty, etc.). Specifications in this 
manual do not apply to vehicles with aftermarket changes.

 Shock Absorber Checks 

The hydraulic shock absorbers are of the direct-acting type. This type 
of shock absorber is non-adjustable and non-refillable and cannot be repaired.

 Vehicle Inspection 

Before replacing a shock absorber, check the action of the shock 
absorbers as follows.

Check the shock absorber to be sure it is securely and properly 
installed. Check shock absorber insulators for damage and wear. Replace any 
worn or damaged insulators. Tighten attachments to specification.

 CAUTION: Replace the shock absorber if leakage is severe. 

Inspect shock absorber for evidence of fluid leakage. A light film of 
fluid is permissible. Make sure any fluid observed is not from sources other 
than shock absorber.

Disconnect lower end of shock absorber. Extend and compress shock 
absorber as fast as possible, using as much travel as possible. Action should 
become smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Higher resistance on 
extension than on compression is a normal condition. Faint swish noises are 
also normal.

If action is smooth but shock absorber is suspected of being weak, 
repeat Step 3 on mating shock absorber installed on opposite side of vehicle, 
and compare results of both tests. If action is similar, it is unlikely that 
either shock absorber is worn or damaged. Connect both shock absorbers.

 CAUTION: Make sure the part number of the replacement is the same as that of the 
original shock absorber. 

If there is a difference between the two, replace shock absorber having 
lower resistance. The replacement shock absorber resistance will appear to be 
higher than either original, due to initial friction of rod seal.

 Hoist Check 

 Noise: Noise can be caused by loose suspension or 
shock attachments. Verify that all attachments or the suspension components 
and springs and shock absorbers are tight. Replace any worn or damaged upper 
mount insulators. Check springs and shock absorbers for external damage.

 Bottom/Hopping: Check condition of the rubber 
suspension travel stops (front suspension bumpers). Replace if worn or 
missing. Examine for evidence of previous overload or damaged components.

 Force-Check: Support axle and remove lower shock 
attachment. Stroke front shock body using as much travel as possible. The 
action should be smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Damping forces 
should be equivalent on both sides of the vehicle.

Replace only the worn or damaged shock absorber.

In the past it was recommended that shock absorbers be replaced in 
pairs if one unit became unserviceable. Improved sealing, new materials, 
design and improved rod machining and hardening techniques have added to the 
reliability of shock absorbers. Therefore, shock absorbers no longer need to 
be replaced in pairs when only one unit is not serviceable.

 Bench Test 

Place the shock absorber right side up in a vise. Hand-stroke the shock 
absorber as fast as possible using as much travel as possible. Action should 
be smooth and uniform throughout each stroke. Higher resistance on extension 
than on compression is normal.

The following conditions are abnormal:

a lag or skip at reversal of travel near mid-stroke when the shock 
absorber is properly primed and in the installed position

seizing

noise, other than a faint swish, such as a clicking upon fast stroke 
reversal

excessive fluid leakage

with rod fully extended, any lateral motion of rod in relation to outer 
cylinder

If the shock absorber action remains erratic after purging air, install 
a new shock absorber, replacing only the damaged shock absorber. Shock 
absorbers do not need to be replaced as sets.

 Suspension, Rear 

Check for leaks on rear shock absorbers.

Check shock absorber operation for stiff, rough or spongy operation.

Check condition or rear suspension bushings and rear suspension springs.

If the above checks reveal evidence of excessive wear, deterioration, 
or improper operation, replace damaged components.

 Spindle Pin Inspection 

These procedures are for determining if front axle spindle pin bushing 
wear (side play) and spindle vertical end play measurements exceed the maximum 
wear limits for normal service and decide if maintenance is necessary.

 Spindle Pin Bushing Wear Check 

Spindle pin and bushings must not have been recently lubricated before 
making this check. Measurements must be made before lubrication.

The simplest method for checking spindle pin looseness is to use a 
camber gauge. Instructions for the use of the camber gauge in this particular 
operation are as follows:

Block the rear wheels.

Raise and support the axle on two jack stands. If the axle is supported 
on only one jack stand, a false reading will be obtained.

Apply brakes to eliminate wheel bearing play and to ensure a correct 
reading. Failure to do so will result in a false reading.

Mark the tire at 444.5-mm (17.5-inch) radius (A in the illustration) 
from the center of the spindle. Position a dial indicator at the 444.5-mm 
(17.5-inch) mark to measure tire movement. Accurate results depend upon 
measurement at specified radius.

Push the wheel inward at the top and measure the movement obtained on 
the dial indicator (B in the illustration) at the 444.5-mm (17.5-inch) radius 
mark on the tire. If more than 3.175 mm (1/8 inch) is obtained at the 444.5-mm 
(17.5-inch) mark, the spindle pin bushings should be replaced.

[FIGURE: F9183A.gif]

 Measuring Spindle Vertical End Play 

Block rear wheels prior to performing this procedure.

Raise and support the axle.

Lift the wheel and tire (spindle only if wheel is removed) so that all 
clearance is taken up between the steering knuckle and the axle spindle pin 
boss.

[FIGURE: F9184A.gif]

Using a feeler gauge, measure clearance between steering knuckle and 
spindle pin boss. If more than 1.524 mm (0.060 inch) is measured, add shims as 
needed to reduce clearance to 0.1270-0.3810 mm (0.005-0.015 inch).

ADJUSTMENTS

Axle Alignment, Front 

As a first step in aligning the front suspension system, the front axle 
must be squared to the frame. If axle-to-frame alignment is not square, loosen 
the U-bolts (which attach the front springs to the front axle) on both sides 
of the vehicle. Shift the axle to the proper square-to-frame position, and 
retighten all U-bolts.

ADJUSTMENTS

Wheel Alignment, Front

Prior to any alignment check, inspect the vehicle tires for the 
following: 

correct tire inflation pressure (with respect to tire temperature and 
vehicle load as specified in the Tire and Rim Association yearbook)

tire condition (tread uniformity, balance, runout, etc.) 

correct tire matching and selection (same tire brand, tread depth, 
tread design, ply rating and construction type on both ends of axles) 

correct wheel bearing adjustment

Check the frame for straightness. The frame rails must be straight 
within 3 mm (1/8 inch) per 2540 mm (100 inches) of length. If the rails are 
not within this specification, they can be straightened by qualified frame 
straightening technicians. 

Check for loose or missing frame crossmember and suspension bracket 
mounting fasteners, which can allow the frame assembly to parallelogram 
(deviate from true rectangular shape). If loose fasteners are found, check for 
egg-shaped holes. If holes have been enlarged, redrill for the next size bolt, 
and retighten all fasteners to the appropriate torque. 

Inspect chassis/suspension systems for worn or damaged components 
(bushings, spring leaves, tie rods, brackets, etc.) and replace prior to the 
alignment check. 

On tandem axle vehicles, check and set the alignment of the drive axles 
before the front axle alignment is performed. 

 Caster 

The caster angle is controlled by the angle of the front spring pads, 
and changes as the load on the front axle increases or as the springs sag. The 
spring pads must be parallel to each other. Any change in the caster angle 
results from a twisted axle or spring sag. 

Caster specifications are based on the assumption that the frame is 
level front to rear. Caster should be checked with the vehicle at empty load.

Measure the frame angle with a bubble protractor or inclinometer.

If the frame is low at the front, add the frame angle to the caster 
angle shown on the checking equipment.

If the frame is high in front, subtract the frame angle from the caster 
angle reading on the checking equipment to get the true caster angle.

[FIGURE: F30091A.gif]

If the springs have sagged, adjust the caster angle by replacing the 
springs or by installing tapered wedges between the springs and the spring 
pads. Use only one wedge per side. The wedges are available in different 
thicknesses. Position the thick edge of the wedge toward the rear of the 
vehicle to increase the caster, or toward the front to decrease the caster. 
When installing wedges, make sure the front spring tie bolts extend through 
the wedge and into the axle pilot hole.

[FIGURE: F30101B.gif]

 Camber 

Camber is built into the axle and cannot be changed. If the camber 
measurement is not within specifications, the axle must be replaced.

 Toe 

If the toe is out of specification, loosen the clamp bolts at each end 
of the spindle connecting rod tube.

Rotate the tube until the correct toe is obtained, and tighten to 43-56 
Nm (32-41 lb-ft) for 1/2-20 clamp bolts or 68-95 Nm (50-70 
lb-ft) for 5/8-18 clamp bolts.

Recheck the toe to make sure no changes occurred when the bolts were 
tightened.

[FIGURE: F30111A.gif]

Clamps that are not fixed should be positioned with the tab against the 
end of the rod. The clamp bolt must be vertical and rearward, with the clamp 
facing forward.

[FIGURE: G3428D.gif]

ADJUSTMENTS

Alignment for Clear Vision

Set wheels in straight-ahead position by driving vehicle a short 
distance and mark the steering wheel relationship to steering column with a 
chalk mark.

If the steering wheel is more than 9 degrees off center, remove the 
steering wheel. Refer to Section 11-04 . Proceed to Step 3.

 NOTE: The steering wheel has serrations equally spaced and can be installed 
in any position.

With the front wheels in the straight-ahead position, install the 
steering wheel on the column so that the spokes are in a horizontal position 
(plus or minus 9 degrees from horizontal).

Install the steering wheel. Refer to Section 11-04 .

ADJUSTMENTS

Alternate Alignment Procedures

 Bee Line Method 

The Bee Line method for aligning tandem axles uses the chassis or frame 
as a primary reference and a laser to measure the perpendicularity 
(squareness) of the rear rear drive axle to the centerline of the vehicle. 

The centerline is established by shooting through a centered target at 
the rear rear drive axle to a second centered target at the front of the 
chassis.

Measure the distance the laser dot is either left or right of the 
centerline of the forward target.

[FIGURE: F8229A.gif]

 NOTE: The acceptable distance of the laser dot to the left or right of center 
on the Bee Line target increases as the distance between the laser and forward 
target increases.

 NOTE: The axle error value is half the maximum value of 5 mm (3/16 inch) 
because it is measured from axle tip to centerline, rather than axle tip to 
axle tip.

Using the following conversion chart, compute the amount of error at 
the rear rear drive axle. Axle error is the amount the axle tip is forward or 
rearward of square from the centerline of the vehicle. Computing axle error 
greater than 2.5 mm (3/32 inch) indicates that the axle is out of square and 
needs adjustment.

For example, on a particular vehicle, the distance measured between the 
laser and the forward target is 306 inches (25.5 ft.). The measured distance 
between the laser dot and the forward target centerline is 1/2 inch. Rounding 
25.5 ft. up to 26 ft., the chart gives an error of 1/16 inch, which is less 
than 3/32 inch and is acceptable. If the measured distance between the laser 
dot and the forward target centerline is 1 inch, the error at the axle is 5/32 
inch, indicating the axle needs adjustment.

Depending on the alignment condition, axle position adjustments can be 
made for each suspension.

 Hunter Method 

The Hunter method aligns axles with each other, without reference to 
chassis or frame. Computerized alignment systems use sensors containing 
calibrated devices and microprocessors attached to individual wheels with 
lines connecting one adapter to the others to measure tandem axle alignment 
angles. The thrust angle is determined for the rear rear drive axle to measure 
perpendicularity (squareness) to the frame. Thrust angle is the resultant 
direction of travel for an axle due to the relative toe setting for the wheel 
at both ends of the axle. An acceptable thrust angle on Hunter alignment 
equipment is within ±0.12 degrees on the rear rear drive axle. Refer to 
the previous illustrations. 

Depending on the alignment condition, axle position adjustments can be 
made for each suspension.

For either Bee Line or Hunter methods, a trammel gauge or other 
suitable device can be used to set the forward rear drive axle parallel to the 
rear rear drive axle. Measure from rear rear drive axle centers to forward 
rear drive axle centers on both sides. If these measurements differ by more 
than 3 mm (1/8 inch), reposition the forward rear drive axle so that B 1 
 = B 2 .
