REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Bushing, Center, Rubber, Beam Removed 

 Removal 

Remove the equalizing beam. 

Inspect the area surrounding the bushing outer metal for signs of 
mushrooming. Remove all signs of mushrooming with a chisel or disc sander.

 WARNING: WHEN REMOVING AND INSTALLING BUSHINGS IN EQUALIZING BEAMS, FOLLOW 
PROCEDURES DESCRIBED IN THIS SECTION. DO NOT USE A TORCH TO REMOVE THE BUSHING 
OUTER METAL PRESSED IN THE BEAM. WELDING, TORCHING OR ATTACHING MATERIAL TO 
THE EQUALIZING BEAM MUST NEVER BE PERFORMED. ALL EQUALIZING BEAMS (ALUMINUM 
AND STEEL) ARE HEAT TREATED FOR STRENGTH AND SERVICE LIFE. THE USE OF HEAT CAN 
ADVERSELY AFFECT THE STRENGTH OF THE BEAMS. AFTER REMOVING EQUALIZING BEAM 
BUSHINGS, THOROUGHLY INSPECT THE BEAM BORES. IF THE BEAM BORES ARE DAMAGED, 
REPLACE WITH A NEW EQUALIZING BEAM. 

 CAUTION: When pressing the bushing out, make sure the equalizing beam is 
securely supported at the center bore area on the press bed to avoid bending 
the equalizing beam. 

Remove the rubber bushing with OTC tool set Y-849 for Series 340 
suspensions and tool set Y-849 and adapter Y-861 for Series 380 and 400 
suspensions. If the tool set is not available, press the bushing out in a 
press of at least 50 tons capacity. On Series 340 suspensions, press the 
bushing out with a piece of tubing with an 88-mm (3-1/2 inch) outside diameter 
and a 178-mm (7-inch) length. On Series 380 and 400 suspensions, press the 
bushing out with a piece of tubing with a 117-mm (4-5/8 inch) OD and a 178-mm 
(7-inch) length.

 Installation 

Inspect the bushing bore for nicks and burrs. Remove any nicks and 
burrs with emery cloth. 

Clean the outer steel sleeve of the rubber bushing with an emery cloth 
to remove the phosphate coating that acts as a rust preventative. 

Apply a coating of Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B around the bushing outer sleeve. 

Position the bushing in the bore and press in with a press of at least 
45,359 kg (50 tons) capacity. Press the bushing in with OTC tool 302031 
(Series 340 suspension) or 302026 (Series 380 and 400 suspension). 

If tool is not available, press the bushing in place with a piece of 
tubing with an outside diameter of 88 mm (3-1/2 inches) and a length of 178 mm 
(7 inches) for Series 340 suspension or an outside diameter of 117 mm (4-5/8 
inches) and a length of 178 mm (7 inches) for Series 380 and 400 suspensions. 

Install the equalizing beam.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Bushing, Center, Rubber, Beam Installed 

 Removal 

Block the front wheels to prevent movement of the vehicle. 

Remove the nuts retaining the saddle caps to the saddle and remove the 
saddle caps. 

Raise the rear of the vehicle until the studs in the saddle clear the 
equalizing beam. 

 CAUTION: Do not use a torch to remove the welded plug; the equalizing beam can 
be damaged. 

Remove the plug welded in the center bushing bore that retains the 
crosstube in the bore. Drill out the plug with a hole saw. Use a 51-mm 
(2-inch) diameter hole saw on Series 340 suspensions or a 64-mm (2-1/2-inch) 
diameter hole saw on Series 380 and 400 suspensions remove the welded plug 
from the right and left equalizer beam.

Remove the crosstube from inside the bushing. 

Inspect the inside face of the equalizing beam center hub. If the 
bushing outer sleeve is excessively worn, and the edge is mushroomed over the 
inner face of the equalizing beam hub, remove the mushroomed surface with a 
chisel or disc sander. 

 WARNING: WHEN REMOVING AND INSTALLING BUSHINGS IN EQUALIZING BEAMS, FOLLOW 
PROCEDURES DESCRIBED IN THIS SECTION. DO NOT USE A TORCH TO REMOVE THE BUSHING 
OUTER METAL PRESSED IN THE BEAM. WELDING, TORCHING OR ATTACHING MATERIAL TO 
THE EQUALIZING BEAM MUST NEVER BE PERFORMED. ALL EQUALIZING BEAMS (ALUMINUM 
AND STEEL) ARE HEAT TREATED FOR STRENGTH AND SERVICE LIFE. THE USE OF HEAT CAN 
ADVERSELY AFFECT THE STRENGTH OF THE BEAMS. AFTER REMOVING EQUALIZING BEAM 
BUSHINGS, THOROUGHLY INSPECT THE BEAM BORES. IF THE BEAM BORES ARE DAMAGED, 
REPLACE WITH A NEW EQUALIZING BEAM. 

Remove the bushing from the equalizing beam with Bushing Remover Tool 
Set 1745 and adapters as shown in the following illustration.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Torque Rod, Straddle (Longitudinal) Mount 

 Removal 

Position a jack under the differential carrier housing to prevent the 
axle from tipping. 

Remove the two retaining nuts and the two bolts that retain the torque 
rod to the axle, and rotate arm clear of housing. 

Remove the two nuts that retain the torque rod and bracket to the frame 
crossmember. Remove torque rod and bracket from vehicle. 

Inspect torque rod and bushings for visual damage and bushing wear. If 
metal to metal contact exists between torque arm housing and torque rod pin, 
if rubber seems excessively worn, or if looseness is encountered between pin 
and bushing, replace torque rod assembly. If unusually damaged (cracks in weld 
or parent metal or rod bent such that ends are not parallel with each other), 
replace torque rod assembly. 

 Installation 

If original axle angle settings are to be retained, install torque rod 
and bracket to frame crossmember with original shims in place and tighten nuts 
to 204-277 Nm (150-205 lb-ft).

If new axle angle settings are to be employed, install torque rod and 
bracket assembly to frame crossmember on top of original spacers. Assemble 
nuts loosely onto bracket retaining bolts. Assemble torque rod to axle and 
tighten to specifications. 

Set new angles by adding or subtracting spacers to original spacer pack 
under torque arm frame bracket. (Remove jack under axle housing during this 
procedure, if necessary.) When desired axle angle is attained, reset jack 
under housing (if removed). 

Assemble spacers properly under torque rod bracket and tighten nuts to 
204-277 Nm (150-205 lb-ft). 

Install torque rod to axle by rotating torque arm into position and 
installing nuts, bolts and washers. Place a washer under bolt head and nut. 
Tighten nuts to 204-277 Nm (150-205 lb-ft). 

Remove jack from under the differential carrier housing.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suspension

The Hendrickson HAS-190L air suspension is made up of two air springs. 
The air springs are supported on main support beams that are fastened to the 
axle and to the frame. A torque rod from the frame bracket to the bottom axle 
cap provides stability. Additional stability is provided by a transverse 
torque rod from the frame to the axle housing. The shock absorbers help to 
control bump and rebound during vehicle operation.

1999 F700, F800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Control System

Air from the air supply system is used to inflate each of the air 
springs.

The suspension air control system uses air supplied from the secondary 
air brake supply system. The air suspension supply line is connected to the 
auxiliary no. 1 port in the dash-mounted air manifold.

The correct vehicle ride height is maintained through use of an 
adjustable bogie crossmember-mounted height leveling valve. The valve senses 
changes in the ride height due to varying loads and either adds or exhausts 
air from the air springs until the correct ride height is reached.

If a loss of air occurs forward (upstream) of the protection valve, air 
pressure within the air spring system will be partially maintained until 
repairs can be made. However, if a loss of air occurs rearward (downstream) of 
the protection valve, the air in the brake system will be protected but the 
air pressure in the air springs will be lost.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Dump Valve System

This system permits deflation of the rear suspension air springs while 
the vehicle is parked to provide a lower bed height for easier loading and 
unloading of cargo.

 CAUTION: This control must not be operated during normal vehicle operation. 
Damage to the system or vehicle can occur.

PAGE 2516

1999 F and B-Series

Section 04-02D: Suspension, Rear, Hendrickson HAS-190L

1999 F700, F800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Control Valve

The toggle control valve is mounted in the instrument panel opening 
below the steering column. To activate the dump valve system, move the toggle 
lever from the normal position to the deflate position. In this deflate 
position, the air will be exhausted from the air springs and the vehicle 
weight will be applied to the rubber bump stops inside each of the air 
springs. The deflate position also activates a warning light in the instrument 
panel above the radio. The purpose of this warning light is to remind the 
driver to move the toggle switch to the normal position before driving to 
prevent damage to the suspension.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Relay Valve

The relay valve is a pilot-operated, inverting, two-way valve. Without 
air pressure on the control, the valve delivers supply air to the delivery 
port and then to the air springs. When air pressure is applied to the control 
port, the supply port is opened to the exhaust port deflating the air springs.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Shock Absorber

 Removal 

Remove the lock nut and the washer that connect the shock absorber to 
the shock absorber mounting bracket.

Remove the nut and the washer that connect the shock absorber to the 
lower shock bracket.

Remove the shock absorber from the stud on the shock absorber mounting 
bracket, and remove the bolt in the lower shock bracket.

If necessary, remove the nuts, the lockwashers and the bolts that 
fasten the shock absorber mounting bracket to the frame. Remove the shock 
absorber mounting bracket.

 Installation

frame. Install the bolts, the washers and the nuts. Make sure that a washer is 
installed on each side of the shock absorber mounting bracket.

Install the shock absorber on the stud of the shock absorber mounting 
bracket and into the lower shock bracket.

Install the washers and the nuts that fasten the shock absorber to the 
stud and lower bracket. Tighten the nuts to 68-95 Nm (50-70 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Main Support Beam

 WARNING: DO NOT USE A CUTTING TORCH TO REMOVE ANY FASTENERS. THE USE OF HEAT ON 
SUSPENSION COMPONENTS WILL ADVERSELY AFFECT THE STRENGTH OF THESE PARTS. A 
COMPONENT DAMAGED IN THIS MANNER CAN CAUSE LOSS OF VEHICLE CONTROL AND 
POSSIBLE PERSONAL INJURY OR PROPERTY DAMAGE. 

 WARNING: EXERCISE EXTREME CARE WHEN HANDLING OR PERFORMING MAINTENANCE IN THE 
AREA OF THE MAIN SUPPORT BEAM. DO NOT CONNECT ARC WELDING GROUND LINE TO THE 
MAIN SUPPORT BEAM. DO NOT STRIKE AN ARC WITH THE ELECTRODE ON THE MAIN SUPPORT 
BEAM. DO NOT USE HEAT NEAR THE MAIN SUPPORT BEAM. DO NOT NICK OR GOUGE THE 
MAIN SUPPORT BEAM. A MAIN SUPPORT BEAM THAT HAS BEEN SUBJECTED TO ANY OF THESE 
CONDITIONS CAN FAIL, CAUSING LOSS OF VEHICLE CONTROL AND POSSIBLE PERSONAL 
INJURY OR PROPERTY DAMAGE. 

 Removal

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Bushing, Torque Rod

 Removal 

 WARNING: DO NOT USE HEAT OR A CUTTING TORCH TO REMOVE THE BUSHINGS FROM THE 
TORQUE ROD. THE USE OF HEAT WILL ADVERSELY AFFECT THE STRENGTH OF THE TORQUE 
ROD. 

Use a press with a minimum capacity of 90,718 kg (10 tons).

 CAUTION: Make sure the torque rod is securely supported on the press bed. 

Support the torque rod on a piece of 6-mm (1/4-inch) wall steel tubing 
that is 127 mm (5.0 inches) long with an inside diameter of 50.8 mm (2.0 
inches).

Push directly on the bar pin of the bushing to remove the bushing from 
the torque rod.

 Installation 

Clean and inspect the inside diameter of the ends of the torque rod. 
Use an emery cloth to remove any nicks and small scratches from the bore.

 CAUTION: Do not use a petroleum or soap base lubricant. 

Lubricate the inside diameter of the torque rod and the new bushing 
with a vegetable base oil such as cooking oil or shortening. 

 CAUTION: Make sure the torque rod is securely supported on the press bed. 

Support the torque rod on the piece of steel tubing used during 
removal. Make sure the bore of the torque rod is centered in the tube.

Put the bushing in the bore of the torque rod so that the mounting 
flats of the bar pin is positioned 10 degrees counterclockwise to the shank of 
the rod.

Press the bushing into the torque rod so that the bushing extends 4.763 
mm (3/16 inch) on the opposite side of the torque rod.

Turn the torque rod over and press on the bar pin so that the bushing 
is centered in the bore of the torque rod.

[FIGURE: F65461A.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Pad, Rear Spring Hanger Bracket

 Removal 

 NOTE: The vehicle must be empty of all load (service empty vehicle, one 
axle/both sides at a time).

Chock the wheels of all the axles.

Support the frame with suitable frame stands.

Support the axles with suitable jack stands.

Release all air from the air springs.

Remove the rebound bolt lock nuts, washers, bolts, spacers and rollers 
from rear spring hangers. The torque rods can remain in place.

Apply an upward force on the crosschannel with a jack or pry bar. This 
will cause the tips of the main support members to drop away from the cam 
surface of the rear spring hangers.

Remove the slipper attaching fasteners, retainer plates and slipper pads.

[FIGURE: F8410C.gif]

 Installation 

Place new slipper pad on rear spring hanger.

Place the retainer plate over the slipper pad and tighten the 3/8-inch 
hex-head self-tapping screws to 48-54 Nm (35-40 lb-ft).

Release the jack or pry bar on the crosschannel or air spring mounting 
brackets, allowing the main support members to come up to the new slipper pads.

Assemble the rebound rollers, spacers, bolts, washers and lock nuts, 
and tighten the lock nuts to 68-95 Nm (50-70 lb-ft) torque.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tires 

Tube-type bias ply and tubeless radial or bias ply tires are used on 
medium and heavy trucks. Tubeless tires are mounted on 15-degree drop-center 
rims and wheels. Tube-type tires are mounted on two-piece flat-base rims or 
wheels and three-piece flat-base rims or wheels.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheels

 NOTE: The material used to make front cast spoke wheels has been changed from 
steel to nodular iron. EPA regulations require that wheel mounting studs be 
converted from cadmium plating to phosphate and oil-coated. The black 
phosphate and oil-coated studs replace the silver cadmium plated studs.

Cast spoke wheels consist of a cast spider and brake drum, and a 
separate demountable rim. Clamps and hold-down nuts on the 3/4-inch studs 
firmly secure the rim to the wheel. On dual rear assemblies, a ring-shaped 
spacer holds the inner and outer rims apart. Optional rear cast spoke wheels 
have five spokes on 13,000, 15,000, 17,500 and 34,000-pound axles, and six 
spokes on 21,000, 23,000, 40,000 and 46,000-pound rear axles. 

[FIGURE: F8385A.gif]

The front cast spoke wheels are of the six-spoke design. 

[FIGURE: F8386A.gif]

 NOTE: Do not mix 10-hole ISO hub mount disc wheels with 10-hole BSN stud 
mount disc wheels. 

Heavy-duty 10-hole BSN stud mount disc wheels have a 285.75-mm 
(11.25-inch) bolt circle diameter. 

[FIGURE: F8387A.gif]

Medium-duty 8-hole ISO disc wheels have a 275-mm (10.8-inch) bolt 
circle diameter with 20 mm x 1.5 wheel mounting bolts. 

[FIGURE: F8919A.gif]

[FIGURE: F2606D.gif]

Heavy-duty 10-hole ISO disc wheels have a 285.75-mm (11.25-inch) bolt 
circle diameter with 22 mm x 1.5 wheel mounting bolts. 

[FIGURE: F8388A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Wheels and Rims 

 Drop-Center Rims 

The one-piece, full drop-center rim has a 15-degree tapered bead seat 
and is used for tubeless tires on demountable rims with cast spoke wheels and 
on disc wheels. 

 Demountable Rims with Cast Spoke Wheels 

[FIGURE: F8379A.gif]

 Disc Wheels 

[FIGURE: F8384A.gif]

The wide base drop-center rim has a 15-degree bead seat. It is used 
with disc wheels or demountable rims for flotation bias and radial tubeless 
tires. 

[FIGURE: F8383A.gif]

 Two-Piece Convertible Rims 

The two-piece flat rim base has a split side ring and is common with FL 
or CR type three-piece (Code D) rim. Disc wheels or demountable rim on cast 
spoke wheels are used with 20-inch tube-type tires. 

[FIGURE: F8380A.gif]

 Three-Piece Rims 

The three-piece flat rim base has continuous side ring and split lock 
ring and is common with FL or CR type flat-base (Code C) two-piece rim. It is 
used for disc wheels or demountable rims on cast spoke wheels. The rims are 
optional with 20-inch tube-type tires. 

[FIGURE: F8381A.gif]

The flat-base three-piece 5-degree rim has a wide seat with split lock 
ring. The rim is used for disc wheels or demountable rims for cast spoke 
wheels and is used with 20-inch tube-type tires. 

[FIGURE: F8382A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety 

 Precautions When Servicing Truck Tires 

CAUTION and SAFETY FIRST are bywords when handling truck tires. Careful 
attention to the suggestions that follow can prevent crippling injuries or 
even death. Make it a rule to respect the terrific force contained in an 
inflated tire.

Wheels must be properly maintained. Improperly maintained wheels and 
wheel components can adversely affect the life of the tire and the wheel. A 
tire is potentially very destructive when inflated. Accidents are caused by 
inexperience and careless handling.

Follow the safety precautions in this manual and obtain safety 
literature from your wheel and rim distributor, wheel and rim manufacturer, 
NHTSA or OSHA. In addition, if you have any questions, consult the distributor 
or manufacturer directly.

The load carrying requirements of each vehicle must be determined 
before selecting the proper tire/wheel combination. Always remember that the 
weakest weight carrying component of the vehicle (i.e., tire, wheel, axle, 
bearings, etc.) determines the overall maximum and safe load carrying capacity 
for the vehicle.

 WARNING: EACH INDIVIDUAL AXLE, WHEEL, RIM AND TIRE HAS ITS OWN MAXIMUM WEIGHT 
AND INFLATION RATING. DO NOT OVERLOAD OR OVERINFLATE BEYOND THE CAPACITY OF 
THE LOWEST RATED COMPONENT OF THE SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: AN INFLATED TIRE AND RIM CAN BE VERY DANGEROUS IF MISUSED OR WORN OUT. 
MANY ACCIDENTS, SOME FATAL, HAVE RESULTED FROM IMPROPER HANDLING AND OPERATION 
OF TRUCK RIMS AND WHEELS. IT IS OF THE UTMOST IMPORTANCE THAT THE PRECAUTIONS 
DESCRIBED ON THESE PAGES BE CAREFULLY FOLLOWED BY ALL PERSONS SERVICING TRUCK 
RIMS AND WHEELS TO AVOID PERSONAL INJURIES AND COSTLY DAMAGE. 

 WARNING: NEVER MOUNT A SMALLER DIAMETER TIRE ON A LARGER DIAMETER RIM/WHEEL. 
WHEN REPLACING TIRES, ALWAYS MATCH THE TIRE SIZE TO THE RIM/WHEEL SIZE. 
IMPROPER MATCHING CAN CAUSE THE TIRE BEAD TO BREAK DURING MOUNTING OR 
INFLATION. THE TIRE CAN EXPLODE DURING INFLATION, EXPELLING BOTH TIRE AND 
RIM/WHEEL OR RIM SIDE AND LOCK RINGS INTO THE AIR WITH ENOUGH FORCE TO INFLICT 
PROPERTY DAMAGE, SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

When replacing tires, use the same size, load range and construction 
type as originally installed on the vehicle. When replacing wheels, use 
original equipment manufacturer's wheels or equivalent available from your 
Ford dealer with equivalent capacity, width, offset and mounting configuration 
as those originally installed on your vehicle. Use of improper replacement 
wheels and tires can adversely affect ride, handling, load carrying capacity, 
bearing life, tire clearance to body and chassis components, vehicle ground 
clearance, vehicle width and brake cooling.

Prepare for any tire repair operation in a safe and efficient way. Use 
caution not to drop the tires, wheels or assemblies on the feet, hands or 
body, or heavily on the floor. Truck tires are heavy. Use a wheel jack such as 
Rotunda Heavy Duty Wheel Dolly 014-00030 or equivalent to maneuver tires.

[FIGURE: E73641A.gif]

 WARNING: EXCESSIVELY CORRODED OR CRACKED RIMS OR RINGS CAN BE DANGEROUS. DEFLATE 
TIRES ON CORRODED OR CRACKED RIMS OR RINGS PRIOR TO REMOVAL OF RIMS OR WHEELS 
FROM VEHICLE. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

Deflating a tire properly is very important to your safety. First, 
reduce the pressure as much as you possibly can by pressing the valve core 
plunger. Only then should you remove the valve core to completely deflate the 
tire before removal from the vehicle or disassembling any components. On 
duals, deflate both tires completely. 

Demounting tires from the wheels or rims requires special care. Follow 
the procedures given for the different types of rims in this section. 

Use only standard tire mounting tools and equipment. The use of 
makeshift tools to force tires on or off the rims or wheels is dangerous and 
must be avoided.

Always lubricate tire beads to ensure sealing of the tire beads on rim. 
Use Rubber Lubricant D9AZ-19583-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications 
ESR-M99B135-A and ESA-M1B6-A. 

Make sure all air is out before removing tires from rims. Use special 
care when using tire irons. 

Grip tire irons firmly and keep them free of oil and grease. They can 
slip and fly with tremendous force. 

Mark all damaged parts for destruction to prevent future use. Always 
remove rust or other foreign matter to ensure proper fitting during 
reassembly. Clean and lightly repaint all rusted rim areas.

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING USED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS, DO NOT USE EXCESSIVE AMOUNTS OF 
PAINT. THIS CAN CAUSE NUT LOOSENING, WHICH CAN LEAD TO PREMATURE WHEEL FAILURE 
OR LOOSE WHEELS, RESULTING IN SERIOUS, PERHAPS FATAL, INJURY. 

 WARNING: WHEN PAINTING ANY WHEEL OR RIM PARTS, ALWAYS ALLOW THE PARTS TO DRY 
THOROUGHLY. IF THE PAINT IS NOT DRY WHEN THE WHEELS/RIMS ARE MOUNTED, TORQUE 
VALUES WILL NOT BE MAINTAINED BECAUSE OF THE PAINT BEING FORCED OUT. EXCESS 
PAINT THICKNESS WILL CAUSE THE DISC WHEELS TO LOOSEN. RETIGHTEN THE WHEEL NUTS 
AFTER 80-160 KM (50-100 MILES) WHEN NEW PAINTED DISC WHEELS ARE REINSTALLED ON 
VEHICLE. 

 NOTE: If replacing one component of an assembly, make sure the size and type 
are a proper match. Never use parts of a different manufacturer than the 
original wheel. Do not use a different size or type.

Replace damaged or excessively corroded parts. Abuse during road 
operations or in mounting tires can cause damage that can weaken the parts. 
Parts that are excessively corroded are weakened. Always inspect for and 
replace damaged or heavily rusted parts. Never use rims, lock rings, side 
rings or flanges that are out of shape, excessively rusted, cracked or broken 
in any way.

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS, SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, SIDE RINGS, LOCK 
RINGS AND RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR OUT OF FLAT, SPRUNG SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RINGS OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE DANGEROUS. THESE COMPONENTS 
CAN FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL 
PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Inspect for and remove light rust and other foreign matter. 
Accumulation of such material on the engagement surfaces of the rim base and 
side rings or lock rings can prevent the proper fit of these parts. Use of a 
rust preventative during mounting will minimize rust. 

 WARNING: ALWAYS WEAR SAFETY GOGGLES OR A FACE SHIELD WHEN PERFORMING ANY BUFFING 
OPERATION. 

Tires and rims often require a buffing operation before being mounted 
once the regular service has been completed. 

 WARNING: AVOID HAMMERING WITH A STEEL HAMMER; YOU CAN DAMAGE THE RIM. ANY 
HAMMERING CAN DISLODGE PARTICLES. NEVER HAMMER ON AN INFLATED ASSEMBLY. 

Make certain the rim ring is seated to full depth of the groove, fits 
tightly all around and is securely locked.

 WARNING: ALWAYS INFLATE THE TIRE IN ROTUNDA INFLATION CHAMBER 104-00104 OR 
EQUIVALENT, OR USE AN OSHA-APPROVED PORTABLE TIRE SAFETY CAGE OR LOCK RING 
GUARD. THIS IS A SAFEGUARD AGAINST IMPROPER ASSEMBLY, INADVERTENTLY MISMATCHED 
PARTS, AND OTHER ASSEMBLY ERRORS. REMEMBER, AN INFLATED TIRE CONTAINS 
POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE ENERGY THAT CAN BLOW IMPROPERLY ASSEMBLED RINGS LOOSE 
AND ASSEMBLIES CAN BE PROPELLED IF THERE IS A SUDDEN RELEASE OF AIR. IN 
EMERGENCY SITUATIONS, WHERE A SAFETY CAGE OR PORTABLE SAFETY DEVICE IS NOT 
AVAILABLE, USE THE VEHICLE'S SPARE WHEEL AND TIRE. 

 WARNING: STAND CLEAR WHEN USING A SAFETY CAGE OR AN OSHA-APPROVED RESTRAINING 
DEVICE. ALWAYS USE A CLIP-ON AIR CHUCK WITH A REMOTE VALVE AND PRESSURE GAUGE. 
DO NOT REST ANY PART OF THE BODY AGAINST THE DEVICE DURING INFLATION. IF THE 
COMPONENTS ARE NOT SEATED PROPERLY AND AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION OCCURS, THE AIR 
BLAST OR MOVEMENT OF THE RESTRAINING DEVICE CAN CAUSE INJURY. 

Place tire assembly in safety cage and inflate to a maximum of ten 
pounds. Check to see that beads are properly seated. Completely deflate tire 
to prevent tube from buckling. Reinflate to recommended pressure.

Use only accurate, tested gauges to ensure proper air pressure. Check 
all gauges regularly with a master gauge. 

Never attempt to short-cut the above procedures.

 WARNING: PROPER PRECAUTIONS SHOULD ALWAYS BE TAKEN WHEN JACKING A VEHICLE UP TO 
PREVENT PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE: 

ALWAYS BLOCK ONE AXLE WITH WHEEL CHOCKS TO PREVENT UNEXPECTED MOVEMENT. 

ALWAYS USE PROPER HEAVY-DUTY JACK STANDS.

MANUALLY CAGE PARKING BRAKE CHAMBERS WHEN WORKING ON THE REAR AXLE. 

APPLY PARKING BRAKE WHEN WORKING ON FRONT AXLE. 

Do not overload rims or wheels. Make sure the combination of load and 
vehicle weight does not exceed the rated load of the rims or wheels. Rims and 
wheels are designed to sustain their rated load using the maximum tire size 
recommended for that rim width by the Tire and Rim Association.

 WARNING: EACH INDIVIDUAL AXLE, WHEEL, RIM AND TIRE HAS ITS OWN MAXIMUM WEIGHT 
AND INFLATION RATING. DO NOT OVERLOAD OR OVERINFLATE BEYOND THE CAPACITY OF 
THE LOWEST RATED COMPONENT OF THE SYSTEM. 

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, SIDE RINGS, LOCK 
RINGS AND RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR OUT OF FLAT, SPRUNG SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RINGS OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

 WARNING: ALLOYS OR METAL SURFACES WITH CRACKS ARE DANGEROUS. THESE COMPONENTS 
CAN FAIL WITHOUT WARNING DURING INFLATION OR LATER ON THE VEHICLE. DESTROY ALL 
PARTS THAT ARE CRACKED. 

Inspect rims and wheels for damage during tire checks and at periodic 
maintenance intervals. Remove and replace worn or damaged parts. 

 WARNING: DO NOT EXCEED MAXIMUM INFLATION PRESSURES. THIS IS DETERMINED BY THE 
SIZE AND PLY RATING OF THE TIRE, BUT IS NOT TO EXCEED THE MAXIMUM COLD 
INFLATION PRESSURE LISTED FOR THE RIM OR WHEEL EVEN IF THE TIRE IS APPROVED 
FOR A HIGHER LOAD OR INFLATION. IT IS ALSO IMPORTANT TO MAINTAIN UNIFORM 
INFLATION IN BOTH TIRES OF A DUAL ASSEMBLY SO THAT WEIGHT IS EQUALLY 
SUSTAINED. 

 WARNING: DO NOT RUN VEHICLE ON ONE TIRE OF DUAL ASSEMBLY. WHEN THERE IS LOSS OF 
AIR IN A DUAL TIRE, THE CARRYING CAPABILITY IS REDUCED AND THE LOAD MUST BE 
SUSTAINED BY THE OTHER TIRE AND RIM AND THE CLAMPING STRENGTH IS LOST IF 
MULTI-PIECE RIMS ARE DEFLATED. INFLATE BOTH TIRES TO BALANCED, RECOMMENDED 
PRESSURES BEFORE FURTHER OPERATION. 

 WARNING: THUMPING OR SIMPLY LOOKING AT THE TIRE DOES NOT GIVE AN ACCURATE 
PRESSURE READING. PERIODICALLY CHECK YOUR AIR PRESSURE GAUGE FOR ACCURACY AND 
ALWAYS USE IT TO CHECK TIRE PRESSURE. 

 WARNING: NEVER ADD AIR TO A TIRE/RIM ASSEMBLY OPERATED IN A RUN FLAT OR 
UNDERINFLATED CONDITION (80 PERCENT OR LESS OF RECOMMENDED PRESSURE). RIMS, 
SIDE RINGS AND LOCK RINGS CAN BECOME DISLODGED, WORN OR DAMAGED. IF AIR IS 
ADDED TO AN ASSEMBLY WITH ANY OF THE PREVIOUS CONDITIONS, AN EXPLOSIVE 
SEPARATION CAN OCCUR, CAUSING SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

 NOTE: When checking inner wheel torque on dual wheel assemblies, back off 
outer nuts first. After the inner nuts are completely tightened, tighten outer 
nuts. 

After first 80-160 km (50-100 miles) of service, recheck clamp and 
wheel nut torque. Loose wheel nuts can cause excessive wear around bolt holes, 
dangerous wheel vibration and metal fatigue failure. Excessive torque is also 
dangerous; it can cause stud or wheel breakage.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Demountable Rims

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, SIDE RINGS, LOCK 
RINGS AND RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR OUT OF FLAT, SPRUNG SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RINGS OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

 WARNING: EXCESSIVELY CORRODED, CRACKED OR DAMAGED RIMS AND RINGS ARE DANGEROUS. 
COMPLETELY DEFLATE TIRE BEFORE REMOVING FROM VEHICLE. IF WORKING ON DUAL 
WHEELS, DEFLATE BOTH TIRES BEFORE REMOVING FROM VEHICLE. IF TIRE OR TIRES ARE 
NOT DEFLATED BEFORE REMOVAL FROM VEHICLE, AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION CAN OCCUR, 
RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: RUST, CORROSION OR ANY FOREIGN MATTER ON THE SIDE RINGS, LOCK RINGS OR 
RIM/WHEEL GROOVE CAN PREVENT THE SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RINGS FROM SEATING 
PROPERLY. THIS CAN CAUSE AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION DURING INFLATION, RESULTING 
IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

 Removal 

Prior to removal of the tire and rim from the vehicle, deflate the tire 
completely by first reducing the pressure as much as possible by depressing 
the valve core plunger, then removing the valve core. If working on dual 
wheels, deflate both tires completely before loosening the mounting bolts. 

 WARNING: WHEN REMOVING WHEEL NUTS FROM SPOKE WHEELS, LOOSEN ALL NUTS 6.35-12.7 
MM (0.25-0.50 IN.) BUT DO NOT REMOVE. RAP ON CLAMPS WITH AN APPROPRIATE TOOL 
TO FREE CLAMPS FROM WHEEL. DO NOT STRIKE ANY PORTION OF THE CAST SPOKE WHEEL. 
IF WHEEL CLAMPS ARE NOT LOOSENED PRIOR TO REMOVING WHEEL NUTS, THE CLAMP OR 
CLAMPS CAN SPRING FROM THE WHEEL UNDER EXTREME FORCE, CAUSING PERSONAL INJURY. 

Loosen, but do not remove the wheel nuts.

 Installation 

Make sure that all parts, including rims, rings, flanges, spacer bands, 
and cast wheel studs are free from damage, dirt or rust. Replace any damaged 
parts.

With dual wheels, place rims and spacer band on wheel and proceed to 
the next step. On single wheels, place the rim on the wheel and proceed to 
Step 7.

 NOTE: Spacer bands are designed to render adequate lateral strength with the 
minimum amount of weight. Spacer bands should not be subjected to loads or 
pressures other than those present during normal use. 

Check the spacer band for concentricity. Make sure it has not been 
distorted, bent or otherwise mishandled in shipment. 

Do not move the vehicles, wheels, axles or assemblies by rolling on 
spacers. 

Place the inside rim over the cast spoke wheel as far as possible up to 
the mounting bevel. On tube-type tires check to see that tire valve does not 
contact drum balance weight. 

Push the spacer band over the cast spoke wheel with a consistent 
pressure on both sides. Guard against cocking. The band must fit snugly to the 
spokes and against the inside rim gutter edge. At this point, the 
concentricity can be checked by turning the spacer band on the wheel.

Install outer rim (or rim in case of single wheel) with the rim drivers 
in between the spokes as shown in the following illustration. Install the 
clamps and start the nuts onto the studs. Refer to the clamp usage chart in 
the Specifications portion of this section.

[FIGURE: F26041A.gif]

 WARNING: DO NOT TIGHTEN A RIM CLAMP IN THE COCKED POSITION. THIS CAN DAMAGE THE 
WHEEL OR CAUSE WHEEL RUNOUT. 

 NOTE: Refer to the following illustration for the cast spoke wheel 
triangulation tightening sequence.

Turn nut No. 1 until snug.

[FIGURE: F2605C.gif]

Rotate the wheel/rim assembly until nut No. 2 is in the top position. 
Turn until snug. 

Rotate the wheel/rim assembly again until nut No. 3 is in the top 
position, and turn the nut until snug. Since the entire weight of the tire/rim 
assembly is on the top spoke position, this procedure allows even application 
of force against three points of the rim for proper alignment. 

Repeat the triangle procedure, this time bringing each nut to 
recommended torque. Refer to the Specifications portion of this section. 

Bring remaining nuts to recommended torque. Refer to the Specifications 
portion of this section.

Check to see that clamps do not bottom out. Make sure rim edges 
consistently meet the spacer band edges on dual wheels. 

After assembly of rims to wheels, rotate the wheels and check 
alignment. Use a block of wood or other object to support marker so the marker 
is at the same level as the edge of the rim. Rotate the tire/wheel assembly 
and note variations in the space between edge of rim and edge of marker as the 
assembly is rotated. Variations in excess of the following measurements 
indicate the rim is not properly mounted.

Demountable rims

front: 2.28 mm (0.090 inch)

dual rear: 3.17 mm (0.125 inch)

Disc wheels

1.52 mm (0.060 inch)

[FIGURE: F3141D.gif]

To correct any misalignment, loosen nut at point of greatest variation 
and tighten nut on opposite side. Recheck and correct until runout is within 
above recommended limits. Tighten nuts to the specified torque. Refer to the 
Specifications portion of this section.

 WARNING: USE ONLY THE SAME TYPE AND STYLE WHEELS, RIMS, LOCK RINGS, SIDE RINGS 
AND MOUNTING HARDWARE TO REPLACE ORIGINAL PARTS. FAILURE TO DO SO CAN RESULT 
IN AN ASSEMBLY THAT LOOKS PROPER, BUT DOES NOT FIT TOGETHER CORRECTLY. THIS 
CAN CAUSE WHEEL OR WHEEL FASTENER FAILURE, RESULTING IN PERSONAL INJURY. NEVER 
MIX FOREIGN (NOT MADE IN THE U.S.A.) PARTS WITH DOMESTIC (MADE IN THE U.S.A.) 
PARTS. 

 CAUTION: Insufficient mounting torque can cause rim slippage, resulting in 
broken valves, worn parts and damaged tires. Excessive mounting torque can 
cause damage by stripping studs, collapsing spacer bands or forcing rims into 
an out-of-round condition. 

 NOTE: Even when the triangulation method is used, nuts will still lose torque 
when the vehicle is operated. This is caused by the seating in of the rim 
assembly to the wheel. After 80-160 km (50-100 miles) of operation, the nuts 
should again be brought to recommended torque and thereafter periodically 
inspected and retightened. The wheel/rim assembly will remain tight, barring 
accidents such as stud breakage or clamp failure. 

Most highway rims look alike, but all vary somewhat in certain design 
features. It is these differences between rims of different types that makes 
part-mixing a hazardous practice. A close, proper fit between rim parts is 
essential to long tire life as well as to operating safety. Often side rings, 
flanges and lock rings of different types appear to be properly seated, but 
wide gaps frequently are present and difficult to see. The rim cross-sections 
in the following illustration show correct, safe matchings of rim parts as 
well as mismatched rings and bases, which almost always create an unsafe 
operating condition.

 NOTE: The following rim part illustrations are intended to depict some 
examples of incorrect procedures. They are not intended to show all incorrect 
and dangerous methods.

 NOTE: Goodyear CR and FL bases and components are interchangeable with 
Firestone/Accuride CR and FL.

 NOTE: Goodyear LB bases and components are interchangeable with 
Firestone/Accuride and Budd LB.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Disc Wheel and Rim 

 Removal 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

Prior to removal of tire and wheel from vehicle, deflate the tire 
completely. Reduce pressure as much as possible by depressing valve core 
plunger, then removing the valve core. Refer to safety precautions. If working 
on dual wheels, deflate both tires completely before loosening the mounting 
bolts.

Loosen, but do not remove the wheel stud nuts. All studs are right-hand 
threads for ISO metric disc wheels. 

[FIGURE: F8389A.gif]

Raise the vehicle until wheel and tire clear floor. 

Remove the wheel stud nuts and wheel and tire from hub and drum. When 
replacing a rear inner wheel, valve extension (if present) must be transferred 
to new wheel. On dual disc wheels, the inner wheel nut will also have to be 
removed if the inner tire is to be removed. 

[FIGURE: F4621B.gif]

 Installation 

 10-Hole BSN Disc Wheels 

Check all parts for damage, including wheels and rings. Make sure 
studs, nuts and mounting faces of hub and wheels are clean and free from 
grease. Refer to Rim and Wheel Maintenance in the Cleaning and Inspection 
portion of this section. Replace any worn or damaged parts. 

Mount single wheel or inner dual wheel over studs, being careful not to 
damage stud threads. Studs and wheel nut threads should be dry. No oil or 
lubricant should be used.

[FIGURE: F2606D.gif]

 NOTE: Left side wheels have left-hand threads.

Draw the single wheel nut or dual inner wheel nut alternately in the 
sequence shown in the following illustration, but do not tighten fully. This 
procedure will permit uniform seating of the nuts and even, face-to-face 
contact of the wheels and hub.

[FIGURE: F2607D.gif]

 CAUTION: Insufficient mounting torque can cause wheel shimmy, resulting in 
damage to parts and extreme tire tread wear. Excessive mounting torque can 
cause studs to break and discs to crack in the stud hole area. 

Tighten the nuts fully to 610-677 Nm (450-500 lb-ft) in the same 
sequence. Mount the outer wheel (for dual wheels) and repeat the tightening 
procedure. Refer to the disc wheel nut usage charts under Specifications in 
this section.

 8- and 10-Hole ISO Disc Wheels 

Check all parts for damage, including wheels and rims. Make sure studs, 
nuts and mounting faces of hub and wheels are clean and free from grease. 
Replace any worn or damaged parts. 

Mount single wheel or inner and outer dual wheel over studs, being 
careful not to damage stud threads. Studs and flange nut threads should be 
dry. No oil or lubricant should be used. 

[FIGURE: F8388A.gif]

Tighten nut and washer assemblies alternately in sequence shown. 
Ten-hole wheel is illustrated; use similar sequence for 8-hole wheel. Do not 
fully tighten. This procedure will permit uniform seating of nuts and even, 
face-to-face contact of wheels and hub. 

[FIGURE: F7947A.gif]

 CAUTION: Insufficient mounting torque can cause wheel shimmy, resulting in 
damage to parts and extreme tire tread wear. Excessive mounting torque can 
cause studs to break and discs to crack in the stud hole area. 

Tighten M20 nuts for 8-hole ISO disc wheels to 380-447 Nm 
(280-330 lb-ft) and M22 nuts for 10-hole ISO disc wheels to 611-677 Nm 
(450-500 lb-ft) in same sequence.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Tires, Tubeless

 Demounting 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH THESE PROCEDURES CAN RESULT IN FAULTY 
POSITIONING OF THE TIRE AND RIM PARTS AND CAUSE THE ASSEMBLY TO BURST WITH 
EXPLOSIVE FORCE, RESULTING IN SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURY OR DEATH. NEVER MOUNT OR 
USE DAMAGED TIRES OR RIMS. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

 CAUTION: Demounting and mounting tires can be extremely dangerous if proper 
safety precautions are not followed. Before starting this procedure, read all 
safety precautions under Safety at the beginning of this section. 

Before demounting, deflate tire completely deflated by removing valve 
core. Run wire through valve to ensure deflation. Loosen both beads from rim 
by driving the flat end of the tire tool between the tire bead and rim flange. 
Straighten tool to a vertical position and hammer downward on the neck to pry 
tire from rim. Repeat about every 203 mm (8 inches) around flanges until beads 
are free from rim. 

[FIGURE: F8392B.gif]

Place wide side of rim down. Lubricate tire bead and rim. Insert curved 
end of both tools, and step on tire opposite valve to direct first bead into 
the well. Hold one tool in position with foot and pull second tool toward 
center of rim. Progressively work first bead off rim. 

[FIGURE: F8393B.gif]

Stand assembly in vertical position with valve near top. Lubricate 
second bead and rim. Insert straight end of tool between tire bead and the 
back rim flange, hooking the tool over the second flange. Lean tire assembly 
toward tool and provide a rocking or bouncing action to pry the rim out of the 
assembly. Be sure opposite side of second bead is into well.

[FIGURE: F8394B.gif]

 Mounting 

Before starting the mounting process, check the rim manufacturer's load 
and inflation rating and the Tire and Rim Association's recommendation for 
proper rim width. Check rims and components carefully for damage. Discard 
bent, cracked, and out-of-round rims. Inspect the valve stem to ensure that it 
is in good condition, is not cracked or bent irregularly, and is capable of 
holding proper air pressure. The rim must be thoroughly cleaned and painted 
for prevention of corrosion. 

Inspect the inside of the tire to make sure it is clean and free of 
foreign material. 

Place valve stem with rubber washer through valve hole from tire side 
of rim. Screw on valve nut from opposite side, making sure the rubber bushing 
and metal collar or nut are centered and fit snugly in valve hole. Finish 
tightening to 5-6 Nm (44-53 lb-in) torque, except aluminum disc wheels, 
which are tightened to 9-15 Nm (6-11 lb-in) torque. 

 WARNING: USING A FLAMMABLE SUBSTANCE SUCH AS GASOLINE OR ETHYL ETHER TO SEAT THE 
BEADS ON A TUBELESS TIRE IS EXTREMELY DANGEROUS. THIS CAN CAUSE AN EXPLOSION 
THAT WILL DAMAGE THE TIRE OR RIM AND RESULT IN SEVERE INJURY OR DEATH. 

Place rim on floor with wide side down. Lubricate both bead seats 
(flanges) of the rim and both tire beads, applying Rubber Lubricant 
D9AZ-19583-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1B6-A with a brush 
or swab.

[FIGURE: F8401B.gif]

Lay tire on the rim. If there is a light balance mark on the tire, line 
this mark up with the valve stem. Push lower bead over flange and into rim 
well. Using straight end of tool (with stop resting on rim flange), take small 
bites to work remaining section of bead into rim. 

[FIGURE: F8402B.gif]

Start upper bead over rim flange into well by standing on tire. When 
necessary, push section of bead into rim well and anchor with vise-grip pliers 
by pinching pliers onto rim flange (snub side toward tire). Using spoon end of 
tire iron, with stop toward rim, work progressively around bead. Use small 
bites until bead slips over flange onto rim base. If necessary, insert second 
tire iron and lubricate last 203 mm (8 inches) of bead before completing the 
procedure. 

[FIGURE: F8403B.gif]

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Rims and Wheels, Two-Piece

 Demounting 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH THESE PROCEDURES CAN RESULT IN FAULTY 
POSITIONING OF THE TIRE AND RIM PARTS AND CAUSE THE ASSEMBLY TO BURST WITH 
EXPLOSIVE FORCE, RESULTING IN SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURY OR DEATH. NEVER MOUNT OR 
USE DAMAGED TIRES OR RIMS. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY KEEP VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

 CAUTION: Demounting and mounting truck tires can be extremely dangerous if 
proper safety precautions are not followed. Before starting this procedure, 
read all safety precautions under Safety at the beginning of this section. 

Before demounting the tire from the rim, deflate tire completely by 
removing valve core. Run wire through valve to ensure deflation. Place on 
floor, side ring up. Insert hooked end of tools between side ring and sidewall 
of tire and pry bead loose from side ring by downward pressure on rim tools. 
Continue prying progressively around tire until bead is completely free from 
side ring. 

[FIGURE: F8395B.gif]

Insert tapered end of tool into prying notch on side ring and pry side 
ring from its groove in rim by prying progressively around tire until ring is 
free. 

[FIGURE: F8396B.gif]

Turn the assembly over and unseat second tire bead from rim. Lift rim 
from tire. Remove tube and flap, if any, from tire. 

Clean and inspect rim and parts. Replace when necessary.

[FIGURE: F8397B.gif]

 Mounting 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING INFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

Insert tube into the tire and partially inflate to round out tube. 
Apply Rubber Lubricant D9AZ-19583-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M1B6-A to inside and outside surfaces of both beads and to that portion of 
tube that appears between beads. Insert flap and lubricate. Lay rim flat on 
floor with valve slot up. Align valve with rim valve slot and place tire onto 
rim and insert valve through valve slot.

[FIGURE: F8404B.gif]

Place side ring on the rim base so that ring split is opposite valve 
stem. Place leading end of ring into the groove in the rim as shown.

[FIGURE: F8405B.gif]

 WARNING: SIDE RING AND LOCK RINGS CANNOT BE SEATED BY ANY FORCE, INCLUDING 
HAMMERING, STRIKING OR FORCING WHILE ASSEMBLY IS UNDER INFLATION. DEFLATE 
ASSEMBLY ACCORDING TO INSTRUCTIONS AND REPEAT SEATING PROCEDURE. FAILURE TO DO 
SO CAN CAUSE THE COMPONENTS TO SEPARATE EXPLOSIVELY, CAUSING SERIOUS INJURY OR 
DEATH. 

Progressively walk side ring into place. Check to make sure ring is 
fully seated in groove.

[FIGURE: F8406B.gif]

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Rims and Wheels, Three Piece

 Demounting 

 WARNING: FAILURE TO COMPLY WITH THESE PROCEDURES CAN RESULT IN FAULTY 
POSITIONING OF THE TIRE AND RIM PARTS AND CAUSE THE ASSEMBLY TO BURST WITH 
EXPLOSIVE FORCE, RESULTING IN SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURY OR DEATH. NEVER MOUNT OR 
USE DAMAGED TIRES OR RIMS. 

 WARNING: NEVER POSITION BODY IN FRONT OF RIM DURING DEFLATION. ALWAYS KEEP EYES 
AWAY FROM VALVE WHEN DEFLATING TIRES. 

 CAUTION: Demounting and mounting vehicle tires can be extremely dangerous if 
proper safety precautions are not followed. Before starting this procedure, 
read all safety precautions under Safety at the beginning of this section. 

Before demounting the tire from the rim, deflate tire completely by 
removing valve core. Run wire through valve to ensure deflation. Place on 
floor, side ring up. Insert hooked end of tire tools between side ring and 
sidewall of tire. Pry bead loose from side ring by downward pressure on rim 
tools. Continue prying progressively around tire until bead is completely free 
from side ring. 

[FIGURE: F8398B.gif]

With side flange and tire bead pushed down, insert tapered end of tool 
into notch near split in lock ring and push downward to pry lock ring from 
gutter groove of rim base.

[FIGURE: F8399B.gif]

Use hooked end of tool to complete removal of lock ring, progressively 
working around tire. Lift off side flange. Turn the assembly over and unseat 
second tire bead from rim. Lift rim from tire. Remove tube and flap, if any, 
from tire. 

Clean and inspect rim and parts, replace when necessary.

[FIGURE: F8400B.gif]

 Mounting 

Insert tube into the tire and partially inflate to round out tube. 
Apply a rubber lubricant meeting Ford specification ESA-M1B6-A to inside and 
outside surfaces of both beads and to that portion of tube that appears 
between beads. Insert flap and lubricate. Lay rim flat on floor with valve 
slot up. Align valve with rim valve slot. Place tire onto rim and insert valve 
through valve slot. 

[FIGURE: F8407B.gif]

Place side flange on rim base and stand on flange to position it below 
gutter grooves in rim base. 

[FIGURE: F8408B.gif]

 WARNING: SIDE RINGS AND LOCK RINGS CANNOT BE SEATED BY ANY FORCE, INCLUDING 
HAMMERING, STRIKING OR FORCING WHILE ASSEMBLY IS UNDER INFLATION. DEFLATE 
ASSEMBLY ACCORDING TO INSTRUCTIONS AND REPEAT SEATING PROCEDURE. FAILURE TO DO 
SO CAN CAUSE THE COMPONENTS TO SEPARATE EXPLOSIVELY, CAUSING SERIOUS INJURY OR 
DEATH. 

Snap leading end of lock ring into gutter groove of rim base and 
progressively walk lock into place. Check to make sure lock ring is fully 
seated in gutter groove. 

[FIGURE: F8409B.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Wheels 

 Steel 

Wheel stud nuts should be inspected and tightened at 160 km (100 miles) 
of operation. At the first 1600 km (1000 miles) of operation they should again 
be inspected and tightened. Loose wheel stud nuts can cause shimmy and 
vibration. Elongated stud holes in the wheels can also result from the loose 
stud nuts. This includes ISO and BSN type disc wheels.

 NOTE: If different types of brake drums or wheels have been interchanged with 
the original, the wheel stud standout can be incorrect. Make sure the wheel 
studs are of the proper type and length for the components used. 

Keep the wheels and hubs clean. Stones or lumps of mud wedged between 
the wheel and drum will unbalance a wheel and tire.

 Aluminum 

Whenever tire is removed, thoroughly examine the complete wheel. Remove 
all grease and road dirt, and use a wire brush or steel wool to remove the 
rubber from the bead seat. 

 Mounting Area 

Smooth all projections in the mounting area to ensure even pressures 
when tightening nuts. 

 Inner Wheel Nut 

Since the disc thickness of aluminum wheels is at least twice that of 
steel wheels, unique inner wheel nuts are required for aluminum wheels to 
ensure thread engagement for both the wheel stud and the outer wheel nut. 
Never replace inner dual aluminum disc wheels with steel disc wheels unless 
you are sure the inner wheel nut will properly clamp the inner dual disc 
wheel. 

 Flange Area 

Nicks and gouges in the vicinity of the flanges can lead to rim 
fracture. 

Check for damage that will affect the runout of the wheels. Wobble or 
shimmy caused by a damaged wheel will eventually damage the wheel bearings and 
cause uneven tire wear. Inspect the wheel rims for dents that will permit air 
to leak from the tires.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Rims 

Rim clamp nut torque should be checked at 160 km (100 miles) of 
operation and at 1600 km (1000 miles) of operation. Loose clamps can allow 
rims to slip and damage the valves. Maximum lateral and radial runout of the 
following measurements should be maintained. 

Demountable rims

front: 2.28 mm (0.090 inch)

dual rear: 3.17 mm (0.125 inch)

Disc wheels

1.52 mm (0.060 inch)

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tires 

Tires should be checked frequently to ensure the air pressures agree 
with those specified for the tires and vehicle model. Inspect the tire tread 
and remove all stones, nails, glass or other objects that may be wedged in the 
tread. Check for holes or cuts that will permit air leakage from the tire. 
Make the necessary repairs. 

Inspect the tire side walls for cuts, bruises and other damage. If 
internal damage is suspected, demount the tire from the wheel for further 
inspection, service or replacement. 

Check the tire valve for air leaks, and replace the valve if necessary. 
Replace any missing valve caps.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Straightening Wheels, Rims or Components 

 WARNING: NEVER ATTEMPT TO REPAIR A DAMAGED, WORN, OR BROKEN WHEEL, RIM OR 
COMPONENT. ATTEMPTS TO REPAIR CAN LEAD TO SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. REPLACE 
DAMAGED, WORN OR BROKEN COMPONENTS AND DESTROY ALL USED, DAMAGED OR BROKEN 
COMPONENTS. THE ALLOY USED IN THESE COMPONENTS IS HEAT-TREATED AND 
UNCONTROLLED HEATING AFFECTS THE PROPERTIES OF THE MATERIAL. REPAIRED 
RIM/WHEEL COMPONENTS CAN FAIL DURING INFLATION OR LATER VEHICLE USE, RESULTING 
IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL PARTS THAT HAVE BEEN DAMAGED.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Valves 

Aluminum and steel drop-center wheels for tubeless tires come from the

valve nut.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Maintenance and Protection in Corrosive Environments 

Due to aluminum's natural resistance to corrosion, aluminum forged disc 
wheels do not need to be painted for most operating conditions. Washing them 
when washing the rest of the vehicle will be enough to keep wheels looking 
good for many years (but do not use highly alkaline cleaning agents). Certain 
environments, created by some operations, can lead to corrosion. Some of these 
include livestock hauling, salt, chloride compounds used for snow removal, and 
highly alkaline materials. When these conditions are encountered, the 
following practice is recommended. 

Clean frequently with steam or high-pressure water from a hose. Use of 
a mild detergent will speed up the cleaning process. 

When tires are removed, clean and inspect the entire wheel. There are 
various types of coatings that give good results and offer maximum protection.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Rim and Wheel Maintenance

 During Tire Inspection 

 WARNING: EXCESSIVELY CORRODED, CRACKED OR DAMAGED RIMS AND RINGS ARE DANGEROUS. 
COMPLETELY DEFLATE TIRE BEFORE REMOVING FROM VEHICLE. IF WORKING ON DUAL 
WHEELS, DEFLATE BOTH TIRES BEFORE REMOVING FROM VEHICLE. IF TIRE OR TIRES ARE 
NOT DEFLATED BEFORE REMOVAL FROM VEHICLE, AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION CAN OCCUR , 
CAUSING SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: RUST, CORROSION OR ANY FOREIGN MATTER ON THE SIDE RING OR LOCK RING OR 
RIM/WHEEL GROOVE CAN PREVENT THE SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RINGS FROM SEATING 
PROPERLY. THIS CAN CAUSE AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION DURING INFLATION, RESULTING 
IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: DAMAGED WHEEL AND RIM PARTS SUCH AS BENT FLANGES, SIDE RINGS, LOCK 
RINGS AND RIMS OUT OF ROUND OR OUT OF FLAT, SPRUNG SIDE RINGS OR LOCK RING OR 
DEEP TOOL MARKS CAN PREVENT COMPONENTS FROM SEATING PROPERLY. THIS CAN LEAD TO 
AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION, RESULTING IN SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH. DESTROY ALL 
UNSERVICEABLE PARTS. 

Check all metal surfaces thoroughly while making tire inspections, 
including areas between duals and on inboard side of wheel. Watch for the 
following conditions:

excessive rust or corrosion buildup 

cracks in metal 

bent flanges, resulting from road obstructions 

deep rim tool marks on rings or in gutter areas 

loose, missing or damaged nuts or clamps 

bent or stripped studs 

damaged or missing rim drive plates 

mismatched rim parts 

Remove damaged rims or wheels.

Inflate tires to recommended air pressures. Do not exceed these 
pressures. 

 During Tire Changes 

Check all metal surfaces. Watch particularly for the following items: 

Cracks in the rim base, in the back flange and gutter areas. These are 
caused by deep rim tool marks, overloading and overinflating tires or using 
larger than recommended tire sizes. 

Cracks in the wheel disc, between the stud holes or hand holes. These 
are caused by loose wheel nuts, improper installation procedures or the use of 
incorrect sizes or types of attaching parts. 

Cracks through the side ring, spreading laterally through the entire 
section. These are caused by improper mounting and demounting techniques, 
impact with road obstructions, or excessive clamping torques. 

Sprung side ring, resulting from improper mounting procedures. 

Erosion and chipping of the bead seat of the lock ring, resulting from 
excessive corrosion. This can occur with this part as well as others if 
protective measures are not taken. 

 WARNING: USE ONLY THE SAME TYPE AND STYLE WHEELS, RIMS, LOCK RINGS, SIDE RINGS 
AND MOUNTING HARDWARE TO REPLACE ORIGINAL PARTS. FAILURE TO DO SO CAN RESULT 
IN AN ASSEMBLY THAT LOOKS PROPER, BUT DOES NOT FIT TOGETHER CORRECTLY. THIS 
CAN CAUSE WHEEL OR WHEEL FASTENER FAILURE, RESULTING IN PERSONAL INJURY. NEVER 
MIX FOREIGN (NOT MADE IN THE U.S.A.) PARTS WITH DOMESTIC (MADE IN THE U.S.A.) 
PARTS. 

 NOTE: Openings between the ends of the split side rings must not be less than 
2.38 mm (3/32 inch) except where the ring design calls for an abutting 
condition, or more than 7.93 mm (5/16 inch) after the ring is seated during 
operation. Split lock rings used with the continuous side rings or flanges 
must not butt. 

Replace the parts as necessary.

Thoroughly remove rust, dirt and other foreign materials from all 
surfaces. Hand or electric wire brushes, sand blasting or chemical baths can 
be used. Clear gutter of rim base of rust and other materials obstructing 
safe, positive seating of rings. Make sure bead seat areas of rim are free of 
rust and rubber deposits. This is especially important for drop-center 
tubeless rims, because the 15-degree bead seat is the air-sealing element. 

Clean rings with wire brush. Pay particular attention to seating 
surfaces and bead seat areas. Paint rim by brush or spray with a fast-drying 
metal primer. Make sure surfaces are clean and dry prior to painting. Make 
sure bare metal areas on the outside or tire side of rim are covered. This is 
especially important on drop-center tubeless rims because warm and sometimes 
moist air is in constant contact with the metal surface on the tire side of 
the rim.

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Inflation, Tube-Type

 WARNING: STAND CLEAR WHEN USING A SAFETY CAGE OR AN OSHA-APPROVED RESTRAINING 
DEVICE. ALWAYS USE A CLIP-ON AIR CHUCK WITH A REMOTE VALVE AND PRESSURE GAUGE. 
DO NOT REST OR LEAN ANY PART OF THE BODY AGAINST THE DEVICE DURING INFLATION. 
IF AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION OCCURS, THE AIR BLAST OR MOVEMENT OF RESTRAINING 
DEVICE CAN CAUSE INJURY. 

Place tire in a suitable, OSHA-approved safety cage such as Rotunda 
Inflation Chamber 104-00104 or equivalent. Using an extension hose equipped 
with an air gauge and clip-on air chuck, inflate to a maximum of 68.95 kPa (10 
psi). Check to see that beads are properly seated. Completely deflate tire to 
prevent tube from buckling. Reinflate to recommended pressure. 

Again check to make sure of proper engagement of lock ring. If assembly 
is not proper, deflate and correct — never hammer on an inflated or 
partially inflated tire/rim assembly. 

 CAUTION: Never inflate beyond the inflation pressure specified for the tire or 
rim. 

 NOTE: Openings between the ends of the split side ring must not be less than 
2.38 mm (3/32 inch) except where the ring design calls for an abutting 
condition, or more than 7.93 mm (5/16 inch) after ring is seated in during 
operation. Split lock rings used with the endless side rings must not butt. 

If assembly is proper, continue to inflate to recommended inflation 
pressure to seat tire beads. Check to see that beads are seated. Completely 
deflate tire to prevent localized overstretching of tube and flap. Reinflate 
to recommended pressure. 

Before removing the tire/rim assembly from the restraining device, 
always inspect for proper seating of all parts. 

The maximum capacity of a wheel or rim load and air pressure is stamped 
on the weather side of the rim, or in some cases, on the wheel disc adjacent 
to the mounting stud holes. Tire pressures are also listed in the Tire 
Capacity Ratings chart at the end of this section.

Never exceed maximum capacities for load or pressure of either the tube 
or wheel/rim.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tire Inflation, Tubeless

 WARNING: STAND CLEAR WHEN USING A SAFETY CAGE OR AN OSHA-APPROVED RESTRAINING 
DEVICE. ALWAYS USE A CLIP-ON AIR CHUCK WITH A REMOTE VALVE AND PRESSURE GAUGE. 
DO NOT REST OR LEAN ANY PART OF THE BODY AGAINST THE DEVICE DURING INFLATION. 
IF AN EXPLOSIVE SEPARATION OCCURS, THE AIR BLAST OR MOVEMENT OF RESTRAINING 
DEVICE CAN CAUSE INJURY. 

Place the tire in a suitable OSHA-approved safety cage such as Rotunda 
Inflation Chamber 104-00104 or equivalent.

 NOTE: Make sure air supply tank incorporates moisture trap when used with 
drop-center tubeless rims in order to reduce the moisture in contact with the 
metal rim surfaces.

Using an extension hose equipped with an air gauge and clip-on type air 
chuck, inflate tire to a maximum of 10 pounds. Check to see that beads are 
properly seated. Deflate tire completely to prevent tube from buckling. 

Check for proper bead seating by referencing any circumferential design 
element on the tire and the top of the rim flange. Make sure these are equally 
spaced around the tire. 

Inflate tire to 138 kPa (20 psi) and then check tire beads for proper 
seating. Never inflate beyond 276 kPa (40 psi) to seat any tire beads. If the 
beads are not seated at 276 kPa (40 psi), STOP! DEFLATE AND DETERMINE THE 
PROBLEM. 

 CAUTION: Never inflate beyond the inflation pressure specified for the tire or 
rim. 

Inflate tire to recommended pressure. The maximum capacity of a wheel 
or rim load and air pressure is stamped on the weather side of the rim, or on 
the wheel disc adjacent to the mounting stud holes. Tire pressures are also 
listed in the Tire Capacity Ratings chart at the end of this section. Never 
exceed maximum capacities for load or pressure of either the tube or 
wheel/rim. 

Before removing the tire/rim assembly from the restraining device, 
always inspect for proper seating of all parts.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Driveshaft, Rear 

The driveshaft or coupling shaft is composed of the universal joints 
(U-joints), connecting shafts and the attaching yokes. 

All the vehicle U-joint spiders and sliding splines are equipped with 
lubrication fittings. They must be lubricated periodically with 
High-Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease E8TZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C198-A.

The vehicles are equipped with center support bearings that are 
prelubricated and sealed for the life of the bearing. 

 NOTE: All driveline shafts are balanced. If a vehicle is to be undercoated, 
cover all shafts to prevent getting undercoating material on the shafts. 

The basic parts of a U-joint assembly are shown in the illustration. 
All U-joints are of the needle bearing type and, in general, are defined by 
the shape of the bearing cap (plate or bearing strap type). The U-joints are 
held in the yoke by bearing straps or bolts.

Vehicles have the following types of driveshafts: 

Driveshaft — The shaft that accommodates the change in length 
(slip) in the driveline system. The driveshaft is the shaft which is the input 
to the rear axle. 

Coupling Shaft — All shafts which connect the transmission to the 
rear axle, except the driveshaft. Coupling shafts are attached to a support 
plate via a shaft support bearing. 

Interaxle Shaft — The shaft that connects the forward axle of a 
tandem drive unit to the rear axle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Driving Axle, Rear

The axle drive pinion receives its power from the engine through the 
transmission. The pinion gear rotates the differential case through engagement 
with the ring gear, which is bolted to the differential case. Inside the 
differential case, four differential pinion gears are mounted on the 
differential pinion spider (cross). These pinion gears are engaged with the 
side gears to which the axle shafts are splined. Therefore, as the 
differential case turns, it rotates the axle shafts and wheels. When it is 
necessary for one wheel and axle shaft to turn faster than the other, the 
faster turning side gear causes the differential pinions to roll on the slower 
turning side gear to allow differential action between the two axle shafts.

Several rear driving axles are available. A single-speed rear axle, a 
two-speed rear axle, and a tandem axle set with different load capacities are 
the types of rear axles available. For more information, refer to Section 05-02A , Section 05-02B or Section 05-02C .

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Axle and Driveshaft

 Inspection and Verification 

Certain rear axle and driveline concern symptoms are also common to the 
engine, transmission, rear wheel bearing, tires, and other parts of the 
vehicle. For this reason, be sure that the cause of the concern is in the rear 
axle before adjusting, repairing or replacing any of the parts. Refer to 
 Section 00-04 .

 U-Joint Inspection 

Perform a visual inspection of the driveshaft and U-joints. Inspect for 
any buildup of foreign material, such as mud or undercoating, on the 
driveshaft or in the U-joints. Check the shaft for damaged or bent tubing or 
missing balance weights. 

Check the U-joint phasing arrows to make sure that U-joint phasing is 
correct. Refer to Adjustments, U-Joint Phasing in this section. Lubricate the 
U-joints and road test the vehicle to see if the condition improves. Refer to 
Lubrication, U-Joints in this section for procedure. 

If the condition does not improve, perform the following steps:

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Manipulate rear axle shaft universal joint in each direction of 
rotation. If U-joint feels stiff or has a "lumpy," "gritty" feel in any 
direction, replace rear axle shaft universal joint. Refer to Section 05-01 .

 Alignment Inspection, Rear Axle 

Refer to Tandem Drive Axle Alignment under Description and Operation in 
 Section 04-00 .

 Noise Acceptability 

A gear-driven unit, especially a truck drive axle, will produce a 
certain amount of noise. Some noise is acceptable and may be audible at 
certain speeds or under various driving conditions such as a newly paved 
blacktop road. The slight noise is not detrimental to operation of the rear 
axle and must be considered normal.

 Failure Analysis 

The following information explains failure analysis of the drive axle 
carrier — the assembly that contains the gears, bearings and 
differential, and is removable from the housing that supports the vehicle 
load. 

A successful failure analysis requires three steps: 

Identify the type of failure. 

Determine the cause of the failure. 

Take corrective action to prevent a recurrence. 

 Reasons for Axle Carrier Failures 

The basic reasons for failure of drive axle carriers fall into the 
following four general categories: 

Vehicle application or usage 

Vehicle operation 

Maintenance 

Design or manufacturing 

 Vehicle Application or Usage 

To prevent drive axle carrier failure, the operator must understand the 
vehicle's intended usage and application. Axles are available in various 
capacities to meet application requirements. If they are used in operations 
that exceed their design limitations, premature failures and reduced life can 
be expected. 

Drive axles are rated in terms of the carrying capacity of the housing 
— in other words, the weight on its back. This is called the Gross Axle 
Weight Rating (GAWR). 

The carrier gearing is rated in terms of total vehicle weight. For 
straight trucks, buses, etc., it is the Gross Vehicle Weight (GVW) — the 
weight of the vehicle itself plus its payload. For tractor-trailer 
combinations, it is the Gross Combination Weight (GCW) — the combined 
weight of the tractor, trailer and payload. The rating (GVW or GCW) determines 
the amount of work the gearing must do to move the vehicle. 

[FIGURE: E80201A.gif]

Road grades and surfaces also affect the carrier gear rating. 

The road surface determines the road rolling resistance. Rolling 
resistance is the force required to push or move the vehicle over that 
surface. The harder and smoother the surface, the lower the resistance. The 
softer and rougher the surface, the greater the effort required. Soft surfaces 
may increase the needed effort as much as two to ten times.

The same axle carrier is rated at a higher GVW/GCW for operation on 
hard surface, level roads than on soft or mountainous roads.

Care in specifying the axle is the first and most important step toward 
ensuring satisfactory performance and life. 

 Vehicle Operation 

Improper vehicle operation or abuse can also cause axle carrier failure.

Improper operation may cause either an instantaneous failure or damage 
leading to a failure later when the vehicle is operating under normal 
conditions. 

To avoid failure, the vehicle operator must be trained to drive 
properly. The operator must be aware that poor driving now may not result in 
an immediate failure but in one that occurs many miles later. 

 Maintenance 

Failures can result from improper or lack of maintenance, or from poor 
rebuilding practices. 

Recommended maintenance and rebuild practices are established when 
vehicles and components are designed. It is important that maintenance 
personnel and supervisors know and follow these recommendations. 

 Design or Manufacturing 

When an axle is designed, a great deal of engineering effort is devoted 
to ensure that the carrier will provide satisfactory performance and service 
at its rated loads. This is followed by exhaustive testing to verify that the 
design objectives have been met. 

Both the operator and the manufacturer influence the useful service 
life of drive axle carriers. The operator must be sure the vehicle is 
specified, operated and maintained properly. The manufacturer is responsible 
for the design and quality of the equipment, and for clear and specific 
maintenance recommendations. 

Some of the most common axle carrier failures are discussed in the 
following pages. This information will be helpful in identifying them and 
their causes, and in initiating action to prevent their recurrence. 

The following conditions are the most common types of drive axle 
carrier failures: 

spinout 

shock 

fatigue 

lubrication 

 Spinout Failures 

Spinout is defined as excessive differential action. On a single rear 
axle, main differential spinout occurs when one wheel remains stationary while 
the other wheel is spinning. In the case of tandems, spinout occurs in the 
interaxle differential when either one wheel or one axle remains stationary 
while its mate spins. The relatively high speed difference between the mating 
parts generates heat. When the heat becomes excessive, it can cause galling of 
the journals of the cross and the mating differential pinion bores. In extreme 
cases enough heat may be generated to weld the differential pinion to the 
cross and cause a catastrophic failure. 

Spinouts can occur in these driving situations: 

Backing under a trailer 

Starting or traveling on a slippery surface 

[FIGURE: E80211A.gif]

 Backing Under a Trailer 

When a tractor is backing under a trailer, particularly one whose 
landing gear is too low, the extra effort can cause loss of traction between 
the tire and the ground. The resulting spinout is most likely to happen on wet 
and slippery pavement, or on unpaved surfaces. 

 Starting on a Slippery Surface 

Spinout can occur when the vehicle is started on a wet or slippery 
surface. It is especially likely to happen when the vehicle is stuck in mud or 
snow and the driver attempts to free it by stepping on the throttle and 
"burning out." 

 Traveling on a Slippery Surface 

Any moving vehicle encountering a wet or slippery surface can lose 
traction and spin out. This usually happens when driving up a hill because of 
the additional torque required to negotiate the grade. 

In all the situations that result in spinouts, the interaxle 
differential (sometimes called a power divider or third differential) and main 
differential assemblies are subject to damage.

The interaxle differential of a tandem axle is more susceptible to 
spinout damage than the main differential. The interaxle differential turns at 
a higher speed. It revolves at the same speed as the prop shaft, while the 
main differential rotates at prop shaft speed divided by the axle gear ratio. 

 Tandem Axle Interaxle Differential 

[FIGURE: E80222A.gif]

The amount of lubricant available to carry off the generated heat and 
lubricate the mating surfaces is a significant factor. Since the main 
differential is actually submerged in the oil reservoir, it is more tolerant 
of spinout friction and heat than the interaxle differential, which is usually 
supplied with lubricant only by gear splash. 

Spinout can be especially damaging when the rear-rear axle of a tandem 
is spinning and the forward-rear axle wheels are stationary, or nearly so. In 
this situation there is excessive differentiation of the interaxle 
differential. It receives no splash lubrication to carry away the heat, since 
the forward rear wheels are not turning. 

All tandems have optional incorporated oil pumps to provide pressurized 
lubrication to the inside of the interaxle differential. Lubrication of the 
cross and pinions and resistance to spinout damage are thereby improved.

[FIGURE: E80231A.gif]

The main differentials of single or tandem axles are also subject to 
spinout damage, but to a much lesser degree. The differential rotates more 
slowly and is partially submerged in lubricant. Even so, the heat generated by 
severe spinout can cause galling and possible seizure of the pinions to the 
cross. 

 Spinout Failures 

[FIGURE: E8024B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Interaxle Differential Action

2

—

Main Differential Action

In summary, spinout damage is due to excessive action of the main or 
interaxle differential caused by severe wheel slippage. Heat generated by 
rapid spinning of the pinions on the cross can result in galled cross legs, 
and this is the most common characteristic of spinout failures.

Typical failed parts resulting from spinout can be seen in the 
following illustration. A close look at the differential cross shows a badly 
galled leg, two legs broken off and destroyed pinions.

[FIGURE: E80251A.gif]

The differential pinions indicate the severity of the spinout — 
they have seized the cross legs and caused them to fail. This is an example of 
how excessive differentiation generates so much heat that the pinions actually 
weld themselves to the cross legs.

[FIGURE: E80261A.gif]

This is an example of one of the cross legs having been welded to the 
differential case, again due to the extreme heat generated by the spinout.

[FIGURE: E80271A.gif]

The intense heat generated transferred metal to the pinion thrust 
washers by friction welding.

[FIGURE: E80281A.gif]

One of the broken cross legs worked its way out of the differential 
case and punched a hole in the differential cover. The result was a lubricant 
loss which caused the carrier to burn up.

[FIGURE: E80291A.gif]

This cross suffered less damage than the one shown previously. However, 
note the characteristic galling on the leg caused by the heat generated by 
spinning pinion.

[FIGURE: E80301A.gif]

Here is a cross that shows wear on its legs caused by low speed 
differential action not severe enough to result in galling. It was, however, 
enough to indicate above-normal differentiation between the axles. This can be 
caused by tires with too great a difference in rolling radii. Mismatched tires 
cause the gearsets in the two axles to turn at different speeds to maintain 
the same road speed, and so result in above-normal interaxle differential 
action. There must be no more than 19.05 mm (0.75 inch) difference on the 
circumference between the tires on the forward and rear axles of a tandem. 
Another cause of this type of damage is different gear ratios in the forward 
and rear axles. 

[FIGURE: E80311A.gif]

After identifying a spinout failure and its probable cause, corrective 
action must be taken to keep it from reoccurring in the future. Or, better 
still, take action that will keep such failures from happening at all. 

If spinout failure is due to excessive differential action caused by 
wheel slippage, then these failures can be avoided by eliminating, or at least 
minimizing, the slippage-induced differential action. 

This can be done in two ways: 

First, by using the interaxle differential lock with which tandem axles 
are equipped. The purpose of the lock is to keep the interaxle differential 
from performing its normal function. 

When conditions exist that can result in wheel slippage, locking the 
interaxle differential will keep it from differentiating and thus prevent 
spinout damage. The circumstances under which the lock should be used are 
backing under a trailer, starting on or traveling over a slippery surface. 

The second way to avoid differential concerns caused by wheel slippage 
centers on the main differential. Locking the interaxle differential in tandem 
axles will not prevent the m
