PAGE 2861
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-07A: Brake, Power, Hydro-Max Booster

1999 P800, F700, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

End Cap, Filter and Seal 

 NOTE: This procedure can be performed with the Hydro-Max booster on the bench 
or installed in the vehicle. 

A trace of automatic transmission fluid (not brake fluid) on the bottom 
of the Hydro-Max booster at the booster master cylinder joint is considered 
normal. 

For more visible leaks, a service replacement filter and seal assembly 
is available.

 Removal 

Disconnect the negative battery cable. 

Remove master cylinder from Hydro-Max booster. Provide support for 
master cylinder. 

Provide container to catch 3 cups of oil that will spill out of 
Hydro-Max booster. 

Have assistant slowly apply brake pedal and hold or block Hydro-Max 
booster stroked to about 25.4 mm (1 inch). 

 CAUTION: Filter and end cap assembly is spring-loaded and may forcefully exit 
the booster housing. Protect hands with a shop rag or gloves to prevent 
injury. 

Filter and end cap assembly may begin to slide out of the booster 
housing. Hold the filter and end cap assembly and remove snap ring from the 
power piston.

Gently pull the filter and end cap assembly out of the booster housing. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: The following references to "lubricate" parts means lubrication with 
fresh, clean automatic transmission fluid such as Motorcraft MERCON® 
ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent. Do not use brake fluid. 

Dip parts in Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® 
equivalent. 

Replace the filter and end cap assembly if cracked or damaged. 

Install the end cap O-rings (2-5/8-inch diameter) in the respective 
outside diameter grooves in the cap. The thick O-ring is installed in the 
groove nearest to the end cap ribs. Install the thin O-ring in the remaining 
groove. 

 NOTE: Make sure the lip of the lip seal faces the power piston when the 
filter and end cap assembly is installed on the power piston shaft. Incorrect 
installation of the lip seal will allow pressurized fluid to leak from the 
interior of the Hydro-Max booster. 

Lubricate and install the 1-inch outside diameter O-ring and lip seal 
in the appropriate grooves in the inside diameter of the filter and end cap 
assembly.

Install the return spring on the output shaft of the power piston, 
small end first. 

 NOTE: From the booster seal rebuild kit, use a seal guide bullet to protect 
the seal during installation. This seal guide bullet is not available for 
service use. A seal protecting guide can be fabricated from a piece of clean 
white writing paper or mylar sheet in the shape of a cone. Coat the paper with 
automatic transmission fluid prior to assembly of the lip seal. Remove the 
seal guide paper after installing the filter and end cap assembly.

Lubricate the lip seal and O-ring in the inside diameter of the filter 
and end cap assembly and install on the power piston shaft. Depress the filter 
and end cap assembly onto the power piston shaft until the snap groove on the 
piston shaft is exposed. Install the Truarc®-type snap ring on the 
power piston shaft, making sure the snap ring is fully seated in the groove. 
Make sure the lip seal does not catch on the retaining ring groove.

Install the snap ring. 

Slowly release the power piston, making sure filter and end cap 
assembly remains square to the Hydro-Max booster and that the O-ring seals 
seat in the Hydro-Max booster without being pinched or dislocated. 

Dry off any excess oil on outside of filter and end cap assembly. Clean 
input end of master cylinder with a clean, dry cloth. 

Install master cylinder on Hydro-Max booster. Tighten nuts to 34-41 
Nm (25-30 lb-ft). 

Connect the negative battery cable to the battery. 

Fill the brake pump reservoir with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent. Crank engine without starting it to 
fill Hydro-Max booster. Refill the brake pump reservoir and repeat as 
necessary until the Hydro-Max booster is filled. 

Start engine, apply and release brakes. Check for leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Flow Switch 

 NOTE: This procedure can be performed with the Hydro-Max booster on the bench 
or installed in the vehicle. 

 Removal 

Disconnect the negative battery cable. 

Disconnect the electrical lead from the flow switch contact assembly. 

Remove the flow switch contact assembly using a 3/4-inch wrench. 

Remove the flow switch piston and spring.

[FIGURE: DH0198A.gif]

 Installation 

Install the flow switch spring along with the flow switch piston in the 
booster housing. 

Lubricate the O-ring with clean Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX 
or MERCON® equivalent and install on the flow switch contact assembly. 

 CAUTION: Do not overtighten the flow switch contact assembly. Leakage and 
eventual failure will result. 

Install the flow switch contact assembly in the booster housing and 
tighten to 2-5 Nm (18-44 lb-in).

Connect the electric power lead to the flow switch contact assembly. 

Connect the negative battery cable to the battery. 

Start engine, apply and release brakes. Check for leaks.

Electric Motor Relay

 CAUTION: The Hydro-Max booster for the 1-3/4-inch and 2-inch brake master 
cylinder produce different boost pressures. The 2-inch master cylinder 
requires a higher boost pressure output from the engine-driven brake pump. 
Failure to replace the 2-inch master cylinder booster with a like unit will 
result in substantially degraded braking performance. Installation of a 2-inch 
booster on a 1-3/4-inch master cylinder will result in overly sensitive brakes 
and excessive pressure output from the master cylinder. 

The following instructions cover service and replacement of the 
hydraulic seals and power piston if leaks are evident. The seals are serviced 
as a complete seal rebuild kit. The power piston is available as a separate 
item. 

 Disassembly 

Remove the capscrew securing the electric motor relay to the booster 
housing. Remove the electric motor relay. 

 NOTE: Approximately three cups of oil will drain out of the Hydro-Max booster 
when the electric pump and motor assembly is removed. Avoid damaging the 
mating surfaces when removing the electric pump and motor assembly.

Remove the two capscrews that secure the electric pump and motor 
assembly to the Hydro-Max booster and remove the electric pump and motor 
assembly.

Remove and discard the two pump motor face seals (oval O-rings). 

Remove the boot from the brake booster rod. 

 CAUTION: Handle power piston with care as aluminum surface will scratch easily. 

 NOTE: During power piston removal, pull power piston straight out to avoid 
scratching rear of power piston.

Push in on brake booster rod to force power piston assembly from 
Hydro-Max booster. Rotate filter and end cap assembly to ease power piston 
removal.

Remove and discard the two power piston input seals from the rear of 
the booster housing. 

Using a 3/4-inch wrench, remove the flow switch contact assembly. 
Remove and discard the O-ring seal from the flow switch contact assembly. 
Extract the flow switch piston and spring. 

 NOTE: Do not clamp onto power piston.

Clamp brake booster rod in a vise. Push against the filter and end cap 
assembly compressing the return spring 6.35-12.7 mm (0.25-0.50 inch). Remove 
the snap ring, filter and end cap assembly, and the return spring. Discard the 
snap ring. 

Clamp the flats of the input plug in a vise. Do not overtighten the 
vise. To remove the input plug, grasp the large diameter of the power piston 
by hand and rotate counterclockwise. Do not grip power piston surface with any 
tool. If additional leverage is required, a drift may be inserted through the 
flow holes in the output shaft. 

 NOTE: Do not disassemble the valve rod and reaction piston assembly. 

Remove the valve rod and reaction piston assembly, poppet valve and 
valve return spring from the power piston. 

Pry the actuator seal retainer from the input plug and discard. Remove 
actuator pin and discard actuator seal. Remove and discard input plug O-ring. 

Remove and discard the O-ring and lip seal from the inside diameter of 
the filter and end cap assembly. 

Remove and discard both O-rings from the outside diameter of the filter 
and end cap assembly. 

Use a hooked piece of wire to remove the inlet check valve and O-ring 
from the inlet pressure port of the booster housing. Discard these and the 
inlet check ball. 

Gently clamp the input plug flats in the jaws of a vise. Insert a 
5/8-inch diameter rod or another appropriate tool through the hole in the 
brake booster rod. Using the 5/8-inch rod as a lever, carefully pull the brake 
booster rod out of the input plug. It may require up to 1000 pounds of load to 
pull the brake booster rod from the input plug. Remove and discard the grommet 
from the brake booster rod. All rubber debris from the sheared grommet must be 
completely removed from the brake booster rod and input plug. 

 Assembly 

 NOTE: The following references to "lubricate" parts means lubrication with 
fresh, clean automatic transmission fluid such as Motorcraft MERCON® 
ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent. Do not use brake fluid.

Replace the filter and end cap assembly if cracked or damaged. 

Install the filter and end cap assembly along with the two O-rings 
(2-5/8-inch diameter) in the respective outside diameter grooves in the end 
cap. The thick O-ring is installed in the groove nearest to the end cap ribs. 
Install the thin O-ring in the remaining groove. 

 NOTE: Make sure the lip of the lip seal faces the power piston when the 
filter and end cap assembly is installed on the power piston shaft. Incorrect 
installation of the lip seal will allow pressurized fluid to leak from the 
interior of the Hydro-Max booster. 

Lubricate and install the 1-inch outside diameter O-ring and lip seal 
in the appropriate grooves in the inside diameter of the filter and end cap 
assembly.

 CAUTION: If the brake booster rod is not properly installed, the brake booster 
rod could become disconnected from the input plug. The result will be a "no 
brake" condition. 

Remove any traces of the old grommet material from the input plug. 
Install a new grommet on the brake booster rod and insert the brake booster 
rod into the input plug. Make sure the grommet is completely seated in the 
input plug and is capable of retaining the brake booster rod.

Lubricate and install the actuator seal in the recess inside of the 
input plug. Lubricate and insert the actuator pin in the actuator seal. 

Install the actuator seal retainer in the input plug with its flat side 
toward the input plug. 

Install the 1-3/16-inch outside diameter O-ring on the input plug. 

Lubricate and install the two booster housing input seals. The lip of 
both seals should face the inside of the booster housing. 

Lubricate and install the inlet check valve O-ring on the inlet check 
valve.

Install the inlet check ball in the inlet pressure port of the booster 
housing. Lubricate and install the assembled inlet check valve and O-ring in 
the inlet pressure port. Push the inlet check valve until it comes to rest. 

Install the flow switch spring and then the flow switch piston in the 
booster housing. 

 CAUTION: Do not overtighten the flow switch contact assembly. Leaking and 
eventual failure will result. 

Lubricate and install the flow switch contact assembly O-ring. Install 
the flow switch contact assembly in the booster housing and tighten to 2-5 
Nm (18-44 lb-in). 

Install the return spring on the output shaft of the power piston, 
small end first. 

 NOTE: From the booster seal rebuild kit, use a seal guide bullet to protect 
the seal during installation. This seal guide bullet is not available for 
service use. A seal protecting guide can be fabricated from a piece of clean 
white writing paper or mylar sheet in the shape of a cone. Coat the paper with 
automatic transmission fluid prior to assembly of the lip seal. Remove the 
seal guide paper after installing the filter and end cap assembly. 

Lubricate the lip seal and O-ring in the inside diameter of the filter 
and end cap assembly and install on the power piston shaft. Depress the filter 
and end cap assembly onto the power piston shaft until the snap ring groove on 
the power piston shaft is exposed. Install a new Truarc® type snap 
ring on the power piston shaft making sure the snap ring is fully seated in 
its groove. Make sure the lip seal does not catch on the retaining ring groove.

 NOTE: Make sure the correct poppet valve is used for the master cylinder. The 
1-3/4-inch master cylinder uses a Hydro-Max booster with a blue poppet valve. 
The 2-inch master cylinder uses a Hydro-Max booster with a white poppet valve. 

Install the valve return spring in the hollow end of the power piston. 
Install the poppet valve. Make sure the poppet valve is installed with the 
cone-shaped end toward the valve return spring.

Install the valve rod and reaction piston assembly in the hollow end of 
the power piston. Insert the reaction piston end in the power piston first.

Screw the input plug and brake booster rod assembly into the power 
piston and hand-tighten. Gently clamp the power piston in the jaws of a vise 
between the snap ring groove and the end of the power piston. Tighten the 
input plug to 10-17 Nm (7-13 lb-ft). 

Lubricate the exterior of the input plug and power piston input shaft. 
Liberally lubricate the outside diameter of the filter and end cap assembly. 
Insert the power piston in the booster housing with a gentle twisting motion 
to start the input plug on its way through the two lip seals in the small 
diameter of the booster housing bore. Make sure the large O-rings slide into 
the booster housing without being pinched. 

Lubricate and install the two oval face seals in the grooves of the 
electric pump and motor assembly. 

 CAUTION: To prevent incorrect installation, the pump motor must be installed 
with its delivery port closest to the brake booster rod end of the booster 
housing. The position of the inlet and return ports on the booster housing 
should have the same relationship to the delivery and return of electric pump 
and motor assembly. A check ball is visible in the delivery port of the 
electric pump and motor assembly. Do not mar the mating surfaces when 
installing the electric pump and motor assembly on the booster housing. 

Before installing the electric pump and motor assembly on t

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Hydro-Max Booster 

Use clean automatic transmission fluid such as Motorcraft 
MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent for cleaning and 
lubricating parts and seals. 

Inspect the power piston input and output shaft surfaces for scratches 
or nicks. Also, make sure the large piston seal surface is smooth and 
continuous without excessive wear. If any wear or damage is found, replace the 
power piston assembly. Confirm that the check ball is in place and is clean 
and free to move. Confirm that the reaction piston bore and poppet valve seat 
surface inside the power piston are clean and undamaged. 

Inspect housing for grooves, scratches or nicks in the input bore area. 
If any are found, replace the housing. Minor wear, as indicated by a shiny 
appearance on the large bore surface area, is normal. 

Inspect the input plug for wear in the actuator pin hole. Replace the 
input plug if wear is evident.

Section 06-07B: Brake, Power, Hydraulic Pump and Reservoir

1999 P800, F700, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake, Power — Hydraulic Pump and Reservoir

The engine-driven brake pump is a constant-displacement vane type pump 
providing hydraulic pressure for the parking brake system, as well as the 
Hydro-Max booster brake system on units so equipped. The internal parts of the 
brake pump operate submerged in oil.

Retaining Ring

The driveshaft is fitted with a pulley and is belt-driven from the 
crankshaft. The rotor is loosely splined to the driveshaft and secured with a 
retaining ring. Ten vanes are mounted in radial slots in the rotor.

A remote brake pump reservoir is employed and is located just above the 
engine-driven brake pump. A non-vented cap on top of the brake pump reservoir 
is used for checking and adding fluid. A vent tube on the brake pump reservoir 
provides for overflow. The parking brake system and Hydro-Max Booster use 
Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent, and are 
filled through the remote brake pump reservoir of the brake pump.

For a more detailed description of the parking brake system with 
hydraulic brakes, refer to Section 06-05B .

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Service Precautions

 WARNING: THE FOLLOWING PRECAUTIONS SHOULD BE OBSERVED WHENEVER SERVICING OR 
REMOVING COMPONENTS IN THE SYSTEM:

ALWAYS BLOCK VEHICLE WHEELS.

STOP ENGINE WHEN WORKING UNDER THE VEHICLE.

RELEASE PRESSURE IN SYSTEM BEFORE SERVICING. TO RELEASE PRESSURE WITH 
THE ENGINE OFF, CYCLE THE PARKING BRAKE HAND CONTROL VALVE TO THE RELEASED AND 
APPLIED POSITION TWO TIMES.

NEVER CONNECT OR DISCONNECT A HOSE OR LINE CONTAINING PRESSURE; IT MAY 
WHIP.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Steering Pump Pulley Remover

T69L-10300-B

 Removal 

Chock vehicle wheels to prevent vehicle movement. 

Release system pressure. To release system pressure with the engine 
off, cycle the parking brake control valve to the released and applied 
positions two times. 

Remove fluid from brake pump reservoir with a suction tool. 

Disconnect the pressure, return and reservoir lines from the brake pump 
and plug them to prevent loss of fluid or entrance of dirt into the system. 
Disconnect and plug the respective lines from the brake pump reservoir. 

Loosen the belt tension adjusting bolt all the way. Remove belt from 
the brake pump pulley. 

Remove reservoir-to-brake pump reservoir bracket bolts and remove brake 
pump reservoir. 

Remove brake pump pulley from brake pump with Steering Pump Pulley 
Remover T69L-10300-B. 

Remove four bolts from brake pump and remove brake pump and reservoir 
bracket from brake pump bracket. 

 Installation 

Position brake pump and reservoir bracket at brake pump bracket. 
Install and tighten attaching bolts. 

Install brake pump pulley onto brake pump until pulley hub is flush 
with pump driveshaft end within ±0.25 mm (0.010 inch). 

Assemble brake pump reservoir to brake pump reservoir bracket and 
secure with attaching bolts. 

Install the drive belt. Adjust the idler pulley or brake pump tensioner 
until the belt has the specified tension. Refer to Section 03A-05 or Section 03C-05 of the Powertrain, Drivetrain Manual. 

Connect the pressure, return and reservoir lines to the brake pump. 
Connect the respective lines to the brake pump reservoir. 

Fill the brake pump reservoir with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent. Bleed the air from the system as 
described in Section 06-05B .

Check system operation, and check system for leaks. 

Remove chocks from wheels.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Rotor Shaft Seal 

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Sector Shaft Seal Replacer

T65P-3D642-A

 Removal 

Remove the brake pump. Refer to Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven in 
the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

Drain as much fluid as possible from the brake pump.

 NOTE: When removing the rotor shaft seal do not pry against the driveshaft or 
housing bore.

Insert a sharp tool between the rotor shaft seal and the brake pump 
housing. Pry out the rotor shaft seal.

 Installation 

Remove the brake pump and bracket from the vise and lay it flat on the 
workbench.

Place a new rotor shaft seal on the driveshaft with the metal backing 
facing the brake pump pulley end of the driveshaft as shown.

[FIGURE: G5040E.gif]

Install the rotor shaft seal using Sector Shaft Seal Replacer 
T65P-3D642-A. Tap the tool lightly with a small hammer until the seal is 
properly seated in the driveshaft hub.

Install the brake pump. Refer to Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven in 
the Removal and Installation portion of this section.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Brake Pump, Engine-Driven

 CAUTION: Take the following precautions when servicing the brake pump: 

 Use a clean workbench and tools. 

 Clean the exterior of the unit with solvent. Drain as 
much fluid as possible. 

 If only the rotor shaft seal is being replaced, refer to 
Rotor Shaft Seal in the Removal and Installation portion of this section. 

 Do not use solvent on seals. 

 Disassembly 

Remove the brake pump bracket and brake pump pulley from the brake 
pump. Refer to Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven in the Removal and 
Installation portion of this section. 

 CAUTION: Do not clamp the brake pump too tightly or bearing damage may result. 

Clamp the front hub of the brake pump in a vise so the extending 
portion of the driveshaft points down.

Pressure Plate Spring

3D589

End Plate

20

384979-S

Retaining Ring

Remove the housing by removing the two studs and the control valve 
retainer.

Rotate the end plate retaining ring so that one end of the ring is over 
the hole in the housing. Insert a small punch in the 3.18 mm (1/8 inch) 
diameter hole in the housing side opposite the flow control valve hole. 
Compress the retaining ring with the punch and remove the ring by twisting a 
screwdriver under the ring.

[FIGURE: G50411A.gif]

Remove the end plate. The end plate is spring-loaded and will generally 
sit above the housing level for easy removal. If the plate sticks, rock it 
back and forth lightly to free it. 

Remove the pressure plate spring. 

Remove the brake pump from the vise and turn it over allowing the flow 
control valve and its spring to fall out. Do not disassemble the flow control 
valve. Service it as a unit. 

With the end plate O-ring removed, tap very lightly on the end of the 
driveshaft until the pressure plate falls free. 

Remove the cam ring, vanes and rotor.

[FIGURE: G5042B.gif]

Remove the cam ring and vanes from the rotor. 

Remove the retaining ring by clamping the driveshaft in a soft-jawed 
vise and prying the ring off the driveshaft with long-nose pliers or a 
screwdriver. Do not damage the driveshaft with the vise jaws. Discard the 
retaining ring. 

Remove the thrust plate from the driveshaft. 

Remove both dowel pins from the housing. 

Remove the pressure plate and end plate O-ring seals from the housing 
bore and discard them. 

Remove the rotor shaft seal only if it is worn or damaged. Removal will 
destroy the rotor shaft seal. 

 Assembly 

Clean all metal parts with solvent. 

If the rotor shaft seal was removed, install a new rotor shaft seal. 
Refer to Rotor Shaft Seal in the Removal and Installation portion of this 
section. 

Lubricate a new pressure plate O-ring seal with Motorcraft 
MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent, and install it in 
the third groove from the rear of the housing. 

Clamp the end hub of the housing in a vise so the extending portion of 
the driveshaft points down. Do not clamp the bearing too tightly or damage may 
occur. 

Insert both dowel pins. 

Install the thrust plate on the driveshaft with the ports toward the 
splined end of the driveshaft. 

Install the rotor on the driveshaft with the counterbored end toward 
the thrust plate. 

Clamp the driveshaft in a soft-jawed vise, using care not to damage the 
driveshaft. Install a new retaining ring on the splined end of the driveshaft 
by prying the ring open and sliding it down over the driveshaft until it seats 
in the ring groove. Use the round wire ring from the retaining ring service kit.

Insert the driveshaft in the housing. Lubricate the driveshaft with 
Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent and make 
sure the thrust plate slides properly on the dowel pins. 

Install the cam ring on the dowel pins with the rotation arrow toward 
the rear of the housing.

[FIGURE: G50431A.gif]

Install the vanes in the rotor slots with the rounded edge of the vanes 
outward. Be sure the vanes slide freely.

[FIGURE: G50441A.gif]

Lubricate the pressure plate with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent to prevent damage to the pressure plate 
O-ring seal. 

Install the pressure plate on the dowel pins with the circular spring 
depression toward the rear of the housing. The narrow slots in the plate 
should engage the dowel pins. To seat pressure plate, press it about 1.588 mm 
(1/16 inch) over the O-ring.

[FIGURE: G50451A.gif]

Lubricate a new end plate O-ring with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent and install it in the second groove 
from the rear of the housing. 

Install the pressure plate spring in the groove in the pressure plate. 

Lubricate the end plate with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or 
MERCON® equivalent to prevent damage to the O-ring, and press it into 
the housing with an arbor press. Depress the end plate only far enough to 
allow installation of the retaining ring in its groove.

[FIGURE: G50461A.gif]

Install the end plate retaining ring. Release the arbor press. 

Place the flow control valve spring in its hole and insert the flow 
control valve with the screened end toward the front of the housing. 

Install the housing by installing the two studs and the control valve 
retainer.

Install the brake pump bracket and brake pump pulley onto the brake 
pump. Refer to Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven in the Removal and 
Installation portion of this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Belt, Engine-Driven Pump

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Belt Tension Gauge

T63L-8620-A

Loosen the belt idler pulley or brake pump tensioner adjustment bolts. 

Adjust the idler pulley or brake pump tensioner until the belt has the 
specified tension. Measure the tension with Belt Tension Gauge T63L-8620-A or 
Rotunda Belt Tension Gauge 014-R1056 or equivalent. For belt tension 
specifications, refer to Section 03A-05 or Section 03C-05 of the Powertrain, 
Drivetrain Manual.

[FIGURE: Q4239C.gif]

With tension still applied, tighten the adjustment bolts.

ADJUSTMENTS

Fluid Level Check 

 NOTE: To minimize parking brake system release and actuation time during 
continuous cold weather operation (constant operation during -18°C 
[0°F]), fill the parking brake system with Esso UNIVIS-N-22 hydraulic 
oil or equivalent. Do not mix with other fluids.

Check the fluid level in the engine-driven brake pump reservoir with 
the parking brakes applied. If required, fill the brake pump reservoir to the 
specified level with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or 
MERCON® equivalent.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Brake Pump/Reservoir, Engine-Driven

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Steering Pump Pulley Remover

T69L-10300-B

 Removal 

Chock vehicle wheels to prevent vehicle movement. 

Release system pressure. To release system pressure with the engine 
off, cycle the parking brake control valve to the released and applied 
positions two times. 

Remove fluid from brake pump reservoir with a suction tool. 

Disconnect the pressure, return and reservoir lines from the brake pump 
and plug them to prevent loss of fluid or entrance of dirt into the system. 
Disconnect and plug the respective lines from the brake pump reservoir. 

Loosen the belt tension adjusting bolt all the way. Remove belt from 
the brake pump pulley. 

Remove reservoir-to-brake pump reservoir bracket bolts and remove brake 
pump reservoir. 

Remove brake pump pulley from brake pump with Steering Pump Pulley 
Remover T69L-10300-B. 

 NOTE: Reservoir bracket removal required on fixed hood vehicles only.

Remove four bolts from brake pump and remove brake pump and reservoir 
bracket from brake pump bracket. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: Reservoir bracket installation required on fixed hood vehicles only.

Position brake pump and reservoir bracket at brake pump bracket. 
Install and tighten attaching bolts. 

Install brake pump pulley onto brake pump until pulley hub is flush 
with pump driveshaft end within ±0.25 mm (0.010 inch). 

Assemble brake pump reservoir to brake pump reservoir bracket and 
secure with attaching bolts. 

Install the drive belt. Adjust the idler pulley or brake pump tensioner 
until the belt has the specified tension. Refer to Section 03A-05 or Section 03C-05 of the Powertrain, Drivetrain Manual. 

Connect the pressure, return and reservoir lines to the brake pump. 
Connect the respective lines to the brake pump reservoir. 

Fill the brake pump reservoir with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent. Bleed the air from the system as 
described in Section 06-05B of the Body, Chassis Manual.

Check system operation, and check system for leaks. 

Remove chocks from wheels.

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Air 

The air brake system consists of three sub-systems; the air supply 
system (refer to Section 06-08A ), the air delivery system (refer to Section 06-08B ) and the parking/emergency system (refer to Section 06-05A ). The 
components that make up the air brake systems of F- and B-Series vehicles may 
differ, but all systems operate in basically the same manner. 

A schematic of the air brake system for the vehicle is illustrated in 
the Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

================================================================================
PAGE 2882
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System Balance 

The air brake system must provide balanced braking at all wheels and 
axles of the unit. This will provide for optimum brake system performance and 
life. The braking effort produced at each wheel and axle of the unit must be 
capable of doing its share of the work in controlling the speed of the unit or 
units. 

Brake system balance can be adversely affected by worn, damaged or 
inoperative components; contaminants in the air supply and delivery system; 
poor system maintenance; or the use of incorrect replacement parts. 
Maintenance and service of the air brake systems on all trucks should be 
performed with these considerations kept clearly in mind. When performance 
difficulties are encountered in the air brake system, the information 
contained in this section can be used to identify and correct the source of 
the concern.

================================================================================
PAGE 2883
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Supply System 

The air supply system is the source of air pressure for the air brake 
system. It consists of the compressor, reservoirs (supply, primary and 
secondary), governor, low pressure indicator, dash gauge, safety valve, drain 
cock or automatic moisture ejector valve, single check valves, double check 
valves and the tank valve. 

The compressor is driven by the engine and controlled by a governor. 
When the reservoir air pressure reaches 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi), the 
governor cuts out the compressor. When reservoir pressure drops to 82-179 kPa 
(12-26 psi) below the cutout pressure, the governor allows the compressor to 
cut in again. When reservoir air pressure drops below 414 kPa (60 psi), the 
low pressure indicator valve closes an electrical circuit to the warning 
buzzer and the warning lamp. If the air reservoir pressure exceeds 1034 kPa 
(150 psi), the safety valve will release the pressure. The single check valves 
between the supply reservoir and the primary and secondary service reservoirs 
keep the air from flowing from the protected service air reservoir should an 
air loss occur in the other service system, supply reservoir, or air 
compressor plumbing. 

The air reservoir is equipped with a manual drain valve or an automatic 
moisture ejector valve. This allows for the removal of moisture from the air 
brake system. 

The tank valve in the supply reservoir can be used to fill the air 
system if the engine is inoperative and the vehicle must be moved.

================================================================================
PAGE 2884
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Delivery System 

The air delivery system delivers the air brake pressure from the air 
supply system service reservoirs to the brake chambers. It controls the amount 
of air pressure that is delivered to the brake chambers and thus controls the 
amount of braking during a stop. It consists of the foot control valve, the 
relay valve, the quick release valve and the brake chamber. 

The foot control valve meters the air pressure delivery, to the front 
brake chamber and the rear relay valve(s), relative to the amount the foot 
pedal is depressed. The rear relay valve(s) is constantly supplied with full 
system pressure from the primary service reservoir. As the foot control valve 
meters the pressure to the relay valve, the relay valve controls and delivers 
air pressure to the rear brake chambers. 

The relay valve's main function is to speed up the delivery and release 
of air pressure to the rear chambers. This is attained by having full system 
pressure available at the rear of the vehicle and controlling the delivery and 
release of this air pressure near the chambers. The brake chamber functions to 
convert air pressure into a mechanical force to apply the brakes.

================================================================================
PAGE 2885
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08: Brake System, Air, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake System, Parking/Emergency 

The parking brake system is composed of a parking brake control valve, 
an inverting relay valve, quick release valves and spring brake chambers. The 
spring brake chambers use a powerful spring to mechanically apply the brakes 
when air pressure is not available (provided the brakes are properly adjusted).

Air pressure compresses the spring in the spring brake chamber when the 
parking brake control valve is in the release position. The air pressure is 
delivered to the spring chamber by an inverting relay valve which is 
controlled by an air pressure signal from the control valve on the instrument 
panel. The inverting relay valve also functions to prevent the application of 
the spring brakes and service brakes at the same time, thus preventing brake 
system damage. 

Emergency brake systems on trucks are different than brake systems on 
tractors. The rear (primary) brake system is used when there is an air 
pressure loss in the front brake system. An air pressure loss in the rear 
brake system lets the front brakes continue to function but additional braking 
power is provided by the modulation of the rear spring brakes application. 
This is controlled by the R-7 inverting or SR-1 inversion valve with an R-8 
relay valve. 

The stopping capabilities of the brakes are reduced during a brake 
concern since not all of the brakes are functional. Upon service of the 
component, the system should return to normal operation. 

The MGM and Maxi II service and spring (parking) brake assemblies are 
available on all vehicles. The brake chamber assembly consists of two separate 
air chambers, each with its own diaphragm and push rod. The service brake 
chamber applies the brake by air pressure and releases it by spring pressure 
when air is exhausted. The parking or emergency brake is applied by spring 
pressure and is released by air pressure.

 Inspection and Verification 

 Brake Squeal 

Occasional brake squeal can be caused by environmental conditions such 
as cold, heat, wet, snow, salt and mud. This occasional squeal is not a 
functional concern and does not indicate any loss in brake effectiveness. 

 Fitting and Tube Seat Leak Inspection 

Since most air leaks occur at the fittings and connections, these areas 
should be checked before any other part is replaced. Refer to the Symptom 
Chart in this section. 

For diagnostic and testing procedures for individual components, refer 
to the Diagnosis and Testing portion of each air brake section.

 Air Brake System Cautions 

 CAUTION: Before attempting to work on air brake system, certain precautions 
should be observed since the compression and storage of air may be compared to 
the energy in a coiled spring and, when released, may present a hazard if not 
properly recognized. The wheels of the vehicle should always be blocked by 
some means other than the air brake system so that depletion of air will not 
permit the vehicle to roll. 

In draining the system, do not look into the air jets or direct them 
toward a person as dirt or sludge particles may be carried in the air stream.

Hoses that contain air pressure should not be disconnected under 
pressure since they will whip as air escapes from the line.

Follow the manufacturers' recommended procedures in working on any air 
device so as to avoid injury or damage from parts which, when released, are 
subject to mechanical (spring) or pneumatic propulsion.

As system pressure is drained and the emergency brakes applied, hands 
should be away from brake chamber push rods and spring actuators which will 
apply automatically with the loss of pressure. This also applies when checking 
service brake system. 

Reservoirs that are closest to the sources of compressed air 
(compressors or auxiliary sources) should contain a safety valve in known 
working order and sufficient capacity to limit the reservoir pressure to a 
safe maximum level.

Old, used reservoirs should not be used as replacements.

The safety valves should not reset higher than specified by the 
reservoir manufacturer, vehicle manufacturer, or code to which the reservoir 
had been manufactured.

Various actuators contain large internal steel springs that require 
special disassembly procedures. Note and be guided by the warning tags on such 
units.

 Engine-Driven Pump Belt Check 

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

 Symptom Chart — Air Brake System 

 AIR BRAKE SYSTEM 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Braking Is Uneven. Vehicle Pulls to One Side

 NOTE: Brake-pull evaluation should be conducted on a smooth level surface.

Low tire pressure or worn tires.

INFLATE tires to recommended pressure. REPLACE worn tires. REFER to 
 Section 04-04 .

Improperly adjusted brakes.

ADJUST brakes to recommended specifications. Make certain that the 
chamber push rod clevis position is to specifications. REFER to Section 06-08C .

Worn or damaged brake chambers.

APPLY brakes and CHECK brake chamber operation. CHECK brake chamber for 
leaking diaphragm, bent push rod or other damage. SERVICE brake chamber 
components as required. REFER to Section 06-08C , Section 06-08D or Section 06-08E .

Improper push rod-to-slack adjuster connection.

CHECK connection from push rod to slack adjuster. Connections must be 
the same on both sides of the axle. Clevis should be free moving. Length from 
clevis to center of brake camshaft must be the same. Do not use heat to free 
camshaft. The camshaft contains nylon bushings that can be damaged.

Worn or damaged brake camshaft.

CHECK for frozen or restricted brake camshaft. LUBRICATE camshaft and 
WORK free or DISASSEMBLE and SERVICE. (Do not use heat to free camshaft. The 
camshaft contains nylon bushings that can be damaged.) REFER to Section 06-08C .

Worn or damaged brake components.

CHECK for greasy drum linings or damaged hoses, rollers, brake shoes 
and return springs. REMOVE grease from linings if possible. If linings are 
saturated REPLACE linings. SERVICE worn or damaged components as required. 
REFER to Section 06-08C .

Worn or damaged air lines.

CHECK for equal air pressure delivery to the chambers on both sides of 
the axle. SERVICE leaking, collapsed or damaged air lines. CHECK for internal 
restrictions in the air lines, fittings or valve ports. REFER to Section 06-08A .

Worn or damaged bearing or overtightened bearing nut.

RAISE each wheel with brakes released. CHECK for free wheel rotation. 
If wheels do not rotate freely, CHECK for worn or damaged bearings. CHECK 
bearing nut torque. TIGHTEN to specifications. REFER to Section 04-01 or 
 Section 04-02B .

Excessive Water in the Brake System

Leaking compressor cooling system.

DRAIN reservoirs to 0 kPa (0 psi) daily. CLEAN, SERVICE or REPLACE the 
drain cocks as required. REFER to Section 06-08A .

CHECK compressor air inlet for signs of excessive wear. CORRECT as 
required.

CHECK compressor cooling system for leaking. SERVICE or REPLACE the 
compressor as required. REFER to Section 06-08A .

Air Pressure Above Normal at Gauge

Inaccurate air gauge.

REPLACE air gauge. (Air gauge accuracy should be 0-96 kPa ± 48 
kPa [0-14 psi ± 7 psi] from test gauge.) REFER to Section 13-10 .

Plugged or damaged air line from tank to governor.

SERVICE or REPLACE plugged or damaged air line. REFER to Section 06-08A .

Worn or damaged compressor governor.

SERVICE or REPLACE governor as required. REFER to Section 06-08A .

Worn or damaged compressor.

CHECK compressor unloader. SERVICE or REPLACE compressor as required. 
REFER to Section 06-08A .

Front Brakes Drag and Are Slow to Release

Worn or damaged brake chambers.

CHECK to see if brake chambers are releasing properly. CHECK linkage 
for binding. LUBRICATE, SERVICE or REPLACE as required. REFER to Section 06-08D and Section 06-08E . CHECK brake ch

ADJUSTMENTS

Brake Hose

Replace a flexible brake hose if it shows signs of softening, cracking 
or other damage with hose of the same type, size, shape and length. Use only 
SAE J1401 rayon braid, low expansion brake hose or equivalent. 

When installing a new brake hose, position the hose to avoid contact 
with other vehicle parts.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Supply System 

The air supply system is the source of air pressure for the brake 
system. It consists of the compressor, reservoirs, governor, low air pressure 
switch, dash-mounted dual air pressure gauge, safety valve, drain cock or 
automatic moisture ejector valve, air dryer (optional), tank valve, single 
check valve and double check valve. 

The compressor is engine-driven and controlled by a governor. When 
reservoir air pressure reaches 931 kPa (135 psi), the governor cuts out the 
compressor. When reservoir pressure drops to 724 kPa (105 psi) the governor 
allows the compressor to cut in again. When reservoir air pressure drops below 
414 kPa (60 psi), the low air pressure switch closes an electrical circuit to 
the warning buzzer and the warning light. If the air reservoir pressure 
exceeds 1034 kPa (150 psi), the safety valve will release the pressure. 

The air reservoir is equipped with a manual drain cock or an automatic 
moisture ejector valve, which can be drained for the removal of moisture from 
the air brake system.

================================================================================
PAGE 2891
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Compressor 

The function of the air compressor is to build up and maintain the 
required amount of air pressure in the air reservoirs of the supply system. 
The rated capacity of a compressor is based on the piston displacement in 
cubic feet per minute when operating at 1250 rpm.

[FIGURE: H5465D.gif]

Compressors are of the one- or two-cylinder, single-stage, 
reciprocating piston design. The compressor is constructed from two major 
assemblies, the head and the crankcase. The head houses the discharge valving 
and is installed on the upper portion of the crankcase. The crankcase is a 
one-piece casting combining the cylinder block and the crankcase. The upper 
portion of the casting houses the cylinder bores and inlet valving; and the 
lower portion, the crankshaft and main bearings. Various mounting and drive 
configurations, required by vehicle engine designs, are obtained by bolting 
different mounting flanges, end covers, and base adapters to the compressor 
crankcase.

 Compressor/Governor System, Typical 

[FIGURE: H1341G.gif]

Piston (Compression)
(Part of 2875)

Since all compressors are connected to the engine's pressurized oil 
system, a continuous flow of oil is provided to the compressor, which is 
eventually returned to the engine. Oil is fed into the compressor in various 
ways. Two examples are through the rear end cover, the drive end of the 
crankshaft or through the front flange adapter. An oil passage in the 
crankshaft conducts pressurized oil to the precision sleeve main bearings and 
to the connecting rod bearings. Splash lubrication of the cylinder bores, 
connecting rod wrist pin bushings, and the ball type main bearings, on some 
models, is obtained as oil is forced out around the crankshaft journals by 
engine oil pressure. 

Air flowing through the engine compartment from the action of the 
engine's fan and the movement of the vehicle assists in cooling the crankcase. 
Coolant flowing from the engine's cooling system enters the head, goes through 
the head's water jacket, and then returns to the engine. Proper cooling is 
important in maintaining discharge air temperatures below the maximum 
204°C (400°F) recommended. 

The compressor operates as follows: 

The unloader piston is in the retracted (non-pressurized) position. 

As the compressor piston is retracted (moved downward), air is drawn 
into the cylinder through the inlet valve which operates like a check valve. 

When the piston moves upward, the air is compressed. The air inlet 
valve is seated thus keeping the air from leaving the cylinder through the 
inlet valve. As the air is compressed further, it overcomes the spring force 
of the discharge valve and allows the compressed air into the discharge line 
and to the reservoir. 

As the compressor piston moves downward, the discharge valve is 
returned to its seat and air is drawn into the cylinder by way of the inlet 
valve and the cycle begins again. 

When air pressure in the air reservoir reaches the governor cutout 
setting of 931 kPa (135 psi) maximum, the governor opens and allows air to the 
compressor unloader piston. The unloader piston is lifted, thus moving the air 
inlet valve off its seat. With the inlet valves unseated, air is pumped back 
and forth between the cylinder or cylinders and the inlet valve cavity. As 
reservoir air pressure is used up, the governor pressure drops to its cut-in 
pressure setting (724 kPa [105 psi] minimum), the governor closes and 
exhausts the air below the unloader piston. The spring then moves the unloader 
piston downward, the inlet valve is seated, and the compressor cycle is 
restarted.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Governor 

The governor operates in conjunction with the compressor unloading 
mechanism to keep air pressure in the supply system within specifications. The 
compressor runs continually with the engine but the compression of air is 
controlled by the governor which starts or stops compression when the maximum 
or minimum governor settings are reached. The governor is non-adjustable.

Air pressure from the reservoir to the reservoir port of the governor 
forces the governor piston to overcome the resistance of the pressure setting 
spring. (The governor piston and the inlet and exhaust valve move up as 
reservoir air pressure reaches the governor cutout setting.) The exhaust stem 
seats on the inlet and exhaust valve and opens the inlet passage. Reservoir 
air pressure then flows by the open inlet valve, through the passage in the 
governor piston and out the unloader port to the compressor unloading 
mechanism. 

As air pressure in the reservoir drops to the governor cut-in setting, 
the force exerted by air pressure on the governor piston is reduced and the 
pressure spring will move it downward. The inlet valve will close and the 
exhaust valve will open. With the exhaust valve open, air in the unloader line 
will escape through the exhaust stem and out the exhaust port. 

The governors are mounted directly to the compressor, allowing direct 
connection between the compressor unloader and the governor unloader port.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Reservoir 

The reservoir is a storage tank; its function is to provide a volume of 
compressed air for braking which will be adequate in relation to the volume 
used by the brake air chambers and auxiliary devices. It also provides a 
location in the system where the air, heated by compression, may be cooled and 
the water vapor condensed. 

 Single Reservoir, Typical 

[FIGURE: H41651A.gif]

The primary reservoir is the air source for the rear brakes, and the 
front brakes are supplied by the secondary reservoir. The combined volumes of 
all service reservoirs and supply reservoirs are 12 times, or more than the 
combined volumes of all service brake air chambers at maximum travel of the 
pistons or diaphragms. The reservoirs are made from steel sheet, with stamped 
heads and rolled shells. The seams are electrically welded, and each reservoir 
is internally coated for corrosion resistance. 

All reservoirs should be drained to 0 kPa (0 psi) daily. If an 
automatic drain device is used, it should be checked periodically for proper 
functioning. If an air dryer or aftercooler is used, the reservoirs should be 
manually drained periodically to verify the proper function of the drying 
device. Reservoirs that have collected a considerable oily emulsion can be 
drained by opening a drain cock and allowing them to drain until all drainage 
stops. 

Minor service to the reservoir consists of examining the reservoir 
mounting, and the inspection of the outside for corrosion or damage. The 
outside should be kept painted to reduce the possibility of corrosion causing 
a failure. 

Service involving welding should never be performed on reservoirs. If a 
reservoir has been damaged so as to be unfit for use, it should be replaced 
with a new one.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety Valve 

The safety valve protects the air brake system against excessive air 
pressure buildup. The safety valve consists of a spring-loaded ball valve 
subjected to reservoir pressure, which will permit air to exhaust from the 
reservoir to the atmosphere if the reservoir pressure rises above the safety 
valve pressure setting. The safety valve pressure setting is determined by the 
force of the spring.

[FIGURE: H3339C.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

—

Exhaust Port (Part of 2A550)

Spring Cage (Part of 2A550)

 NOTE: It is recommended that the safety valve be installed in a vertical 
position. If it must be mounted horizontally, the exhaust port must point 
downward and the safety valve stem must face the rear of the vehicle. 

The safety valve should be installed in the same reservoir that the 
compressor discharge line is connected to. It can be installed in a convenient 
location in a top port of the reservoir.

A safety valve setting of 985-1082 kPa (143-157 psi) is used, and is 
not adjustable. Should system pressure rise to approximately 1034 kPa (150 
psi), air pressure can force the ball valve off its seat, and allow reservoir 
pressure to vent to the atmosphere through the exhaust port in the spring 
cage. 

When reservoir pressure decreases sufficiently, the spring force will 
seat the ball valve, sealing off reservoir pressure. This occurs at 930 kPa 
(135 psi) for the 1034 kPa (150 psi) setting. It is important to note that the 
desired pressure setting of the safety valve is determined by the governor 
cutout pressure. The opening and closing pressures of the safety valve must 
always be in excess of the governor cutout pressure setting. The pressure 
setting is stamped on a wrench flat of the safety valve. 

Normally, the safety valve remains inoperative and only functions when 
reservoir pressure rises above the setting of the valve. Constant popping off 
or exhausting of the safety valve can be caused by a worn or damaged safety 
valve, governor, compressor unloader mechanism, or a combination of any of the 
preceding items.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drain Cock 

A drain cock is provided as standard on air reservoirs that do not have 
the automatic moisture ejector valves. Drain cocks have a brass body fitting 
with a tapered brass key. The drain cock is open when the handle is parallel 
to the body and closed when the handle is at right angles to the body. Drain 
cocks are installed in the bottom of each reservoir in the air brake system to 
provide a convenient means of draining the condensation and contamination that 
normally collects in the reservoirs.

[FIGURE: H41661A.gif]

Air reservoirs should be drained daily to 0 kPa (0 psi). If they are 
not drained to 0 kPa (0 psi) the moisture and contamination may not be drained 
fully. High pressure air will blow through the water keeping the moisture in 
the reservoir while air is being released. Always open a drain cock by hand. 
To prevent damage and leakage, never strike the handle with a hammer or any 
other instrument.

The Bendix DV-2 Automatic Moisture Ejector Valve expels moisture and

The automatic moisture ejector valve may also be drained manually by 
depressing the stem wire located in the exhaust port.

The automatic moisture ejector valve has a die cast aluminum body and 
cover, and is mounted in the bottom or lower end port of the air system 
reservoir.

With no air pressure in the system, the inlet and exhaust valves are 
closed. Upon charging the air system, a slight pressure opens the inlet valve 
which permits air and contaminants to collect in the sump. The inlet valve 
remains open when pressure is increasing in the system until (governor) cutout 
pressure is reached. The spring action of the valve guide in the sump cavity 
closes the inlet valve. The inlet valve and the exhaust valve are now closed.

When reservoir pressure drops approximately 13 kPa (2 psi), air 
pressure in the sump cavity opens the exhaust valve and allows moisture and 
contaminants to be ejected from the sump cavity until pressure in the sump 
cavity drops sufficiently to close the exhaust valve. The length of time the 
exhaust valve remains open and the amount of moisture and contaminants ejected 
depends upon the sump pressure and the reservoir pressure drop that occurs 
each time air is used from the system.

To drain the automatic moisture ejector valve manually, use a tool to 
move the wire in the exhaust port upward and hold it in until draining is 
completed to 0 kPa (0 psi).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Tank Valve 

A tank valve is provided in the supply reservoir to allow air pressure 
to build up in the brake system from an external air source. The tank valve is 
similar to a tire valve stem and operates similarly.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Gauge 

Air brake systems have either dual or split brake systems which provide 
an emergency brake system, a primary or a secondary service system, should a 
failure occur in any part of the brake system. The dual air pressure gauge 
provides a direct reading of each service system's air pressure.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Check Valve

 Single 

Single check valves are used in the air brake supply systems on all 
vehicles. They protect the primary and secondary air reservoirs against air 
pressure loss in the compressor or the supply tank. They protect against a 
loss of either primary or secondary system pressure by sealing off the 
remaining system's operation to allow an emergency stop. The single check 
valve is located in the air line from the supply tank to each reservoir. It 
allows air to flow in one direction only and prevents the flow of air in the 
reverse direction. Airflow in the normal direction moves the check valve disc 
from its seat, and the flow is unobstructed. Flow in the reverse direction is 
prevented by the seating of the disc, which is caused by a drop in the 
up-stream air pressure and assisted by the spring.

 Double 

Double check valves are used in an air brake system to direct a flow of 
air into a common line from either of two sources, whichever is at the higher 
pressure. They may be used for directing airflow for specific functions, or to 
select the higher pressure of either of two sources of air as a supply source. 
It is recommended that double check valves be mounted so that the shuttle 
operates horizontally.

As air under pressure enters either end of the double check valve 
(inlet port) the moving shuttle responds to the pressure and seals the 
opposite port, assuming it is at a lower pressure level. The airflow continues 
out the delivery port or ports of the double check valve. The position of the 
shuttle will reverse if the pressure levels are reversed. Double check valves 
are designed so that the shuttle can never impede the backflow of air in the 
exhaust mode.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Dryer 

The purpose of the air dryer is to collect and remove solid, liquid and 
vapor contaminants from the air brake system. It provides clean, dry air to 
brake system components, increasing the life of the system and reducing 
maintenance cost. 

The Bendix AD-9 Air Dryer consists of a desiccant cartridge and a die 
cast aluminum end cover that is attached to an outer cylinder by capscrews and 
nuts. The end cover contains a purge valve mechanism, a check valve, a 
pressure relief valve and three threaded air connections. 

A cast-in heater element, a screw-in desiccant cartridge and an 
external electrical terminal are also included in the air dryer. The 
electrical requirements of the heater and thermostat are shown in the recess 
near the port marked CON. 

Air dryer operation consists of two cycles, the charge cycle and the 
purge cycle. 

For ease of serviceability, a replaceable desiccant cartridge, 
discharge valve and a heater and thermostat assembly with an external 
electrical connector are provided. The heater and thermostat are only 
serviceable as part of the purge valve assembly.

 Charge Cycle 

When the air compressor is operating, air, along with oil vapor, water 
and water vapor flows through the compressor discharge line to the air dryer 
supply port. As the air enters the port and moves through a baffle system, the 
flow direction changes by 180 degrees several times. These changes in 
direction cause air contaminants to condense and drop into the air dryer end 
cover sump. After leaving the air cover baffle system, the air flows into a 
desiccant cartridge that removes oil, oil vapor and solid contaminants.

[FIGURE: H72551A.gif]

Air leaves the oil separator and enters the desiccant drying bed. The 
air is still 100 percent saturated with water vapor. Air flowing through the 
column of desiccant becomes progressively drier as water vapor adheres to the 
desiccant material. The desiccant material removes 95 percent of the water 
vapor from the air. 

The dry air leaves the desiccant cartridge through an integral single 
check valve. Some air also exits the cartridge through the purge orifice next 
to the check valve. 

Dry air flows through the single check valve and out the delivery port 
to the air system supply reservoir. 

The air dryer will remain in the charge cycle until the air brake 
system pressure builds to the governor cutout setting. 

 Purge Cycle 

When the air brake system pressure reaches the governor cutout setting, 
the compressor continues to turn but stops compressing. This is the point at 
which the air dryer purge cycle begins. The governor unloader port-to-air 
dryer control port line becomes pressurized when the governor unloads the 
compressor. Air pressure at the air dryer end cover control port is also 
present on the purge valve piston. The purge valve piston moves and causes the 
purge valve to open to the atmosphere. Contaminants in the end cover sump are 
expelled immediately. In addition, air which was flowing through the desiccant 
cartridge changes direction and begins to flow toward the open purge valve. 
Oil and solid contaminants collected by the oil separator are removed by air 
flowing from the desiccant drying bed to the open purge valve.

[FIGURE: H72561A.gif]

The initial purge and desiccant cartridge decompression lasts only a 
few seconds. It can be heard as a burst of air at the air dryer exhaust. 

Dry air flows from the purge volume through the desiccant cartridge 
purge orifice and into the desiccant drying bed. Pressurized air from the 
purge volume expands after passing through the purge orifice. Its pressure is 
lowered and its volume is increased. The flow of dry air through the drying 
bed reactivates the desiccant material by removing the water vapor that 
adheres to it. It usually takes 15 to 30 seconds for the entire purge volume 
of a standard air dryer to flow through the desiccant drying bed. 

The end cover single check valve prevents air pressure in the brake 
system from returning to the air dryer during the purge cycle. After the purge 
cycle is complete, the air dryer is ready for the next charge cycle to begin. 
The purge valve will remain open after the purge cycle is completed and will 
not close until air brake system pressure is reduced and the governor allows 
the compressor to begin compressing.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Air Pressure Switch 

The low air pressure switch is a safety device designed to give an 
automatic warning to the driver whenever air pressure in the air brake system 
is below 414 kPa (60 psi), the safe minimum for normal vehicle operation. It 
is usually used to operate an electrical buzzer or warning lamp, or both, that 
are audible or visible to the driver. Low air pressure switches are located in 
both the primary and secondary air supply lines.

[FIGURE: H8176A.gif]

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air Supply

 Inspection and Verification 

Before testing the air brakes, operate the engine until the air 
pressure builds up to 621 kPa (90 psi). Then open the drain cocks and drain 
the air pressure to zero in each reservoir. Close the drain cocks. Some models 
may have automatic moisture ejector valves which can be manually operated to 
completely drain the reservoirs. 

If the air supply system is not properly maintained, the system can 
become filled with moisture and other contaminants which can cause damage to 
the brake system internal components (diaphragms, valve seats, seats, etc.). 
Daily draining of the air reservoir to 0 kPa (0 psi) or periodic maintenance 
of the automatic moisture ejectors is very important to make sure brake system 
performance is trouble-free. More frequent maintenance is required in dusty, 
high humidity or low temperature environments. 

 Symptom Chart — Air Supply Brake 

 AIR SUPPLY BRAKE 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging

Excessive system air leaks.

TEST for excessive air leaks and SERVICE as necessary. Allowable air 
leaks are: Single vehicle, 7 kPa/minute (1 psi/minute); Tractor trailer, 21 
kPa/minute (3 psi/minute)

Excessive air leaks in fittings, hoses and tubing connected to the 
compressor, air dryer and supply reservoir.

Using soap solution, TEST for leaks at fittings, drain cock (if used) 
and pressure relief valve in supply reservoir. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary.

Worn or damaged check valve in the air dryer cover.

TEST check valve. START the engine, ALLOW pressure to build in the 
system to the governor cutout. WAIT two minutes for the purge cycle to 
complete. Using soap solution, CHECK for air at the purge valve exhaust. Air 
leaks should not exceed a 25-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds. REPLACE check 
valve if necessary.

Worn or damaged air compressor governor.

TEST governor for proper cut-in or cutout pressures and excessive leaks 
in both positions. REPLACE or SERVICE governor or compressor as necessary.

Leaking purge valve in the air dryer end cover on the control side.

REMOVE air dryer end cover. APPLY 827 kPa (120 psi) at the control 
port. SOAP both sides around the purge valve to test for control piston leaks. 
Air leaks should not exceed a 25-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds.

Compressor unloader mechanism leaking excessively.

REMOVE compressor air strainer or fitting at inlet cavity. With 
compressor unloaded, CHECK for unloader piston air leaks. Slight air leaks are 
allowed.

Air Dryer Pressure Relief Valve Popping or Exhausting Air

Desiccant cartridge plugged or saturated.

CHECK for proper compressor installation. CHECK for excessive oil 
passing the compressor piston rings. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary. REBUILD 
or REPLACE cartridge.

Worn or damaged end cover check valve.

CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE.

Worn or damaged fittings, hose or tubing between air dryer and the 
supply reservoir.

CHECK if air reaches supply reservoir. INSPECT for kinked tubing or 
hoses, undrilled or restricted hose and tube fittings.

Constant Exhaust of Air at Air Dryer Purge Valve Exhaust or Unable to 
Build System Pressure

Air dryer purge valve leaking excessively.

With compressor loaded, APPLY soap solution to purge valve exhaust and 
CHECK for excessive leaks. SERVICE purge valve if necessary.

Worn or damaged air compressor governor.

CHECK governor for proper cut-in, cutout pressure and excessive leaks 
in both positions. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary.

Purge control line connected to reservoir or governor exhaust port.

CONNECT purge control line to the governor unloader port.

Purge valve stuck open, worn or damaged heater and thermostat, wiring, 
blown fuse.

TEST heater and thermostat. REFER to the air dryer component test 
procedure in this section.

Inlet and outlet connections reversed.

CONNECT lines properly. The compressor discharge line must enter the 
air dryer at the inlet port.

Worn or damaged check valve between air dryer and supply reservoir.

CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE.

Kinked or plugged discharge line.

CLEAR line. STRAIGHTEN or REROUTE line as necessary.

Excessive bends in discharge line, water collects and freezes.

REROUTE discharge line to slope away from compressor to air dryer, with 
as few bends as possible.

Excessive system air leaks.

REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging."

Air Dryer Does Not Purge or Exhaust Air

Broken, kinked, frozen, plugged or disconnected purge control, input or 
output lines.

When the compressor is unloaded, TEST to determine if air flows through 
the purge control line. CHECK for undrilled fittings.

Worn or damaged air dryer purge valve.

SERVICE purge valve.

Worn or damaged compressor governor.

CHECK governor for proper cut-in, cutout pressure and excessive leaks 
in both positions. SERVICE or REPLACE as necessary. CONNECT lines properly. 
The compressor discharge line must enter the air dryer at the inlet port. 
CHECK if air passes through the check valve. SERVICE or REPLACE. CHECK 
discharge line. STRAIGHTEN or REROUTE the discharge line as necessary. REROUTE 
discharge line to slope away from compressor to air dryer, with as few bends 
as possible. REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging."

Desiccant Material, Whitish Liquid or Paste or Small Beads Expelled 
from Air Dryer Purge Valve Exhaust or Unsatisfactory Desiccant Life

This condition is usually accompanied by one or more of the preceding 
conditions. See related possible sources for those conditions.

REFER to appropriate conditions in this symptom chart.

Air dryer not securely mounted, excessive vibration.

ADD bracket supports or CHANGE the air dryer mounting location if 
necessary to minimize vibration.

Worn or damaged cloth-covered perforated plate in air dryer desiccant 
cartridge or improperly rebuilt desiccant cartridge.

REPLACE desiccant cartridge.

Compressor passing excessive oil.

CHECK for proper compressor installation. If symptoms persist, REPLACE 
the compressor.

Ice blocking the purge orifice — cold weather operation.

CHECK air dryer fuse. TEST heater and thermostat. REFER to procedure in 
the air dryer component test in this section.

Water in Air Reservoir

Desiccant needs replacement.

REPLACE the desiccant cartridge.

Improper discharge line length or improper line material.

USE a minimum 1.8 m (6 feet) of metal tubing between the compressor 
discharge port and the air dryer supply port.

Air system charged from outside air source, outside air not passing 
through the air dryer.

Outside air must pass through the air dryer if system has an outside 
air fill provision. An outside air fill system is not recommended.

Air dryer not purging.

REFER to "Air Dryer Does Not Purge or Exhaust Air."

Purge time is insufficient because of excessive system air leaks.

REFER to "Air Dryer Constantly Cycling or Purging."

Air dryer/vehicle application requires additional purge volume.

Additional purge volume may be necessary when the compressor is 
operating longer than 90 seconds during normal operation.

Air dryer not compatible with vehicle air system requirements. Improper 
air dryer/vehicle application.

Air dryer requires a minimum purge time of approximately 30 seconds. If 
the air compressor stays loaded longer than 90 seconds, and additional purge 
volume is added, a longer purge time is required. Air dryer efficiency will 
decrease as compressor loaded time increases beyond 120 seconds, during the 
normal operation of the vehicle. This limitation assumes that the compressor 
is approximately 12CFM and engine operation is 1600-1900 rpm. The air dryer 
will accommodate occasional longer loaded times, such as system initial 
pressure buildup.

 Component Tests 

 Compressor 

 NOTE: Tractor must be disconnected from the trailer to run this test. 

Bleed both the primary and secondary reservoirs down to 586 kPa (85 
psi) as measured with a test gauge. Run the engine at full governed rpm until 
the air pressure in the reservoirs reaches 689 kPa (100 psi). If the pressure 
buildup time exceeds 40 seconds, the compressor is not operating properly and 
one or more of the following conditions may exist. 

clogged engine air cleaner or compressor inlet hose 

excessive air system leakage 

drive belt slipping 

restricted discharge cavity in compressor or restricted discharge line 

discharge valve stuck or broken 

unloader piston inside the compressor stuck 

excessively worn compressor piston rings or cylinder walls 

governor out of adjustment or fouled 

 Governor 

Install a test gauge in the air lines, in the supply or service 
reservoir. Run the engine to build up air pressure. Note the reading on the 
test gauge at which the pressure stops rising. This is the point that the 
governor shuttles the compressor unloader piston and stops the compression 
cycle of the compressor. This is the compressor cutout pressure. The 
compressor cutout pressure should be between 793-861 kPa (115-125 psi). If the 
instrument panel dual air pressure gauge is used, the pressure should range 
between 752-903 kPa (109-131 psi), allowing for dual air pressure gauge 
accuracy. 

With the engine running, slowly reduce the amount of air pressure in 
the system by applying and releasing the brakes. Note on the dual air pressure 
gauge the level at which pressure starts to bu

To Reservoir

 Removal 

Drain the cooling system. Open the air reservoir drain cocks to exhaust 
air pressure from the system. 

Remove the air cleaner assembly. 

Disconnect the oil supply and oil return lines at the compressor. 

Disconnect the air supply and return lines at the compressor. 

Disconnect the air supply line at the governor. 

Disconnect the coolant supply and return lines from the compressor. 

Loosen the air pump pivot bolt locknut to loosen and then remove the 
drive belt. 

Remove the compressor mounting bolts and nuts. Remove compressor. 

Remove governor retaining bolts and remove governor and gasket. 

Remove oil, air and coolant fittings to be installed on replacement 
unit. 

Remove air outlet tube (manifold) and gasket. 

Remove the air compressor pulley nut. 

Using a suitable puller, remove pulley and key. 

 Installation 

Position key and install air compressor pulley and air compressor 
pulley nut. Tighten nut to 122-163 Nm (90-120 lb-ft). 

Position air outlet tube (manifold) and gasket, and install one 
retaining bolt at this time. 

Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to oil, air and 
coolant fittings and install fittings. 

Position governor and gasket and install retaining bolts. 

Position compressor in vehicle and install mounting bolts and nuts. 

Install drive belt. Adjust tension and tighten pivot bolt nut. 

Connect coolant lines to compressor. 

Connect air lines and oil lines to compressor. 

Connect air line to governor. 

Install air cleaner assembly. 

Fill and bleed the cooling system. 

Close the air reservoir drain cocks. 

Start the engine and check for air, coolant and oil leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Governor 

The governor is mounted to the compressor with two attaching bolts. 
Mating ports in the governor and compressor bodies connect governor pressure 
to the unloading pistons in the compressor. Reservoir pressure is connected to 
the governor through a hose or tube. 

 Removal 

Exhaust the air brake system. 

Disconnect the pressure lines at governor. 

Remove the attaching bolts and remove the governor. 

 Installation 

Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A to the governor bolt 
threads. 

Using a new gasket, position the governor and bolts on the compressor. 
Tighten the governor bolts to 20-25 Nm (15-18 lb-ft).

Transfer the pressure lines to replacement governor. 

Test the governor. Refer to Component Tests in the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Dryer 

 Removal 

To make servicing the air dryer easier, it is recommended that it be 
removed from the vehicle except for the purge valve which can be serviced in 
place. 

Park the vehicle on a level surface and chock the wheels. 

Drain the air system to 0 kPa (0 psi). 

Identify, tag, and disconnect the three air lines from the end cover. 

Unplug the wiring harness from the heater and thermostat assembly 
connector on the purge valve housing assembly. 

Loosen the bolts securing the upper mounting strap. 

Mark, remove and retain the end cover capscrews, lock nuts and special 
washers retaining the lower mounting bracket to the end cover. Mark these 
holes in the end cover. 

Remove the air dryer from the vehicle.
