REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Heater and Thermostat Assembly 

 Removal 

Unplug the wiring harness from the heater and thermostat assembly 
connector on the purge valve housing. Make sure connector seal is present on 
vehicle wiring harness connector.

 NOTE: Mark the relationship of the purge valve assembly to the air dryer.

Remove the three self-tapping screws securing the purge valve housing 
assembly to the end cover assembly. Remove the purge valve assembly from the 
end cover assembly. 

Remove and discard the three (two in certain assemblies) O-rings from 
the purge valve assembly.

Remove and discard the two screws securing the heater and thermostat 
assembly to the purge valve assembly.

 CAUTION: Do not pull the heater and thermostat assembly straight out of the 
purge valve body. Read this step before attempting removal. 

Remove the heater and thermostat assembly by gently rotating the 
connector to the left until the thermostat clears the purge valve housing. 
Then, slide the heater element out, to the right and up. Discard the heater 
and thermostat assembly along with its sealing ring(s).

[FIGURE: H9946A.gif]

 Installation 

Make sure the square-cut sealing ring(s) on the back side of the 
connector has not slipped off or twisted.

Position the heater and thermostat.

First install the heater element into the heater element slot until the 
connector contacts the purge valve housing. 

Gently move the connector and thermostat to the left until the 
thermostat clears the cavity in the housing. 

Gently rotate the connector to the right while inserting the thermostat 
down into the cavity until the thermostat is inside the cavity and the 
connector seats against the housing. 

Make sure the sealing ring(s) is not pinched.

While holding the connector against the purge valve housing, install 
the two heater connector-to-purge valve housing screws that secure the 
connector to the housing. Torque to 1.13-2.26 Nm (10-20 lb-in).

Lubricate the O-rings and the respective grooves on the purge valve 
assembly. Install the O-rings on the purge valve.

Install the purge valve assembly, with the O-rings, into the air dryer 
end cover using the relationship mark made during the removal to align the 
parts.

Install the three screws and flatwashers or extended exhaust cover if 
present at removal. Start screws by hand then tighten to 6-9 Nm (50-80 
lb-in).

With the key on, test for vehicle power at the two pins of the vehicle 
wiring harness connector. If voltage is not detected, check for a blown fuse, 
broken or pinched wiring.

Reconnect the vehicle wiring harness connector to the purge valve 
assembly. Make sure that the seal is present on the vehicle wiring harness, 
then plug the wiring harness connector into the purge valve assembly connector 
until the lock tab snaps in place.

Charge the system and test for leaks.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Moisture Ejector Valve, Automatic 

The automatic moisture ejector valve is used in place of the reservoir 
drain cock on some models, and must be disassembled and cleaned every 80 450 
km (50,000 miles) or six months. The automatic moisture ejector valve must be 
removed from the air reservoir for cleaning. 

 Disassembly 

Remove the capscrews and lockwashers. 

Remove the cover and sealing rings. 

Remove the valve guide. 

Remove the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Wash metal parts with solvent. Wipe rubber parts with a clean cloth. 

Inspect all parts for wear or deterioration. 

Replace all worn or damaged parts. 

 Assembly 

 CAUTION: Do not apply oil to the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Before assembling the valve, apply a light film of grease to inlet 
valve seat. 

Place the sealing ring in groove of cover. 

Place the valve guide over the inlet and exhaust valve. 

Place the valve guide over the inlet and exhaust assembly into the 
cover. The manual release wire will project through the exhaust port. 

Place the body on the cover and install the capscrews and lockwashers.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Safety Valve 

 Disassembly 

Clamp lower wrench flat in vise (flat nearest pipe thread). 

Using upper wrench flat, unscrew lock nut. Unscrew and remove spring 
cage from body of safety valve. 

Remove ball valve, spring and release pin from spring cage. 

Clean all parts in mineral spirits. Inspect all parts. All parts 
requiring replacement should be replaced with genuine Bendix® 
replacement parts. 

 Assembly 

Place the ball valve in body. 

Install spring and release pin in spring cage with adjusting screw. 

Position the release pin over ball valve. Screw body with ball into the 
spring cage. Tighten securely. The safety valve is not adjustable.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Air Dryer 

 NOTE: The desiccant change interval may vary from vehicle to vehicle. 
Although typical desiccant cartridge life is three years, many can perform 
adequately for a longer time period. 

In order to take maximum advantage of desiccant life and to make sure 
that replacement occurs only when necessary, it is important that operation 
and leakage tests be performed as described in Air Dryer in the Component 
Tests in the Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

Rebuild the air dryer, including the desiccant cartridge every 10,800 
hours, 480,000 km (300,000 miles) or every 36 months.

 Disassembly 

 NOTE: Several replacement parts and maintenance kits are available which do 
not require full disassembly. The instructions provided with these parts and 
kits should be followed. 

 NOTE: New O-rings are provided in the rebuild kit. Discard all old O-rings.

Remove the delivery port check valve assembly and O-ring. Discard the 
O-ring.

 CAUTION: Do not use any clamping device to hold the end cover as damage may 
occur. The end cover may be held by installing a pipe nipple into the supply 
port and clamping the nipple in a vise. 

Using a machinist's scribe, matchmark the air dryer housing and end 
cover. Remove the three self-tapping screws retaining the purge valve assembly 
to the end cover. Remove the purge valve assembly from the end cover. 

Remove the three O-rings from the exterior of the purge valve assembly.

Remove the six 3/8-inch air dryer housing bolts, air dryer housing nuts 
and twelve special washers and remove the end cover and desiccant cartridge 
assembly.

Remove and discard the end cover O-ring. 

Place a strap or chain wrench around the desiccant cartridge 
approximately two to three inches away from the end cover. Rotate the 
dessicant cartridge counterclockwise and separate it from the end cover. 

Remove the desiccant cartridge O-ring from the end cover. 

 NOTE: Do not remove the heater and thermostat assembly unless proven damaged. 
Refer to Air Dryer in Component Tests in the Diagnosis and Testing portion of 
this section. 

 NOTE: A Torx® head socket or a twelve point 1/4-inch socket is 
required.

Disassemble the purge valve assembly. 

Remove the 1/4-inch purge piston nut from the bottom of the purge valve 
assembly with a socket wrench and one of the sockets mentioned above to hold 
the purge piston bolt head. Remove the exhaust diaphragm, diaphragm (if used) 
and purge valve. 

Remove the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt, purge piston, 
spring and the O-rings; one from the inside and one from the outside of the 
purge piston.

 Assembly 

Wash all parts thoroughly in a quality commercial solvent such as 
mineral spirits. Make sure that all parts are thoroughly dry before assembly.

Inspect all components for wear and damage. Replace as necessary. 

Lubricate the new O-rings and bores with a barium-base lubricant. 

Install the O-rings in the purge piston inside and outside O-ring 
grooves. 

Install the spring into the top inside diameter of the purge valve 
housing. Install the purge piston in the inside diameter of the spring. 
Install the 1/4-inch Torx® head purge piston bolt in the purge piston. 
Depress the purge piston into the exhaust cover. 

Hold the purge piston and, from the opposite end of the exhaust cover, 
install the purge valve, rubber side up on the purge piston bolt. Install the 
diaphragm and diaphragm washer (if used) or the flatwasher and purge piston 
nut. Tighten the purge piston nut to 7-9 Nm (60-80 lb-in). 

Install the three O-rings on the exhaust cover and install the exhaust 
cover into the end cover aligning the scribe marks. Install the three 1/4-inch 
self-tapping exhaust cover screws and tighten to 6-9 Nm (50-80 lb-in). 

Install the O-ring on the check valve assembly and install the assembly 
in the end cover. Tighten to 23-28 Nm (17-21 lb-ft). 

Install the desiccant cartridge sealing ring in the end cover. 
Lubricate the bottom of the cartridge at the O-ring seal and end cover contact 
area with a light coating of barium grease. 

Screw the desiccant cartridge into the end cover until it contacts the 
O-ring. With a strap or chain wrench positioned two to three inches from the 
bottom of the cartridge, turn the cartridge clockwise 180-225 degrees. Do not 
overtighten. 

Install the end cover O-ring on the end cover, place the housing over 
the cartridge and align the holes. 

 NOTE: The longer 3/8-inch capscrews are used to secure the dryer assembly to 
its support bracket. 

Install the six 3/8-inch capscrews, lock nuts and 12 special washers 
making sure they are in proper position as removed. Tighten the capscrews 
using a cross pattern. Tighten to 31-43 Nm (23-32 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Delivery System 

The air delivery system delivers the air brake pressure from the air 
supply system to the brake chambers. It controls the amount of air pressure 
that is delivered to the brake chambers, and controls the amount of braking 
during a stop. It consists of the foot control valve, the relay valve, quick 
release valve and the brake air chamber.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Foot Control Valve 

The E-7 foot control valve is mounted to the dash panel and uses a 
suspended brake pedal. The foot control valve is the dual brake valve type 
which provides two separate circuits to control the primary and secondary 
systems of the dual (or split) systems.

[FIGURE: H3758C.gif]

The foot control valve is connected to each of the air supply systems. 
The air from supply tanks is metered by the foot control valve as the driver 
applies the brake pedal during a brake stop. The metered air pressure is then 
delivered to a rear axle relay valve which controls the amount of air to the 
brake air chambers. This amount of air is proportional to the air delivered 
from the foot control valve. 

The front brakes are supplied directly from the foot control valve.

The circuits in the foot control valve are identified as follows: 

The number one (primary) circuit is the portion of the valve between 
the primary piston and the secondary piston.

The number two (secondary) circuit consists of the area between the 
secondary piston and the exhaust cavity. 

The supply, delivery and exhaust ports of the foot control valve are 
identified by designations cast into the valve body next to the port. The 
primary supply and delivery ports are located in the valve's primary body. The 
secondary supply and delivery ports are located in the secondary body. 

The primary circuit of the foot control valve is similar in operation 
to a standard single circuit air brake valve. Under normal operating 
conditions the secondary circuit is similar in operation to a relay valve. 

Both the primary and secondary circuits use a common exhaust, protected 
by an exhaust diaphragm.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Relay Valve 

The R-12 relay valve speeds up the application and release of the air 
at the rear brake air chambers. The valve is constantly supplied with air 
pressure from the air reservoir to its supply port. As an application is made 
to the foot control valve, air pressure is delivered to the relay valve 
service port. The air supply to the relay valve is then metered to the rear 
brakes from the valve delivery port proportional to the air pressure at the 
service port.

[FIGURE: H5840C.gif]

(Part of 2A449)

Air pressure delivered to the service port enters the small cavity 
above the piston and moves the piston down. The exhaust seat moves down with 
the piston and seats on the inner or exhaust portion of the inlet/exhaust 
valve and seals off the exhaust passage. At the same time, the outer or inlet 
portion of the inlet/exhaust valve moves off its seat, permitting supply air 
to flow from the reservoir, past the open inlet valve and into the brake air 
chambers. 

The air pressure being delivered by the open inlet valve also is 
effective on the bottom area of the relay piston. When air pressure beneath 
the piston equals the service air pressure from above, the piston lifts 
slightly and the inlet spring returns the inlet valve to its seat. The exhaust 
remains closed as the service line pressure balances the delivery pressure. 
The R-12 relay valve is equipped with a piston return spring which will assist 
the lifting of the piston. As delivered air pressure is changed, the relay 
valve reacts instantly to the change and holds brake application at that 
level. 

When air pressure is released from the service port as the foot control 
valve is released, and air pressure in the cavity above the piston is 
exhausted, air pressure beneath the piston lifts the piston and the exhaust 
seat moves away from the exhaust valve, opening the exhaust passage. With the 
exhaust passage open, the air pressure in the brake air chambers is permitted 
to exhaust through the exhaust port and releases the brakes.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brake Air Chamber 

A brake air chamber converts the energy of air pressure into mechanical 
force. This force is used to push a lever to rotate a brake camshaft, forcing 
the brake shoes against the brake drum. Air pressure delivered to the brake 
air chambers (delivered through the inlet port) acts on the diaphragm, moving 
the push rod and plate. The amount of force coming from the brake air chamber 
is equal to the air pressure multiplied by the effective area of the 
diaphragm. This force is proportional to the air pressure delivered to the 
brake air chambers.

[FIGURE: H3342C.gif]

When air pressure is released from the brake air chamber, the push rod 
return spring and the brake shoe return spring return all the affected 
components (push rod and plate, diaphragm, brake camshaft) to their released 
position, releasing the brakes. 

Spring brake air chambers also have an integral service chamber which 
applies the spring brakes the same as the service chamber above. Refer to 
 Section 06-05A for spring brake air chamber operation.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Quick Release Valve 

The quick release valve is used for several functions in the brake 
system. Its function is to speed up the exhaust of air from a particular part 
of the brake system. It is used to exhaust air from brake air chambers, front 
and rear, near the brake air chamber, to speed up the release of air without 
the air traveling all the way back to the source of air. It is used in 
tractors to release air pressure in the service line to the trailer. It is 
used in the parking brake system to provide a faster brake application and to 
eliminate the undesirable exhausting of large quantities of air into the cab.

[FIGURE: H4959E.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

2A095

Quick Release Valve

2

—

Supply Port (Part of 2A095)

3

—

Delivery Port (Part of 2A095)

4

—

Exhaust Port (Not Threaded) (Part of 2A095)

When a brake application is made, air pressure enters the supply port. 
The diaphragm moves down and seals the exhaust port. At the same time, air 
pressure forces the edges of the diaphragm down and air flows out the delivery 
port. 

When the air pressure being delivered (beneath the diaphragm) equals 
the pressure being delivered by the foot control valve (above the diaphragm), 
the diaphragm outer edge will seal against the body seat. The exhaust port is 
still sealed by the center portion of the diaphragm. When the foot control 
valve application is released, the air pressure above the diaphragm is 
released back through the foot control valve exhaust. Air pressure beneath the 
diaphragm forces the diaphragm to rise, opening the exhaust and allowing air 
to exhaust.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Brakes 

Cam air brakes are used on the front and rear axles. The cam-type brake 
is an air-operated, two-shoe brake. The front brake shoes each use a one-piece 
shoe lining. The rear shoes each use a two-piece lining. Air applied to the 
brake air chamber push rod causes a cam to rotate against the rollers, forcing 
the brake shoes outward against the brake drum. For more information, refer to 
 Section 06-08C .

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air Delivery

 Inspection and Verification 

Since most air leaks occur at the fittings and connections, these areas 
should be checked before any other part is replaced. For diagnostic and 
testing procedures for individual components, refer to the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of each air brake section.

 WARNING: WHEN DRAINING THE SYSTEM, DO NOT LOOK INTO THE AIR JETS OR DIRECT THEM 
TOWARD A PERSON, AS DIRT OR SLUDGE PARTICLES MAY BE CARRIED IN THE AIR STREAM. 
HOSES WHICH CONTAIN AIR PRESSURE SHOULD NOT BE DISCONNECTED UNDER PRESSURE 
SINCE THEY WILL WHIP AS AIR ESCAPES FROM THE LINE. FOLLOW THE MANUFACTURERS' 
RECOMMENDED PROCEDURES IN WORKING ON ANY AIR DEVICE SO AS TO AVOID INJURY OR 
DAMAGE FROM PARTS WHICH, WHEN RELEASED, ARE SUBJECT TO MECHANICAL (SPRING) OR 
PNEUMATIC PROPULSION. AS SYSTEM PRESSURE IS DRAINED AND THE EMERGENCY BRAKE 
APPLIES, HANDS SHOULD BE AWAY FROM BRAKE CHAMBER PUSH RODS AND SPRING 
ACTUATORS WHICH WILL APPLY AUTOMATICALLY WITH THE LOSS OF PRESSURE. THIS ALSO 
APPLIES WHEN CHECKING SERVICE BRAKE SYSTEM. 

Reservoirs which are closest to the sources of compressed air 
(compressors or auxiliary sources) should contain a safety valve in known 
working order and sufficient capacity to limit the reservoir pressure to a 
safe maximum level. Old, used reservoirs should not be used as replacements. 
The safety valves should not reset higher than specified by the reservoir 
manufacturer, vehicle manufacturer, or code to which the reservoir had been 
manufactured. Various brake air chambers contain large internal steel springs 
that require special disassembly procedures. Note and be guided by the warning 
tags on such units.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Component Tests — Brake, Air Delivery

 Foot Control Valve 

 Operation Test 

Check the delivery pressure of both primary and secondary circuits 
using test gauges known to be accurate in the appropriate delivery ports of 
the foot control valve. Press the brake pedal to several positions between the 
fully released and fully applied positions, and check the delivered pressure 
on the test gauges to see that it varies proportionately with the movement of 
the brake pedal.

When the brake pedal is fully applied, the reading on the test gauge 
should fall off to zero promptly when the application is released. It should 
be noted that the primary circuit delivery pressure (primary-green) will be 
about 13.7-27.5 kPa (2-4 psi) greater than the secondary circuit delivery 
pressure (secondary-red) with primary and secondary circuit supply reservoirs 
at the same pressure. This is normal for the foot control valve. 

An increase in stopping distance or a low air pressure warning 
indicates one or the other brake circuit is inoperative, and although the 
vehicle air brake system may continue to function, the vehicle should not be 
operated until the necessary service has been performed and both braking 
circuits are operating normally. 

 Leakage Test 

 NOTE: If the foot control valve does not function as described or leakage is 
excessive, it is recommended that it be replaced with an identical new or 
remanufactured unit.

Make and hold full brake application. 

Coat the exhaust port and body of the foot control valve with soap 
solution. 

Leakage should not exceed a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in three seconds 
in both the applied and released position. 

 Relay Valve 

 Operation and Leakage Test 

Fully charge air brake system and adjust brakes. 

Make several brake applications and check for prompt application and 
release at all appropriate wheels. If brakes are slow to apply or release, 
make sure the brake camshaft is properly lubricated and any excessively worn 
brake parts are replaced before proceeding. 

With foot control valve in released position, coat the exhaust port 
with soap solution and check for inlet valve and valve guide O-ring leakage; a 
25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in five seconds leakage is permitted. 

Make and hold a foot control valve application; coat the exhaust port 
with soap solution and check for leakage; a 25.4-mm (1-inch) bubble in three 
seconds leakage is permitted. 

 NOTE: If leakage is detected, replacing the inlet/exhaust valve may correct 
the concern. If leakage still occurs, leakage may be caused by relay piston 
O-ring or exhaust valve seat. 

Make and hold a foot control valve application; coat outside of foot 
control valve body in area where cover joins the body for cover O-ring 
leakage. No leakage is permitted. If the foot control valve does not function 
as described above, or if leakage is excessive, it is recommended that the 
foot control valve be replaced with an identical new or remanufactured unit. 

 Service Air Chamber 

 Operation Test 

Apply brakes and verify whether the brake air chamber push rods move 
out promptly and without binding. If any binding is evident, make sure brake 
camshaft is properly lubricated and that any excessively worn brake parts are 
replaced before proceeding. 

Release brakes and observe that the brake air chamber push rods return 
to the released position promptly and without binding. 

Check brake air chamber push rod travel. Adjust travel of brake air 
chamber push rod at slack adjuster if necessary. Refer to Section 06-08C for 
adjustment. 

 Leakage Test 

Make and hold a full brake application. 

 CAUTION: Do not overtighten as this can distort sealing surface or clamping ring. 

Using soap solution, coat clamping ring(s). If leakage is detected, 
tighten clamping ring only enough to stop leakage. 

Coat area around push rod hole. No leakage is permitted. If leakage is 
detected, the diaphragm must be replaced. If the diaphragm of one brake air 
chamber of an axle is replaced, replace the other chamber diaphragm to make 
sure braking is even. 

 Quick Release Valve 

 Operation Test 

With the air brake system fully charged, apply the brakes. Observe the 
brake action on the wheels controlled by the quick release valve or relay 
valve in question. The brakes should apply promptly. 

Release the brakes and inspect to be sure the air pressure is exhausted 
rapidly from the exhaust port. Be sure the exhaust port is not restricted. 

 Leakage Test 

 CAUTION: Leakage is not permissible. Service or replace a leaking quick release 
valve. 

With brakes applied, coat the exhaust port with soap solution.

Inspect for leaks.

Service as required.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

 Removal

To remove the foot control valve from the dash panel, identify and tag

Connect the two supply and delivery lines to their respective ports and

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brakes, Cam

 WARNING: DO NOT INHALE DUST FROM BRAKES, CLUTCHES OR ASSOCIATED COMPONENTS. 
INHALATION OF DUST CAN BE INJURIOUS TO YOUR HEALTH. COMPRESSED AIR OR BRUSHES 
MUST NOT BE USED TO CLEAN BRAKES, BRAKE DRUMS, CLUTCHES AND ASSOCIATED 
COMPONENTS. USE BRAKE AND CLUTCH SERVICE VACUUM, MODEL 164-R3600 OR EQUIVALENT 
EQUIPPED FOR THIS PURPOSE TO CAREFULLY REMOVE ANY DUST. ADHERENT DUST SHOULD 
BE REMOVED WITH A DAMP RAG. ANY DUST SHOULD BE CONTAINED IN A SEALED AND 
LABELED BAG FOR DISPOSAL. WEAR AN APPROVED HIGH EFFICIENCY CARTRIDGE OR AIR 
LINE RESPIRATOR AND USE EXTRA CAUTION TO AVOID BREATHING THIS DUST. 

The cam-type brake is an air-operated two-shoe brake. The front brake 
shoes each use a one-piece shoe lining. The rear shoes each use two-piece 
lining.

 Front Brake Assembly, Rockwell Q-Plus Series 

[FIGURE: H7405B.gif]

Camshaft Bracket

As the brake pedal application is made, air pressure is applied to the 
brake air chamber. The brake air chamber has an internal diaphragm that will 
push against the brake chamber push rod with a force proportional to the air 
pressure being applied. The push rod then pushes on the automatic slack 
adjuster arm, which causes rotation of the brake camshaft. The rotation causes 
the rollers of the brake shoes to roll up the cam ramp forcing the brake shoes 
against the brake drum. When the brake pedal is released, the retracting (or 
return) spring of the brake pulls the shoes away from the brake drum, and a 
return spring in the brake air chamber returns the slack adjuster to the 
released position.

PAGE 2939
================================================================================

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Slack Adjuster, Automatic 

The automatic slack adjuster design uses both brake chamber push rod 
travel and shoe-to-brake drum force to maintain proper brake adjustment. On 
brake application, the brake chamber push rod rotates the slack adjuster until 
the adjusting link engages a one-way cone clutch on the wormshaft. At this 
point, if the brake shoes are not in contact with the brake drum, the cone 
clutch will remain engaged with the shaft and the link will rotate the 
wormshaft. This shaft rotation adjusts the brake shoes by reducing 
shoe-to-drum clearance. Adjustment continues until the brake linings are 
forced against the brake drum. The shoe-to-brake drum force creates a 
resistance torque that exceeds the slip torque of the clutch, and allows the 
clutch to slip on the wormshaft for the remainder of the slack travel. During 
the return stroke the one-way cone clutch allows the link to return without 
shaft movement. The adjustment cycle will repeat until shoe-to-brake drum 
contact force occurs simultaneously with the initial link to clutch engagement.

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake, Air, Cam-Type

 Inspection and Verification 

It is important that a careful parts inspection be made before 
assembly. Check all parts for wear or damage and service or replace as required.

Check the brake backing plate for expanded anchor pin holes and for 
cracks. Replace damaged backing plate and anchor pin bushings.

Check the camshaft bracket for broken welds, cracks and correct 
alignment. Replace damaged brackets.

Check anchor pins for corrosion and wear. Replace damaged anchor pins.

Check brake shoes for rust that may impair operation, expanded rivet 
holes, broken welds and incorrect alignment. Service or replace as necessary.

On 16.5 inch brake shoes only: anchor pin holes must not exceed 25.63 
mm (1.009 inches) in diameter. The distance from the center of the anchor pin 
hole to the center of the roller hole must not exceed 324.59 mm (12.779 
inches). Replace any shoe whose measurements are not to specifications.

Check the brake camshaft for cracks, wear and corrosion. Check the cam 
head, bearing journals and splines. Replace damaged brake camshafts.

Check the slack adjusters:

For slack adjusters with "quick connect" type clevis, check the gap 
between the clevis and the collar. If the gap exceeds 1.52 mm (0.060 inch) 
replace the clevis.

Check the clevis pins and the bushing in the arm of the slack adjuster. 
Replace the pins if they are worn. Replace the bushing if its diameter exceeds 
16.7 mm (0.656 inch).

[FIGURE: DH0175A.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Brake Shoe and Camshaft

 Lining/Drum Replacement Procedure 

Special attention must be given to proper maintenance procedures of the 
automatic slack adjuster when the brake linings or brake drums are replaced.

If the axle is equipped with spring brake chambers, manually cage the 
spring brakes, following the manufacturer's recommended procedures.

Applying 69-137 kPa (10 to 20 psi) air pressure to the service brake 
chamber is recommended. This relieves the internal pressure on the adjusting 
mechanism, minimizing wear when backing off the slack adjuster.

Rotate the hex extension counterclockwise until adequate clearance is 
reached for the new brake linings or brake drum.

Release the 69-137 kPa (10-20 psi) in the system.

Proceed with the lining change or brake drum replacement.

 Clean Parts 

 WARNING: INCORRECT USE OF HOT SOLUTION TANKS OR ALKALINE SOLUTIONS CAN CAUSE 
SERIOUS PERSONAL INJURY. TO PREVENT INJURY, FOLLOW MANUFACTURER'S 
INSTRUCTIONS. DO NOT USE GASOLINE TO CLEAN PARTS. GASOLINE CAN EXPLODE. 

Ground or polished parts

Use a cleaning solvent, kerosene or diesel fuel to clean ground or 
polished parts. To prevent corrosion, do not use hot solutions, water, steam 
or alkaline solutions.

Rough parts

Rough parts may be cleaned in hot solution tanks or a weak alkaline 
solution. After cleaning, rinse and dry the parts thoroughly.

 Corrosion Prevention 

Apply brake lubricant to cleaned or new brake parts as needed. Do not 
apply lubricants to brake linings or drums.

 Parts Inspection 

Check all parts for wear or damage. Service or replace as necessary. 
Rockwell recommends replacement of springs, rollers and anchor pins each time 
the brake shoes are relined or replaced.

 NOTE: Anchor pin holes must not exceed 25.63 mm (1.009 inches) in diameter. 
The distance from the center of the anchor pin hole to the center of the 
roller hole must not exceed 324.59 mm (12.779 inches).

Check the backing plate for cracks or expanded anchor pin holes. 

Check the camshaft bracket for cracked or broken welds. Check for 
correct bracket alignment.

Check anchor pins for corrosion or wear. Replace as necessary.

Check brake shoes for cracks, heat damage, loose or missing rivets and 
loose or damaged lining. Replace as necessary.

Check the brake camshaft for cracks, wear and corrosion. Check the cam 
faces, shaft bearing journals and splines. Replace damaged brake camshafts.

Check the slack adjusters:

For slack adjusters with quick connect clevis, the clevis-to-collar gap 
must not exceed 1.52 mm (0.060 inch). Replace clevis if not within 
specification.

Replace worn clevis pins. Replace clevis pin bushings with diameter 
greater than 13.5 mm (0.531 inch).

Check slack adjusters by rotating the adjusting nut counterclockwise 
with a torque wrench. Turn the gear 360 degrees. The torque must be a minimum 
of 20 Nm (15 lb-ft) for the full rotation of the gear. Service or 
replace a slack adjuster not meeting specification.

[FIGURE: DH0175A.gif]

 WARNING: TO AVOID POSSIBLE SERIOUS PERSONAL INJURY, DO NOT INSTALL A BRAKE DRUM 
NOT MEETING MANUFACTURER'S SPECIFICATION. 

Check the brake drums.

Measure the inside diameter of the brake drum at several points with a 
drum caliper or inside micrometer. Replace if the brake drum exceeds 
manufacturer's specifications.

[FIGURE: H10254A.gif]

Check dust shields for rust or distortion. Service or replace as 
necessary.

 Rockwell Front or Rear (16.5 x 5, 6, 7), Q-Series 

 Removal 

Secure vehicle by chocking the wheels, put transmission in neutral, 
cage the spring brake.

Rotate the slack adjuster adjustment nut counterclockwise until shoes 
no longer touch the brake drum.

Raise axle and remove tire, wheel and brake drum. 

Press down on the bottom brake shoe and remove the lower cam roller. 
Next, lift the top shoe and take out the top cam roller.

[FIGURE: H10255A.gif]

Lift out the shoe return spring which is now free of tension.

[FIGURE: H10256A.gif]

Swing the lower shoe back approximately 180 degrees to relieve the 
tension on the retainer springs, remove the springs and slip the shoes off the 
stepped anchor pins.

[FIGURE: H10257A.gif]

After removing shoes, completely inspect brake components, servicing as 
necessary.

Remove the slack adjuster clevis pins.

Remove retainer and washers on end of brake camshaft.

Remove the automatic slack adjuster.

Check the camshaft bracket bushing wear by moving the camshaft up and 
down and side to side. If the total movement is more than 0.76 mm (0.030 
inch), remove the brake camshaft from the camshaft bracket.

[FIGURE: H10292A.gif]

Use an appropriate driver to remove the camshaft bracket bushings and 
seals.

[FIGURE: H10293A.gif]

 Installation 

If necessary, use an appropriate driver and install new camshaft 
bracket bushings.

If the camshaft was removed, install new camshaft bracket seals. Use an 
appropriate driver and install with the seal lips pointing toward the slack 
adjuster.

[FIGURE: H10294A.gif]

Coat the camshaft splines, bushings and bearing journals with Ford Disc 
Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or equivalent meeting Ford 
specification ESA-M1C172-A.

Install the brake camshaft. It should turn by hand without binding.

Install the camshaft flatwasher and slack adjuster and fasten the slack 
adjuster in place. Add spacing washers to limit the end play to approximately 
1.57 mm (0.062 inch) and install a new snap ring.

 CAUTION: Always use all new springs. 

Install the relined or new shoes by reversing the procedure used to 
remove them.

Reconnect slack adjuster clevis to air chamber push rod. Lubricate the 
clevis pins with Ford Disc Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C172-A.

Reinstall brake drum and wheel and tire assembly.

Lube brake camshaft tube cavity with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or 
-K or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Adjust brakes as required, as described in Adjustments, Manual 
Adjustment in this section.

MAINTENANCE

Brake, Air — Cam Type

Perform the following periodic maintenance every three months or 40,225 
km (25,000 miles).

Check the condition of the foundation brakes, including brake drums, 
shoes and linings, cams, rollers, bearings, etc.

Check for structural damage of the automatic slack adjuster and 
condition of the boot for cuts, tears, etc. Replace if necessary.

After allowing brake drum to cool to room temperature, check for 
correct brake air chamber stroke.

================================================================================
PAGE 2947
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

LUBRICATION

Brake, Air — Cam Type

The automatic slack adjusters should be lubricated every 39,000 km 
(24,000 miles) or six months, whichever occurs first, more frequently under 
adverse conditions. Use the following procedure.

Locate the grease fitting on the slack adjuster. With a conventional 
grease gun, fill the inside of the slack adjuster until new grease flows from 
the grease plug hole or automatic grease relief opening.

Lubricate the slack adjuster with Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B.

Lubricate the brake camshaft splines every 39,000 km (24,000 miles) or 
12 months, whichever occurs first. Lubricate more frequently under adverse 
conditions. Use Ford Disc Brake Caliper Slide Grease D7AZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C172-A. Do not lubricate the cam 
faces.

 Section 06-08D for the Maxi-Brake II and to Section 06-08E for the MGM.

ADJUSTMENTS

Adjusters, Automatic

 Inspection 

Free stroke is the amount of slack adjuster movement required to bring 
the brake shoe and linings into contact with the brake drum. Check the slack 
adjuster free stroke as follows:

With the brakes released, measure and record the distance from the 
brake air chamber face to the center of the large clevis pin. Distance "A."

Using a lever, extend and hold the air chamber push rod at the point at 
which the brake shoe and lining is felt to come into contact with the brake 
drum.

Make the same measurement as in Step 1. Distance "B."

[FIGURE: H10290A.gif]

Subtract "A" from "B" to obtain the free stroke measurement. For a 
properly installed slack adjuster, with the brakes properly adjusted, the free 
stroke should be 10-16 mm (3/8-5/8 inches). A free stroke that is longer than 
specified is caused by a foundation brake concern. Inspect the foundation 
brakes for proper installation, loose, missing or broken parts. Service or 
replace as necessary.

================================================================================
PAGE 2950
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-08C: Brake, Air, Cam-Type

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Manual Adjustment

Rotate the slack adjuster hex extension clockwise until the brake shoe 
and lining contacts the brake drum.

Back off the slack adjuster by rotating the hex extension 1/2 turn 
counterclockwise. A loud clicking will be heard during counterclockwise 
rotation.

[FIGURE: DH0175A.gif]

With the brakes released, measure and record the distance from the face 
of the brake air chamber to the center of the large clevis pin. Distance "A."

Have an assistant make and hold a 586 kPa (85 psi) brake application. 
Allow the air chamber push rod its full travel.

Make and record the same measurement as in Step 3. Distance "B." The 
difference between "A" and "B" is the air chamber stroke.

The air chamber stroke must be within the DOT Adjusted Air Chamber 
Stroke specifications.

 DOT ADJUSTED AIR CHAMBER STROKE LIMITS

550-620 kPa (80-90 psi) Pressure in Air Chamber

 Clamp Type Air Chamber

Chamber Type (Size)

Adjust the stroke as short as possible without the brakes dragging. The
vehicle may be put out of service if the stroke is not:

9

less than 34.9 mm (1-3/8 inches)

12

less than 34.9 mm (1-3/8 inches)

16

less than 44.4 mm (1-3/4 inches)

20

less than 44.4 mm (1-3/4 inches)

24

less than 44.4 mm (1-3/4 inches)

24 long stroke

less than 50.8 mm (2 inches)

30

less than 50.8 mm (2 inches)

36

less than 57.1 mm (2-1/4 inches)

If the air chamber stroke is not within specifications, inspect the 
foundation brake system to locate loose, broken, worn, missing or improperly 
installed parts. Service or replace as necessary.

Section 06-08D: Brake, Air Chamber, Maxi-Brake II

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake, Air Chamber, Maxi-Brake II

 WARNING: BEFORE ATTEMPTING DISASSEMBLY, MAKE SURE THE SPRING IS MECHANICALLY 
CAGED. REMOVE THE PLUG AND INSTALL THE EXTERNALLY STORED T-BOLT. TURN THE 
T-BOLT 90 DEGREES CLOCKWISE UNTIL IT CONTACTS THE INTERNAL STOP. INSTALL THE 
T-BOLT RELEASE NUT AND HAND-TIGHTEN THE NUT OVER THE WASHER. DO NOT USE IMPACT 
WRENCHES AS THEY CAN DAMAGE THE ALUMINUM DIE CASTINGS AND PREVENT PROPER 
CAGING OF THE SPRING. 

The Midland Maxi-Brake II brake air chamber (used on the rear axles 
only) is much like a conventional brake air chamber. It consists of an 
emergency chamber, a service chamber and a bulkhead assembly. 

The service chamber applies the brake by air pressure and releases it 
by spring pressure when air pressure in the service brake chamber is released. 
The emergency brake in the end cap is applied by spring pressure and released 
by air pressure.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Brake Air Chamber 

 Removal 

Chock the wheels to prevent vehicle movement.

 CAUTION: To avoid damage to the brake air chamber aluminum housing, do not use 
impact tools to tighten the T-bolt nut. Turn down the T-bolt nut and tighten 
it against the washer. 

Cage the main spring with the following procedure:

Remove the T-bolt from its storage position on the brake air chamber 
housing.

Pull the weather seal plug from the end of the brake air chamber.

Insert and turn the T-bolt until the T head locks in the internal slot.

Install the washer and T-bolt release nut and hand-tighten the nut over 
the washer.

Tighten the T-bolt release nut until the T-bolt protrudes at least 76 
mm (3 inches).

Release all air pressure from the system.

Disconnect the clevis from the slack adjuster. Discard the cotter pins.

Disconnect the air lines from the brake air chamber.

Remove the brake air chamber mounting nuts and remove the brake air 
chamber from the vehicle.

 Installation 

 CAUTION: To avoid cutting the push rod too short, make sure that the main spring 
is fully caged before cutting the push rod. If installing a new brake air 
chamber, cut the new push rod to the same length as the old one. 

Install the brake air chamber on the mounting bracket. Tighten the 
mounting nuts to 136-197 Nm (100-145 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: H7073D.gif]

Remove the clevis/snap nut assembly and the jam nut from the old brake

Using new cotter pins, attach the slack adjuster to the brake air 
chamber push rod.

 NOTE: After installing the clevis, the push rod should not be less than 3 mm 
(1/8 inch) below or extend more than 1.6 mm (1/16 inch) past the end of the 
clevis threads. 

Adjust the snap nut so that the centerline of the large clevis hole is 
63-69 mm (2-1/2-2-3/4 inches) from the mounting face of the brake air chamber.

[FIGURE: H10049A.gif]

hole.

Adjust the brakes. Refer to Section 06-08C .

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Service Brake Diaphragm

 NOTE: If a new diaphragm is installed in the brake chamber on one side of the

 Disassembly 

 WARNING: BEFORE ATTEMPTING DISASSEMBLY, MAKE SURE THE SPRING IS MECHANICALLY 
CAGED. REMOVE THE PLUG AND INSTALL THE EXTERNALLY STORED T-BOLT. TURN THE 
T-BOLT 90 DEGREES CLOCKWISE UNTIL IT CONTACTS THE INTERNAL STOP. INSTALL THE 
T-BOLT RELEASE NUT AND HAND-TIGHTEN THE NUT OVER THE WASHER. DO NOT USE IMPACT 
WRENCHES AS THEY CAN DAMAGE THE ALUMINUM DIE CASTINGS AND PREVENT PROPER 
CAGING OF THE SPRING. 

 WARNING: TO AVOID RISK OF INJURY, DO NOT ATTEMPT TO REPAIR THE SPRING BRAKE 
PORTION OF THE BRAKE AIR CHAMBER. 

Scribe a mark on the non-pressure housing and bulkhead and across the 
clamp band for alignment purposes during assembly.

[FIGURE: H3774C.gif]

Remove the non-pressure housing clamp band nuts and bolts. Separate the 
clamp band halves by prying the bands off with a screwdriver. 

Remove the clevis, if still installed. 

Remove the non-pressure housing from the bulkhead. Place the housing 
down on a bench and push down on the housing. Remove the jam nut from the push 
rod and slowly allow the return spring to push up the non-pressure housing. 
Remove the return spring and push rod.

[FIGURE: H37751A.gif]

Remove the diaphragm from the bulkhead.

[FIGURE: H3776B.gif]

Inspect all components for rust and wear. If the spring shows signs of 
rust, clean with a wire brush and coat with a rust inhibitor. Replace any worn 
or damaged parts. 

 Assembly 

 WARNING: TO MAINTAIN EVEN BRAKING, DIAPHRAGMS AND SPRINGS MUST BE REPLACED IN 
AXLE SETS. 

Install a new diaphragm in the bulkhead. 

Position the push rod and return spring in the non-pressure housing. 
Push down on the housing and install the jam nut. Run the jam nut down as far 
as it will go on the push rod to make sure the return spring is properly 
seated. This will prevent return spring force from pushing apart the bulkhead 
and non-pressure housing while installing the clamp bands. A spacer may be 
used between the jam nut and non-pressure housing if necessary.

[FIGURE: H37771A.gif]

Place the assembly on the bulkhead and align the scribe marks made at 
disassembly. Install the clamp bands in alignment with the scribe marks. 
Install nuts and bolts and tighten to 22-26 Nm (16-19 lb-ft). Make sure 
the clamp bands are evenly spaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Brake Assembly 

The MGM double diaphragm brake air chamber assembly, used on rear wheel 
brakes, contains a spring applied parking brake which acts as an emergency 
brake in case of air pressure loss. This assembly is used with S-cam brakes 
only. 

The brake air chamber assembly consists of two separate air chambers, 
each having its own application and release mechanism. The only difference 
between the two chambers is that the service chamber applies the brake by air 
pressure and releases it by spring pressure; the spring brake chamber applies 
the brake by spring pressure and releases it by air pressure. 

During normal driving (brakes released), the service brakes are held in 
the released position by the diaphragm return spring in the service air 
chamber assembly. Air reservoir pressure against the spring brake chamber 
piston and diaphragm keeps the parking-emergency spring compressed.

 Normal Driving 

[FIGURE: H9915A.gif]

During normal braking (service brakes applied) air pressure from the 
brake valve working against the service brake diaphragm applies the brakes. 
Air reservoir pressure in the spring brake chamber keeps the parking-emergency 
spring compressed. Normal service brake operation is not affected by the 
spring brake. 

 Normal Service Brakes 

[FIGURE: H9916A.gif]

During parking or an emergency brake application, air is exhausted from 
the spring brake chamber permitting the parking-emergency spring to expand, 
moving the spring brake piston and the service brake push rod against the 
slack adjuster assembly to apply the brakes. 

 Parking Brake 

[FIGURE: H9917A.gif]

Loss of air pressure at the spring brake chamber will result in 
automatic application of the brakes. If it is necessary to move the vehicle 
before air pressure can be restored, the parking-emergency spring must be 
manually compressed. The procedure for manually releasing and then resetting 
the spring brake after service has been performed is described below. Do not 
drive vehicle until the air system is serviced.

 Manual Release 

[FIGURE: H9918A.gif]

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Chamber, Complete Unit 

 Removal 

Place chocks under the wheels to prevent the vehicle from moving. 

Manually cage the spring brake as described in Manual Release in the 
Adjustments portion of this section. 

Loosen the jam nut above the clevis. 

After releasing system air pressure, disconnect the air lines and the 
clevis pins. Discard the cotter pins.

Remove the mounting stud nuts and remove the unit from the mounting 
bracket. 

 Installation 

If a new unit is being installed, make sure the push rod and the clevis 
are the correct length and all ports are aligned with the air lines. New units 
are equipped with a 203 mm (8-inch) push rod. Cut the push rod the same length 
as the old unit. When cutting the push rod, the spring brake must be fully 
compressed (release bolt fully extended) as described in Manual Release in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

[FIGURE: H4038D.gif]

If necessary, remove the clevis/snap nut assembly and the jam nut from 
the old air chamber and install them on the new unit. Tighten jam nut to 45-67 
Nm (33-50 lb-ft). 

 NOTE: When installing brake air chambers to brake assemblies, chambers must 
be placed to top of slots in brake assembly bracket in normal vehicle position.

Install the unit in position on the bracket. Make sure the washers are 
on the outside of the bracket and not against the service chamber housing. 
Install the nuts and tighten to 136-196 Nm (100-145 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Service Diaphragm or Service Chamber 

 Removal 

Chock the wheels to prevent vehicle movement.

Manually cage the spring brake. Refer to Manual Release in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

 CAUTION: Pad the jaws of the locking pliers to prevent push rod damage. 

Extend the service brake push rod by applying the brake pedal or by 
pushing the slack adjuster. Clamp and hold the push rod with locking pliers.

Release system air pressure.

Disconnect the clevis from the slack adjuster. Discard the cotter pins.

[FIGURE: H4042C.gif]

Disconnect the air lines from the air chamber.

Remove the air chamber-to-air chamber bracket nuts and remove the air 
chamber from the vehicle.

Pull the one end of the breather tube out of the rubber elbow.

Make a mark across the two chamber assemblies and the clamp ring to aid 
reassembly alignment.

Remove the two clamp ring nuts and bolts. Remove the clamp ring.

Separate the non-pressure housing from the spring brake chamber assembly.

Remove the service brake diaphragm from the spring brake chamber 
assembly.

Inspect all components for cracks, corrosion or other damage. Replace 
as necessary. 

 Installation 

 WARNING: TO INCREASE BRAKING BALANCE, AIR CHAMBER DIAPHRAGMS AND SPRINGS MUST BE 
REPLACED IN AXLE SETS ONLY. 

Install the new diaphragm into the spring brake chamber assembly.

 NOTE: To help seat the clamp ring, tap around the ring with a hammer. 

Using the alignment marks made at disassembly, position the spring 
brake chamber and clamp ring on the non-pressure housing. Install the clamp 
ring bolts and nuts. Tighten the clamp ring nuts to 41-47 Nm (30-35 
lb-ft).

Insert the breather tube into the rubber elbow.

Position the air chamber on the air chamber bracket and install the air 
chamber-to-air chamber bracket washers and nuts. Tighten the nuts to 136-196 
Nm (100-145 lb-ft).

Apply Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent 
meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-AZ and ESR-M18P7-A on the air line 
fittings. Install the fittings and tighten to 33 Nm (24 lb-ft) maximum. 
Position the fittings by turning in the tightening direction only.

Using new cotter pins, attach the clevis to the slack adjuster. 

Remove the locking pliers from the push rod.

Build up air system pressure and test for leaks.

With air system at normal pressure, uncage the spring brake. Remove and 
store the T-bolt and nut.

Press the weather seal into the hole in the spring brake chamber.

Adjust the brakes. Refer to Section 06-08C .

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock, Front and Rear

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Description 

The anti-lock brake system (ABS) is optional on F-Series with air brake 
 systems. ABS provides precise axle braking control during aggressive braking 
and prevents wheel lockup. On vehicles equipped with ABS, steering control, 
stability and safety are maintained when the brakes are applied. In addition, 
the stopping distance can be reduced.

The particular system covered is called the full vehicle ABS system or 
two-channel system.

The major components of a two-channel (full vehicle ABS) system are a 
control module, two front wheel speed sensors, two drive axle wheel speed 
sensors, a rear modulator/relay valve and a front modulator valve. 

[FIGURE: H9484C.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

2B372

Front Wheel ABS Speed Sensors

2

4B409

Rear Wheel ABS Speed Sensor

3

—

Rear Modulator/Relay Valve

4

2C219

ABS Module Assy

5

2B373

ABS Modulator Valve

The control module is the computer or "brain" controlling the ABS 
system. It is an electronic device that receives electrical input signals 
from several anti-lock system components. Based on these signals, the control 
module is programmed to send output signals to control other ABS components 
during aggressive braking. The control module has a diagnostics window that 
helps to troubleshoot the system. The ABS system uses an EC-14 control module. 

[FIGURE: H9485B.gif]

Wheel speed sensors send wheel speed signals to the control module. 
ABS systems have four wheel speed sensors: two for the front axle and two for 
the drive axle. 

[FIGURE: DH0346A.gif]

The rear axle brakes on the ABS system are controlled by the M-12 rear 
modulator/relay valve. Inside the rear modulator/relay valve there are two 
solenoids. These solenoids are controlled by the control module.

[FIGURE: H9487B.gif]

The control module is mounted on top of the M-12 rear modulator/relay 
valve. On the ABS system, which uses an EC-14 control module, this assembly is 
called an MC-14. 

[FIGURE: H9488E.gif]

The front modulator is designed to prevent lockup of the brakes on the 
front axle. This modulator is called the M-21. Like the rear modulator, it has 
two solenoids which are controlled by the EC-14 control module.

[FIGURE: H9489B.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 2967
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock, Front and Rear

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Inputs/Outputs

All components in the ABS system either send or receive a signal from 
the control module. Components that send signals to the control module are 
module inputs and components that receive signals are module outputs.

 ABS Component Layout 

[FIGURE: DH0347B.gif]

[FIGURE: H8787A.gif]

 Module Inputs 

Module inputs are the components of an anti-lock brake system that send 
signals to the control module. Wheel speed sensors are an example of 
components that provide input signals. In addition to wheel speed sensors, ABS 
inputs to the control module include electrical power and the stoplight switch.

 Electrical Power 

Vehicle power is continually input to the control module from the 
ignition switch through a fuse or circuit breaker. The electrical ground for 
the control module is the vehicle chassis. The system will operate normally if 
voltage is between 10 to 17 volts.

 Stoplight Switch 

The stoplight switch sends a 12-volt signal to the EC-14 that indicates 
that the brakes have been applied. If the signal is not available, the EC-14 
will still function. 

 Module Outputs 

Module outputs are the components of an anti-lock brake system that 
receive signals from the control module. Modulators are an example of an 
output component. In addition to modulators, ABS output signals from the 
control module include the anti-lock warning light LEDs (diagnostic window), 
engine/transmission retarder, and the serial link.

 Anti-Lock Warning Light 

The main components in the anti-lock warning light electrical circuit 
consist of:

dash-mounted amber ABS warning light

ABS warning light relay

control module

The amber ABS warning light is located in the instrument cluster. When 
the key is turned to RUN, the amber light blinks twice and stays on as the 
control module performs a self test.

If the amber light does not blink, it means that a fault has been 
detected. The self test is completed when vehicle speed exceeds 16 km/h (10 
mph) and the light goes out. To eliminate false anti-lock, the control module 
will shut down and turn on the amber light if it sees too much variation in 
wheel speed sensor signals after 15 seconds (front to rear or left to right). 
This condition can be caused by towing, dynamometer or accelerating on an icy 
surface. If this occurs, the vehicle must slow down or stop and then 
accelerate normally. When the control module receives uniform wheel speed 
signals, the anti-lock function will be reactivated and the amber light will 
be turned off.

The ABS warning light relay is located near the circuit breaker panel. 
Voltage is supplied to the relay through the fuse and ignition switch.

When the key is turned to RUN, current flows through the relay and ABS 
warning light.

To turn the ABS warning light off, the control module grounds the relay 
coil. This allows current to flow through the relay coil winding and creates a 
magnetic field. The magnetic field around the coil opens the relay contacts 
and turns the amber warning light off.

 LEDs, Diagnostic Window 

A self test is performed each time the key is turned to RUN. The 
flashing amber warning light indicates that the self test is in progress. 
During this time the control module sends out an electrical signal to each of 
the windings in the wheel speed sensors and modulator valves and brake switch. 
Excessive electrical resistance, opens, shorts or grounds in any of these 
circuits (including the wiring harness) will affect the self test signal and 
turn on a combination of LED (light emitting diode) lights on the control 
module.

If any single ABS component fails, the dash-mounted anti-lock warning 
light will illuminate. A troubleshooting LED on the control module will also 
light. Depending on the type of failure and where it occurs, the control 
module will continue anti-lock function, but at a lower performance level, or 
it will disable all or some of the anti-lock functions on the vehicle. When 
the anti-lock function is disabled, the affected axle(s) will revert to 
standard air braking.

If a single speed sensor fails on one axle, the system will not be 
disabled. The remaining sensor will be used to continue anti-lock operation, 
but with slightly less efficiency.

The ABS will try to provide the vehicle with the best possible braking 
and stability, even after a failure has occurred. Standard air braking will 
still be available on those brakes where the anti-lock has been disabled.

The ABS system will completely shut down if:

electrical power is below or above the 10 to 17 volt operating range.

a control module failure is detected.

two or more failures are detected regardless of where the concern 
exists, or the modulator fails on the rear axle(s).

If a failure is detected on the front modulator, only the front ABS 
will be disabled.

When servicing an ABS system, observe the following precautions:

It is generally advisable to replace a wire harness rather than repair 
individual wires in the harness. If a splice repair must be made, it is 
important that the splice be properly soldered with a rosin flux (not acid 
based) and made waterproof. 

Do not pierce wire insulation when checking for continuity. Check for 
power, ground or continuity by disconnecting the connector and testing the 
individual pins or sockets in the connector(s). 

Always check the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for wire 
and connector identification. 

While the retarder disable and serial link connections (three total) 
are present on all control modules, they are not always used.

================================================================================
PAGE 2968
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 06-09: Brake System, Anti-Lock, Front and Rear

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Operation

The wheel speed sensors send signals to the control module. These 
signals tell the control module how fast each wheel is rotating. When the 
driver applies the brakes, the control module uses these signals to detect if 
one or more wheels on the front or rear axle is about to lock up. The control 
module signals the front and rear modulators to adjust air pressure to the 
service brakes to control wheel lockup. The control module and modulator are 
able to apply and exhaust air the same way as if the driver was pumping the 
brakes.

 Rear Brake Application 

The rear brakes on the ABS system are controlled by the control module 
and the M-12 rear modulator/relay valve. The M-12 rear modulator/relay valve 
delivers equal brake application pressure to the service chambers on the rear 
axles during normal braking. Two wheel speed sensors on the rear axle send 
changes in wheel acceleration and deceleration to the control module. Based on 
this information, the control module activates two solenoids in the M-12 rear 
modulator/relay valve. When the solenoids are activated air is exhausted from 
the service brakes to prevent wheel lockup.

 Front Brake Application 

The front axle (steering axle) brakes are controlled by the control 
module and the M-21 front modulator. During normal braking when the brakes are 
applied, air passes through the M-21 front modulator to the front axle service 
chambers. Two wheel speed sensors on the front axle send changes in wheel 
acceleration and deceleration to the control module. When ABS braking is 
required, the control module activates the M-21 front modulator solenoids to 
control the air pressure to the front service brakes.

 Control Module, Anti-Lock Brake 

Wheel speed information is provided to the control module (EC-14) by a 
wiring harness from individual wheel speed sensors. The control module 
receives and interprets all speed signals at the same time. During aggressive 
braking, the control module uses the modulator to regulate air pressure to the 
service brakes based on information from the wheel speed sensors. The brake 
switch also provides braking information.

The EC-14 control modules has self-test capabilities and a diagnostic 
display window for troubleshooting.

The EC-14 self test and diagnostic circuitry continuously checks for 
proper operation of the entire anti-lock system. If a circuit or component 
concern is detected, one or more LEDs (light emitting diodes) in the 
diagnostic window will be turned on along with the dash-mounted warning light.

 Multiple Faults 

The LEDs will only show one fault at a time. After correcting the first 
fault (and clearing the first fault code with the RESET function) the second 
fault will be displayed. Intermittent faults, however, must be recreated in 
order to reactivate second fault display.

 EC-14 Control Module 

The EC-14 has a 30-pin connector. It monitors the speeds of four wheels 
and controls the braking on two axles.

The EC-14 has the following nine LEDs:

FRONT (front component)

MID (middle) (see following note)

REAR (rear component)

RIGHT (right component)

LEFT (left component)

MOD (modulator)

SENS (wheel speed sensor)

ECU (control module)

VOLT (voltage to control module)

 NOTE: The MID LED is not used in the diagnostic process for the EC-14. It 
will, however, light when a magnet is placed on the RESET switch in the 
diagnostic window.

[FIGURE: H8790B.gif]

 M-12 Rear Modulator/Relay Valve 

The purpose of the M-12 rear modulator/relay valve is to modify driver 
applied air pressure to the service brakes. It is a combination valve that has 
two components: a standard relay valve and solenoids (inlet and exhaust) which 
rapidly apply and exhaust air during an ABS stop. It is located between the 
brake pedal and the rear brake air chambers. It replaces the standard drive 
axle relay valve used to speed up the application and release of the rear axle 
brakes. The M-12 has the following three air connections:

SUP — supply air from the reservoir

DEL — delivery to the rear brake actuators

CON — air pressure from the brake valve

 NOTE: Do not remove or tamper with plugged port on solenoid body. It will 
disable the anti-lock system.

[FIGURE: H8788C.gif]

 M-21 Front Modulator Valve 

The M-21 is a high capacity, on/off air valve that has two electrical 
solenoids that are controlled by the EC-14. The M-21 has one exhaust and one 
supply solenoid. Each solenoid winding has between 3.5 and 5 ohms of 
resistance. The solenoids are connected to the EC-14 by a three-wire 
connector. One wire supplies source voltage (+) to both windings. The 
remaining two wires are used by the EC-14 to control the supply and exhaust 
solenoids. The M-21 has the following three ports:

SUP — air pressure from the brake valve

DEL — delivery to the front brake actuators

EXH — air exhaust during anti-lock control

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Brake System, Anti-Lock

 Inspection and Verification 

 General 

While the diagnostic display locates a specific area, it is still 
necessary to confirm whether the concern resides in the component itself or 
the wiring. Basically, the troubleshooting procedure that follows is devoted 
to narrowing the concern to either the wiring or a specific anti-lock 
component. It should be noted however that all troubleshooting begins by 
observing the anti-lock warning light on the dash. All troubleshooting should 
begin by first performing Pinpoint Test A: Initial Start-up Procedure and 
following the directions contained in it. 

To assist the troubleshooting technician in keeping track of the 
procedure and also to provide a record of the services performed, use a 
troubleshooting record. Refer to Troubleshooting Tips in the Diagnosis and 
Testing portion of this section.

 Troubleshooting Tips 

No voltage or resistance tests are performed at the control module. All 
voltage and resistance tests are performed by beginning at the wire harness 
half of the connector and moving away from the control module toward an 
anti-lock system component (modulator, wheel speed sensor, etc.). 

Record all findings and the action taken while troubleshooting on a 
troubleshooting record sheet. The troubleshooting sheet should be filed in the 
vehicle maintenance folder for future reference and comparison. 

 Troubleshooting Record Sheet 

[FIGURE: CH8792A.gif]

 Safety 

 WARNING: WHERE CIRCUMSTANCES REQUIRE THAT THE ENGINE BE IN OPERATION, EXTREME 
CAUTION SHOULD BE USED TO PREVENT PERSONAL INJURY RESULTING FROM CONTACT WITH 
MOVING, ROTATING, LEAKING, HEATED OR ELECTRICALLY CHARGED COMPONENTS. 

When working in the engine compartment, the engine should be shut off.

Park the vehicle on a level surface. Apply the parking brakes, then 
chock the wheels. Stop the engine when working around the vehicle. 

Drain the air pressure from all reservoirs before beginning any work on 
the vehicle. 

Never connect or disconnect a hose or line containing pressure; it may 
whip. Never remove a component or plug unless you are certain all system 
pressure has been depleted. 

Never exceed recommended pressures and always wear safety glasses. 

Do not attempt to install, remove, disassemble or assemble a component 
until you have read and thoroughly understand the recommended procedures. Use 
only the proper tools and observe all precautions pertaining to use of those 
tools. 

Replacement hardware, tubing, hose fittings, etc., should be of 
equivalent size, type and strength as original equipment and be designed 
specifically for such applications and systems. 

Components with stripped threads or damaged parts should be replaced 
rather than serviced. Service requiring machining or welding should not be 
attempted. 

Prior to returning the vehicle to service, make sure all components and 
systems are restored to their proper operating condition. Repeat initial 
check-out procedure. 

 Pin Tests 

When performing checks at the control module connector pins, be careful 
not to damage the pins. Also, check the pins for corrosion and damage. Make 
sure the terminals and pins make good contact.

 Ground Tests 

Make sure all ground connections are tight and that all ground voltage 
measurements are zero volts.

 Resistance Tests 

Make sure the wiring harnesses are tight and in good condition without 
any damaged insulation or frayed wires. Measure resistance or continuity at 
the control module to verify the condition of the wiring harness and component.

[FIGURE: H9501C.gif]

 Component Resistance 

If the resistance or continuity test results are not within 
specifications, measure the resistance of each component at the connector. If 
the resistance is not correct, check the component and service or replace the 
parts as necessary.

[FIGURE: H9502A.gif]

 Checking Continuity, Power and Ground 

When checking for continuity, do not pierce the wire insulation. Check 
for power, ground or continuity by disconnecting the connector and testing the 
individual pins or sockets in the connector(s).

 Retarder Disable and Serial Link Connections 

The retarder disable and serial link connections are on all control 
modules but are not always used.

connector numbers in the pinpoint tests.

electrical pinpoint tests.

 Pinpoint Tests 

There are nine LEDs plus a magnetically actuated reset switch in the 
control module diagnostic window. The first five LEDs locate a concern to a 
specific area of the vehicle while the last four indicate the component or its 
wiring. The LEDs are controlled by the control module and are either on or off 
depending upon their monitor function. 

 NOTE: Right and left, front and rear are determined from the driver seat. 
Left front is therefore the corner closest to the driver. 

 NOTE: The MID LED shown in the chart is not used in the diagnostic process 
for the control module. However, it will light when a magnet is placed on the 
RESET switch in the diagnostic window. 

LED

Description

FRONT

 (See Note)

Red LED

 Front LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on in order to indicate the 
location of a worn or damaged component or its wiring. It will light in 
conjunction with either the RIGHT or LEFT LED and the SENS LED when indicating 
a speed sensor malfunction. The FRONT LED will also light in conjunction with 
the MOD LED to indicate that the front modulator or its wiring has 
malfunctioned. 

 Mid LED 

This red LED is not used in troubleshooting the control module and 
should light only when a magnet is held on the RESET switch. 

 Rear LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on in order to indicate the 
location of a worn or damaged component or its wiring. It will light in 
conjunction with either the RIGHT or LEFT LED and the SENS LED when indicating 
a speed sensor malfunction. The REAR LED will also light in conjunction with 
the MOD LED to indicate that the rear modulator/controller has malfunctioned. 

 Right LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on in order to indicate the 
location of a worn or damaged component or its wiring. It will light in 
conjunction with either the FRONT or REAR LED and SENS LED. This LED should 
not light when a MOD LED is on. 

 Left LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on in order to indicate the 
location of a worn or damaged component or its wiring. It will light in 
conjunction with either the FRONT or REAR LED and SENS LED. This LED should 
not light when a MOD LED is on. 

 Mod LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on to indicate a permanent or 
intermittent open or short circuit in the solenoids of one of the two 
modulators or the wiring connecting them to the system. The MOD LED will 
illuminate in conjunction with either the FRONT or REAR LED. 

 Sens LED 

This red LED illuminates and latches on to indicate permanent or 
intermittent failure. The failures indicated are open or shorted wheel speed 
sensor, open or shorted wheel speed sensor wiring, wheel speed signal not 
present or not to specification. The SENS LED will illuminate in conjunction 
with either the FRONT or REAR LED and either the RIGHT or LEFT LED. 

 ECU LED 

This red LED, when illuminated, indicates that the control module has 
failed. It is latched on for all control module failures except low voltage. 
For voltages less than 10, the LED illuminates to indicate the controller is 
inoperative. However, when the voltage again exceeds 11 volts the LED will 
turn off automatically. 

 Volt LED 

This green LED illuminates and remains on during vehicle operation to 
indicate that vehicle power is reaching the control module. If vehicle power 
is out of range for proper operation (below 10 or above 17 volts), this LED 
will flash until power is brought into range. The VOLT LED will also flash if 
a marginal low voltage condition existed at the time of an anti-lock event. 

 Reset 

Beneath the RESET area of the window display is a magnetically 
sensitive switch that is used to reset the diagnostic system. The device will 
respond to a magnet which has strength sufficient to lift a 3-ounce weight. 
Holding a magnet against the RESET will cause all LEDs to light during the 
time the magnet is against it.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Control Module, Anti-Lock Brake

 Removal 

Make sure all system air pressure has been relieved. Identify and 
remove all air lines connected to the rear modulator. 

Disconnect the electrical connector from the control module. 

Note and mark the mounting position of the modulator controller 
assembly on the vehicle. Loosen, remove and save the nuts on the mounting 
hardware that attaches the modulator control assembly bracket to the vehicle. 
Remove the modulator controller assembly from the vehicle. 

Remove any contamination from the exterior of the assembly, making sure 
to keep the contamination away from the open ports. 

 NOTE: If gasket is damaged during removal, replace it with a new gasket.

Note and mark the position of the control module relative to the rear 
modulator. Remove and retain the four hex capscrews that secure the control 
module to the modulator. Carefully separate the control module from the 
modulator enough to expose the wire harness that connects both units 
electrically. Disconnect the wire harness by separating the four-pin connector 
at the control module. Peel the gasket from the modulator and retain for 
reuse. 

 Installation 

After noting the positioning marks made prior to disassembly, reconnect 
the modulator wire harness to the control module. Position the gasket on the 
control module and secure the control module to the modulator using the four 
capscrews. Tighten the capscrews to 6-9 Nm (53-80 lb-in). 

Mount the modulator controller assembly on the vehicle and orient it in 
the position marked prior to removal. 

Reconnect all air lines. 

Reconnect the electrical connector to the modulator controller. 

Test the modulator controller assembly for operation and air leakage 
prior to placing the vehicle in service. 

Perform Pinpoint Test A: Initial Start-up Procedure in the Diagnosis 
and Testing portion of this section. Make sure the anti-lock system is 
operating properly.

Wheel Speed Sensor, Front

 Removal

Remove the sensor from the steering knuckle, using a twisting motion if 
necessary. Do not pull on the cable.

Disconnect any fasteners that hold the sensor cable to other components.

Disconnect the sensor cable from the chassis harness.

[FIGURE: H9705A.gif]

Install any fasteners used to hold the sensor cable in place.

Push the sensor spring clip into the bushing in the steering knuckle 
until it stops.

Push the sensor completely into the sensor spring clip until it stops 
against the tooth wheel.

Remove the chocks from the rear tires.

MAINTENANCE

Preventative Maintenance 

Every three months, 25,000 miles or 900 operating hours, perform the 
following: 

Check all wiring and connectors to make sure they are secure and free 
from visible damage. 

Although the control module incorporates a diagnostic routine, the LED 
display should be inspected to make sure they are functional. With the vehicle 
ignition on, a magnet (800 gauss; capable of picking up 3 ounces) held to the 
diagnostic window reset switch, should cause all of the LEDs to illuminate. If 
one or more of the LEDs does not illuminate and the anti-lock warning light on 
the dash indicates the system is functioning properly, the non-illuminated 
LED(s) should be noted for future reference. Although the diagnostic 
capabilities will be limited, the system will continue to function as 
designed. 

Road test the vehicle by making an anti-lock stop from a vehicle speed 
of 32 km/h (20 mph). When an anti-lock stop is made, the modulator solenoids 
pulsate and an audible burst of air can be heard from outside of the cab. The 
wheels should not enter a prolonged "lock" condition.
