DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Description — 4-Channel ABS

 Anti-Lock Warning Light — 4-Channel ABS 

The main components in the anti-lock warning light electrical circuit 
consist of:

dash-mounted amber ABS warning light

ABS warning light relay

control module

The amber ABS warning light is located in the instrument cluster. When 
the key is turned to RUN, the amber light will flash, then go out as the 
control module performs a self test.

If the amber light stays on, it means that a fault has been detected. 
The self test is completed when vehicle speed exceeds 8-11 km/h (5-7 mph) and 
the light goes out. To eliminate false anti-lock, the control module will shut 
down and turn on the amber light if it sees too much variation in wheel speed 
sensor signals after 15 seconds (front to rear or left to right). This 
condition can be caused by towing, dynamometer or accelerating on an icy 
surface. If this occurs, the vehicle must slow down or stop and then 
accelerate normally. When the control module receives uniform wheel speed 
signals, the anti-lock function will be reactivated and the amber light will 
be turned off.

The ABS warning light relay is located near the circuit breaker panel. 
Voltage is supplied to the relay through the fuse and ignition switch.

When the key is turned to RUN, current flows through the relay and ABS 
warning light.

To turn the ABS warning light off, the control module grounds the relay 
coil. This allows current to flow through the relay coil winding and creates a 
magnetic field. The magnetic field around the coil opens the relay contacts 
and turns the amber warning light off.

Modulator

Fit retaining clip into groove in neck of modulator control. Clip tabs 
must face toward transmission. Tighten clip retaining bolt to 18-22 Nm 
(13-16 lb-ft). 

Attach cable hub to mounting bracket and tighten retaining nuts to 
20-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft). 

Position modulator lever and washers on the fuel pump lever shaft. 
Install retaining snap ring. 

With fuel pump lever set at wide-open throttle, turn the kick-down 
adjuster to provide 3 mm (1/8 inch) between modulator lever and fuel pump lever.

Set fuel pump indent lever to wide-open throttle position. Push 
modulator cable rod end to internal stop and check for a clearance between 
modulator lever and fuel pump lever. Readjust at idle if clearance does not 
exist. In wide-open throttle, the modulator must be within 3 mm (1/8 inch) of 
it's stop position (full indent). 

Check for proper return to idle and ease of movement. 

Once adjustment is complete, tighten adjuster lock nuts to 5-7 
Nm (44-62 lb-in). 

To adjust the modulator, rotate governor shaft to WOT position. 

Push modulator cable end to stop and adjust clevis until it can be 
installed on transmission control shift lever assembly. 

Check for proper operation.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Fluid Drain and Refill Procedure

If the fluid is cold, operate the transmission until a normal operating 
temperature of 71°-93°C (160°-200°F) is reached.

Remove drain plug from the transmission pan and allow the fluid to drain.

When the fluid has stopped draining, reinstall drainplug and tighten to 
20-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft).

Remove the dipstick and pour approximately 17.5 liters (37 pints) of 
transmission fluid into the transmission through the filler tube. Use fluid 
type C-4 or equivalent meeting Ford specification WSA-M2C195A.

With the vehicle standing level, apply the parking brake and place the 
selector lever in N. Operate the engine at idle speed.

Shift the selector lever through all the range positions to make sure 
that warm fluid is distributed throughout the transmission. Return the 
selector lever to N.

Check the fluid level on the dipstick. The safe operating level is 
between the two COLD marks on the dipstick. If fluid level is low, add 
sufficient fluid to bring level to the bottom COLD mark. If level is too high, 
drain excess fluid to proper level. Fluid temperature should be 16-49°C 
(60-120°F) for cold check.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission 

 Removal 

From inside the vehicle, remove the right and left door sill scuff 
plate screws and remove the plates. Position the floor covering out of the 
way. Remove the bolts securing the transmission access cover to the floor pan 
and remove the cover. 

Open the hood and disconnect the coil wire (7.0L). 

Remove exhaust flanges and disconnect heated oxygen sensor (7.0L). 

Remove right side exhaust rear hanger (7.0L). 

On a one-piece driveshaft, disconnect the shaft from the yoke at the 
transmission. On a two-piece driveshaft, disconnect the coupling shaft from 
the yoke and remove the center support bearing bracket. Move the forward end 
of the driveshaft or coupling shaft out of the way. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Place a drain pan under the transmission. Remove the drainplug from the 
transmission and allow fluid to drain. Then disconnect the filler tube from 
the transmission pan. 

Disconnect the speedometer wiring from the rear of the transmission. On 
F-Series only, unplug the park/neutral position and backup light switch.

Disconnect the fluid cooler lines at the transmission. 

Remove heat shield from left side of transmission (7.0L). 

Disconnect the vacuum line from the modulator, if so equipped (7.0L). 

Remove the modulator retainer bolt and remove the retainer. Remove the 
modulator and valve actuating rod from the case. 

Disconnect fluid fill tube. 

Disconnect the shift cable from the manual lever at the transmission. 

Remove the two bolts securing the shift cable bracket to the 
transmission and position the cable and bracket out of the way. 

Remove the inspection cover from the bottom front side of the flywheel 
housing. 

Remove the six torque converter-to-flywheel retaining bolts. If 
required, turn the crankshaft manually (only after disconnecting the coil 
wire). 

Remove four upper and two lower converter housing-to-flywheel housing 
retaining bolts. 

Remove the bolts and nuts securing the two rear engine supports to the 
crossmember. Remove the lower insulators and flatwashers. 

Loosen the front engine support bolts. 

Position a transmission jack, such as Rotunda Truck Transmission Jack 
164-R3510 or equivalent, under the transmission and secure the transmission to 
the jack with a safety chain. 

Place a jack under the engine, then raise both jacks to take the weight 
off the crossmember. 

Remove the two upper engine rear support insulators from the 
crossmember. 

Remove the bolts securing the engine rear support brackets to the 
transmission and remove the brackets. 

With both jacks supporting the engine and transmission, remove the 
remaining converter housing-to-flywheel housing retaining bolts. 

 WARNING: THE TORQUE CONVERTER ASSEMBLY IS NOT SECURED TO THE TRANSMISSION. IT 
CAN FALL OUT IF THE TRANSMISSION IS TILTED FORWARD, CAUSING DAMAGE TO THE 
CONVERTER AND POSSIBLY CAUSING PERSONAL INJURY. IF THE TRANSMISSION IS TO BE 
TRANSPORTED OR SHIPPED, RETAINING BRACKETS SHOULD BE ATTACHED TO THE CONVERTER 
AND HOUSING TO HOLD THE CONVERTER IN PLACE. 

Pull the transmission rearward until the torque converter housing 
contacts the body sheet metal. Then tilt the rear of the transmission up until 
the bottom of the converter housing clears the crossmember. Lower the assembly 
and remove it from under the vehicle. If necessary, raise the rear of the 
truck to permit the transmission to clear the frame.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Prior to installing the transmission, the flexplate must be checked for 
runout. The maximum TIR should be 0.762 mm (0.030 inch). Also, flywheel 
housing transmission mounting face alignment inspection should be made of the 
engine flywheel housing transmission surface. The face and bore runout should 
not exceed 0.203 mm (0.008 inch) TIR. 

 WARNING: REMOVE SHIPPING BRACKETS AND ATTACHING HARDWARE IF SO EQUIPPED. THE 
CONVERTER WILL BE LOOSE IN THE ASSEMBLY. USE CARE DURING INSTALLATION SO THE 
CONVERTER DOES NOT FALL OUT WHEN THE TRANSMISSION ASSEMBLY IS TILTED. 

Position the torque converter to the transmission, engaging the turbine 
shaft with the converter turbine, the stator shaft with the stator and the hub 
with the oil pump drive gear. 

With the converter properly installed, place the transmission on the 
jack. Secure the transmission to the jack with a safety chain. 

Raise the converter and transmission on the jack, then move the 
assembly into position over the crossmember. Align the holes in the converter 
with the holes in the flywheel. 

Install six converter-to-flywheel retaining bolts (three on each side). 
Tighten the bolts to 42-56 Nm (32-41 lb-ft). 

Lower the engine jack and remove it from under the vehicle. 

Position the engine rear support brackets to the sides of the 
transmission and secure with the retaining bolts. Tighten to 53-62 Nm 
(39-46 lb-ft). 

Position the two upper engine rear support insulators on the 
crossmember. Position the lower insulators and flatwashers to the crossmember 
and install the rear support-to-crossmember bolts and nuts. Tighten the bolts 
to 102-142 Nm (75-105 lb-ft). 

Lower the transmission jack and remove it from under the vehicle. 

Tighten the front engine support bolts to 102-142 Nm (75-105 
lb-ft). 

Install six adapter ring-to-flexplate bolts. Tighten bolts to 47-54 
Nm (35-40 lb-ft). If required, turn crankshaft manually.

Install the cover on the bottom front side of the flywheel housing.

Position the shift cable bracket to the transmission and install the 
retaining bolts. 

Connect the shift cable to the manual lever at the transmission. 

Install the modulator actuating rod and modulator into the case. 
Install the modulator retainer and secure with the retaining bolt. Tighten the 
bolt securely.

Install the heat shield. 

Connect the vacuum line to the modulator, if so equipped (gas engine 
only). 

Connect the fluid cooler lines to the transmission case. 

Connect the speed sensor wiring. On F-Series only, connect the 
park/neutral position and backup light switch connector. 

Connect the fluid fill tube to the fluid pan. Tighten the nut to 95-108 
Nm (70-80 lb-ft). 

Install the driveshaft, or the center support bearing bracket and the 
coupling shaft, if so equipped. Connect the driveshaft or coupling shaft to 
the yoke. Tighten all bolts and nuts to specifications. Refer to Section 05-01 . 

Install exhaust. 

Connect heated oxygen sensor (gas engine only). 

Position the transmission access covers to the floorpan and secure with 
the retaining bolts. Reposition the floor covering. Install the door sill 
scuff plates and secure with the retaining screws. 

Connect coil wire (gas engine only). 

Replace fluid filter. Refer to Section 07-02 .

Fill transmission. Refer to Transmission Drain and Refill Procedure in 
the Removal and Installation portion of this section. 

Add enough automatic transmission fluid to the converter and 
transmission to bring the fluid up to a level between the bottom two COLD 
marks on the dipstick with the engine at idle and transmission in neutral. 

Check the transmission, converter assembly and fluid cooler lines for 
leaks.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Universal Joint Flange 

 Removal 

The transmission can be placed in a horizontal position on the sump pan.

Remove flange retaining bolt with washer and O-ring seal. Do not remove 
washer and O-ring from the bolt.

Remove the flange. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: Do not allow the output shaft to turn until the flange is installed, 
seated and the retaining bolt has been tightened. If the output shaft is 
allowed to rotate, damage to the pilot tube or governor will result. 

Lubricate the output seal with Multi-Purpose Grease DOAZ-19584-AA or 
equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M1C159A and ESB-M1C93-A. 

Install the output flange using a 1/2-20-inch UNF bolt, flange 
retaining plate, spacer and nut as installation tools. The length of the bolt 
and spacer will vary depending on the type of flange being installed. 

During installation, exercise care to avoid damage to the seal journal 
or the oil seal. Inspect the flange seal journal for nicks or scratches and 
seal for cuts and tears. 

Seat the flange by tightening the 1/2-20-inch nut. Remove the 
installation bolt, nut, plate and spacer. Install retaining bolt including 
O-ring seal and washer. 

Tighten the bolt to 139-164 Nm (103-121 lb-ft). 

Rotate flange by hand to check for binding or interference.

ADJUSTMENTS

Selector Lever Linkage

With the engine stopped, position the transmission selector lever in 
the R position, fully counterclockwise.

Disconnect the shift cable sleeve at the transmission control arm.

Shift the transmission control arm to R (all the way forward and upward).

With the transmission control arm in the R position, adjust the sleeve 
until it freely enters into the hole of the control arm.

Connect the sleeve to the control arm with the flatwashers, spring 
washer and cotter pin.

Operate the selector lever in all positions to make sure that the 
control arm at the transmission is in full detent in all gear ranges. It may 
be necessary to readjust the sleeve slightly to obtain the detent position in 
all drive ranges.

ADJUSTMENTS

Flywheel Housing Alignment

Whenever the flywheel housing has been replaced, or when the original 
housing is to be used on another engine, check the alignment of the housing 
bore and rear face with the engine crankshaft.

Check the mating surfaces of the engine and the flywheel housing for 
raised metal, paint, nicks or burrs. Remove any marks or material that would 
affect alignment.

Position the flywheel housing on the two dowel pins in the engine. Bolt 
the housing in place.

Check the runout of the flywheel housing bore and rear face with Dial 
Indicator/Magnetic Base D78P-4201-B or equivalent mounted on the engine 
crankshaft. If the total indicator reading of the bore runout exceeds 0.203 mm 
(0.008 inch), or if the total indicator reading of the rear face runout 
exceeds 0.203 mm (0.008 inch), repeat the check with another housing.

 CAUTION: Be careful not to drill the upper dowel pin too deeply as the dowel pin 
is in a blind hole which can break through into the water jacket or cylinder 
wall. 

If either runout on the housing checked is not within limits, remove 
the two dowel pins from the engine.

Bolt the flywheel housing in place without dowel pins, then adjust the 
housing to get the correct bore runout. Tighten the bolts and ream the dowel 
pin holes large enough for oversize dowel pins.

Check the runout with the new oversize dowel pins in place, and with 
the mounting bolts tightened to 55-61 Nm (41-45 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Modulator, MT Transmission 

 NOTE: Before performing any adjustments on modulator, the throttle linkage 
must be adjusted first. Refer to Section 10-02 .

 Removal 

Remove the bolt and modulator retainer clip from the side of the 
transmission. 

Remove the modulator from the transmission. 

Remove the snap ring from the fuel pump lever shaft. 

Remove the modulator lever from the fuel pump lever shaft. 

Loosen the cable hub retaining nuts from the mounting bracket and 
remove the lever, modulator and cable assembly from the engine. 

 Modulator Assembly, MT-Series Transmissions

 Installation 

Lubricate modulator shaft O-ring with the appropriate automatic 
transmission fluid and fit on neck of modulator control. 

Position modulator in transmission mounting opening. Make sure 
modulator valve actuating rod is in place in transmission. 

Rotate modulator control until modulator cable is pointing 40 to 50 
degrees upward from horizontal. 

Fit retaining clip into groove in neck of modulator control. Clip tabs 
must face toward transmission. Tighten clip retaining bolt to 18-22 Nm 
(13-16 lb-ft). 

Attach cable hub to mounting bracket and tighten retaining nuts to 
20-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft). 

Position modulator lever and washers on the fuel pump lever shaft. 
Install retaining snap ring. 

Adjust the modulator. 

With fuel pump lever set at idle position, turn adjuster to provide 3 
mm (0.12 inch) between modulator lever and fuel pump lever. 

Set fuel pump lever to wide-open throttle position. Push modulator 
cable rod end to internal stop and check for a clearance between modulator 
lever and fuel pump lever. Readjust at idle if clearance does not exist. 

Check for proper return to idle and ease of movement. 

Once adjustment is complete, tighten adjuster lock nuts to 5-7 
Nm (44-62 lb-in).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Fluid Drain and Refill Procedure

If the fluid is cold, operate the transmission until a normal operating 
temperature (71°-93°C [160°-200°F]) is reached. 

Remove drain plug from the transmission pan and allow the fluid to 
drain. 

When the fluid has stopped draining, reinstall drain plug and tighten 
to 20-27 Nm (15-20 lb-ft). 

Replace fluid filter. Refer to Section 07-02 .

Remove the dipstick and pour approximately 14.2 liters (15 quarts) of 
Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent into the 
transmission through the filler tube. 

With the vehicle standing level, apply the parking brake and place the 
selector lever in N. Operate the engine at idle speed. 

Shift the selector lever through all the range positions to make sure 
that fluid is distributed throughout the transmission. Return the selector 
lever to N. 

Check the fluid level on the dipstick. The safe operating level is 
between the two COLD marks on the dipstick. If fluid level is low, add 
sufficient fluid to bring level to the bottom COLD mark. If level is too high, 
drain excess fluid to proper level. 

Fluid temperature should be between 16-49°C (60-120°F) for cold 
check.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission 

Nothing fastens the torque converter to the transmission. A retaining 
strap must be used for handling. 

The torque converter and transmission must be removed from and 
installed in the vehicle as a unit. The transmission cannot be removed from or 
installed on the converter in the vehicle. 

Except where noted, these removal and installation procedures apply 
generally to all vehicles. 

The transmission should be at operating temperature of 71°-93°C 
(160°-200°F) when the fluid is drained. This will make sure drainage 
is quicker and better. 

 Removal 

From inside the vehicle, remove the right and left door sill scuff 
plate screws and remove the plates. Position the floor covering out of the 
way. Remove the bolts securing the transmission access cover to the floorpan 
and remove the cover. 

Remove the drain plug from the fluid pan and allow the fluid to drain. 

Remove the fluid filler tube. 

Install a protective plug in the drain hole and fluid filler tube hole. 

On a one-piece driveline, disconnect the shaft from the pinion flange 
and from the yoke. Do not remove the bolt that attaches the flange on the 
transmission output shaft. On a two-piece driveline, disconnect the coupling 
shaft from the yoke at the parking brake drum, and then remove the center 
support bearing bracket. Move the forward end of the drive shaft, or coupling 
shaft, out of the way. Refer to Section 05-01 . 

Disconnect the speedometer and fluid temperature switch wiring from the 
transmission. Unplug the neutral start and backup lamp switch. 

Disconnect the vacuum line, if so equipped, from the modulator and 
disconnect the selector lever cable from the transmission control arm and the 
throttle control rod to the lever on the left side of the transmission 
housing. Remove the cable clamp bracket from the housing. 

Disconnect the pin and clevis and position the modulator cable aside.

Disconnect the fluid cooler lines from the fittings on the 
transmission. Plug the lines and transmission openings. If desired, the lines 
can be drained, but they should be plugged before removing the converter and 
transmission from the vehicle. 

If necessary, remove or disconnect exhaust manifold to exhaust pipe.

Remove the dust shield from the bottom front side of the flywheel 
housing on 7.0L gasoline engine only. For the Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 diesel 
engines, remove the cover from front face of flywheel housing. 

For the Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 engines, remove the bolts holding the 
flexplate to the converter ring. 

Place an engine support under the rear end of the engine, then raise 
the engine to take the weight off the crossmember. 

Remove the two lock nuts, bolts and washers that hold the transmission 
rear support to the support side rail brackets and remove the support 
assembly, if so equipped. 

Support the transmission with a 454 kg (1000-pound) transmission jack 
such as Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or equivalent. 
The jack should be placed so the fluid pan does not support the entire weight 
of the transmission. Fasten a safety chain over the top of the transmission 
and to both sides of the jack. 

Remove the bolts and lockwashers that attach the converter housing to 
the flywheel housing. 

Move the converter and transmission away from the engine until the 
converter housing clears the crossmember, then lower the unit. If necessary, 
raise the floor pan slightly to permit the converter housing to clear the 
crossmember. 

 Installation 

If the engine, flywheel, or flywheel housing has been replaced, check 
the flywheel housing alignment and flywheel shim adjustment before installing 
the torque converter and transmission. Refer to Flywheel Housing Alignment in 
the Adjustments portion of this section. 

 NOTE: Prior to installing the transmission, it is mandatory that the 
flexplate be checked for runout. The maximum total indicated runout (TIR) 
should be 0.762 mm (0.030 inch). Also, flywheel housing transmission mounting 
face alignment inspection should be made of the engine flywheel housing 
transmission surface. The face and bore runout should not exceed 0.203 mm 
(0.008 inch) TIR. 

Raise the converter and transmission on the jack, then move the unit 
into position over the crossmember that supports the converter. Align the 
studs in the converter cover with the holes in the flywheel or flexplate. 
Install two guide studs in the flywheel housing, then push the unit forward so 
that the converter studs enter the holes in the flywheel. 

Install six new self-locking nuts and flatwashers that hold the 
converter on the engine flywheel, and tighten to 43-56 Nm (32-41 lb-ft) 
for 3/8-24 and 28-33 Nm (21-24 lb-ft) for M10-1.5 x 40.

Install the transmission on the engine flywheel housing and tighten as 
follows:

3/8-16 x 1.5 bolts, MT-643/653, gasoline engines: 23-31 Nm 
(17-23 lb-ft)

M10-1.5 x 40, MT-643/653 Cummins 5.9 and C8.3 diesel engines: 51-61 
Nm (38-45 lb-ft)

Install the dust shield on the bottom front side of the flywheel 
housing for the 7.0L gasoline engine. For the Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 diesel 
engines, install cover to front face of flywheel housing. 

Install the two bolts, washers and lock nuts that hold the support 
crossmember to the side rail brackets. Tighten securely. 

Lower the Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, remove it from under the vehicle, then remove the engine support 
from under the rear end of the engine. 

Remove the protective plugs, and install the fluid cooler lines. 

Install the selector lever cable bracket on the left side of the 
transmission housing, and tighten the screws to 11-13 Nm (8-10 lb-ft). 

Connect the selector lever cable to the transmission control arm on the 
left side of the housing and connect the vacuum line, if so equipped, to the 
modulator. 

Position and install the modulator cable clevis and pin.

Remove the protective plug and connect the fluid filler tube to the 
fluid pan, then install the tube support strap bolt. 

If the exhaust manifold to exhaust pipe was removed or disconnected 
during removal, install and connect it. 

Install the driveshaft, or the center bearing support bracket, and the 
coupling shaft. Connect the shaft to the output flange. Tighten all nuts and 
bolts to specifications given in Section 05-01 . 

Connect the speedometer and fluid temperature switch wiring to the rear 
of the transmission. 

Adjust the selector lever linkage. Refer to Selector Lever Linkage in 
the Adjustments portion of this section.

Connect the neutral start switch and backup lamp switch.

Check all fluid line connections for tightness, then lower the vehicle 
to the floor. 

Replace fluid filter. Refer to Section 07-02 .

Fill transmission. Refer to Transmission Fluid Drain and Refill 
Procedure in the Removal and Installation portion of this section. 

Add enough automatic transmission fluid to the converter and 
transmission to bring the fluid level to between the bottom two COLD marks on 
the dipstick with the engine idling and the transmission in neutral. 

Position the transmission access covers to the floorpan and secure with 
the retaining bolts. Reposition the floor covering. Install the door sill 
scuff plates and secure with the retaining screws. 

 Transmission Installation, Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 Diesel Engines,

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Universal Joint Flange, MT-643 and MT-653

 Removal 

The transmission can be placed in either a vertical or horizontal 
position on the input drive cover or sump pan. Remove flange retaining bolt, 
with washer and O-ring seal. Do not remove washer and O-ring from the bolt. 
Remove the flange. 

Do not allow the output shaft to turn until the flange is installed, 
seated and the retaining bolt or nut has been tightened. If the output shaft 
is allowed to rotate, damage to the pilot tube or governor will result. 

 Installation 

Install the output flange, using a 1/2-20-inch UNF bolt, flange 
retaining plate, spacer, and nut as installation tools. The length of the bolt 
and spacer will vary depending on the type of flange being installed. 

During installation, care should be exercised to avoid damage to the 
seal journal or the oil seal. Inspect the flange seal journal for nicks or 
scratches and seal for cuts and tears. 

Seat the flange by tightening the 1/2-20-inch nut. Remove the 
installation bolt, nut plate and spacer. Install retaining bolt including 
O-ring seal and washer. Tighten the bolt to 139-164 Nm (102-121 lb-ft).

ADJUSTMENTS

Selector Lever Linkage

Proper adjustment of the manual selector lever linkage is important as 
the shift detents must correspond exactly to those in the transmission. 
Periodic inspections should be made for bent or worn parts, loose threaded 
connections, loose bolts, and accumulation of grease and dirt. All moving 
joints must be kept clean and well lubricated. 

The following procedures are applicable to most vehicles. 

The selector lever should move easily and give a crisp detent feel in 
each position. The linkage should be adjusted so that the stops in the column 
(selector lever and bracket) match the detents in the transmission. 

When the linkage is correctly adjusted, the pin that engages the 
control arm at the transmission can be moved freely in each range. 

 CAUTION: Proper installation of the control arm is imperative to the function of 
the transmission. Excessive torque applied to the external selector lever 
retaining nut can damage the internal selector lever arm. 

With the engine stopped, position the transmission selector lever in 
the R position. 

Disconnect the selector cable adjusting sleeve at the control arm. 

 Linkage Installation, 7.0L Gasoline Engine

Connect the sleeve to the control arm with flatwashers, spring washer 
and cotter pin. 

Operate the selector lever in all positions to make sure the control 
arm at the transmission is in full detent in all gear ranges. It may be 
necessary to readjust the sleeve slightly to obtain the detent position in all 
drive ranges. (The pin that engages the control arm can be moved freely in 
each range.)

ADJUSTMENTS

Throttle Position (TP) Sensor

To adjust throttle position (TP) sensor for MD-Series transmissions, 
bear in mind that the TP sensor should open and close before the throttle. 
Therefore, when the throttle cable is at the maximum full throttle position, 
the TP sensor should be adjusted to the fully extended position. Likewise, 
when the throttle cable is set at the minimum closed throttle position, the TP 
sensor should be adjusted to the fully retracted position. Refer to the 
following illustration.

ADJUSTMENTS

Flywheel Housing Alignment 

Whenever the flywheel housing has been replaced, or when the original 
housing is to be used on another engine, check the alignment of the housing 
bore and rear face with the engine crankshaft. 

Check the mating surfaces of the engine and the flywheel housing for 
raised metal, paint, nicks, or burrs. Remove any marks or material that would 
affect alignment. 

Position the flywheel housing adapter on the two dowel pins in the 
engine, then bolt the housing in place. 

If either runout on the housing is not within limits, remove the two 
dowel pins from the engine. 

 CAUTION: Be careful not to drill the upper dowel pin too deeply as the dowel pin 
is in a blind hole which can break through into the water jacket or cylinder 
wall. 

Bolt the flywheel housing adapter in place without dowel pins, then 
adjust the housing to get the correct bore runout. Tighten the bolts and ream 
the dowel pin holes large enough for oversize dowel pins. 

Check the runout with the new oversize dowel pins in place, and with 
the mounting bolts tightened to 55-61 Nm (41-45 lb-ft).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Transmission Temperature Indication Light 

The instrument panel-mounted TRANS TEMP warning light (available for 
MT-Series transmissions) comes on to indicate maximum transmission-to-cooler 
fluid temperature of 149°C (300°F). Should the light come on, stop the 
vehicle and shift the transmission to NEUTRAL. Accelerate the engine to 
1200-1500 rpm to allow the transmission to return to normal, 71-104°C 
(160-219°F), before resuming operation. Check transmission fluid level.

Section 07-02: Transmission, Automatic, Cooling

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Transmission Cooler Line Filter 

Normal transmission wear may cause debris which can move around within 
the transmission fluid cooling system and become trapped in the transmission 
fluid cooler, preventing efficient cooling. In most cases there is no 
effective method to completely remove this material from the transmission 
fluid, yet it must be eliminated as much as possible. MT-Series transmission 
fluid cooler systems use an external filter in the fluid return circuit to 
remove any debris present in the fluid. MD-Series transmissions have two 
internal filters providing protection against excessive transmission wear, 
overheating, or damage due to contamination.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Fluid Filter

 Removal 

 WARNING: ALWAYS DISPOSE OF USED AUTOMOTIVE FLUIDS IN A RESPONSIBLE MANNER. 
FOLLOW YOUR COMMUNITY'S STANDARDS FOR DISPOSING OF THESE TYPES OF FLUIDS. 
CONSULT YOUR LOCAL RECYCLING CENTER. 

Drain transmission fluid. 

Carefully loosen the transmission fluid filter by hand or with an oil 
filter wrench. 

Remove transmission fluid filter from the transmission filter mounting 
adapter. 

 Installation 

Fill new external filter almost to the top with the specified grade of 
new automatic transmission fluid. 

Lightly coat the filter O-ring with a thin coat of the automatic 
transmission fluid. 

Rotate the new filter carefully onto the transmission fluid filter 
mounting adapter. Avoid spilling the fluid out of the filter. 

Hand-tighten the filter until snug. Using an oil filter wrench 
carefully rotate it an additional 1/3 to 1/2 revolution. Do not overtighten 
filter. 

Fill transmission system with specified automatic transmission fluid to 
the specified level. 

Start engine and check for leaks. 

Recheck automatic transmission fluid level.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Transmission Fluid Cooler

When internal wear or damage has occurred in the transmission, metal 
particles, clutch plate material or band material may have been carried into 
the converter and fluid cooler. These contaminants are a major cause of 
recurring transmission troubles and MUST be removed from 
the system before the transmission is put back into service.

Whenever a transmission has been disassembled to replace worn or 
damaged parts or because the valve body sticks due to foreign material, the 
converter and transmission fluid cooler MUST be cleaned 
by using a mechanically agitated cleaner, such as Rotunda Torque Converter/Oil 
Cooler Cleaner 014-00028 or equivalent.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Transmission, Manual

 Inspection and Verification 

 Vibration 

Although the effects of vibration will show up in the transmission, 
vibration usually originates somewhere else in the drivetrain. Vibration can 
usually be felt and can be accompanied by noise. 

Some of the problems found in the transmission due to drivetrain 
vibration are as follows: 

gear rattle at idle 

gear and shaft splines fretted

[FIGURE: C94901A.gif]

noise 

fretted bearings 

repeated rear seal leakage 

broken or loose synchronizer pins

[FIGURE: C94911A.gif]

continuous loosening of capscrews, brackets and mountings 

input shaft spline wear

[FIGURE: C94921A.gif]

worn universal joints (not a transmission symptom, but an indicator of 
vibration) 

driveline imbalance or misalignment 

unbalanced wheels or brake drums 

rough running engine 

broken or worn engine mounts 

worn suspension 

 Gear Slipout and Jumpout 

 Front Section 

When a sliding clutch is moved to engage with a mainshaft gear, the 
mating teeth must be parallel. Tapered or worn clutching teeth will try to 
walk apart as the gears rotate. Under the right conditions, slipout will 
result. Some of these conditions are: 

transmission mounted eccentrically with engine flywheel pilot 

excessive gear clashing, which shortens clutching teeth 

gear clutching teeth wearing to a taper

[FIGURE: C94931A.gif]

insufficient pressure on detent ball from weak or broken detent spring

[FIGURE: C94941A.gif]

excessive wear on detent notch of yoke bar

[FIGURE: C94951A.gif]

Slipout will generally occur when pulling with full power or 
decelerating with the load pushing. 

Jumpout will occur when a force sufficient to overcome the detent 
spring pressure is applied to the yoke bar, moving the clutch gear to a 
neutral position.

[FIGURE: C94961A.gif]

Some conditions contributing to jumpout are:

Extra-heavy and long shift levers that swing pendulum-fashion from 
operating over uneven terrain. Whipping action of the lever overcomes detent 
spring tension. 

Relative movement between engine-transmission package and frame can 
force transmission out of gear. Worn or broken engine mounts increase the 
effects of this condition. 

 Auxiliary Section 

Slipout in the auxiliary section can be caused by the clutching teeth 
being worn, tapered, or not fully engaged. These conditions cause the clutch 
gear to walk out of engagement as the gears turn. Causes of these clutching 
defects are clashing or normal wear after long life. Vibrations set up by an 
improperly aligned driveline and low air pressure add to the slipout problem.

[FIGURE: C94971A.gif]

Jumpout in the auxiliary section usually occurs with the splitter gear 
set. If torque is not sufficiently broken during splitter shifts, the sliding 
clutch gear may not have enough time to complete the shift before torque is 
reapplied to the gears. As torque is reapplied, the partially engaged clutch 
gear jumps out of the splitter gear. Since the gears have torque applied to 
them, damage will be done to the clutching teeth of the mating gears. 

 Hard Shifting 

To determine if the transmission itself is the cause of hard shifting, 
remove the shift lever from the top of the transmission. Move the shift blocks 
into each gear position using a prybar or screwdriver. If the trouble is in 
the transmission, it will generally be caused by one of the following: 

Splines of the sliding clutch gear binding on the mainshaft as a result 
of a twisted mainshaft, bent shift yoke or bowed mainshaft key.

[FIGURE: C94981A.gif]

Yoke bars binding in the bar housing as a result of cracked housing, 
overtorqued shift block lock screw, sprung yoke bar or swelled areas of the 
yoke bar. 

If hard shifting occurs only in first and reverse, the shift block 
detent plunger movement may be restricted. This can result from burrs on the 
plunger or from overtightening the plunger spring plug. With the plunger 
blocked in the depressed position, the plug should be tightened until it 
bottoms out against the spring and backed out one-quarter to one-half turn. 

Gear clashing should not be confused with hard shifting. Gear clashing 
occurs when an attempt is made to engage the clutch gear before it has reached 
synchronization with the mainshaft gear. 

 Heat 

The transmission operating temperature should never exceed 120°C 
(248°F) for an extended period of time. If it does, the oil will break 
down and shorten transmission life. 

Because of the friction of moving parts, transmissions will produce a 
certain amount of heat. In most cases normal operating temperature is 
approximately 40°C (104°F) above ambient. Heat is dissipated through 
the transmission case. When conditions prevent the proper dissipation of heat, 
overheating occurs. 

Before checking for possible causes of overheating, the oil temperature 
gauge and sending unit should be inspected to make sure they are giving 
correct readings. 

Some of the causes of overheating are as follows: 

improper lubrication (oil level too low or too high, wrong type of oil, 
or an operating angle of more than 12 degrees) 

operating consistently under 32 km/h (20 mph) 

high engine rpm 

restricted airflow around the transmission, due to the transmission 
being boxed in by frame rails, deck lids, fuel tanks and mounting brackets, or 
by a large bumper assembly 

exhaust system too close to transmission 

high ambient temperature 

high horsepower, overdrive operation 

coasting downhill with the clutch depressed 

 Noise 

 Knocking or Thudding Gears 

Knocking or thudding can be a result of bumps or swells on gear teeth. 
Such bumps or swells can be removed with a hone or small hand grinder. These 
areas can be identified as highly polished spots on the face of the gear 
tooth. Generally, this noise is more prominent when the gear is loaded. The 
problem gear can be located as the noise occurs in a specific gear position. 
Bumps or swells are caused by improper handling of gears before or during 
assembly.

[FIGURE: C94991A.gif]

 Cracked Gear 

A gear cracked or broken by shock loading or by pressing on a shaft 
during installation will produce a knocking or thudding sound at low speeds. 
At high speeds a howl will be present.

[FIGURE: C95001A.gif]

 High-Pitched Whine or Squeal 

A high-pitched whine or squeal is the result of normal gear wear, 
including gear tooth pitting from excessive use. In advanced deterioration, a 
howl will result. 

 Mismatched Gear Sets 

Such gear sets are identified by an uneven wear pattern on the face of 
gear teeth. 

 Bearings 

Noise comes in at low shaft speeds in any position. It is caused by 
bearings with damaged balls or rollers, or with pitted and spalled raceways. 

Pinched bearings, having insufficient axial or radial clearance can be 
a cause of whining or squealing noise. 

 Growling 

A growling noise can be produced by improper timing of the transmission 
during reassembly, or improper timing due to gear turning on the countershaft. 
Both conditions produce error in tooth spacing. 

 Causes or Types of Noise Other Than Transmission 

Sources of noise other than transmission include the following:

rough idling engine 

engine operating noise 

clutch driven plates in which the dampening action of springs or rubber 
blocks has been eliminated by wear set or fracture 

driveline out of balance 

unequal joint working angles 

worn crosses in universal joints 

loose or worn center bearings 

worn or pitted teeth on ring gear and pinion of driving axle (rear axle 
bearing failure) 

wheels out of balance 

worn spring pivot bearing 

loose U-bolts 

brake drums warped or out of balance 

 Clashing 

Snubbing and clashing gears while shifting are frequent abuses to which 
unsynchronized transmissions are subjected. Light snubbing will do little 
damage. The real damage is done by the hard clash shift caused by engaging 
gears which are far out of synchronization. This can break pieces of metal 
from the ends of the clutching teeth.

[FIGURE: C95011A.gif]

Clashing gears can be traced to one of three causes: 

Improper shifting — This applies to drivers who are not familiar 
with the shift pattern or have not learned the rpm spread between shifts. 

Clutch — Clashing when starting up in first or reverse gear can 
be caused by insufficient clutch clearance or a dragging clutch not releasing 
properly. This makes the transmission countershafts and mainshaft gears 
continue rotating while the clutch pedal is depressed. Clashing results when 
the nonrotating sliding clutch is forced to mesh with a rotating mainshaft 
gear. Double clutching during lever shifts will also reduce snubbing and 
clashing. 

Inertial force — Countershafts and mainshaft gears usually take 
from three to five seconds to stop rotating after the clutch has been 
disengaged. Attempting to mesh a clutch gear with a mainshaft gear before the 
mainshaft gear stops will result in clashing. If the transmission is not 
equipped with a clutch brake or countershaft brake, pause a few seconds after 
depressing the clutch pedal before attempting initial engagement of the 
transmission. 

 Gear Rattle at Idle 

Mainshaft gears are designed to have a specified amount of axial 
clearance which allows them to rotate freely on the mainshaft. The amount of 
clearance is governed by the use of washers. A rough idling engine can set up 
vibrations, causing the mainshaft gears to rattle as they strike mating gears. 
This condition can usually be cured by improving the idling characteristics of 
the engine. Tolerance washers may have to be changed to bring the axial gear 
clearance to within tolerance on high mileage units. 

 Gear Manufacturing Marks 

Sometimes gears are replaced or thought to be defective because of 
marks left on the gear by manufacturing processes. These blemishes do not 
contribute to gear failure and the gear should not be replaced because of 
these marks. 

Hob marks are cutting marks or lines formed during the initial cutting 
of the gear teeth. Hob marks on the tooth face will be removed by the shaving 
process, but hob marks in the root of the tooth will most likely remain, and 
may be found even on gears with much wear on them.

[FIGURE: C95021A.gif]

Shaving marks are the distinct diagonal marks left on the face of the 
gear tooth during the shaving operation. These marks can be distinguished from 
scoring marks by the fact that they are diagonal, while scoring marks are more 
nearly vertical. Most shaving marks are removed during normal gear operation.

[FIGURE: C43691A.gif]

Lipping or shaving burrs are formed at the tip of the gear teeth during 
machining. These lips will not harm the gear.

[FIGURE: C95031A.gif]

 Shaft Twist and Failure 

Failure of transmission shafts through fracturing or twisting is caused 
when stresses are imposed on them which are greater than they were designed to 
withstand. Following are the main causes for these failures: 

improper clutching techniques 

starting in too high gear (either front or auxiliary section) 

lugging 

attempting to start with brakes locked 

transmission used for application it was not designed to withstand. 

bumping into dock when backing 

improper mounting of adjustable 5th wheel 

Following the recommended action, refer to the appropriate section in 
Group 07.

As with gear teeth, shafts can fracture as a result of fatigue or impact.

[FIGURE: C95041A.gif]

Loads not severe enough to cause shaft fractures may cause the shaft to 
twist.

[FIGURE: C94981A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Transmission, Manual 

 Cleaning 

After the transmission has been disassembled, soak all the parts, 
except the bearings, in a cleaning solvent until all the old lubricant is 
dissolved or loosened. Brush or scrape all foreign matter from the parts. Be 
careful not to damage any of the parts with the scraper. 

An excessive amount of foreign material usually results from a bearing 
failure, gear seizure, tooth breakage, extreme synchronizer wear or clashing 
gears. In such cases, the input and output shaft bearings should be carefully 
inspected and replaced if necessary. Since countershaft bearings, output shaft 
pilot bearings and reverse idler bearings are not so susceptible to damage 
from foreign material in the lubricant, they need not be replaced if they seem 
satisfactory. 

Wipe the parts or blow compressed air on them until they are thoroughly 
dry. 

To clean the bearings, rotate them in clean solvent until all lubricant 
is removed. Hold the bearing assembly to prevent it from rotating, and dry it 
with compressed air. 

When the bearings are dry, lubricate them thoroughly with transmission 
lubricant and cover them with a clean, lint-free cloth until ready for use. 

 Inspection 

Inspect all transmission parts before reassembly to determine if they 
need to be replaced. 

 Transmission Case Service 

 NOTE: Steam clean the transmission or transfer unit case to remove grease, 
oil, or road dirt. Clean the service area thoroughly. Epoxy resin will not 
stick to a dirty or oily surface.

Inspect the case for cracks, worn or damaged bearing bores, damaged 
threads or similar damage. If such is found, replace the case. However, if the 
cracks do not extend into bearing bores or bolt holes in the machined surface, 
the case can be welded or brazed.

Holes smaller than 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) in diameter, such as sand holes 
or casting porosity can be serviced using an epoxy resin material meeting Ford 
Manufacturing Standard M3D35A(E).

Holes larger than 6.35 mm (1/4 inch) can be serviced by drilling, 
tapping and plugging. 

The recommended procedure for servicing sand holes or casting porosity 
using the epoxy resin is as follows: 

 NOTE: Steam clean the transmission or transfer unit case to remove grease, 
oil, or road dirt. Clean the service area thoroughly. Epoxy resin will not 
stick to a dirty or oily surface. 

Prepare the surface to be serviced by grinding or rotary filing to a 
clean, bright metal surface. Chamfer or undercut the hole or porous area to a 
depth greater than that in the surrounding cleaned surface. Solid metal must 
surround the hole. 

Apply the service mixture with a suitable clean tool (putty knife, wood 
spoon, etc.), forcing the mixture into the hole or porosity. 

Allow the service mixture to harden by either of two methods: heat cure 
with a 250-watt lamp placed 254 mm (10 inches) from the serviced surface, or 
air dry for 10 to 12 hours at temperatures above 10°C (50°F). 

Sand or grind the serviced area, blending it with the general contour 
of the surrounding surface. Do not use this method to service casting cracks. 

Inspect the front face of the case, and file or grind off any minor 
nicks or burrs that could cause misalignment of the transmission with the 
clutch housing.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Shift Housing

equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B. Replace cover if it is bent 
or distorted. Make sure the vent hole in the case is open.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Seals and Gaskets 

When disassembling a later-design, twin-countershaft Eaton 
transmission, you may notice a small rubber lip seal on the input shaft under 
the front cover. This shipping seal was added for the sole purpose of 
eliminating oil leakage during shipment. 

When this seal is found during service on a twin-countershaft 
transmission, it should be removed. There is no need to install a replacement 
as this is a nonserviceable item. The transmission continues to be sealed 
during operation by the spiral cut grooves on the input shaft.

[FIGURE: C10324B.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Synchronizer Blocking Rings 

Check synchronizer cones and clutching teeth.

Replace synchronizer if cone wear is excessive or clutching teeth are 
chipped.

Inspect the synchronizer blocking rings for widened index slots, 
rounded clutch teeth and smooth internal surfaces (must have machined 
grooves). With the blocker ring on the cone, the distance between the face of 
the gear must not be less than 0.254 mm (0.010 inch). 

Check the synchronizer sleeves for free movement on the hubs. Make sure 
the alignment marks (etched marks) are properly indexed.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Bearings 

Inspect the bearing assemblies. If any of the following conditions are 
present, replace the bearings. 

 Bearing Raceways 

Examine the races for discoloration, pitting, flaking, fretting, 
scoring, scratches, cracks or other damage.

 Bearing External Surfaces 

Examine the bearings for looseness, discoloration, pitting, scoring, 
scratches or other damage.

 Spin Test 

 CAUTION: Do not spin bearings with compressed air as this will damage bearing. 

Spin bearings by hand. Bearings should spin freely without roughness.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Gear Inspection 

Some forms of grind marks and tooth wear contact patterns are 
acceptable and should not be considered as a source of gear noise. Grind marks 
are distinctive from wear or damage which are local swells (polished raised 
projections), nicks and chips. All gears have possible factory service grind 
marks. Phosphate coated gears are especially easy to recognize since the grind 
operation removes a patch of phosphate and base metal exposing the lighter 
metallic color.

 Countershaft Gear and Countershaft 

Replace the countershaft gear if the teeth are chipped or excessively 
worn. Replace the countershaft if the shaft is bent or grooved. 

 Reverse Idler Gear 

Replace the reverse idler gear if the gear or bushing is badly worn or 
if the teeth are chipped or burred. Replace the reverse idler gear shaft if it 
is excessively worn or scored.

PAGE 3033
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 07-03: Transmission, Manual, General

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Shaft Inspection

 Input Shaft 

Replace the input shaft if it is worn, bent, or twisted, if the gear 
has chipped, worn, or missing teeth, or if the cone surface is damaged. 
Replace the pilot bearing if scored, and inspect input shaft for damage. 

 Output Shaft 

Replace all output shaft gears that are chipped, burred, or badly worn. 
Check the intermediate gear end play, and replace the gear if the end play is 
not within specifications. Replace the output shaft if it is out of round or 
worn, or if the bearing surface is scored. 

Replace the speedometer drive gear if the gear teeth are worn or 
broken. Be sure to install the correct replacement gear.

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Thrust Washers, Synchronizer Discs and Bearing Covers 

Check the surfaces of all thrust washers. Replace washers that are 
scored or reduced in thickness. 

Replace synchronizer discs that are scored, burned, or warped. Also 
replace bearing covers that are grooved or showing wear from the thrust or 
adjacent bearings. Check the oil return threads in the bearing cover. If the 
sealing action of the threads has been destroyed by contact from the input 
shaft, replace the cover.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Identification

[FIGURE: C11744B.gif]

The FS-4205 series transmissions are five-speed synchronized units 
which feature a constant mesh low and reverse, and offer an efficient ratio of 
torque capacity to weight. Transmission features include split-pin 
synchronizers in second, third, fourth and fifth gears, tapered roller 
bearings, and needle roller bearings at main support locations.

The shift forks have steel-backed bronze wear pads that can be 
replaced, if necessary. The shift pattern is the standard progression type 
with all shifts having the same throw at the shift lever. Transmissions are 
available with either standard ratio or the soft ratio which splits the step 
in a two-speed axle. The FS-4205-A is the standard ratio and the FS-4205-B is 
the soft-fourth ratio.

The FS-4205 series transmissions have five forward speeds and one 
reverse speed with gear ratios as follows:

 Power Flow 

The transmission must efficiently transfer the engine's power (torque) 
to the vehicle's rear wheels. Knowledge of what takes place in the 
transmission during torque transfer is essential when troubleshooting and 
performing service.

 NOTE: The numbers in these steps correspond to the numbers in the following 
illustration.

Power (torque) from the engine is transferred to the transmission's 
input shaft.

Torque is transferred to the countershaft drive gear.

Torque is delivered along the countershaft to all countershaft gears.

Torque is transferred to engaged mainshaft gear. The cross section 
illustrates first speed gear position.

Engaged mainshaft gear external clutching teeth transfer torque to 
mainshaft through synchronizer assembly.

Mainshaft transfers torque directly to the driveshaft through the rear 
yoke.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Oil Drain and Refill Procedure

 CAUTION: The use of mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil is not 
recommended, but if these gear oils are used, be sure to adhere to the 
following limitations. 

 CAUTION: Do not use mild EP gear oil or multi-purpose gear oil when operating 
temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). Many of these gear oils, 
particularly 85W140, break down above 230°F and coat seals, bearings, and 
gears with deposits that can cause premature failures. If these deposits are 
observed (especially a coating on seal areas causing oil leakage), change to 
Eaton Roadranger® CD50 transmission fluid, heavy-duty engine oil,
mineral gear oil, or Emgard 2924 Synthetic Transmission Lubricant SAE50 or
equivalent to ensure maximum component life and to maintain your warranty with
Eaton. Refer to Operating Temperatures in this section. 

 CAUTION: Additives and friction modifiers are not recommended for use in Eaton 
Fuller transmissions. 

Correct lubrication procedures are the key to a good all-around 
maintenance program. If the oil is not doing its job, or if the oil level is 
ignored, all the maintenance procedures in the world are not going to keep the 
transmission running or ensure long transmission life.

Eaton Fuller transmissions are designed so that the internal parts 
operate in an oil circulating bath by the motion of the gears and shafts.

All parts are amply lubricated if these procedures are closely followed:

Maintain oil level. Inspect regularly.

Change oil regularly.

Use the correct grade and type of oil.

Buy from a reputable dealer.

 Proper Oil Level 

Make sure oil is level with the filler opening. Because you can reach 
oil with your finger does not mean oil is at proper level. An oil level of 
25.4 mm (one inch) is equal to approximately 3.7 liters (one gallon) of oil.

[FIGURE: C11745A.gif]

 Draining Oil 

Drain transmission while oil is warm. To drain oil, remove the drain 
plug at case bottom. Clean the drain plug before reinstalling.

 Refilling 

 CAUTION: When adding oil, do not mix types and brands of oil because of possible 
incompatibility. 

Clean case around filler plug and remove plug from case side. Fill the 
transmission to the level of the filler opening. If the transmission has two 
filler openings, fill to the level of both openings.

The exact amount of oil depends on the transmission inclination and 
model. Do not overfill — this causes oil to be forced out of the case 
through the front bearing cover. 

 Proper Lubrication Levels As Related to Transmission Installation Angles 

If the transmission operating angle is more than 12 degrees, improper 
lubrication can occur. The operating angle is the transmission mounting angle 
in the chassis plus the percent of upgrade (expressed in degrees).

The chart below illustrates the safe percent of upgrade on which the 
transmission can be used with various chassis mounting angles. For example: if 
you have a four-degree transmission mounting angle, then eight degrees (or 14 
percent of grade) is equal to the limit of 12 degrees. If you have a 
zero-degree mounting angle, the transmission can be operated on a 12-degree 
(21-percent) grade.

Any time the transmission operating angle (or 12 degrees) is exceeded 
for an extended period of time, the transmission should be equipped with an 
oil pump or cooler kit to make sure transmission is correctly lubricated.

Note on the chart the effect low oil levels can have on safe operating 
angles. Allowing the oil level to fall one-half inch below the filler plug 
hole reduces the degree of grade by approximately three degrees (5.5 percent). 
Correct lubrication levels are essential.

[FIGURE: C11746A.gif]

 Operating Temperatures 

 With Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid, Heavy Duty 
Engine Oil, Mineral Oil, or Emgard 2924 Synthetic Transmission Lubricant SAE 50 

The transmission should not be operated consistently at temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F). However, intermittent operating temperatures to 
149°C (300°F) will not harm the transmission. Operating temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F) increase the lubricant's rate of oxidation and 
shorten its effective life. When the average operating temperature is above 
120°C (250°F), the transmission may require more frequent oil changes 
or external cooling.

The following conditions in any combination can cause operating 
temperatures of over 120°C (250°F).

operating consistently at slow speeds

high ambient temperatures

restricted airflow around transmission

exhaust system too close to transmission

high horsepower, overdrive operation

External oil coolers are available to reduce operating temperatures 
when the above conditions are encountered.

Transmission oil coolers are recommended with the following engines:

350 HP and above with overdrive transmissions

Transmission Oil Coolers are required with the following engines:

399 HP and above with overdrive transmissions and GCWs over 40,824 kg 
(90,000 lbs).

399 HP and above and 1898 Nm (1400 lb-ft) or greater torque

450 HP and above

 With EP or Multipurpose Gear Oil 

Mild EP gear oil and multipurpose gear oil are not recommended when 
lubricant operating temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). In addition, 
transmission oil coolers are not recommended with these gear oils, since the 
oil cooler materials may be attacked by these gear oils. The lower temperature 
limit and oil cooler restriction with these gear oils generally limit their 
success to milder applications.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission

 Removal 

Raise hood.

Disconnect battery(s).

Remove floor mat and floor plate.

Position shift lever in neutral. Remove four screws retaining shift 
lever housing to shift bar housing. Jar housing lightly to break the gasket 
seal. Remove shift lever housing and gasket. Cover opening in the shift bar 
housing.

Position a suitable drain pan under transmission. Remove drain plug and 
drain the transmission oil. Reinstall drain plug and tighten to 61-75 
Nm (45-55 lb-ft).

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Disconnect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Position Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent under the transmission.

Fabricate two guide pins from standard bolts as shown.

[FIGURE: C52661A.gif]

Remove two lower screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing. Install the two fabricated guide pins into the lower holes. 
Remove the two upper screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing.

Remove transmission from the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Lower transmission from vehicle.

 Installation 

If removed, reinstall the two fabricated guide pins into lower holes of 
clutch housing.

Using Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, raise and align transmission to the clutch housing. Install 
transmission to the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Install two upper transmission-to-clutch housing retaining screws and 
washers and tighten to 122-136 Nm (90-100 lb-ft).

Remove fabricated guide pins. Install two lower transmission-to-clutch 
housing retaining screws and washers and tighten to 122-136 Nm (90-100 
lb-ft).

Connect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Install driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Clean the shift lever housing gasket mating surfaces. Make sure the 
shift block and yoke notches are aligned in the neutral position. Install 
gasket and the shift lever housing. Apply Threadlock® and Sealer 
EOAZ-19554-AA or equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G315-A5 to the 
screw threads. Then, install and tighten the retaining screws to 27-34 
Nm (20-25 lb-ft).

Install floor plate and floor mat.

Fill transmission with the appropriate type and quantity oil. Refer to 
Specifications.

Connect battery(s).

Close hood.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Mainshaft Taper Bearing Adjustment

 NOTE: Each time a change is made, tighten nuts and roll mainshaft.

Place transmission in vertical position with main drive gear pointing 
down. Install yoke and nut. Tighten mainshaft flange nut to 407-475 Nm 
(300-350 lb-ft). Roll main drive gear and mainshaft to seat front and rear 
taper bearings. Position Dial Indicator with Bracketry TOOL-4201-C or 
equivalent as shown. Pry on output flange to get mainshaft end play. End play 
must be between 0.203-0.305 mm (0.008-0.012 inch). Add shims for more end play 
or remove shims for less end play.

[FIGURE: C66401B.gif]

Apply Gasket and Trim Adhesive D7AZ-19508-B or equivalent meeting Ford 
specifications ESR-M11P17-A and ESE-M2G52-A to both sides of each shim during 
final assembly. Apply a band of Pipe Sealant with Teflon® D8AZ-19554-A 
or equivalent meeting Ford specifications ESR-M18P7-A and WSK-M2G350-A2 to 
bearing cap retaining nuts. Install and tighten bearing cap retaining nuts to

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Identification

The transmission identification number indicates torque capacity, 
design levels, number of forward speeds and ratio group.

[FIGURE: C11747B.gif]

The FS-5205 transmissions are five-speed synchronized units that 
feature a constant mesh low and reverse, and offer an efficient ratio of 
torque capacity to weight. The FS-5205 series is available in two models, 
FS-5205A and FS-5205B. Transmission features include split-pin synchronizers 
in second, third, fourth and fifth gears; two tapered roller bearings on the 
mainshaft and two on the countershaft. The shift forks have steel-backed 
bronze wear pads that can be replaced, if necessary. The shift pattern is of 
the standard progression type with all shifts having the same throw at the 
shift lever. Transmissions are available with either standard ratio or the 
soft-fourth ratio, which splits the step in a two-speed axle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Power Flow

The transmission must efficiently transfer the engine's power (torque) 
to the vehicle's rear wheels. Knowledge of what takes place in the 
transmission during torque transfer is essential when troubleshooting and 
performing service.

 NOTE: The numbers in these steps correspond to the numbers in the following 
illustration.

Power (torque) from the engine is transferred to the transmission's 
input shaft.

Torque is transferred to the countershaft drive gear.

Torque is delivered along the countershaft to all countershaft gears.

Torque is transferred to engaged mainshaft gear. The cross section 
illustrates first speed gear position.

Engaged mainshaft gear external clutching teeth transfer torque to 
mainshaft through synchronizer assembly.

Mainshaft transfers torque directly to the driveshaft through the rear 
yoke.

 Power Flow, FS-5205 Series

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission Oil Drain and Refill Procedure

 CAUTION: The use of mild EP gear oil or multipurpose gear oil is not 
recommended, but if these gear oils are used, be sure to adhere to the 
following limitations. 

 CAUTION: Do not use mild EP gear oil or multipurpose gear oil when operating 
temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). Many of these gear oils, 
particularly 85W140, break down above 110°C (230°F) and coat seals, 
bearings, and gears with deposits that can cause premature failures. If these 
deposits are observed (especially a coating on seal areas causing oil 
leakage), change to Eaton Roadranger® CD50 transmission fluid, 
heavy-duty engine oil, mineral gear oil, or Emgard 2924 Synthetic Transmission
Lubricant SAE 50 or equivalent to ensure maximum component life and to
maintain your warranty with Eaton. Refer to Operating Temperatures in this
section. 

 CAUTION: Additives and friction modifiers are not recommended for use in Eaton 
Fuller transmissions. 

Correct lubrication procedures are the key to a good all-around 
maintenance program. If the oil is not doing its job, or if the oil level is 
ignored, all the maintenance procedures in the world are not going to keep the 
transmission running or ensure long transmission life.

Eaton Fuller transmissions are designed so that the internal parts 
operate in an oil circulating bath by the motion of the gears and shafts.

Thus, all parts are amply lubricated if these procedures are closely 
followed:

Maintain oil level. Inspect regularly.

Change oil regularly.

Use the correct grade and type of oil.

Buy from a reputable dealer.

 Proper Oil Level 

Make sure oil is level with the filler opening. Because you can reach 
oil with your finger does not mean oil is at proper level. An oil level of 
25.4 mm (one inch) is equal to approximately 3.7 liters (one gallon) of oil.

[FIGURE: C11745A.gif]

 Draining Oil 

Drain transmission while oil is warm. To drain oil, remove the drain 
plug at case bottom. Clean the drain plug before reinstalling.

 Refilling 

 CAUTION: When adding oil, do not mix types and brands of oil because of possible 
incompatibility. Do not overfill — this causes oil to be forced out of 
the case through the front bearing cover. 

Clean case around filler plug and remove plug from case side. Fill the 
transmission to the level of the filler opening. If the transmission has two 
filler openings, fill to the level of both openings.

The exact amount of oil depends on the transmission inclination and 
model. 

 Proper Lubrication Levels As Related to Transmission Installation Angles 

If the transmission operating angle is more than 12 degrees, improper 
lubrication can occur. The operating angle is the transmission mounting angle 
in the chassis plus the percent of upgrade (expressed in degrees).

The following chart illustrates the safe percent of upgrade on which 
the transmission can be used with various chassis mounting angles. For 
example: if you have a four-degree transmission mounting angle, then eight 
degrees (or 14 percent of grade) is equal to the limit of 12 degrees. If you 
have a zero-degree mounting angle, the transmission can be operated on a 
12-degree (21-percent) grade.

Anytime the transmission operating angle or 12 degrees is exceeded for 
an extended period of time, the transmission should be equipped with an oil 
pump or cooler kit to make sure transmission is lubricated correctly.

Note on the chart the effect low oil levels can have on safe operating 
angles. Allowing the oil level to fall one-half inch below the filler plug 
hole reduces the degree of grade by approximately three degrees (5.5 percent). 
Correct lubrication levels are essential.

[FIGURE: C11746A.gif]

 Operating Temperatures 

 With Eaton Roadranger® CD50 Transmission Fluid, Heavy Duty 
Engine Oil, Mineral Oil, or Emgard 2924 Synthetic Transmission Lubricant SAE 50 

The transmission should not be operated consistently at temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F). However, intermittent operating temperatures to 
149°C (300°F) will not harm the transmission. Operating temperatures 
above 120°C (250°F) increase the lubricant's rate of oxidation and 
shorten its effective life. When the average operating temperature is above 
120°C (250°F), the transmission may require more frequent oil changes 
or external cooling.

The following conditions in any combination can cause operating 
temperatures of over 120°C (250°F).

operating consistently at slow speeds

high ambient temperatures

restricted airflow around transmission

exhaust system too close to transmission

high horsepower, overdrive operation

External oil coolers are available to reduce operating temperatures 
when the above conditions are encountered.

Transmission oil coolers are recommended with the following engines:

350 HP and above with overdrive transmissions

Transmission oil coolers are required with the following engines:

399 HP and above with overdrive transmissions and GCW's over 40 824 kg 
(90,000 lb)

399 HP and above and 1898 Nm (1400 lb-ft) or greater torque

450 HP and above

 With EP or Multipurpose Gear Oil 

Mild EP gear oil and multipurpose gear oil are not recommended when 
lubricant operating temperatures are above 110°C (230°F). In addition, 
transmission oil coolers are not recommended with these gear oils, since the 
oil cooler materials may be attacked by these gear oils. The lower temperature 
limit and oil cooler restriction with these gear oils generally limit their 
success to milder applications.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Transmission

 Removal 

Raise hood.

Disconnect battery(s).

Remove floor mat and floor plate.

Position shift lever in neutral. Remove four screws retaining shift 
lever housing to shift bar housing. Jar housing lightly to break the gasket 
seal. Remove shift lever housing and gasket. Cover opening in the shift bar 
housing.

Position a suitable drain pan under transmission. Remove drain plug and 
drain the transmission oil. Reinstall drain plug and tighten to 61-75 
Nm (45-55 lb-ft).

Remove driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Disconnect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Position Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent under the transmission.

Fabricate two guide pins from standard bolts as shown.

[FIGURE: C52661A.gif]

Remove two lower screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing. Install the two fabricated guide pins into the lower holes. 
Remove the two upper screws and washers retaining the transmission to the 
clutch housing.

Remove transmission from the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 . 

Lower transmission from vehicle.

 Installation 

If removed, reinstall the two fabricated guide pins into lower holes of 
clutch housing.

Using Rotunda Heavy-Duty Truck Transmission Jack 164-R3510 or 
equivalent, raise and align transmission to the clutch housing. Install 
transmission to the clutch housing. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Install two upper transmission-to-clutch housing retaining screws and 
washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm (145-155 lb-ft).

Remove fabricated guide pins. Install two lower transmission-to-clutch 
housing retaining screws and washers and tighten to 197-210 Nm (145-155 
lb-ft).

Connect speedometer sensor and backup lamp switch.

Install driveshaft. Refer to Section 05-01 .

Clean the shift lever housing gasket mating surfaces. Make sure the 
shift block and yoke notches are aligned in the neutral position. Install 
gasket and the shift lever housing. Apply Threadlock and Sealer EOAZ-19554-AA 
or equivalent meeting Ford specification WSK-M2G315-A5 to the screw threads. 
Then, install and tighten the retaining screws to 27-34 Nm (20-25 lb ft).

Install floor plate and floor mat.

Fill transmission with the appropriate type and quantity oil. Refer to 
Specifications.

Connect battery(s).

Close hood.
