REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Accelerator Cable, 7.0L MFI Gasoline Engine

 WARNING: SURROUNDING ENGINE COMPARTMENT COMPONENTS, SUCH AS WIRING OR HOSES, 
MUST NOT CONTACT ANY MOVING MEMBER OF THE ACCELERATOR CONTROLS. CHECK ALL 
VEHICLES FOR RETURN TO IDLE. PERCEPTIBLE HESITATION OR PREVENTION OF RETURN TO 
THE IDLE POSITION MUST NOT OCCUR DURING SLOW REMOVAL OF THE FOOT FROM THE 
ACCELERATOR PEDAL AND SHAFT, STARTING AT THE FULLY DEPRESSED, WIDE-OPEN 
THROTTLE (WOT) POSITION. 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery negative cable.

Disconnect the governor electrical connector.

Disconnect the throttle cable at the accelerator pedal by lifting the 
ball out of the slot at the top of the pedal arm.

Disconnect the cable from the ball on the throttle body lever.

Remove the one nut and the two bolts that hold the throttle cable 
bracket to the upper intake manifold.

Remove the two nuts that hold the governor bracket to the throttle 
body. Remove the two nuts from the studs on the lower intake manifold. Remove 
the governor, bracket and throttle cables as an assembly.

Remove the bolts securing the governor to the bracket.

Remove the bracket from the throttle cable.

 Installation 

Install the throttle bracket to the new governor and cable assembly. 

Reverse the removal procedures to install the governor and cable 
assembly.

Tighten accelerator cable bracket mounting screws and nut to 4-6 
Nm (35-53 lb-in).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Accelerator Cable, Hand, 7.0L MFI Gasoline Engine

 Removal 

Loosen setscrew at accelerator pedal lever.

Remove retainer screw and clip at throttle control bracket. Remove 
throttle cable from lever.

Unscrew the jam nut from the back of the steering column support 
bracket. Remove the throttle cable.

 Installation 

Position the throttle cable through the steering column support bracket.

Install the washer and jam nut.

Attach the throttle cable to the throttle control bracket and tighten 
the retainer screw.

Loosely attach the throttle cable to the accelerator pedal lever.

With the accelerator pedal at the closed throttle position, and the 
hand throttle knob pushed all the way in, tighten the setscrew on the pedal 
lever.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Accelerator Pedal and Shaft, Cummins B5.9 and C8.3 Diesel Engines

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Accelerator Pedal — Electronic-Electronic

Engine speed is controlled by an electronic accelerator pedal. The 
electronic accelerator pedal uses a throttle position sensor to send a signal 
to the Engine Control Module (ECM). Based on this input, the ECM sends a 
signal to an actuator (mounted on the fuel injection pump). The actuator 
adjusts the fuel injection pump lever to correspond to the throttle pedal 
position.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Steering System

 Inspection and Verification 

The procedure used to diagnose a steering system condition must be 
systematic and thorough. Short cuts or a hit-or-miss approach will result in a 
misdiagnosis and can cause unnecessary repairs and customer comebacks.

The data sheet included in this section ensures a thorough and 
systematic procedure. The sheet must be completely filled in and the results 
evaluated before any repair is made.

The data sheet begins with a description of the customer concern. 
Interview the driver whenever possible. Use the Description of Common Steering 
System Conditions in this section to properly label the condition and then 
enter the driver's description of what, when, where and how on the data sheet.

The Vehicle Information portion of the data sheet includes items that 
must be noted during a vehicle inspection and road test. Entries in the test 
results are specifically for the power steering system tests. As each test is 
performed, the test data is entered on the sheet. A procedure for this test 
sequence is included in this section.

With a completed data sheet, a complete evaluation of the steering 
system can be made. If a test result is not within the acceptance standards, 
the pinpoint tests can be used to determine the correct service. Items listed 
under Vehicle Information can be used in the symptom charts to isolate a 
concern and make the necessary service. After service, the final step in a 
systematic approach to diagnosis is a road test to verify that the customer 
concern has been resolved.

 Description of Common Steering System Conditions 

A customer will use a wide variety of terms to describe a steering 
condition. The following description of common steering system conditions is 
intended to establish a common terminology between a customer's description of 
a condition and the terms used in the following symptom charts and test 
procedures.

Wander is described as the vehicle not tracking properly on the road 
surface. The vehicle tends to drift from side to side. Continual correction is 
required to keep the vehicle on the road.

The customer may describe wander in the following ways:

squirrelly

continually correcting

constantly fighting the wheel

can't hold it on the road

all over the road

loose steering

hard to steer

To determine if wander is present, drive the vehicle on a flat, 
straight road with no traffic and carefully release the steering wheel. If the 
vehicle has a wander condition, the vehicle will tend to drift from side to 
side. Refer to Wander in the symptom chart for possible causes.

Pulling is a term used to describe a constant movement of the vehicle 
in one direction.

The driver may describe pulling in the following ways:

won't track

pushes to one side

wanders

drives one way

To determine if a pull condition exists, drive the vehicle on a 
straight, flat road with no traffic. Carefully release the steering wheel. If 
the vehicle tracks to one side, a pull condition exists. Refer to Pulls in the 
symptom chart for possible causes.

Binding is an increase in steering wheel effort that is momentary or 
intermittent.

The driver may describe binding in the following ways:

high spot

hangs up

locks up

catches when turning

seizes

intermittent loss of power steering or power assist

Binding can be the result of either a mechanical or hydraulic system 
concern with steering components. A mechanical bind will occur at the same 
position on the steering wheel while turning. A bind caused by a hydraulic 
system problem will occur randomly. Refer to Binding, Uneven or Intermittently 
Hard Steering in symptom chart for possible causes.

No return or poor returnability is used to describe the poor return of 
the steering wheel to center after a turn or steering correction is completed.

The driver may describe poor returnability in the following ways:

the wheel won't come back

hangs up in turns

wheel sticks

steering does not return

Refer to Poor Returnability in symptom chart for possible causes.

Excessive steering effort/hard steering is experienced when steering 
wheel effort exceeds 18-22 pounds measured at the steering wheel rim. Hard 
steering can remain constant through the full turn or occur near the end of a 
turn. Do not confuse hard steering with binding.

The driver may describe hard steering in the following ways:

no power assist

steers like a manual gear

won't turn all the way

hard steering

Hard steering can result from either hydraulic or mechanical problems. 
A complete mechanical and power steering diagnosis is necessary to determine 
the cause. It is extremely important to know if the driver concern occurs 
during driving or during very slow or static park maneuvers. Refer to 
Excessive Steering Effort in symptom chart for possible causes.

Excessive free play or unresponsive motion is a condition in which 
there is too much steering wheel movement before the tires move. A small 
amount of free play is considered normal.

The driver may describe free play in the following ways:

too much slop in the wheel

too much backlash

slack in the wheel

Free play is normally a function of looseness in the steering linkage. 
Refer to Excessive Free Play or Unresponsive Motion in symptom chart for 
possible causes.

Shimmy is a shake or vibration of the front tires that is transmitted 
through the steering wheel.

The driver may describe shimmy in the following ways:

steering wheel shake

cab shakes

steering wheel chatter

Typically, once something triggers a shimmy condition, it is sustained 
until the driver does something (such as slow down) to dampen the condition. 
Refer to Shimmy in symptom chart for possible causes.

Steering wheel kick is felt when the road wheels hit a bump that the 
steering wheel reacts to. The kick is usually dampened out quickly.

Some level of steering wheel kick is normal when operating the vehicle 
on poor roads. Excessive wheel kick on normal roads is generally caused by 
out-of-balance tires, excessive wheel runout or worn shock absorbers. Refer to 
 Section 00-04 for tire and wheel inspection procedures or to Section 04-00 for 
suspension component inspection procedures.

The driver may describe steering wheel kick in the following ways:

kickback

backlash

bump steer

Refer to Steering Wheel Kick in symptom chart for possible causes.

 NOTE: A power steering system should not generate excessive noise in normal 
highway driving and typical maneuvering of a moving vehicle. Noise is normally 
accompanied by poor steering performance if caused by the steering system. In 
some cases, the noise heard by the driver is not caused by the steering 
system. 

Noise in the steering system can come from any number of components. 
Hydraulic system noise can be caused by fluid flow. Metallic or grinding 
noises come from component parts.

The driver may describe noise in the following ways:

growls

swishes

pops when steering

moans/drums

Some noise of an acceptable level is common in all systems, and should 
not be interpreted as a system failure or near failure. High-pressure and 
high-efficiency systems are prone to some noise due to severe operating 
conditions. 

Increased noise may occur during such operating conditions as 
stationary vehicle steering at abnormally high or low engine speed with 
maximum axle loads, or during a rapid steering maneuver, and are considered 
normal for the additional system work requirements.

When noise is present, it must first be determined if it is a 
mechanical or hydraulic noise. Most mechanical noises are a result of 
looseness or wear in components. Hydraulic noise will normally be associated 
with problems in pump flow, such as cavitation or low fluid levels. Refer to 
Steering System Noise symptom chart for possible causes.

External leakage — The actual source of external leakage may be 
difficult to locate because of visual obstruction by other components, fan 
blast, road grime and the fact that fluid tends to run and drip from the 
lowest point, which may not be close to the leakage source. Some leakage may 
only occur with the engine off while other leakage may require pressure. The 
system may have to be cleaned and dried to find the source. The source of the 
leak needs to be found before removing or changing parts.

The driver may describe external leakage in the following ways:

loss of steering fluid

addition of fluid to reservoir continually required

oil on components

oil puddle under vehicle after being parked

leaks at gear box

Refer to External Oil Leakage — Steering Gear or Power Steering 
Pump in symptom chart for possible causes.

 Steering System Test Cycle 

If a standard road test does not verify a steering system condition, 
the following road test can be used to diagnose and resolve customer concerns 
about binds, hard steering or intermittent loss of power assist.

 NOTE: The best place to drive is a large asphalt or concrete parking lot that 
has sufficient space to conduct the maneuvers.

Move vehicle to test drive site. Place wheels straight ahead, place 
transmission in neutral and engage parking brake. Do not test with foot on the 
service brake.

Remove cover from reservoir and note fluid level.

Start engine and run at idle speed for 3 to 5 minutes. 

Shut down engine and note fluid level. If oil level increases, there is 
an air pocket trapped in the steering gear. Air can be sucked into the system 
through cracks in hoses, loose clamps or loose fittings on the inlet side of 
the pump.

Measure fluid temperature and install cover on reservoir. Make sure 
filter is properly positioned before installing cover.

Start engine. With engine at idle speed, slowly rotate steering wheel 
to right and left between the axle stops. Increase speed of steering wheel 
rotation as rapidly as possible and repeat.

Increase engine rpm to 2000 and repeat. Note any discrepancies.

Disengage parking brake and put vehicle into gear. With engine at as 
low a speed as possible, move vehicle in a tight figure eight.

Repeat test if space permits with engine at 1100-1500 rpm. Depending on 
the gear ratio and type of transmission, the figure eight may become larger.

Note anything unusual felt in the steering wheel and compare with the 
information provided by the driver. This test cycle will detect many of the 
different types of steering concerns.

If air in the system is suspected, bleed system and drive vehicle 
again. Determine if steering performance feels different. Concern may have 
been air in the system. Whatever the results, run Power Steering System Test 
Sequence to ensure that the system is working properly.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

System Diagnostic Tips

 Importance of Proper Fan Clutch Operation 

On a vehicle equipped with an on-off fan clutch, a duty cycle used by 
the customer that has many slow-speed steering maneuvers at low ambient 
temperatures may cause excessive system temperatures. Fan clutch operation is 
controlled by coolant water temperature. When ambient temperature is cool and 
vehicle speed is slow, the fan clutch does not engage and air is not 
circulated around the reservoir, plumbing and steering gear. If the vehicle is 
run at these conditions for an extended time period, the power steering system 
can overheat, reducing pump output flow, damaging the seals in the pump and 
steering gear, and causing excessive internal leakage. Continued operation at 
elevated temperatures can damage the steering gear relief valve spring, 
causing a reduction in output pressure. The fluid temperatures can be reduced 
by addition of a power steering cooler. Fan clutch performance should be 
checked before adding a cooler. If the fan clutch is not working properly, 
this is the cause of the high temperatures and no cooler is required.

 Effects of Vehicle Loads 

Although a vehicle can be at a rated axle load, there are at least two 
events in a duty cycle that can cause the front axle to be overloaded. 
Understanding the duty cycle will help with the diagnosis.

When backing up a ramp, weight is transferred to the front axle. If the 
customer has the concern during this mode, high efforts can be expected.

A vehicle in city delivery operation that is equipped with a long body 
with a high amount of rear overhang can have an overloaded front axle near the 
end of its duty cycle. When fully loaded, the load on the front axle does not 
exceed the front axle rating. As the vehicle is partially unloaded from the 
rear at each stop, more weight can be transferred to the front axle. The 
amount of weight transferred is dependent on the commodity. Steering efforts 
will increase as weight is added to the front axle.

 Tires and Their Relation to Steering Efforts 

Low inflation pressures will increase steering efforts because of a 
larger footprint and higher friction on the ground. Inflation pressures should 
be set to vehicle load.

Oversized tires will increase steering efforts. The high effort will be 
noted during maneuvers at one mile per hour or less, or when wheels are turned 
with brakes applied. After determining that system is operating normally by 
performing Test Sequence Procedures, high efforts under these conditions are 
normal.

The data taken during this test can be helpful in determining not only 
if the end-of-travel valves are operating correctly, but can be used as a 
guide to help solve other steering-related concerns.

The test starts with the steering wheel in the vehicle straight-ahead 
position. The pressure buildup should be rapid during the first turn of the 
steering wheel and begin to level off as the amount of turning is increased. 
Effort should be constant. As the road wheels near full turn capability, a 
large effort increase will be felt as the end-of-travel dump valves are 
activated.

The pressure as it levels off should be in the 5516-9653 kPa (800-1400 
psi) range. The actual pressure will vary from vehicle to vehicle depending on 
front end weight and tires.

If an extreme increase in effort is felt and no increase in pressure 
occurs, look for a mechanical fault between the steering gear control valve 
and steering wheel. If a pressure spike or large pressure increase and effort 
increase are observed, look for a mechanical fault in the steering gear or 
between the steering gear and road wheel.

 Turning the Steering Wheel with Brakes Applied 

Depending on front axle weight, turning the steering wheel with brakes 
applied will produce high efforts. This is because the front tires cannot 
rotate as they are turned. With front brakes applied, the efforts can be even 
higher. After determining that the system is operating normally by conducting 
Test Sequence Procedure A1, turn steering wheel with brakes applied. Note 
effort level. Release brake and turn steering wheel. If efforts are reduced, 
system is operating normally.

 High Efforts Near End of Steering Wheel Travel 

Vehicles equipped with a steering gear with end-of-travel unloader 
valves will experience higher steering effort when the valves are activated. 
When the valve is actuated, it permits fluid to flow from the high-pressure 
side of the steering gear piston to the low-pressure side. This reduces the 
amount of available power assist. Additional effort is required to steer the 
vehicle to overcome the reduced level of power assist. Condition is normal if 
all requirements of Test Sequence Procedures test have been met. Unloader 
valves should operate just before the wheel stop contacts the axle beam. 
Always check that correct wheel stop is installed before adjusting unloader 
valves.

 Air Bleeding 

If bubbles are visible in the power steering fluid, bleed air from the 
system as follows:

Check the power steering reservoir fluid level. Add fluid if necessary. 

Run the engine until the fluid reaches normal operating temperature. 

 WARNING: DO NOT HOLD THE STEERING WHEEL IN THE FAR LEFT OR FAR RIGHT POSITION 
FOR MORE THAN FIVE SECONDS TO AVOID HIGH TEMPERATURE AND POSSIBLE DAMAGE TO 
COMPONENTS. 

Turn the steering wheel all the way to the left and right several times 
and return to center.

Recheck fluid level and add Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or 
MERCON® equivalent if necessary. 

 Fluid Level 

Check the fluid level in the power steering reservoir with the engine 
off. Use the HOT or COLD markings on the dipstick, depending upon the fluid 
temperature. 

Use COLD for checking at room temperature, 20°C (70°F). 

Use HOT for normal operating temperatures, 80°C (175°F). 

The fluid level must show between the ADD and FULL markings on the 
dipstick. If the fluid is below the ADD mark, add Motorcraft MERCON® 
ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

 NOTE: After any major power steering system or component overhaul, the system 
should be purged of old fluid and the oil filter discarded, and new fluid and 
a new filter installed.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

External Leakage

 Belt-Driven Power Steering Pump 

If leakage exists between the reservoir and the pump body housing, 
check the retaining bolts for proper torque. If bolts are tight, check the 
reservoir O-rings for cuts, twisting or flat spots and replace where required. 

If leakage exists at the reservoir cap, check the fluid level for 
overfilling. Siphon the excess fluid out with a suction gun to the proper 
level. If leakage persists, check if the cap provides proper sealing and 
tightness. If the cap remains loose, inspect the cap or reservoir neck for 
damage. Service or replace as necessary. 

If leakage exists between the body housing and cover, check if the 
retaining bolts are tight. If bolts are tight, remove the cover and replace 
the O-ring between the cover and body. Refer to Section 11-02B .

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Fluid Leak

With the engine off, wipe the power steering hoses, steering gear and 
reservoir to aid in leak detection. 

If the power steering fluid does not already include dye, mix one 
teaspoonful of oil-soluble aniline dye into power steering fluid and fill the 
reservoir to specification if necessary. 

 CAUTION: Do not hold the wheels against the far right or left position for more 
than 5 seconds to prevent damage to pump. 

With the engine running at 1000-1500 rpm, turn the steering wheel all 
the way to the left and right several times.

Shut off the engine and check for leaks. 

Determine the exact source of leakage. Since most fluid leaks occur at 
fittings and connections in a power steering hydraulic system, the following 
areas should be checked before any other part is replaced. 

 CAUTION: Adjustable hose clamps at oil cooler should not exceed 1.35 Nm 
(12 lb-in). 
Return line hose clamps — tighten or reposition adjustable hose 
clamps to eliminate leakage.

Adapters at gear/assist cylinder ports — if leakage is evident at 
a straight adapter, tighten adapter to 48 Nm (35 lb-ft). If leakage 
persists, remove adapter and replace O-ring on the adapter. If adapter cannot 
be tightened one full turn or if leak persists, remove adapter, replace O-ring 
on adapter, and reinstall directional adapter as follows: 

Make sure jam nut is in loose position on adapter, and metal backup 
washer is positioned against threads for jam nut with O-ring against backup 
washer. 

Install adapter and tighten until metal backup washer contacts pump or 
gear boss. 

Position adapter by loosening adapter no more than one turn. 

Holding adapter in desired direction, tighten jam nut and washer 
against pump or gear boss. 

Thread damage — if leakage is due to damaged threads 
(cross-threaded), replace the connector, the hose fitting end or the hose 
assembly where required. If housing threads on the gear, pump or cylinder are 
badly stripped and cannot be re-dressed with a proper sized tap, replace the 
gear housing, pump body or cylinder.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Start-Up Procedure After Power Steering Pump or Gear Overhaul

Upon initial engine start-up, there is frequently noise and aeration. 
This is due to air trapped in the overhauled unit which mixes with the surging 
fluid and causes aeration. The problem can be minimized if the following 
procedure is used. 

 Fill Process 

Whenever a steering gear, pump or cooler is replaced, follow Steps 1-5.

Place front wheels in straight-ahead position and engage parking brake. 
Do not turn steering wheel during initial fill procedure. 

Fill reservoir with fluid and allow the fluid to gravity-feed the 
system. Crack the pressure line fittings at the pump and steering gear. 
Tighten fittings when fluid is visible. Keep adding fluid to reservoir as 
required.

When fluid level in reservoir no longer goes down, start engine. 
Continue to add fluid to reservoir as required. Do not exceed full mark.

After fluid level in reservoir no longer goes down, rotate steering 
wheel to full right and left turns, stop to stop. Add fluid as required.

Continue process until fluid level no longer changes. Fluid level is 
correct when it is in the full range on the dipstick.

Whenever a minor leak is corrected, follow Steps 6-8.

Place front wheels in straight-ahead position and engage parking brake.

Fill reservoir to full mark on dipstick. Start engine and let idle for 
several minutes. Check fluid level and add as required.

Rotate steering wheel to full right and left turn, stop to stop, 
several times. Stop engine and check fluid level. Fill reservoir to full range 
indicated on dipstick.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering System, Power

TAS power steering gears are the latest design in the Ross family of 
integral hydraulic power steering gears. Integral hydraulic power steering 
means that the gear contains a manual steering mechanism, a hydraulic control 
valve, and a hydraulic power cylinder, all in a single, compact package.

================================================================================
PAGE 3296
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-02A: Steering Gear, Integral Power, Ross TAS40, 55 and 65

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hoses, Pressure and Return

There are two possible leak points at the steering gear fittings.

A leak can occur between the power steering hose (pressure or return 
hose) and the hose nut, or between the hose nut and the steering gear housing 
or pump outlet fitting.

================================================================================
PAGE 3297
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-02A: Steering Gear, Integral Power, Ross TAS40, 55 and 65

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Mechanical Operation

Power is transmitted to the steering gear output shaft (sector shaft) 
by gear teeth on the rack piston. The gear teeth on the rack piston mate with 
the teeth on the sector shaft. Fluid from the engine-driven pump is directed 
to the power cylinder via the control valve, which is concentric to the input 
shaft. 

When force is exerted on the steering wheel to start a steering 
maneuver, the force is transmitted to the input shaft of the steering gear. 
The input shaft is connected to the wormshaft by a torsion bar centering 
device and applies a rotational force to the wormshaft through this 
connection. In response to this rotational force, the wormshaft, acting 
through the recirculating ball mechanism, tries to move the rack piston 
axially. The rack piston axial movement is resisted by its engagement to the 
sector shaft. Because of this resistance, the torsion bar is twisted by the 
input shaft. 

The steering gear input shaft is also the inner member (spool) of the 
rotary control valve. The outer valve member is integral with the wormshaft 
and rotates as a unit. As the torsion bar transmits rotational force from the 
input shaft to the wormshaft, it acts as a spring, deflecting and allowing the 
input shaft to rotate relative to the wormshaft and valve unit. This relative 
rotation between the input shaft and the wormshaft actuates the control valve.

================================================================================
PAGE 3298
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-02A: Steering Gear, Integral Power, Ross TAS40, 55 and 65

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hydraulic Operation

The control valve is an open-center type and when it is in the neutral 
position, the inlet and outlet ports and both cylinder cavities are 
interconnected and there is no flow going to either cylinder cavity. However, 
fluid is circulated from the pump through the control valve and back to the 
reservoir. The pressure in both cylinder cavities is equal and low, sufficient 
only to overcome friction in the lines and the fittings from the outlet port 
to the reservoir. 

As the valve is actuated, the valving edges begin to close, restricting 
flow through the control valve. This restriction directs a portion of the 
fluid flow from the pump to one or the other cylinder cavities. That portion 
of the flow that is not required for the steering maneuver passes through the 
control valve and back to the reservoir. At the same time, the other cylinder 
cavity is opened to the return port and expels fluid back to the reservoir. 

The amount of flow that is directed to the cylinder cavity is 
proportional to the speed at which the steering wheel is being turned. 
Pressure required to complete a steering maneuver is dependent on the amount 
of resistance presented by the steered wheels. The control valve senses these 
requirements and supplies fluid to the cylinder at the proper flow rate and 
pressure. 

As fluid is supplied to the cylinder, the rack piston moves axially, 
rotating the sector shaft and steering the vehicle. The wormshaft is now able 
to rotate in response to the force being applied by the rack piston through 
the recirculating ball and helical screw. Steering action will continue in 
this manner as long as the driver continues to turn the steering wheel. When 
the steering maneuver is completed and effort on the steering wheel is 
relaxed, the torsion bar brings the control valve back to its neutral 
position. 

If the steered wheels are subjected to shock loads, forces are 
transmitted through the sector shaft to the rack piston and on to the worm 
shaft. This actuates the control valve which directs high pressure fluid to 
the proper cylinder to resist the shock load. By absorbing the shock loads 
hydraulically, objectionable kickback at the steering wheel is prevented. 

The gear is equipped with a pressure relief valve, which limits maximum 
supply pressure to protect the pump and gear, but does not reduce the pressure 
as the steered wheels approach the axle stops. 

Tripping the relief valve maintains a constant pressure in the power 
cylinder by allowing a portion of the flow from the pump to circulate through 
the gear and back to the reservoir. Since fluid is allowed to circulate 
through the gear, the pressure relief valve is not required to activate when 
the wheels reach full turn and the amount of heat generated by the pump is 
reduced greatly. 

The TAS gear is equipped with two hydraulic relief poppet valves that 
were automatically set to trip and relieve pressure just before reaching the 
axle stops. This was achieved after initial installation in the vehicle at the 
first right and left turn. The pressure relief poppet valves will 
automatically reset themselves within the poppet adjustment limits if the axle 
stops are reset for increased steering gear travel. These limits are based on 
acceptable equipment revisions from original factory installations. 

If the axle stops are set for decreased steering gear travel, the 
steering gear must be removed from the vehicle and disassembled. The poppet 
adjustment seat and the sleeve assemblies must be reset for automatic 
adjustment after installation.

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Rotary Valve 

The rotary control valve combines simplicity of construction with 
desirable performance characteristics. The speed at which the driver can turn 
the steering wheel with power assist is dependent upon the pump flow (measured 
in gallons per minute, gpm; or liters per minute, lpm) directed to a cylinder 
cavity. The rotary valve controls the flow. 

The pressure (measured in pounds per square inch or bar) required for 
the gear to steer the vehicle is created by the power steering pump to 
overcome resistance at the steered wheels. The control valve senses these 
requirements and directs fluid to the appropriate cylinder cavity in the 
steering gear at the proper flow rate and pressure. 

The higher pressure a steering gear can withstand, the more work it can 
perform. The maximum operating pressure for all TAS gears is 150 bar (2175 
psi). Maximum flow rate for TAS40, 55 and 65 is 7 gpm (26.5 lpm). 

The TAS series gears can steer a vehicle within its front end weight 
rating through a turn at low speed and engine idle. As the driver turns the 
steering wheel faster or slower, more or less fluid will be required by the 
gear.

TAS axle application:

TAS40 6000-7000-lb. front axles

TAS55 8000-9000-lb. front axles

TAS65 10000-, 12000- and 14600-lb. front axles

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Input Shaft Seal 

 NOTE: This procedure uses the vehicle's power steering pump to force out the 
input shaft seal; the input shaft seal is forced out by pressure. To use this 
procedure, the power steering pump should have a minimum of 103.5 bar (1500 
psi) available.

 Removal 

Disconnect return line from the steering gear and plug the line. Also 
cap the return port of the gear with a high-pressure fitting.

[FIGURE: G7885A.gif]

Remove the steering intermediate shaft from the gear input shaft.

[FIGURE: G7886A.gif]

Remove the dirt and water seal from the steering gear.

[FIGURE: G7887A.gif]

 NOTE: Be careful not to scratch the bore with the screwdriver. 

Wipe out the grease and then remove the spiral retaining ring. Use a 
screwdriver inserted into the notch formed in the end of the ring. 

[FIGURE: G7888A.gif]

Slip the steering intermediate shaft back onto the input shaft with the 
pinch bolt installed, but not tightened.

[FIGURE: G7889A.gif]

Tie or wrap a shop towel around the input shaft area and place a drip 
pan under the vehicle to catch the oil.

[FIGURE: G7890A.gif]

 WARNING: DO NOT MIX OIL TYPES. ANY MIXTURE OR ANY UNAPPROVED OIL CAN LEAD TO 
SEAL DETERIORATION AND LEAKS. A LEAK CAN ULTIMATELY CAUSE LOSS OF FLUID, WHICH 
CAN RESULT IN A LOSS OF POWER STEERING ASSIST. 

Add fluid as necessary to the full line on the dipstick.

With the vehicle in neutral, momentarily turn the starter (quickly turn 
off the engine if it starts). 

Remove the shop towel. Disconnect the steering column, and remove the 
input shaft seal.

[FIGURE: G7891A.gif]

Check the seal area of the valve housing for any seal fragments. Remove 
any that are found.

[FIGURE: G7892A.gif]

Check the seal for heat damage. If the seal is stiff and brittle, and 
not pliable like the new seal, it is probably heat-damaged. Determine and fix 
the cause of excessive heat in the power steering system.

[FIGURE: G7893A.gif]

 Installation 

 CAUTION: Do not use a socket to install the input shaft seal. You will not be 
able to control seal installation depth, possibly causing a leak. 

Put clean Ford High-Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease 
E8TZ-19590-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C198-A between the 
seal lips on the inside diameter of the new input shaft seal and place it over 
the input shaft, garter spring side first. Place Input Seal Installer J-37073 
or equivalent over the input shaft and against the seal, small diameter end 
first. Tap the seal installer tool until the tool shoulder is square against 
the valve housing. Remove any seal material that may have sheared off in the 
seal bore or retaining ring groove.

[FIGURE: G7894A.gif]

Insert new retaining ring into the groove.

[FIGURE: G7895A.gif]

Pack the end of the valve housing bore around the input shaft with Ford 
High-Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing Grease E8TZ-19590-A or 
equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C198-A. Apply more of the grease 
to a new dirt and water seal and install it over the input shaft. Seat it in 
the groove behind the serrations and against the valve housing.

[FIGURE: G7896A.gif]

Reconnect the steering intermediate shaft to the input shaft and 
tighten the pinch bolt to torque level specified.

[FIGURE: G7897A.gif]

 CAUTION: Make sure poppets are set correctly before beginning this procedure. 

Reconnect the return line to the steering gear return port.

[FIGURE: G7898A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not allow the fluid level to drop significantly or run out of the 
reservoir. This can induce air into the system. 

Fill the reservoir nearly full. Do not steer. Start and run the engine 
for 10 seconds, then shut it off. Check and refill the reservoir. Repeat at 
least three times, checking the reservoir each time.

Start the engine and let it idle for two minutes. Do not steer. Shut 
off the engine and check the fluid level in the reservoir. Refill as required. 

Start the engine again. Steer the vehicle from full left to full right 
several times. Shut off engine and check the fluid level in reservoir. Add 
fluid as necessary, to the full line on the dipstick. 

Automatic bleed systems should now be free of trapped air. For manual 
bleed systems, continue with Step 10. 

Start engine and let it idle, steer from full left to full right 
several times. Stop steering and loosen the manual bleed screw about one turn. 
Allow air and aerated fluid to "bleed out" until you see only clear fluid. 
Close the bleed screw. Shut off engine and check and refill the reservoir as 
required. 

 CAUTION: Do not turn steering wheel with bleed screw loosened. 

Repeat Step 10 three or four times until all the air is discharged. 
Tighten the manual bleed screw to 3.4 Nm (30 lb-in).

 CAUTION: Do not use a hammer on the pitman arm to remove it from sector shaft as

T64P-3590-F to remove the pitman arm from the sector shaft. 

Remove the bolt and the nut that fasten the pitman arm to the sector 
shaft. Remove the pitman arm from the sector shaft using Pitman Arm Puller 
T64P-3590-F.

 CAUTION: Do not pound the intermediate shaft U-joint or input shaft coupling off 
the input shaft as internal damage to the steering gear can result. 

Remove the bolt and the nut holding the U-joint to the steering gear 
input shaft.

Remove the bolts and the nuts holding the steering gear to the frame 
side rail. Remove the steering gear.

 Installation 

Place the steering gear on the side rail. Install the bolts, the nuts 
and the washers and tighten to 299-406 Nm (220-300 lb-ft) for 3/4-inch 
bolts and 488-650 Nm (360-480 lb-ft) for 7/8-inch bolts. 

 CAUTION: Do not pound the intermediate shaft U-joint or input shaft coupling on 
the input shaft as internal damage to the steering gear can result. 

Place the intermediate shaft U-joint on the steering gear input shaft. 
Tighten to 70-95 Nm (52-70 lb-ft).

 WARNING: WHEN USING A CHISEL TO SPREAD A PINCH BOLT-TYPE PITMAN ARM BOSS FOR 
ASSEMBLY TO THE SHAFT, MAINTAIN A FIRM GRIP ON THE CHISEL AT ALL TIMES. 
FAILURE TO DO THIS CAN RESULT IN THE CHISEL FLYING LOOSE WHICH COULD CAUSE AN 
INJURY. NEVER LEAVE THE CHISEL WEDGED IN THE PITMAN ARM BOSS. DO NOT USE A 
HAMMER ON THE PITMAN ARM TO INSTALL THE PITMAN ARM ON THE SECTOR SHAFT AS 
INTERNAL DAMAGE TO STEERING GEAR CAN RESULT. 

Place the pitman arm on the steering gear sector shaft, making sure the 
timing mark on the pitman arm aligns with the timing mark on the sector shaft. 
Use a chisel to help spread the pitman arm to slide on the shaft.

Install the bolt and nut. Tighten the nut to 299-406 Nm (220-300 
lb-ft). 

Connect the power steering pressure and return lines to the gear. 

Fill the reservoir with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or 
MERCON® equivalent.

Start the engine, turn the steering wheel from left to right and check 
for fluid leaks.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Steering Gear 

 Disassembly 

 CAUTION: Do not clamp against the body of the housing as this can damage the 
housing and cause difficulties during the disassembly and assembly procedures. 
If mounting boss or flange is not accessible, fabricate and attach a mounting 
plate to the housing mounting bosses. 

Put the steering gear in a vise so that the input shaft is in a 
horizontal direction. Tighten the jaws of the vise on the mounting flange or 
the housing boss.

Put a pan under the steering gear. Unplug the hydraulic ports on the 
gear. Drain the fluid from the gear. 

Use a 3/4- or 11/16-inch twelve-point socket to rotate the input shaft 
and valve worm assembly until the timing mark on the end of the sector shaft 
is aligned with the timing mark on the end of the housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G68061A.gif]

Use a small screwdriver to remove the dirt and water seal from the 
housing trunnion. Remove any paint or corrosion from the exposed area of the 
sector shaft with a fine grade of emery cloth.

[FIGURE: G6807B.gif]

Tape the serrations and the bolt groove of the sector shaft with one 
layer of masking tape. The tape must not extend onto the diameter of the 
sector shaft bearing.

[FIGURE: G8405A.gif]

Remove the jam nut from the sector shaft adjusting screw.

[FIGURE: G8406A.gif]

 NOTE: The bolts that fasten the side cover (end cover) to the housing are 
equipped with a ring or a washer under the head of the bolt. If you replace 
one or more bolts, you must replace them with bolts of the same design and 
length as the bolt being removed. Do not use a substitute. 

Be prepared for more fluid drainage and remove the six bolts that 
fasten the side cover to the housing. 

[FIGURE: G6808B.gif]

Remove the side cover and sector shaft assembly as a unit from the 
gear. If necessary, lightly tap on the end of the shaft with a soft mallet. 
Remove and discard side cover gasket.

[FIGURE: G8407A.gif]

Remove and discard vent plug. Remove reverse-threaded sector shaft 
adjusting screw by turning the screw clockwise through the side cover. Pull 
the sector shaft out of the side cover.

[FIGURE: G6809B.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not damage the bore or DU bushing when removing the seal. 

Clamp the side cover in a vise. Place a standard 5/8-inch or 11/16-inch 
3/8 drive socket in the center of the side cover. Pry seal out with a rolling 
head pry bar, using the socket for support. Discard seal and remove the socket.

Inspect the sector shaft assembly for damaged adjusting screw threads. 
The staked retainer must be locked in place and have no cracks. The adjusting 
screw must rotate by hand with no perceptible end play (lash). 

If replacement is required, refer to Adjusting Screw and Retainer in 
the Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section. If no damage is noted, 
proceed to Step 13.

[FIGURE: G8408A.gif]

If so equipped, remove relief valve cap, O-ring and two-piece relief 
valve, from valve housing. Discard O-ring.

[FIGURE: G8409A.gif]

Remove and discard dirt and water seal from input shaft. Note position 
of spring to relief valve.

[FIGURE: G8410A.gif]

Clean any paint or corrosion from exposed area of input shaft.

[FIGURE: G8411A.gif]

Remove the four Torx® head valve housing bolts.

[FIGURE: G8412A.gif]

 CAUTION: The set position of poppet seat and sleeve assemblies must not be 
disturbed if the poppets are not going to be replaced or pushed in during 
assembly. 

Be prepared for more fluid drainage and remove the rack piston 
subassembly. Place the assembly on a clean cloth. It may help to rotate the 
input shaft to move the rack piston toward the lower end of the housing. This 
will force the valve housing to exit the main housing.

[FIGURE: G8413A.gif]

 CAUTION: If the automatically set poppets are not to be removed for replacement 
or to be reset for automatic repositioning after the next installation, make 
sure the set position of the poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly is not 
disturbed. The steering gear should be identified to the vehicle it is removed 
from and noted that the poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies are set for 
that particular vehicle only. 

 NOTE: If the Teflon® rack piston seal is on the end of the rack 
piston away from the rack piston bore opening, cut the seal. Remove the seal 
ring from the rack piston when it is exposed in the sector shaft cavity of the 
housing during the removal of the rack piston assembly, the input shaft valve, 
worm assembly and the valve piston. This prevents the seal from "hanging up" 
as it exits the housing sector shaft cavity. 

Remove and discard the seal rings from the valve housing.

[FIGURE: G68121A.gif]

If the clip-type ball return guide is used, bend down the tabs that are 
against the hex-head bolts. Remove the bolts and the clip. Discard the clip.

[FIGURE: G68131A.gif]

If a cap-type return guide is used, remove and discard the two special 
sealing screws that fasten the cap to the piston using 5/32 Allen wrench or 
T-30 Torx® wrench. Remove the cap and cap seal. Discard the seal.

[FIGURE: G68141A.gif]

 NOTE: Left ball return guide halves are copper-plated for identification and 
right guides are not plated. 

Make sure the rack piston is on a cloth so the steel balls that fall 
out won't roll very far. Remove ball return guide halves by carefully 
inserting a screwdriver between the rack piston and guides.

 CAUTION: The steel balls are a matched set. If any are lost, the complete set 
must be replaced by service balls. Number of factory balls installed: TAS40 
— 29, TAS55 — 31 (30 if date code is 337-89 or earlier) and TAS65 
— 32. 

Remove the steel balls from the rack piston by rotating the input 
shaft, valve, worm assembly until the balls fall out. Place the balls and 
return guides in a cup or other container and make sure all the balls have 
been removed.

[FIGURE: G8414A.gif]

Remove the input shaft, valve worm and valve housing subassembly from 
the rack piston.

[FIGURE: G6815B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Description

1

3K748

Rack Piston

2

3B541

O-Ring

3

—

Seal Ring (Part of 3504)

4

3647

Balls

5

3523

Return Guide

Cut and remove the Teflon® seal ring and the O-ring from the 
rack piston if not removed during Step 17.

[FIGURE: G8415A.gif]

 NOTE: TRW recommends the poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies not be 
removed unless replacement of poppet components is required. 

Inspect poppet stems and seat and sleeve assemblies for damage. Push 
poppet stems; they should spring back. Push poppet seat; it should not move by 
hand. If components are bent or broken, or if poppet stems don't spring back 
or poppet seat moves by hand, refer to Poppet Component Replacement in the 
Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section. Otherwise, proceed to Step 26.

Inspect valve housing/worm screw subassembly for heat damage or bearing 
roughness. If these conditions are present, or if there is excessive internal 
leakage, or if preload adjustment is required, refer to Worm and Valve Sleeve 
in the Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section. If not, proceed to 
Step 27.

[FIGURE: G8416A.gif]

Remove the retaining ring that is closest to the output end of the 
housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G68231A.gif]

Remove and discard the dirt seal from the housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G68241A.gif]

Insert a screwdriver from the trunnion end of the housing and carefully 
push the seal and the spacer washer out of the other end of the housing 
without damaging the sealing area or the spacer washer. Discard the seal.

[FIGURE: G68251A.gif]

Inspect roller bearing in the housing for brinelling or spalling. 
Inspect retaining ring for damage. If replacement of either part is required, 
refer to Housing Roller Bearing or Retaining Ring Replacement in the 
Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section. If not, proceed to Step 31. 

Inspect the following for damage: 

poppet fixed stop screw and washer 

poppet adjusting screw and sealing nut 

pressed-in grease fitting 

auto-bleed plug 

manual bleed screw 

auxiliary port plugs and O-rings

If any are damaged, refer to Housing Ports, Plugs, Screws and Fittings 
in the Disassembly and Assembly portion of this section. If not, proceed to 
Cleaning and Inspection in this section. 

 Assembly 

 NOTE: Bolt torques are given for both dry threads and lubricated threads. TRW 
recommends lubricating threads with oil and using the lubricated torque 
specifications. 

 NOTE: Replace all of the seals, the seal rings and the gaskets every time the 
gear is disassembled. 

Install a new dirt seal into the trunnion end of the sector shaft bore 
of the housing. Make sure the seal is installed against the bearing and the 
lip of the seal faces outward.

[FIGURE: G68321A.gif]

Install the second retaining ring. Make sure the ring is firmly seated 
in the groove in the housing.

[FIGURE: G68331A.gif]

 NOTE: A dab of grease applied to the small diameter of the washer will hold 
it in place during installation of the seal. 

Install washer into the side cover side of housing seal bore with small 
diameter piloted into retaining ring. 

[FIGURE: G8418A.gif]

Assemble new seal onto Bearing and Seal Tool J37705 (TAS40) or J37071 
(TAS55 and 65) or equivalent so the lip with the garter spring is toward the 
shoulder of the tool. 

Working from the side cover side of the housing, pilot the seal tool 
into the washer and bearing and press with a force of 445-3,560 N (100-800 
lbf) until the seal is seated against washer.

[FIGURE: G8419A.gif]

Liberally pack the area between dirt seal and pressure seal including 
roller bearing with Ford High-Temperature 4x4 Front Axle and Wheel Bearing 
Grease E8TZ-19590-A or equivalent meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C198-A.

[FIGURE: G8420A.gif]

Lightly oil new seal ring and assemble in valve housing mounting face 
groove. 

[FIGURE: G8421A.gif]

Install a new backup O-ring and then a new Teflon® seal ring on 
rack piston. Do not overstretch these rings as you install them. Do not allow 
the Teflon® seal ring to be twisted.

[FIGURE: G8422A.gif]

Apply clean oil to housing cylinder bore. Place the rack piston in a 
V-block with ball return guide holes up.

[FIGURE: G8423A.gif]

Insert the worm screw into the rack piston close to maximum depth, 
without the valve housing making contact with the poppet stem. Insert two 
7/16-14 Ready Bolts through valve housing bolt holes and tighten into housing 
to support the worm screw. Line up rack piston ball guide holes with the worm 
ball track grooves by rotating the input shaft.

[FIGURE: G8424B.gif]

 WARNING: DO NOT SEAT GU

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Adjusting Screw and Retainer 

 Disassembly 

 NOTE: A service sector shaft will come assembled with the adjusting screw and 
retainer. 

Inspect the sector shaft bearing and sealing areas and sector teeth 
contact surfaces for brinelling, spalling or cracks. Run your fingernail edge 
across these areas to detect steps. Remove masking tape from the shaft and 
inspect for twisted or otherwise damaged serrations. If any of these 
conditions exist, replace the sector shaft.

[FIGURE: G68291A.gif]

If damage was not found in Step 1, place the sector shaft firmly in a 
soft-jawed vise and unstake the retainer. Turn the retainer out of the sector 
shaft pocket. 

If necessary, remove the adjusting screw. If adjusting screw is 
replaced, retainer must also be replaced.

[FIGURE: G8440A.gif]

 Assembly 

If the adjusting screw has been removed, coat the expanded end of the 
new adjusting screw with a suitable grade of wheel bearing grease and insert 
into recess in end of sector shaft.

[FIGURE: G8441A.gif]

 WARNING: STAKE THE RETAINER SECURELY INTO THE SECTOR SHAFT SLOTS. IF THE 
RETAINER IS BROKEN OR CRACKED DURING THE STAKING, REPLACE IT. FAILURE TO DO SO 
CAN RESULT IN THE LOSS OF MANUAL AND POWER STEERING CONTROL. 

Thread a new sector shaft screw retainer into the sector shaft. Tighten 
and then stake the retainer in the two slots provided. The adjusting screw 
should rotate freely by hand, with very little end play, 0.05 mm (0.000-0.002 
inch).

[FIGURE: G8442A.gif]

================================================================================

Section 11-02A: Steering Gear, Integral Power, Ross TAS40, 55 and 65

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Poppet Component Replacement 

 Disassembly 

If the poppet assemblies are to be removed for replacement or 
internally reset for fully automatic poppet adjustment after reinstallation, 
place rack piston in a soft-jawed vise.

 CAUTION: Poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies are retained by 
Loctite® applied to the threads, which makes the assemblies difficult 
to remove. 

Slide special Poppet Adjusting Seat Tool J36452-A or equivalent over 
the seat of poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly and engage tool in the 
slots in the threaded sleeve. Hit the end of the tool firmly four or five 
times with a 2-lb. hammer to loosen Loctite®.

[FIGURE: G8443A.gif]

With a ratchet applied to the tool, turn one adjuster seat and sleeve 
assembly out of the rack piston. If the ratchet does not turn easily, strike 
the adjuster removal tool again with a hammer. If the engaging tangs won't 
stay in place while tightening, it might be necessary to hold in place with an 
arbor press while applying loosening torque. Discard poppet seat and sleeve 
assembly.

[FIGURE: G8444A.gif]

Remove the two poppets, spring, spacer rod and push tube.

[FIGURE: G8445A.gif]

 NOTE: One poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly can often be reset for 
automatic poppet adjustment while it is in the rack piston if one adjuster 
seat and sleeve assembly and the poppets, spring, spacer rod and push tube are 
removed. 

Remove remaining poppet seat and sleeve assembly as required.

 Assembly 

Clean threads on poppet seat and sleeve assemblies. Use a 7/16-20 UNF 
thread chaser. 

Screw poppet seat and sleeve assembly loosely into its threaded hole in 
the rack piston for full thread length with slotted end in.

[FIGURE: G8446A.gif]

 NOTE: If one poppet seat and sleeve assembly was left in rack piston, it can 
be reset for automatic poppet adjustment by inserting a 9.52 mm (3/8-inch) 
diameter x 152.4 mm (6-inch) drill rod down through the poppet seat hole at 
the opposite end of the rack piston and against the adjuster seat to press the 
seat in until it bottoms against the adjuster sleeve. 

Press the adjuster seat into the sleeve using 2,224-11,120 N (500-2,500 
lbs.) force until shoulder on the seat bottoms against the sleeve. Remove the 
adjuster seat and sleeve assembly from the rack piston, and repeat procedure 
for other poppet seat and sleeve assembly if removed.

[FIGURE: G8447A.gif]

 WARNING: WEAR EYE PROTECTION WHILE ASSEMBLING POPPETS, AS SPRING-LOADED POPPETS 
CAN EJECT AND CAUSE EYE INJURY. 

 CAUTION: Do not allow Loctite® or Locquic to get on the adjuster seat 
component of the adjuster seat and sleeve assembly. The poppets will not 
function properly. 

Carefully apply Locquic T primer to the threads in poppet holes, and 
threads on the seat and sleeve assemblies. Allow to dry for ten minutes, then 
carefully apply Loctite® RC680 to same threads.

[FIGURE: G8448A.gif]

Place rack piston in a soft-jawed vise and turn one poppet adjuster 
seat and sleeve assembly (slotted end out) into the poppet hole in one end of 
rack piston, if both seat and sleeve assemblies were removed.

From other end of the poppet hole in the rack piston, install the 
following: 

one poppet 

poppet spring 

nylon spacer rod 

push tube 

other poppet 

other poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assembly

[FIGURE: G8449A.gif]

Tighten both poppet adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies to 14 Nm 
(10 lb-ft), using Poppet Adjusting Seat Tool J36452-A or equivalent and a 
torque wrench.

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Worm and Valve Sleeve

 Disassembly 

With worm vertical, place the valve housing, input shaft, valve, worm 
assembly in a vise.

[FIGURE: G8450A.gif]

Unstake the valve housing where it was upset into the adjuster lock nut 
slot. Also unstake adjuster nut from adjuster.

[FIGURE: G8451A.gif]

Using Adjuster Locknut Tool J37464 or equivalent, turn bearing adjuster 
lock nut out of the valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8452A.gif]

Using Bearing Adjuster Tool J37070 or equivalent, turn bearing adjuster 
out of the valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8453A.gif]

Remove and discard seal ring and O-ring from bearing adjuster.

[FIGURE: G8454A.gif]

Remove the input shaft, valve, worm assembly from the valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8455A.gif]

Remove thin thrust washer and thrust bearing from input shaft.

[FIGURE: G8456A.gif]

 CAUTION: Input shaft, valve, worm assembly must not be disassembled further. The 
components were a select fit at assembly and are available only as part of 
this subassembly. If disassembled further, the subassembly must be replaced. 

Remove thick thrust washer and thrust bearing from valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8457A.gif]

 CAUTION: Exercise special care when removing seal to prevent damaging the valve 
housing seal bore. 

Remove and discard seal rings and O-rings from valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8459A.gif]

Turn over valve housing and remove retaining ring.

[FIGURE: G8460A.gif]

 NOTE: The valve housing also uses a ball plug for manufacturing purposes that 
must not be removed. 

Tap input shaft seal out of valve housing. Discard seal.

[FIGURE: G8461A.gif]

 Assembly 

Inspect the sealing areas of input shaft and valve for nicks and run 
your fingernail edge across the sealing surfaces to detect steps. Inspect for 
discoloration from excess heat. Inspect input shaft ball track grooves for 
brinelling or spalling. If any of these conditions exist, you must replace the 
input shaft, valve, worm assembly, valve housing and balls. Also replace rack 
piston if brinelling or spalling is found.

[FIGURE: G68281A.gif]

Inspect the thrust bearing rollers for any deterioration. Inspect 
thrust washers for brinelling, spalling, or cracks. Replace any part with 
these conditions.

[FIGURE: G8462A.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not clamp against threaded port hole or relief valve hole sealing 
faces when placing valve housing in vise. 

Place valve housing firmly in a vise so the input shaft, valve, worm 
assembly can be assembled vertically with worm end up.

[FIGURE: G8463A.gif]

Oil and assemble a new O-ring into its counterbore in valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8464A.gif]

Lightly oil and assemble new O-ring and new seal ring into the large 
diameter seal ring groove in valve housing, bending and working them in and 
smoothing them out as necessary.

[FIGURE: G8465A.gif]

Install roller thrust bearing and then the thick washer onto input 
shaft end of input shaft, valve, worm subassembly, seating them against the 
input shaft thrust face.

[FIGURE: G8466A.gif]

Lightly oil and assemble new seal ring onto input shaft and against the 
thick thrust washer to hold the bearing components in place.

[FIGURE: G8468A.gif]

Dip the input end of the input shaft, valve, worm assembly into oil up 
to the worm lead. Assemble the input shaft end of the assembly into the valve 
housing until it is firmly seated.

[FIGURE: G8469A.gif]

Apply oil and assemble the other thrust bearing then the thin thrust 
washer over the ball groove end of worm, and seat them against the shoulder of 
input shaft, valve, worm assembly.

[FIGURE: G8470A.gif]

 NOTE: Make sure the valve housing, adjuster lock nut and bearing adjuster 
threads are clean and free of any staking burrs that can impede the lock nut 
from turning freely on adjuster or the adjuster turning freely in valve 
housing. 

Lightly oil a new O-ring and assemble into the seal groove in bearing 
adjuster. Oil and work a new seal ring into the same groove and smooth it out.

[FIGURE: G8471A.gif]

Lightly oil and assemble bearing adjuster over worm and into valve 
housing. Tighten adjuster to 18 Nm (13 lb-ft), using a torque wrench 
inserted in Bearing Adjuster Tool J37070 or equivalent. This will seat the 
components. Back off adjuster 1/4 to 1/2 turn.

[FIGURE: G8472A.gif]

Reverse assembly in vise so the worm end is down. With an inch-pound 
torque wrench on the input shaft, note torque required to rotate input shaft 
360 degrees in each direction. Tighten the bearing adjuster to increase the 
maximum torque at the input shaft 0.5-1.0 Nm (5-9 lb-in) over that 
which was previously noted.

[FIGURE: G8473A.gif]

 NOTE: The bearing adjuster, lock nut and valve housing flange should be 
flush. If not, the seal or O-ring may be out of position, which will result in 
axial lash.

Again reverse assembly in vise. Lightly oil and assemble new lock nut 
onto bearing adjuster with radius (slightly rounded) side down. Tighten lock 
nut while holding bearing adjuster in position established in Step 12 with 
appropriate Bearing and Seal Tool, J37705 (TAS40) or J37071 (TAS55 and 65) or 
equivalent. When using a torque wrench in Adjuster Locknut Tool J37464 or 
equivalent, the torque wrench reading should be 152 Nm (112 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: G8474A.gif]

Recheck input shaft torque. It should match torque measured in Step 12. 
Repeat Steps 12 and 13 if necessary. 

[FIGURE: G8475A.gif]

Stake valve housing into the clockwise-most corner of two opposing 
slots in lock nut. Stake the locknut into the adjuster in two places (180 
degrees apart) at threaded area. Choose areas that have not been previously 
staked. 

After staking, torque required to rotate input shaft must be 0.5-1.0 
Nm (5-9 lb-in) greater than the torque noted in Step 12. Torque value 
must not exceed 2.5 Nm (22 lb-in). Unstake and readjust if necessary.

[FIGURE: G8476A.gif]

Reposition worm screw/valve housing subassembly in soft-jawed vise, 
clamping tightly against valve housing, so that the worm screw is pointing 
sideways.

Apply clean grease to the outside and inside diameters (fill cavity 
between the lips) of the new input shaft seal and assemble it, garter spring 
side first over the input shaft. Align seal in the valve housing seal bore. 

Assemble Input Seal Installer Tool No. J37073 or equivalent, small 
diameter end first, over the input shaft and against the seal. Tap the seal 
installer tool until the tool shoulder is squarely against the valve housing. 
This will correctly position the seal in the housing bore just beyond the 
retaining ring groove.

[FIGURE: G8477A.gif]

 CAUTION: The input shaft seal must be square in the seal bore and installed to 
the correct depth. 

Remove any seal material that may have sheared off and is in seal bore 
and retaining ring groove.

Insert new retaining ring into its groove in valve housing.

[FIGURE: G8478A.gif]

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Housing Roller Bearing or Retaining Ring Replacement 

 Disassembly 

 CAUTION: The bearing must be pressed out from the side cover to protect seal 
counterbore. Be sure to use a bearing removal tool that will clear the 
retaining ring. 

If roller bearing in housing needs to be replaced, place the bearing 
removal end of the Bearing and Seal Tool J37705 (TAS40) or J37071 (TAS55 and 
65) or equivalent, against the side cover end of the bearing and press it out 
of trunnion end of the bearing bore. Discard bearing.

[FIGURE: G8479A.gif]

If the retaining ring that is still in the housing bearing bore needs 
to be replaced, remove it through the trunnion end of the bearing bore to 
protect the pressure seal bore area from being damaged.

[FIGURE: G8480A.gif]

 Assembly 

Insert retaining ring, if it was removed, into the housing bore from 
the trunnion end (to protect sealing area). Make sure it is seated in the 
retaining ring groove closest to side cover end of the bearing bore. Lubricate 
the bearing bore.

[FIGURE: G8481A.gif]

 CAUTION: Use the bearing installation end of the tool. If the bearing removal 
end of the bearing and seal tool is used to press in bearing, the cage on the 
new bearing can be damaged. 

Using Bearing and Seal Tool J37705 (TAS40) or J37071 (TAS55 and 65) or 
equivalent, press the roller bearing into the housing from the trunnion end of 
bearing bore until it is seated against the retaining ring. Make sure the 
housing is square with the press base and the bearing is not cocked.

[FIGURE: G8482A.gif]

 Disassembly and Assembly

[FIGURE: G8483A.gif]

[FIGURE: G8484A.gif]

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Final Adjustment 

 NOTE: The worm preload adjustment is part of the wormshaft and valve sleeve 
disassembly and assembly procedure.

 CAUTION: Do not rotate the input shaft more than one and one-half revolutions 
from the center position until the steering gear is installed, during the 
poppet setting procedure. Doing so can make the automatic poppets inoperative, 
which requires disassembly of the steering gear to reposition poppet seat and 
sleeve assemblies. 

 NOTE: Initial poppet contact will occur at less than one input shaft rotation 
in one direction from the steering gear center position if new or reset poppet 
adjuster seat and sleeve assemblies are installed in the unit. 

Use a 3/4- or 11/16-inch twelve-point socket to rotate the input shaft, 
valve, worm assembly until the timing mark on the end of the sector shaft is 
aligned with the timing mark on the end of the housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G68061A.gif]

 NOTE: This procedure will properly mesh and seat the rack piston and the 
sector shaft teeth for final adjustments. 

Turn the sector shaft adjusting screw clockwise to provide 5.0-5.5 
Nm (45-50 lb-in) of torque required to rotate the input shaft and valve 
worm assembly through 180 degrees each side of center.

[FIGURE: G8437A.gif]

Turn the sector shaft adjusting screw counterclockwise one-half turn 
and note the maximum torque required to rotate the input shaft, valve, worm 
assembly through 180 degrees each side of center.

[FIGURE: G8438A.gif]

Adjust the sector shaft adjusting screw clockwise to increase the 
maximum torque noted in Step 3 by 0.8 Nm (7 lb-in). Tighten jam nut 
firmly against side cover while holding the adjusting screw in place. 

Tighten the jam nut to 58 Nm (43 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: G8439A.gif]

Check the rotating torque of the input shaft, valve, worm assembly 
again. Readjust if the torque exceeds 4.5 Nm (40 lb-in). 

Plug all ports until the gear is installed in the vehicle.

[FIGURE: G68631A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Steering Gear

 WARNING: SINCE SOLVENTS ARE FLAMMABLE, BE EXTREMELY CAREFUL WHEN USING ANY 
SOLVENT. EVEN A SMALL EXPLOSION OR FIRE CAN CAUSE INJURY OR DEATH. 

 WARNING: WEAR EYE PROTECTION AND MAKE SURE TO COMPLY WITH OSHA OR OTHER MAXIMUM 
AIR PRESSURE REQUIREMENTS. 

Make sure that all seal surfaces and seal cavities are free from nicks 
and corrosion. If any part is nicked or corroded where sealing occurs, replace 
the parts to make sure they seal properly. 

Wash all parts in a clean petroleum-base solvent. Air blow the parts 
until dry.

Inspect the teeth of the rack piston for cracks and wear. If a step is 
detected by running a fingernail horizontally across the tooth surface, the 
rack piston, the sector shaft and the set of 29 service balls for TAS40, 31 
balls for TAS55 (30 if date code is 337-89 or earlier) or 32 balls for TAS65 
must be replaced.

[FIGURE: G68261A.gif]

Inspect the internal ball track grooves of the rack piston for 
brinelling (dents) or spalling (flaking). If either condition exists, replace 
the rack piston, input shaft, worm valve assembly and the set of balls as an 
assembly.

[FIGURE: G68271A.gif]

Inspect the input shaft, worm valve assembly, ball track grooves, 
thrust bearing, and the ball bearing areas for brinelling (dents) or spalling 
(flaking). Inspect the sealing areas of the input shaft and valve for nicks. 
Run a fingernail edge across the sealing surfaces to detect steps. Inspect for 
discoloration from excess heat. If any of these conditions exist, replace the 
input shaft, valve housing, valve worm assembly and the set of balls as an 
assembly. Also replace rack piston if brinelling or spalling is found.

[FIGURE: G68281A.gif]

 NOTE: In performing the internal leakage test after assembling the gear, make 
sure internal leakage over 1.0 gpm (3.8 liters/min) is not caused by the 
improper installation of seals on the wormshaft, rack piston and valve 
assembly. 

Replace the housing only if internal leakage is greater than 1.0 gpm 
(3.8 liters/min). Make sure a seal is not causing the leak. The bore of the 
housing may show signs of scoring but these signs may indicate normal wear.

Inspect the face of the housing for nicks that prevent proper sealing. 
Replace the housing if the nicks cannot be easily removed with a fine-tooth 
flat file without damage to the housing. 

Inspect side cover DU bushing for damage. Also check side cover bushing 
to sector shaft clearance. If damage exists or if clearance exceeds 0.20 mm 
(0.008 inch), replace side cover/bushing assembly.

[FIGURE: G8417A.gif]

 NOTE: A service sector shaft assembly will have the adjusting screw and the 
retainer installed. The screw and the retainer can be serviced separately. 

Remove all masking tape from the sector shaft. Inspect the bearing, 
sealing and tooth contact surfaces on the sector shaft for brinelling, 
spalling or cracks. Run the edge of a fingernail across these areas to detect 
steps. Inspect for cracks. Look for twisted or damaged serrations. Replace the 
sector shaft if any of these conditions exist.

[FIGURE: G68291A.gif]

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Steering Gear Housing

Inspect the steering gear housing for cracks and stripped threads and 
the mating surfaces for burrs. Inspect the piston bore for scoring or wear. If 
necessary, replace the steering gear housing. Surface burnishing is acceptable 
if no significant step can be felt.

ADJUSTMENTS

Sector Shaft Adjustment 

Refer to the Power Steering Gear illustration in the Removal and 
Installation portion of this section. 

 CAUTION: This adjustment must be performed with the sector shaft on its center 
of travel. 

 CAUTION: The input shaft must not be rotated more than 1.5 revolutions when the 
drag link is disconnected from the steering gear to avoid possible 
misadjustment of the automatic poppet system. 

 NOTE: If the adjusting screw jam nut is accessible, this adjustment can be 
completed on the vehicle. Otherwise, the steering gear must be removed from 
the vehicle. 

 NOTE: If this adjustment is being performed with the steering gear on the 
vehicle, remove the drag link from the pitman arm. 

Put the sector shaft in the center of travel. Rotate the input shaft 
until the timing marks across the end of the sector shaft are perpendicular to 
the input shaft and the valve worm is in line with the timing mark on the end 
of the housing trunnion.

[FIGURE: G67711A.gif]

With the steering gear in the center position, grasp the pitman arm and 
gently try to move the arm back and forth in the direction of travel. 
Fingertip force is adequate to detect the lash of a loose sector shaft. There 
must be no movement of the input shaft or the sector shaft.

[FIGURE: G6772B.gif]

Loosen the jam nut on the sector shaft adjusting screw. If no lash was 
detected, turn the adjusting screw counterclockwise until lash is detected at 
the output shaft. 

 CAUTION: Overadjustment of the shaft adjusting screw in the clockwise direction 
can result in a no-recovery, oversteering or darting condition of the vehicle. 

To adjust, slowly turn the adjusting screw clockwise until no lash is 
felt at the pitman arm. Use no more than 14 Nm (10 lb-ft) of torque. 
From the no-lash position, turn the screw clockwise an additional 1/8-3/16 
turn. Hold the adjusting screw in place and tighten the jam nut to 58 
Nm (43 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: G67731A.gif]

Turn the input shaft one-quarter turn each side of center and recheck 
the pitman arm for lash. No lash should be felt. If lash exists, repeat Steps 
1-4. 

 CAUTION: Maintain grease in the sector shaft bearing through the grease fitting 
in the housing using only a hand-operated grease gun. Add grease until it 
begins to extrude past the dirt and water seal. Do not use a power grease gun 
because it will supply grease too fast. This can adversely affect the 
high-pressure seal and contaminate the hydraulic fluid. 

If the adjustment was done with the steering gear on the vehicle, 
install the drag link to the pitman arm. If the steering gear was removed from 
the vehicle, install the gear in the vehicle.
