1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Poppet Valve Manual Readjustment

The steering gear is equipped with two hydraulic pressure-relieving 
poppet valves that were automatically set to trip, relieving pressure just 
before reaching the axle stops. This was achieved after initial installation 
into the vehicle at the first full right and left turns. The 
pressure-relieving poppet valves will automatically reset themselves within 
the poppet adjustment limits if the axle stops are reset for increased 
steering gear travel based on acceptable equipment revisions from original 
factory installations. 

To determine if the poppets require readjustment or if they are 
performing properly, install Rotunda Power Steering Analyzer 014-00230 or 
equivalent between the power steering pump and the steering gear. If poppet 
readjustment is necessary, you can leave the analyzer in the system to verify 
that the following procedure is completed properly. 

Poppets might need to be readjusted because of the following: 

changing to larger tires 

reduced vehicle wheelcut 

pitman arm mistimed, condition corrected 

steering gear being installed on a different truck 

steer axle stop bolt(s) were bent or broken 

steer axle U-bolt(s) were bent or broken 

An alternate method of manually resetting the poppet valves with the 
steering gear installed in the vehicle is done by using Ross special service 
tools, Bearing Adjusting Tool J37070 and Adjuster Lock Nut Tool J37464 or 
equivalents. 

This resetting procedure will work in most cases with at least 1-3/4 
hand wheel turns from each side of center. If you are making a large reduction 
in wheel cut and this procedure does not work, you may have to internally 
reset the poppets using the procedure described in Poppet Component 
Replacement procedure in this section.

Check the maximum turn angle of the front wheels. Refer to the 
Specifications portion of Section 04-00 for the correct specifications. 

 NOTE: The steering gear will have either a fixed stop screw or an adjusting 
screw. If the adjusting screw is already part of the steering gear, back the 
nut off the adjusting screw until it is flush with the end of the adjusting 
screw. 

 NOTE: Only perform the following step with the wheels in the straight-ahead 
position, the steering gear in its center position and only when the timing 
marks on the end of the sector shaft and the housing trunnion are aligned. 

Turn adjusting screw into the non-sealing end of jam nut until the 
drive end of the screw is flush with the nut. Refer to Special Service 
Tools/Equipment in this section for the proper adjusting screw kit number.

[FIGURE: G6774C.gif]

 NOTE: If the unit has a poppet adjusting screw and sealing nut that need to 
be replaced, remove and discard them. 

With the vehicle unloaded, the engine off and the wheels in the 
straight-ahead position, remove and discard the fixed stop screw, if so 
equipped, and the washer from the lower end of the housing.

[FIGURE: G8401A.gif]

Install the adjusting screw and the sealing nut assembly (without 
moving the nut on the screw) into the housing until the nut is firmly against 
the housing. Tighten the sealing nut against the housing. 

[FIGURE: G6775B.gif]

 CAUTION: Do not mix fluid types. Mixing transmission fluid, motor oil, or other 
hydraulic fluids will cause seals to deteriorate faster. 

Fill the power steering reservoir with the specified fluid, Motorcraft 
MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

Place a jack under the center of the front axle and jack up the front 
end of the vehicle so the steering axle tires are off the ground. 

Start the engine and let it run at idle speed.

Note which output shaft timing mark is nearest the housing piston bore.

 CAUTION: Do not hold the steering wheel in this position for more than 10 
seconds at a time. Excessive heat buildup can damage components. 

Turn the steering wheel in the direction that makes this timing mark 
move toward the adjusting screw just installed. Turn in this direction until 
axle stop contact is made.

Pull hard on the steering wheel (put 30 pounds rim pull on a 20-inch 
diameter steering wheel) after the axle stop is contacted. 

Turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction (end of timing mark 
away from adjusting screw) until the other axle stop is contacted.

Pull hard on the steering wheel (put 30 pounds rim pull on a 20-inch 
diameter steering wheel).

Release the steering wheel and shut off the engine. Do not steer again 
until Step 15 is completed. 

Loosen the sealing nut and back out the adjusting screw until it is 
past the nut:

1 inch for TAS55/65 gear

3/4 inch for TAS40 gear

Then tighten the sealing nut against the housing. 

Start the engine and let it idle.

Turn the steering wheel in the original direction (end of timing mark 
toward adjusting screw) until axle stop contact is made.

Hold the steering wheel in this position (with 30 pounds rim pull) for 
10 seconds, then release. Repeat the hold and release process as many times as 
necessary while completing Step 19.

With steering wheel held tightly at full turn, loosen the jam nut and 
hold it in place with a wrench.

Turn the adjusting screw in (clockwise) finger-tight (do not use a 
ratchet), until the Allen wrench comes to a stop. Do not attempt to turn the 
adjusting screw in any further. Pause the turning of the screw each time the 
driver releases the steering wheel; continue turning the screw only while the 
wheel is held at full turn.

 WARNING: THE LENGTH OF THE ADJUSTING SCREW BEYOND THE NUT MUST BE NO MORE THAN 
1-1/16 INCH FOR PROPER THREAD ENGAGEMENT. 

Back off the adjusting screw 3-1/4 turns and tighten sealing nut to 47 
Nm (35 lb-ft). 

Check the reservoir and fill if required. 

The length of adjusting screw beyond the sealing nut may be different 
for each vehicle.

Lower the vehicle.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering Pump, Power

The ZF power steering pump has been specially designed to supply 
pressurized oil to power steering units.

The ZF power steering pump is driven by the engine. As the driven shaft 
rotates the rotor, the slipper vanes inside the pump also move. The 
centrifugal force and pressurized oil force the slipper vanes against the 
track of the cam ring. The oil passes from the two pressure chambers to the 
area between the rear cover and faceplate, pressing this plate against the cam 
ring at operating pressure. The oil then passes through a flow-limiting valve 
to the pressure line.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Pulley, Power Steering Pump

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Steering Pump Pulley Remover

T69L-10300-B

Power Steering Pump Pulley Replacer

T91P-3A733-A

 Removal 

Using a suction gun, remove as much fluid as possible from the 
reservoir through the filler opening.

 NOTE: Always tag pump hoses before removal so they can be easily connected to 
their proper ports during installation.

Disconnect all hoses from the pump. Fasten all hoses in a raised 
position or plug the disconnected ends to prevent the fluid from draining out.

Loosen the tensioner to relieve tension of drive belt. Remove power 
steering pump and power steering pump pulley assembly from the engine.

Place power steering pump and power steering pump pulley assembly into 
vise against the two rear pump mounting holes.

Install Steering Pump Pulley Remover T69L-10300-B on the pulley hub.

 CAUTION: Do not apply in-and-out pressure on the power steering pump shaft. 
Pressure will damage the internal thrust areas. 

Hold the small hex-head, and rotate the tool nut counterclockwise to 
remove the pulley.

[FIGURE: G8928A.gif]

 Installation 

 NOTE: If belt noise is present after pump installation, visually check power 
steering pulley alignment with adjacent pulleys. Adjust pulley by positioning 
the pulley away from the pump or push it to the pump to adjust. A washer with 
an inside dimension larger than the shaft can be used as a spacer on the pump 
shaft. This adjustment is made by moving the fan shroud aside.

Place the power steering pump pulley on the power steering pump shaft, 
and install Power Steering Pump Pulley Replacer T91P-3A733-A or equivalent. 
The small diameter threads on the tool should be engaged in the power steering 
pump shaft.

 CAUTION: Do not apply in-and-out pressure on the power steering pump shaft. 
Pressure will damage the internal thrust areas. 

Hold the small hex-head, and rotate the tool nut clockwise to install 
the power steering pump pulley on the shaft. The power steering pump pulley 
face must be flush within 0.25 mm (0.010 inch) of the end of the pump shaft.

Remove installation tool.

Install pump and drive belt.

Connect all hoses to pump. Fill with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Steering Pump, Power, Direct Drive

 Removal 

Using a suction gun, remove as much fluid as possible from the 
reservoir through the filler opening.

 NOTE: Always tag pump hoses before removal so they can be easily connected to 
their proper ports during installation.

Disconnect all hoses from the pump. Fasten all hoses in a raised 
position or plug the disconnected ends to prevent the fluid from draining out.

Remove nuts or bolts attaching the pump mounting flange to the engine 
and remove the complete pump assembly and gasket.

 Installation 

Using a new gasket, install the pump assembly onto the engine drive.

Align holes in the pump mounting flange with the engine mounting holes 
and tighten bolts to 30-40 Nm (22-30 lb-ft).

Connect all hoses to the pump. Make sure to connect all lines to the 
correct ports.

Fill the reservoir to specification with Motorcraft MERCON® ATF 
XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Reservoir, Power Steering

 NOTE: This procedure applies to reservoir attached to belt-driven pump.

 Removal 

Remove filler cap.

Using suction gun, drain reservoir.

Remove nut, washer, cover and cover gasket.

Remove spacer, retainer, filter, washer and sleeve.

Remove center stud.

Remove flow bolt.

Remove bolt, support plate and reservoir body from pump.

Remove O-rings from pump body.

 Installation 

Install O-rings in pump body.

Install reservoir, support plate, washer and bolt on pump. Do not 
tighten bolt.

Install flow bolt and center stud. Alternately tighten flow bolt and 
center stud.

Install sleeve, washer, new filter, retainer and spacer.

Install cover gasket and cover.

Install washer and nut and tighten.

Fill reservoir with MERCON® ATF XT-2-QDX or MERCON® 
equivalent.

Install filler cap.

 NOTE: This procedure refers to remote reservoir used with direct drive pumps

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Filter Element

 NOTE: After a major power steering system failure due to pump or gear damage

Remove inter nut and filter.

 Installation 

Install replacement filter and inter nut.

Install cover to reservoir by installing washer and hex nut.

XT-2-QDX or MERCON® equivalent.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Pump

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Steering Pump Pulley Remover

T69L-10300-B

Steering Pump Pulley Replacer

T65P-3A733-C

 Disassembly 

Clean all dirt and oil from the external surface of the pump after 
removal. Handle all pump parts carefully to avoid nicks, burrs, scratches and 
dirt.

 CAUTION: To make sure reassembly is correct, record or mark all information as 
specified in the procedure. 

For integral reservoirs on the pump, remove the filler cap from the 
reservoir and drain the balance of the oil. For pumps with remote reservoirs, 
tip the pump to drain oil from the intake tube. Rotate shaft to remove oil 
from internal cavities.

 CAUTION: Do not clamp on the pump, reservoir or pulley. 

Using the pump mounting bracket, clamp the pump assembly into a bench 
vise in such a position as to facilitate pump disassembly.

Remove pulley using Steering Pump Pulley Remover T69L-10300-B for 
gasoline engine pump. Remove the drive gear, Woodruff key and retaining nut on 
Ford diesel engine pumps.

[FIGURE: G3806C.gif]

Compress rear pump cover.

Remove hook spring ring from radial groove in housing using pliers.

[FIGURE: G62021A.gif]

 NOTE: O-ring is inboard of backup ring.

Remove cover and pressure spring. Remove internal O-ring and backup 
ring from rear cover.

[FIGURE: G6203B.gif]

Remove the circlip from the groove.

[FIGURE: G50841A.gif]

 NOTE: O-ring is outboard of backup ring.

 NOTE: Check and record direction of rotation (arrow on cam ring) and location 
of the set pin. Pump cannot be reassembled properly without recording this 
information, as well as set pin location in pump housing, faceplate and cam 
ring.

Turn the housing over and remove the rear faceplate. Remove O-ring and 
backup ring for the rear faceplate from the housing. Remove the rotor assembly 
(rotor, cam ring, vanes and set pin) and front faceplate from the housing.

[FIGURE: G6204C.gif]

 Assembly 

If removed, press in a new needle bearing.

If removed, install a new shaft seal in the housing.

If removed, press a new bearing onto the driveshaft. Install the 
retaining ring in the driveshaft groove.

Install the driveshaft and bearing assembly into the housing.

Install the bearing circlip in the groove.

Install O-ring and backup ring on the rear faceplate in accordance with 
disassembled view.

 NOTE: The cam ring of the rotor assembly must be installed with the arrow 
pointed in the direction of rotation (7.0L, clockwise; Cummins B5.9 and 
Cummins C8.3, clockwise as viewed from the front drive end of the pump). Set 
pin is installed in location recorded during disassembly.

Install the set pin, front faceplate, and rotor assembly into the 
housing.

Install the O-ring and backup ring in the rear cover housing in 
accordance with disassembled view. Place the rear pressure spring in the rear 
faceplate. Position the rear cover in the housing.

Press down on the rear cover plate and install the hook spring ring in 
the groove in the housing.

Install the helical drive gear and Woodruff key. Install the nut and 
tighten to 80-90 Nm (59-66 lb-ft) on Ford diesel engines, or press on 
the pulley with Steering Pump Pulley Replacer T65P-3A733-C.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering Linkage

The steering linkage on F- and B-Series consists of right- and 
left-hand spindle assemblies attached to an I-beam front axle. Separate 
steering and spindle arms attach to the spindles. A tie rod, adjustable for 
toe-in, is connected between the left- and right-hand spindle arms. The drag 
link is connected between the steering arm and the pitman arm on the steering 
gear.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drag Link 

 Removal 

Replace the drag link if the ball stud at the pitman arm or the 
steering arm has lash or if the drag link is damaged.

Remove cotter pins and nuts from ball studs. 

Remove ball studs from arms. 

 Installation 

Position new drag link ball studs in arms with axle end installed in 
steering arm and install nuts.

Tighten nuts to 102-142 Nm (75-105 lb-ft) for 6K and 7K axles, 
and 149-203 Nm (110-150 lb-ft) for 8K-12K axles. Install new cotter 
pins. If required, advance the nut to the next castellation to install new 
cotter pins.

================================================================================
PAGE 3334
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-03: Steering Linkage

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Grease Seals

 Removal 

Remove cotter pin and nut from end of tie rod or drag link with damaged 
seal.

Disconnect end of tie rod or drag link from spindle or pitman arm.

Remove old seal.

 NOTE: Do not use liquid solvents of any type to clean these parts.

Thoroughly wipe away all grease and dirt from tie rod or drag link end.

 Installation 

Snap new grease seal into place.

Reinstall tie rod or drag link end and tighten nuts to 102-142 
Nm (75-105 lb-ft) for 6K and 7K axles and 149-203 Nm (110-150 
lb-ft) for 8K-12K axles.

Install cotter pin.

Lubricate drag link or tie rod end.

================================================================================
PAGE 3335
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-03: Steering Linkage

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Tie Rod Ends

 Removal 

If the tie rod end ball stud is excessively loose, replace the tie rod 
as follows. 

Remove cotter pin and nut from tie rod end ball stud. 

Remove ball stud from spindle arm.

Loosen clamp bolt and turn tie rod end out of the front wheel spindle 
tie rod. Count the number of turns needed to remove the tie rod end.

 Installation 

Lubricate threads of tie rod end. Turn it into rod to about the same 
distance old rod end was installed. This will provide an approximate toe-in 
setting. 

Install ball stud in spindle arm. Tighten nut to 102-142 Nm 
(75-105 lb-ft) for 6K and 7K axles or to 149-203 Nm (110-150 lb-ft) for 
8K-12K axles.

 NOTE: Clamps that are not fixed should be positioned with the tab against the 
end of the rod. The clamp bolt must be vertical and rearward, with the clamp 
facing forward.

Check the toe-in and adjust, if necessary. Refer to Section 04-00 . 
Tighten the tie rod end clamps to 68-95 Nm (50-70 lb-ft).

[FIGURE: G3428D.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 3336
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-03: Steering Linkage

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Tie Rod, Front Wheel Spindle

 Removal 

Replace the wheel spindle tie rod if the end threads are stripped or if 
the rod is damaged. Do not attempt to straighten a bent rod.

Loosen both wheel spindle tie rod end clamps. 

Unthread the wheel spindle tie rod until the connecting rod drops off 
both ends. Count number of turns needed to remove rod ends. The right rod end 
has a right-hand thread, the left rod end has a left-hand thread.

 Installation 

Lubricate threads on tie rod ends and turn a rod end into the tube 
about one thread.

Start the other end and continue to turn rod until rod ends have 
entered rod to about the same distance the old rod was installed. This will 
provide an approximate toe-in setting. 

Tie rod ends should be parallel with each other and in the same plane 
within 5 degrees.

Check toe-in and adjust, if necessary. Be sure to tighten tie rod end 
clamps after adjusting toe-in. Refer to Section 04-00 .

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Steering Gear Pitman Arm

 SPECIAL SERVICE TOOL(S) REQUIRED

Description

Tool Number

Pitman Arm Puller

T64P-3590-F

 Removal 

 NOTE: Replace the pitman arm if it is bent, if the ball stud hole is 
excessively worn or if the serrations are damaged or excessively worn. Do not 
attempt to straighten the pitman arm.

Remove cotter pin and nut from drag link ball stud at the pitman arm. 

Remove drag link ball stud from pitman arm. 

Remove cotter pin and nut from the pinch bolt that secures pitman arm 
to sector shaft. 

 CAUTION: Do not use heat or pound on the pitman arm or sector shaft as damage 
can result. These components must be replaced rather than serviced if they are 
damaged. 

Remove pitman arm from the steering gear sector shaft using Pitman Arm 
Puller T64P-3590-F.

 Installation 

Install a pitman arm on sector shaft, being careful to align index mark 
on steering gear sector shaft with index mark on pitman arm.

Secure pitman arm on sector shaft with pinch bolt and nut. Tighten 
attaching nut to 299-406 Nm (220-300 lb-ft).

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install new cotter pin.

Install the drag link ball stud into the pitman arm and tighten the nut 
to 102-142 Nm (75-105 lb-ft) for 6K and 7K axles and 149-203 Nm 
(110-150 lb-ft) for 8K-12K axles.

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install new cotter pin.

1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-03: Steering Linkage

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Spindle/Steering Arm

 Removal 

Replace the spindle or steering arm if it is bent or damaged. Do not 
attempt to straighten a bent spindle or steering arm. 

Remove spindle tie rod end ball stud or drag link ball stud from 
spindle or steering arm. 

Remove cotter pin and attaching nut from arm. Remove arm from spindle. 
Drive arm out of spindle, if necessary.

 Installation 

 NOTE: Unique arms are used for different front axles and wheelbases. Refer to 
the Master Parts Catalog for part number information. 

Install a new spindle/steering arm in spindle.

 NOTE: The spindle hole is slotted to align the arm with a key.

Insert key in slot from nut side of spindle. Make sure key is flush 
with slot face of spindle. 

Install spindle/steering arm retaining nut. Tighten to 299-406 
Nm (220-300 lb-ft) for 1-inch nut, 489-650 Nm (360-480 lb-ft) 
for 1-1/8-inch nut and 733-989 Nm (540-730 lb-ft) for 1-1/4-inch nut.

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install a new cotter pin through the nut and spindle/steering arm. 

Install tie rod end ball stud or drag link ball stud in arm. Install 
ball stud nut. Tighten to 102-142 Nm (75-105 lb-ft) on 6K and 7K axles 
or to 149-203 Nm (110-150 lb-ft) on 8K-12K axles.

If necessary, advance nut to next castellation to install new cotter 
pin. Install new cotter pin through the nut and ball stud. 

Check toe and adjust, if necessary. Refer to Section 04-00 . 

 NOTE: The spindle arms have fixed steering stops and do not require 
adjustment. 

Install correct steering stop bolts to specification listed in Section 04-00 .

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Steering Column

The steering column is attached to the steering gear by means of an 
intermediate shaft. The column design features a concentric outer tube, 
internal shift tube and steering shaft. The shifter unit is built into the 
automatic transmission column. 

Features on the column include an emergency flasher switch and a turn 
signal indicating switch with lane change position feature.

Fixed Column

electrical switches.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Upper Shaft Bearing, Upper Flange and Shift Socket/Flange Extension 

These components can be serviced without removing the column from the 
vehicle. 

 Removal 

Set parking brake. 

Disconnect battery cable from negative terminal. 

Remove steering column shroud and instrument panel opening cover. 

Disconnect turn signal hazard warning and ignition switch electrical 
connections. 

Remove ignition switch. Refer to Section 11-05 .

Remove steering wheel. 

If shift socket is to be removed, drive out pivot pin and remove lever. 

Remove turn signal lever. 

Remove automatic transmission hood and lens (if so equipped). 

Remove screws from turn signal hazard warning switch and slip switch 
off steering shaft. 

Remove snap ring from above upper shaft bearing. 

Loosen nuts retaining upper flange casting to column until one or two 
threads on each remain engaged. Pinching nuts toward each other, withdraw 
upper flange from steering column. Some tapping on steering shaft upper end 
with a light hammer may be required. 

Remove upper shaft bearing and insulator cover by driving out from 
opposite side of flange. 

Remove shift tube retaining screw at bottom of shift socket and 
withdraw shift socket. 

Remove three flange extension retaining screws and remove extension. 

 Installation 

Install shift socket/flange extension. 

Place flange on steering column tube and tighten nuts to 6.8-8.5 
Nm (60-75 lb-in). 

Prick-punch steering shaft serration diameter to obtain an interference 
fit to inner face. Place bearing and insulator on shaft, working them as far 
down the shaft as possible. Place a piece of pipe 3/4-inch inside diameter x 
2-1/8-inch long over the end of shaft. 

Install steering wheel attaching nut as shown. Tighten nut until 
bearing is seated in flange. Remove nut and pipe from steering shaft.

[FIGURE: G5919C.gif]

Install snap ring in the groove on steering shaft as shown. 

Install turn signal switch on flange. Tighten screws to 1.7-2.8 
Nm (15-24 lb-in). 

Install turn indicator lever. 

Connect electrical connections to steering column. 

Install steering wheel. 

Connect negative battery cable to terminal. 

Test steering column for proper operation.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Ignition Switch Lock Cylinder, Lock Cylinder Functional

The following procedure pertains to vehicles that have functional lock 
cylinders and ignition keys that are available or the ignition key numbers are 
known and the proper key can be made. 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable. 

Remove horn button and steering wheel. 

Place gearshift in neutral and turn lock cylinder with ignition key to 
RUN position. 

Place 1/8-inch diameter wire pin or small drift punch in hole located 
inside column near base of lock cylinder housing and depress retaining pin 
while pulling out on lock cylinder to remove it from column housing. 

 Installation 

To install lock cylinder, turn lock cylinder to RUN position and 
depress retaining pin, then insert lock cylinder into its housing in flange 
casting. Make sure cylinder is fully seated and aligned into interlocking 
washer before turning key to OFF position. This action will permit cylinder 
retaining pin to extend into cylinder cast housing hole. 

Using ignition key, rotate lock cylinder to make sure mechanical 
operation is correct in all positions. 

Install steering wheel and trim pads. 

Connect battery ground cable. 

Check for proper start in neutral. Also check to make sure the start 
circuit cannot be actuated in drive and reverse positions.

================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 11-04: Steering Column

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Ignition Switch Lock Cylinder, Lock Cylinder Non-Functional

The following procedure applies to vehicles on which the ignition lock 
is inoperative and the lock cylinder cannot be rotated due to a lost or broken 
ignition key (key number not known) or the lock cylinder cap is damaged or 
broken to the extent that the lock cylinder cannot be rotated. 

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable. 

Remove horn button and steering wheel. 

Remove turn signal lever from steering column. 

To gain access to ignition switch, remove steering column trim shrouds 
from steering column. Detach and lower steering column assembly from brake 
pedal support bracket. 

Remove ignition switch by removing attaching nuts and lifting ignition 
switch up to permit removal of actuating rod.

[FIGURE: G5920B.gif]

Remove turn signal switch from column assembly. 

Remove upper bearing snap ring and two T-bolt retaining nuts that 
secure flange casting to outer tube. Remove entire flange casting assembly, 
upper shaft bearing, lock cylinder assembly, ignition switch actuator and 
ignition switch actuator rod by pulling the assembly over end of steering 
column shaft as shown.

[FIGURE: G5588C.gif]

 NOTE: Retain ignition switch actuating rod from the removed casting assembly 
for use with new flange casting assembly. 

Replace the above assembly with a new assembly consisting of the 
following:

flange 

lock cylinder assembly 

lock gear, steering column lock 

bearing, steering column lock 

retainer, steering column upper bearing 

actuator assembly, steering column lock

 Installation 

Reassemble the above parts, installing a new upper shaft bearing and 
set the actuator to drive gear. 

Install turn signal switch. 

Install ignition switch. Check and adjust for proper function. 

Install instrument cluster. 

Install steering column trim shrouds, steering wheel and pad assembly. 

Install turn signal lever. 

Using ignition key, rotate the lock cylinder to make sure mechanical 
operation is correct in all positions. 

Connect battery ground cable.

Check for proper start in neutral. Also check to make sure the start 
circuit cannot be actuated in drive and reverse positions.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Ignition Lock Drive Gear 

 Removal 

Remove lock cylinder assembly. 

Insert a flat-bladed screwdriver in the recess of the drive gear at the 
bottom of the lock cylinder housing. Turn lock drive gear counterclockwise 
three notches. 

Remove snap ring, washer and lock drive gear from lock cylinder 
housing. Note position of drive gear to rack teeth. 

 Installation 

Install lock drive gear in housing in the same position as noted during 
removal. Installation is correct if the last tooth on drive gear is meshed 
with the last tooth on rack. Install washer and snap ring. 

Using screwdriver blade, turn drive gear clockwise three notches. 

Install lock cylinder.

Snap Ring

Remove turn signal-hazard warning switch retaining screws and partially 
withdraw switch from upper flange. 

Remove snap ring from steering shaft above upper shaft bearing. 

With a light hammer, tap steering shaft out the bottom of steering 
column. 

Remove ignition switch. 

Remove automatic transmission hood and lens assembly (if so equipped). 

Loosen upper flange retaining nuts until one or two threads remain 
engaged. Pinch nuts toward each other, and pull flange off outer tube. 

Remove shift tube retaining bolt from the bottom of the shift socket. 

Remove shift/socket flange extension. 

Remove lower bearing retainer, if so equipped. 

Remove shift tube from top or bottom of steering column. 

Remove lower shift arms and spacer from column outer tube. 

Remove lamp from flange and separate turn signal-hazard warning switch 
from flange. 

Remove upper shaft bearing and insulator cover from upper flange by 
tapping with light hammer from opposite side of flange. 

Disassemble upper flange and locking mechanism. 

Remove floor opening cover plate from outer tube. 

 Assembly 

Place bushing in socket retainer in outer tube. 

Place bushing on upper hub and wave washer on lower hub of shift socket. 

Insert lower shift arms and spacer in outer tube. 

Insert shift tube assembly from top or bottom of column. 

Install shift socket onto shift tube in outer tube or flange extension 
onto outer tube. Tighten bolts to 1.7-2.8 Nm (15-24 lb-in). 

Install shift tube retaining screw in the bottom of the shift socket. 

Place turn signal-hazard warning switch wiring harness through flange. 

Press lamp and wire into flange. 

Feed turn signal harness through shift socket. Pinching flange casting 
subassembly retaining nuts toward each other, install flange. 

Install ignition switch actuation rod and ignition switch. Hand-start 
washer nuts retaining the switch. 

Adjust ignition switch. Refer to Section 11-05 .

Install steering shaft from the column bottom. 

Install lower bearing retainer. 

Install upper shaft bearing and insulator cover. 

Install snap ring on shaft above the upper bearing. 

Loosen lower bearing retainer so it is free to slide on steering shaft. 

Seat upper bearing by tapping on upper end of shaft with a rubber 
mallet. 

Preload lower bearing by sliding bearing retainer against bearing with 
thumb and forefinger while holding steering shaft as shown. Tighten retainer 
nut to 2-3 Nm (18-27 lb-in) while holding bearing retainer.

[FIGURE: G70151A.gif]

Install turn signal-hazard warning switch and tighten three retaining 
screws. 

Install automatic transmission hood and lens, if so equipped. 

Install hand shift lever and pivot pin. 

Install turn signal lever. 

Install steering column.

Steering Column Flange and Locking Mechanism Subassembly 

Install lock actuator insert in rear of flange and tighten screw to

rearward.

Position spring on lock release lever assembly and position lever 
assembly through hole in front of flange torque spring until lever assembly is 
allowed to drop into place. 

Install snap ring on lock release lever assembly. 

Install flange retaining bolts through holes in flange and hand start 
nuts one or two threads on rear side.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Turn Signal Switch 

The turn signal switch is mounted on a plate attached to the steering 
column main housing. The switch is operated by a lever that extends through a 
boot on the left side of the steering column. When the switch is moved upward 
or downward through the detent, it remains in this position until moved back 
to the center position by hand or automatically by the cancelling switch.

[FIGURE: K42111A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Ignition Switch 

 Blade Type 

The steering column-mounted switch has blade-type terminals that engage 
with one multiple connector. The multiple connector is secured to the switch 
by integral locking fingers.

[FIGURE: K55781A.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hazard Flasher Switch 

The flasher switch is located on the steering column. Push the switch 
inward to start the flashers; pull the switch out to stop the flashing action. 
It can be used with the ignition lock cylinder in the RUN or OFF position. Be 
sure the turn signal lever is in the OFF (center) position before turning on 
the warning flasher system.

 Ignition Switch Continuity Test 

 NOTE: For an "engine won't crank" condition with an automatic transmission, 
determine if the condition exists with the shift lever in the neutral position 
before performing ignition switch continuity tests. If the "no crank" 
condition occurs in one shift lever position but not the other, a more 
probable cause is the neutral start switch located on the transmission.

Disconnect the multiple connector by spreading apart the locking 
fingers and pulling the plugs from the switch. Test the continuity through the 
switch by connecting a self-powered test lamp following manufacturer's

 Ignition Switch Mechanical Test 

 NOTE: Do not apply lubricant to the inside of the ignition switch.

Test the steering column ignition system mechanical operation by 
rotating the lock cylinder key through all switch positions. The movement 
should not stick or bind and should return from the start position back to the 
run position without assistance (spring return). If sticking or binding is 
encountered, check for the following: 

burrs on the lock cylinder key 

insufficient lube on lock cylinder 

binding lock cylinder 

shroud rubbing against lock cylinder 

burrs or foreign material around the rack-and-pinion actuator in the 
lock cylinder housing 

insufficient lube on actuator

binding ignition switch

Turn Signal/Hazard Flasher Switch, Hub Mounted 

 Removal

Disconnect the multiple connector immediately below the switch assembly

secure with two screws.

column.

Connect negative battery cable. Test operation of switch assembly.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Ignition Switch 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable. 

Remove steering column shroud and lower the steering column. Refer to 
 Section 11-04 . 

Disconnect the switch wiring at the multiple plug. 

Remove the two nuts that retain the switch to the steering column. 

Lift the switch vertically upward to disengage the actuator rod from 
the switch and remove switch.

[FIGURE: K11761E.gif]

 Installation 

 NOTE: When installing the ignition switch, both the locking mechanism at the 
top of the column and the switch itself must be in LOCK position for correct 
adjustment. 

To hold the mechanical parts of the column in LOCK position, move the 
shift lever into PARK (with automatic transmissions) or REVERSE (with manual 
transmissions), turn the key to LOCK position, and remove the key. New 
replacement switches, when received, are already pinned in LOCK position by a 
metal shipping pin inserted in a locking hole on the side of the switch. 

Engage the actuator rod in the switch. 

Position the switch on the column and install the retaining nuts, but 
do not tighten them. 

Move the switch up and down along the column to locate the mid-position 
of rod lash. Then, tighten the retaining nuts (top nuts first to minimize rod 
binding) to 4.51-7.34 Nm (40-65 lb-in). 

Remove the locking pin. Connect the battery ground cable and check for 
proper start in PARK or NEUTRAL. Also make sure the start circuit cannot be 
actuated in the DRIVE and REVERSE positions. 

Raise the steering column into position at instrument panel. Refer to 
 Section 11-04 . Install steering column shroud.

Confirm that accessories are deactivated with key off, and that 
accessories are operable with key in RUN.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Flasher Indicator, F-Series

Remove unit from fuse panel and install new unit.

When replacing a flasher unit, be sure to install a new flasher unit 
having the same color code and number as the one removed.

 NOTE: Do not replace turn signal switch or wiring if the following conditions 
exist:

Turn signal lamps do not flash on demand with key in the RUN position.

Turn signal flasher makes normal pulsing noise.

Turn signal lamps prove satisfactory when bench-tested or checked by 
activating brake stoplamp switch for rear only.

Check for power at the turn signal flasher output connector (pulsing 
noise indicates power is coming into the flasher). 

If there is no power or very weak power at the flasher output connector 
(12-volt test lamp will not light or is dim), replace the turn signal flasher.

ADJUSTMENTS

Ignition Switch 

Rotate the key back and forth to either side of lock, until a 5/64-inch 
drill bit can be inserted through the locking pin hole as far as possible 
(minimum 9.53 mm [3/8 inch]). The lock pin hole is located on the right 
of the switch next to the steering column tube. 

Loosen the two ignition switch mounting nuts. 

Turn the key to LOCK (feel for detent) and remove the key. 

Move the switch up and down along the column to locate the mid-position 
of rod lash. Tighten the two ignition switch mounting nuts to 4.51-7.34 
Nm (40-65 lb-in). 

Remove the drill bit from the ignition switch locking pin hole. 

Plug in electrical connector and operate the lock cylinder to ensure 
the switch is positioned properly.

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Heat Transfer

Vehicle air conditioning is the cooling or refrigeration of the air in 
the passenger compartment. Refrigeration is accomplished by making practical 
use of three laws of nature. These laws of nature and their practical 
application are outlined in the following paragraphs.

If two substances of different temperature are placed near each other, 
the heat in the warmer substance will always travel to the colder substance 
until both are of equal temperature. For example, a piece of ice in an ice box 
does not communicate its coldness to the bottle of milk standing nearby. 
Rather, the heat in the warm milk automatically flows into the ice.

To determine the amount of heat that transfers from one substance to 
another, science uses the British Thermal Unit or BTU. One BTU is the amount 
of heat required to raise the temperature of 0.45 kg (1 lb) of water 
0.556°C (1°F). For example, to raise the temperature of 0.45 kg (1 lb) 
of water from 0 to 100°C (32 to 212°F), one BTU of heat must be added 
for each degree rise in temperature or a total of 180 BTUs of heat. 
Conversely, in order to lower the temperature of 0.45 kg (1 lb) of water from 
100-0°C (212 to 32°F), 180 BTUs of heat must be removed from the water.

================================================================================
PAGE 3368
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Latent Heat of Vaporization

When a liquid boils (changes to a gas) it absorbs heat without raising 
the temperature of the resulting gas. When the gas condenses (changes back to 
a liquid), it gives off heat without lowering the temperature of the resulting 
liquid.

For example, place 0.45 kg (1 lb) of water at 0°C (32°F) in a 
container over a flame. With each BTU of heat that the water absorbs from the 
flame, its temperature rises 0.556°C (1°F). Thus, after it has 
absorbed 180 BTUs of heat, the water reaches a temperature of 100°C 
(212°F). Even though the flame continues to give its heat to the water, 
the temperature of the water remains at 100°C (212°F). The water, 
however, starts to boil or change from the liquid to the gaseous state. It 
continues to boil until the water has passed off into the atmosphere as vapor. 
If this vapor was checked with a thermometer, it also would show a temperature 
of 100°C (212°F). In other words, there was a rise of only 100°C 
(from 0°C to 100°C) or 180°F (from 32°C to 212°F) in the 
water and vapor temperature even though the flame applied many more than 180 
BTUs of heat. In this case, the heat is absorbed by the liquid in the process 
of boiling and disappears in the vapor. If the vapor was brought in contact 
with cool air, the hidden heat would flow into the cooler air as the vapor 
condensed back to water. Scientists refer to this natural law as the latent 
(hidden) heat of vaporization.

Water has a latent heat of vaporization of 970 BTUs and a boiling point 
 of 100°C (212°F). This means that 0.45 kg (1 lb) of water at 
100°C (212°F) will absorb 970 BTUs of heat in changing to vapor at 
100°C (212°F). Conversely, the vapor will give off 970 BTUs of heat 
in condensing back to water at 100°C (212°F).

This tremendous heat transfer, that occurs when a liquid boils or a 
vapor condenses, forms the basic principle of all conventional refrigeration 
systems.

For a liquid to be a refrigerant, it must also have a low boiling 
point. That is, the temperature at which it boils must be lower than the 
substance to be cooled. Refrigerant-134a is a liquid used in automotive air 
conditioning systems because its temperature/pressure relationship makes it 
suitable for mobile air conditioning systems. Here is a liquid that boils or 
vaporizes well below passenger compartment temperatures and, in vaporizing, 
will absorb tremendous amount of heat without getting any warmer.

================================================================================

BASIC PRINCIPLES

Effect of Pressure on Boiling or Condensation

The temperature of a liquid or vapor increases or decreases according 
to the pressure exerted on it.

Heat can be transferred from a comparatively cooler passenger 
compartment to the hot outside air because of the difference between the 
refrigerant pressure in the evaporator and the pressure in the condenser. In 
the evaporator, the orifice tube reduces the pressure and thereby reduces the 
boiling point below the temperature of the passenger compartment. Thus heat 
transfers from the passenger compartment to the boiling refrigerant. The high 
pressure produced by the compressor raises the gas temperature above the 
temperature of the outside air. As a result, in the condenser, the heat 
transfers from the condensing refrigerant to the outside air. The orifice tube 
and the compressor simply create pressure conditions that permit the laws of 
thermodynamics to function.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Safety Precautions

The refrigerant R-134a is a hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant. R-134a is 
noncorrosive, nonexplosive, nonflammable and has a slight ether-type odor. 
R-134a is heavier than air. Although it is classified as a safe refrigerant, 
certain precautions must be observed to protect the parts involved and the 
person working on the unit.

 WARNING: AVOID BREATHING A/C REFRIGERANT AND LUBRICANT VAPOR OR MIST. IF 
ACCIDENTAL SYSTEM DISCHARGE OCCURS, VENTILATE THE WORK AREA BEFORE RESUMING 
SERVICE. LIQUID R-134A, AT NORMAL ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURES AND TEMPERATURES, 
EVAPORATES SO QUICKLY THAT IT HAS THE TENDENCY TO FREEZE ANYTHING IT CONTACTS. 
 FOR THIS REASON, EXTREME CARE MUST BE TAKEN TO PREVENT ANY LIQUID REFRIGERANT 
 FROM COMING IN CONTACT WITH THE SKIN AND ESPECIALLY THE EYES. 

 WARNING: WEAR NON-POROUS GLOVES AND SAFETY GOGGLES AT ALL TIMES WHEN HANDLING 
LIQUID REFRIGERANT. SHOULD ANY LIQUID REFRIGERANT GET INTO THE EYES OR ON THE 
SKIN, IMMEDIATELY FLUSH EYES AND SKIN WITH PLENTY OF WATER FOR AT LEAST 15 
MINUTES. REMOVE CONTAMINATED CLOTHING AND SHOES. CALL A PHYSICIAN. 

 WARNING: REFRIGERANT R-134A IS ALWAYS UNDER PRESSURE. BECAUSE THE SYSTEM IS 
TIGHTLY SEALED, HEAT APPLIED TO ANY PART CAN CAUSE THIS PRESSURE TO BUILD UP 
EXCESSIVELY. TO AVOID A DANGEROUS EXPLOSION, KEEP AWAY FROM OPEN FLAMES, 
GLOWING METAL SURFACES, BLOW TORCHES, STEAM CLEANING AND WELDING. R-134A CAN 
BE DECOMPOSED AT HIGH TEMPERATURES. MAKE SURE THAT CONTAINERS ARE NEVER HEATED 
TO OVER 52°C (125°F). CONTAINERS MUST BE STORED AND INSTALLED IN 
ACCORDANCE WITH ALL STATE AND LOCAL ORDINANCES. 

 CAUTION: Use only R-134a refrigerant. Due to environmental concerns, when the 
air conditioning system is drained, the refrigerant must be collected using 
refrigerant recovery/recycling equipment. R-134a must never be removed without 
the appropriate equipment or released into the atmosphere. Use of a recovery 
machine dedicated for R-134a is necessary to reduce the possibility of oil and 
refrigerant incompatibility concerns. Refer to the instructions provided by 
the equipment manufacturer when removing refrigerant from or charging the air 
conditioning system. 

 CAUTION: When admitting R-134a into the refrigerant system, always keep the 
tank in an upright position. If the tank is on its side or upside down, 
liquid R-134a will enter the system and can damage the compressor. Refrigerant 
 R-134a must not be mixed with air for leak testing or used with air for any 
other purpose above atmospheric pressure. R-134a is combustible when mixed 
with high concentrations of air and higher pressures. 

 CAUTION: A number of manufacturers are producing refrigerant products which are 
described as being direct replacements for R-134a. The use of any 
unauthorized substitute refrigerant can severely damage the A/C components. If 
service is required, use only NEW or RECYCLED R-134a. 

Whenever components in the engine compartment or instrument panel areas 
 are being serviced, the battery ground cable must be disconnected to 
eliminate the possibility of electrical shorts or burned-up wiring. Extreme 
care must be exercised when performing electrical tests where the battery must 
be connected to operate the system.

Carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless and dangerous. If necessary to 
operate the engine with the vehicle in a closed area such as a garage, always 
use an exhaust collector to vent the exhaust gasses outside the closed area.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Precautions

Observe the following service precautions.

Never open or loosen a connection before discharging the system.

When loosening a connection, if any residual pressure is evident, allow 
 it to leak off before opening the fitting.

Evacuate a system which has been opened to replace a component or one 
which has discharged through leakage before charging.

Seal open fittings with a cap or plug immediately after disconnecting a 
component from the system.

Clean the outside of the fittings thoroughly before disconnecting a 
component from the system.

Do not remove the sealing caps from a replacement component until ready 
 to install.

Refrigerant oil will absorb moisture from the atmosphere if left 
uncapped. Do not open an oil container until ready to use and install the cap 
immediately after using. Store the oil only in a clean, moisture-free container.

Install a new O-ring before connecting an open fitting. Coat the 
fitting and O-ring with refrigerant oil before connecting.

When installing a refrigerant line, avoid sharp bends. Position the 
line away from the exhaust or any sharp edges which may chafe the line.

Tighten fittings only to specifications. The steel and aluminum 
fittings used in the refrigeration system will not tolerate overtightening.

When disconnecting a fitting, use a wrench on both halves of the 
fitting to prevent twisting of the refrigerant lines or tubes.

Do not open a refrigerant system or uncap a replacement component 
unless it is as close as possible to room temperature. This will prevent 
condensation from forming inside a component which is cooler than the 
surrounding air.

Keep service tools and the work area clean to avoid contamination of 
the refrigerant system.

Suction Accumulator/Drier (Low-Pressure Vapor)

During stabilized conditions (air conditioning system shutdown), 
refrigerant system pressures are equalized on both the high and low pressure 
sides of the system.

When the heater blower motor is on and the function selector lever is 
in any air conditioner position, the A/C compressor clutch field coil is 
energized and the clutch plate is pulled into contact with the compressor 
clutch pulley. The clutch plate and hub assembly then rotates the compressor 
shaft.

When the compressor shaft is rotated, the pistons are alternately moved 
 back and forth with respect to their cylinder bores. As each piston is pulled 
 through its cylinder bore, the pressure in the cylinder suddenly reduces to a 
pressure (or vacuum) considerably lower than the refrigerant system. The 
higher refrigerant system vapor pressure overcomes the suction reed valve 
spring pressure, forcing itself through the reed valve and into the lower 
pressure (or vacuum) area inside the compressor cylinder. The spring pressure 
on the reed valve closes the valve when the refrigerant system suction vapor 
pressure and the compressor cylinder vapor pressure are equalized.

As each piston is forced into its respective cylinder bore, the 
refrigerant vapors from the suction side of the refrigerant system are 
compressed into a decreasingly smaller area, thus increasing the refrigerant 
vapor pressure and also raising the refrigerant vapor temperature. The higher 
refrigerant vapor pressure now assists in sealing the suction reed valve 
closed and also opens the discharge (high pressure) reed valve as the cylinder 
pressure exceeds the higher pressure side of the refrigerant system. When the 
compressed higher pressure and temperature refrigerant vapor is discharged 
into the high pressure side of the refrigerant system, the discharge reed 
valve spring pressure and the high side refrigerant pressure closes and seals 
the reed valve, thus preventing the discharge gas from entering the compressor 
cylinder. The compressor's refrigerant vapor compression cylinder then begins 
again.

The high-pressure and high-temperature compressor discharge refrigerant 
 gas is released into the top of the A/C condenser core, via the compressor's 
discharge hose. The A/C condenser core, being close to ambient temperature, 
causes the refrigerant vapor to condense into a liquid when heat is removed 
from the refrigerant by ambient air passing over the fins and tubing.

Liquid refrigerant from the A/C condenser core exits from the bottom of 
the A/C condenser core and enters the condenser to evaporator tube and then 
the inlet side of the A/C evaporator core orifice located in the inlet tube. 
The inlet filter screen of the A/C evaporator core orifice removes coarse 
contaminant particulates, which may be present in the liquid refrigerant, 
before the liquid refrigerant enters the calibrated opening of the A/C 
evaporator core orifice. The outlet end of the A/C evaporator core orifice has 
a fine mesh filter with four open side slots in the body of the A/C evaporator 
core orifice, upstream from the filter. This filter removes fine contaminants 
and causes some of the refrigerant to exit through the non-filtered side 
slots. The side slots and filter act as a refrigerant flow noise suppressor.

Pressure in the A/C evaporator core is reduced as a result of air 
conditioner compressor suction. As the pressure is lowered and the condenser 
to evaporator tube pressure increases, the liquid refrigerant passes through 
the A/C evaporator core orifice and enters the A/C evaporator core at a low 
pressure and as a cold liquid. As airflow passes over the plate/fin sections 
of the A/C evaporator core, the refrigerant inside absorbs the heat and 
changes into a vapor.

Compressor suction draws the vaporized refrigerant and oil mixture into 
 the suction accumulator/drier where the heavier oil-laden vapors fall to the 
bottom and the lighter vapors and oil mixture continue their path to the 
compressor via the top of the vapor return tube. A desiccant bag, located 
inside the suction accumulator/drier, absorbs and retains moisture which may 
be circulating in the refrigerant system. The heavier oil-laden refrigerant 
also returns to the compressor through a small liquid bleed hole near the 
bottom of the vapor return tube. The liquid bleed hole provides a controlled 
second opportunity for the accumulated refrigerant and oil mixture to 
revaporize as it passes through the opening to re-enter into the main vapor 
flow path to the suction side of the compressor.

 Refrigerant Flow 

The compressor pumps the low pressure refrigerant (containing the 
absorbed heat) from the evaporator and accumulator and forces it under high 
pressure into the condenser which is located in the outside air stream at the 
front of the vehicle. The increase in pressure raises the refrigerant vapor 
temperature to a point higher than that of the outside air. In the condenser, 
the heat transfers from the hot vapor to the cooler air and the refrigerant 
condenses back to a liquid. The liquid under high pressure now returns to the 
orifice tube in the evaporator inlet to repeat the cycle.

 Refrigerant Systems 

The refrigerant used in this refrigerant system is HFC-134a 
(tetrafluoroethane-CF 3 CH 2 F) which is a 
hydrofluorocarbon refrigerant. HFC-134a, also known as R-134a, is 
non-corrosive, non-explosive, non-flammable and has a slight ether-type odor. 
R-134a is heavier than air. Although it is classified as a safe refrigerant, 
certain precautions must be observed to protect the parts involved and the 
person working on the unit.

Use only R-134a refrigerant and R-134a compatible refrigerant oil. Due 
to environmental concerns, when the air conditioning system is drained, the 
refrigerant must be collected using refrigerant recovery/recycling equipment 
meeting SAE-J1990 and J2210. R-134a must never be removed without the 
appropriate equipment or released into the atmosphere. Use of a recovery 
machine dedicated for R-134a is necessary to reduce the possibility of oil and 
refrigerant incompatibility concerns. Refer to the instructions provided by 
the equipment manufacturer when removing refrigerant from or charging the air 
conditioning system.

Several refrigerants are used in today's air conditioning systems. The 
refrigerants are not compatible. While system operations and procedures are 
the same, the equipment is unique and cannot be used interchangeably.

The label stating A/C refrigerant use in the vehicle is attached in the 
engine compartment so the proper service procedure and equipment can be 
referenced in the service manual. An R-134a refrigerant system will have gold 
R-134a NON-CFC tags in addition to the refrigerant charge tag.

[FIGURE: M4526A.gif]

If a component has been used with R-12, it cannot be used again in an 
R-134a system. If used in an R-134a system, it cannot be put into an R-12 
system. Contamination can occur and performance can be adversely affected 
because each system uses a different refrigerant oil designed for that system.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Refrigerant System Protection

 A/C Compressor Pressure Relief Valve 

Under extreme pressure conditions, the A/C compressor pressure relief 
valve will momentarily open, allowing refrigerant vapor to escape. This 
relieves excessive pressure that can damage the compressor. The valve closes 
as soon as pressure is lower than the relief setting. This prevents loss of 
the complete refrigerant charge. The A/C compressor pressure relief valve is 
located in the A/C manifold and tube at the rear of the compressor.

 A/C Pressure Cutoff Switch 

A refrigerant cutoff switch is used with air conditioning to interrupt 
A/C compressor operation in the event of high system discharge pressures which 
can result in the loss of refrigerant charge. The switch is located in the 
discharge line between the compressor and the A/C condenser core. The switch 
is sensitive to the discharge pressure and functions to interrupt the A/C 
compressor operation if the discharge pressure exceeds a setting of 2751-3068 
kPa (399-445 psi).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Condenser Core

The condenser receives compressed (therefore heated) refrigerant gas 
from the compressor.

As the hot refrigerant gas flows down through the condenser, it is 
cooled by air passing between the sections of the condenser. The cooled, 
compressed refrigerant gas condenses to liquid refrigerant which then flows 
into the receiver.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Evaporator Core Orifice

The fixed orifice tube meters the flow of liquid refrigerant during 
cool-down (while the vehicle interior and evaporator core are cooling down). 
After initial system start-up, compressor suction pressure drops, the 
evaporator core pressure reduces toward 175 kPa (25.5 psi), and the evaporator 
fin temperature approaches freezing. The clutch cycling pressure switch then 
opens the compressor clutch coil circuit to disengage the compressor clutch 
and prevents evaporator icing.

The fixed orifice tube is located in the evaporator inlet tube and has 
filter screens located on the inlet and outlet ends of the tube body. The 
filter screens act as a strainer for the liquid refrigerant flowing through 
the fixed orifice opening. O-rings, on the tube body, prevent the high 
pressure liquid refrigerant from bypassing the orifice. Adjustment or repairs 
cannot be made to the fixed orifice tube assembly and it must be replaced as a 
unit.

PAGE 3377
================================================================================

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

A/C Evaporator Core

The evaporator core is a multi-pass plate-fin core similar to passenger 
 car cores. The liquid line connects to the bottom of the core and the suction 
 (low-pressure) line connects to the top of the core. A liquid bleed line is 
not used in this system. The liquid line tube is fitted with an evaporator 
core orifice tube to control refrigerant flow. This orifice tube can be 
removed from the evaporator core tube for replacement if it becomes necessary. 
However, Special Service Tool, Fixed Orifice Tube Tool D80L-19990-A is 
necessary to prevent breaking the orifice tube.

When the cooling system is in operation, the liquid refrigerant flows 
through the orifice tube in the evaporator where it is allowed to evaporate at 
a reduced pressure, to cool the evaporator. Air is blown through the 
evaporator fins and is thus cooled by the evaporator.

PAGE 3378
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 12-00: Climate Control System, Service

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Suction Accumulator/Drier

The suction accumulator/drier is a canister that receives the output of 
low-pressure vapor from the evaporator.

The suction accumulator/drier stores excess liquid refrigerant not used 
under varied conditions of air conditioning operation. The accumulator 
separates the liquid from the gas returning to the compressor. A 
small-diameter oil bleed hole is located in the side of the outlet tube near 
the bottom of the canister. This bleed hole is covered with a filter and 
allows a small amount of the heavier liquid refrigerant and oil mixture to 
re-enter the suction line at a controlled rate. When the heavier liquid 
refrigerant and oil mixture enters the compressor suction line, it has a 
second opportunity to vaporize and circulate through the compressor without 
causing damage to the compressor due to refrigerant slugging.

A desiccant bag is mounted inside the suction accumulator/drier 
canister to absorb any moisture in the refrigerant system.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Special Service Equipment

In order to minimize the discharge of ozone depleting 
chlorofluorocarbons into the atmosphere, the Ford Motor Co. supports the 
efficient usage, recovery, and recycling of R-134a used in vehicle air 
conditioners. Ford Motor Co. recommends the use of U.L. approved 
recycling/charging equipment such as Rotunda R-134a A/C Service Center 
176-00001 or R-134a A/C Service Center 023-00150 or equivalent during any air 
conditioning system service and recharge procedure which requires the air 
conditioning system to be discharged.

R-134a systems require the use of special servicing equipment designed 
specifically for R-134a systems. R-12 servicing equipment cannot be used when 
servicing R-134a A/C systems. R-134a special service equipment includes R-134a 
recovery/recycling/recharging station, R-134a leak detector, R-134a vacuum 
pump and R-134a manifold gauge set.

 CAUTION: Do not use R-12 special tools and equipment when servicing an R-134a 
system. Doing so can cause damage to the R-134a A/C system.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Service Gauge Port Valves

 NOTE: The A/C service port fittings are composed of an adapter which is

 Inspection and Verification 

Obstructed air passages, broken belts, disconnected or broken wires, 
loose clutch, loose or broken mounting brackets can be determined by visual 
inspection of the parts.

Check air conditioner compressor drive belts for proper tension 
(445-533 N [100-120 lb]). Check compressor and pulley mounting bolts for 
looseness. Refer to Section 03A-05 , Section 03B-05 , Section 03C-05 or Section 03D-05 of the Powertrain, Drivetrain Manual for additional information on 
drive belts.

Start engine and adjust controls for air conditioner operation. Make 
sure that compressor is operating. Check for proper air distribution.

Check suction line at outlet of evaporator by feel to determine if cold 
(approximately -1.1-7.2°C [30-45°F]). In high humidity, 
condensation will form on suction line and condensate will drip from 
evaporator drain.

Check recirculation inlet for air restrictions.

Check operation of outside/recirculation air door.

Check condenser for airflow restrictions.

Check for broken, burst or cut hoses and loose fittings on all air 
conditioner components.

A refrigerant leak will usually appear as an oily residue at the 
leakage point in the system. The oily residue soon picks up dust or dirt 
particles from the surrounding air and appears greasy. In time, this will 
build up and appear to be heavy, dirt-impregnated grease.

Many leaks are caused by damaged or missing O-ring seals at the various 
 hose and component connections. When these O-rings are replaced, lubricate 
the new O-rings with refrigerant oil. Be careful to keep shop towel lint or 
dirt from contaminating the internal surfaces of the connection.

If the system contains no refrigerant or is extremely low in 
refrigerant, the clutch will not engage for compressor operation. A rapid 
cycling compressor clutch is usually an indication that the system is low in 
refrigerant. Normally, clutch cycling will not occur when the engine is 
operating at curb idle speed.

 Pinpoint Tests 

Prior to diagnosis and testing, make sure the battery is fully charged 
and that sufficient coolant is present in the heating system.

Various tests to check heater system operations are included in this 
section. In addition to these tests, visual inspection of all heater system 
components and connections can be made to make sure the system is operating 
properly.

The following pinpoint tests can be used to determine the system 
conditions for the climate control system.

Always check the engine coolant level before diagnosing an inoperative 
heating system. Also make sure that the thermostat is capable of maintaining 
the specified engine coolant temperature.

Pinpoint tests should be used together with the appropriate wiring 
diagrams to accurately diagnose and correct system concerns.

Use of the guides and the applicable wiring diagram(s) in the 
Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual will enable the cause of the 
electrical circuit problem to be quickly isolated.

When service or replacement of any component has been completed, the 
system must be tested again to make sure the condition has been corrected.

Refer to the following charts for performance testing procedures. Use 
Rotunda 73 Digital Multimeter 105-R0051 to perform electrical system tests.

 Vacuum Leak Diagnosis 

The air handling system is designed to provide defrost when no vacuum 
is applied to any of the three air door vacuum motors. This is done to prevent 
a situation where defrost cannot be obtained due to a system vacuum leak. 
Instead, a leak in the vacuum control circuit will send all airflow to the 
defroster outlets. This condition can occur during acceleration (slow leak), 
can exist at all times (large leak) or can happen only when certain specific 
functions are selected, indicating a leak in that portion of the circuit.

The vacuum hoses used in the passenger compartment control circuit are 
constructed from PVC plastic material. The vacuum hoses used in the engine 
compartment are constructed of Hytrel. Because of the materials used, the 
vacuum hoses must never be pinched off during diagnosis to locate a leak. Use 
Rotunda Vacuum Tester 014-R1054 or equivalent to locate vacuum leaks. A wood 
golf tee can be used as a plug when it is necessary to plug one end of a 
vacuum hose for leak test purposes.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Refrigerant System Tests

Follow the appropriate pinpoint test in this section to locate the 
electrical or refrigerant system problem.

To check the refrigerant system pressures, install the suction (low 
pressure) gauge on the suction side of the compressor and the discharge (high 
pressure) gauge on the discharge side of the compressor. Operate the system on 
A/C, COOL and HI blower speed for 10-15 minutes to stabilize the pressure 
readings. Operate the engine at 1500 rpm to analyze the refrigerant system.

If a refrigerant system has lost its charge or after servicing the 
refrigerant system, leak check, purge and then evacuate the system for at 
least 30 minutes.

The following refrigerant system diagnosis procedures can be used to 
determine the system conditions for given customer concerns.

To diagnose a concern in the refrigerant system, note the system 
pressure (shown by the manifold gauges) and the clutch cycle rate. Then 
compare readings to the charts.

 NOTE: The test conditions specified at the top of each of the charts must be 
met to obtain accurate test results.

Connect a manifold gauge set to the system.

When the system has stabilized, record the high and low pressures, as 
shown by the manifold gauges.

Determine the clutch cycling rate-per-minute (clutch ON time plus OFF 
time is a cycle).

Record clutch OFF time in seconds.

Record clutch ON time in seconds.

Note center register discharge temperature.

Determine and record the ambient temperature.

Compare test readings and appropriate chart data.

Plot a vertical line for the recorded ambient temperature from the 
scale at the bottom of each chart to the top of the chart.

Plot a horizontal line for the other test readings from the scale at 
the left side of the appropriate chart.

If the point where the two lines cross on each chart falls within the 
dark band, the system is operating normally. If the lines cross outside the 
dark band on one or more of the charts, there is a concern and the specific 
cause must be determined. Refer to the following Refrigerant System and Clutch 
Cycling Time Evaluation chart.

 NOTE: The following five system operating conditions are determined by the 
location of the point where the lines cross on the chart:

System high (discharge) pressure is high, low or normal.

System low (suction) pressure is high, low or normal.

Clutch cycling rate is fast, slow or clutch runs continuously.

Clutch ON time is long or short.

Clutch OFF time is long or short.

Match these conditions with the conditions shown in the five columns 
toward the left in the Refrigerant System Pressure and Clutch Cycling Time 
Evaluation chart. All five system conditions will be indicated on one line. 
The most likely component or components causing the concern are listed in the 
right column.

Exemplary conditions follow the chart.

Refrigerant Leaks

 a Compressor may make noise on initial run. This is slugging condition
caused by excessive liquid refrigerant.

 b Compressor clutch may not cycle in ambient temperatures above
26°C (80°F) depending on humidity conditions.

 c Low-pressure reading will be normal to high if pressure is taken at
accumulator and if restriction is downstream of service access valve.

 d Low-pressure reading will be low if pressure is taken near the
compressor and restriction is upstream of service access valve.

 Exemplary Conditions 

Example:

High (discharge) pressure is low.

Low (suction) pressure normal.

Clutch cycle rate is very fast.

Clutch ON time is very short.

Clutch OFF time is very short.

In this example, the condition is caused by the clutch cycling pressure 
switch. The clutch range is too close. Replace the switch and recheck the 
system.

Example:

High (discharge) pressure normal to low.

Low (suction) pressure is normal.

A badly contaminated system contains water, carbon and other products 
of the decomposition process. Where such a condition exists, the system must 
be flushed with a special flushing agent using equipment designed especially 
for this purpose. Follow the suggestions and procedures outlined to make sure 
the system is thoroughly cleaned.

These conditional requirements for the air conditioning evaporator core

clutch cycle timing.

 Air Conditioner Performance Test 

[FIGURE: M1940C.gif]

Diagnosis of the refrigerant system must be done by analyzing the 
system's high pressure and evaporator pressuring readings. Compare the 
pressure readings to the charts shown in the following illustration to 
determine if the system pressures are normal. The conditional requirements for 
the refrigerant system tests must be satisfied to obtain accurate pressure 
readings.

 Refrigerant System Pressure Readings 

[FIGURE: L7309C.gif]

If the conditional requirements are not satisfied, the pressure 
readings will not be accurate and can indicate that a normal system is not 
functioning properly. If the conditional requirements cannot be satisfied, the 
pressure readings will be inaccurate but can be used to determine what is 
causing the condition in the system. Compare the pressure results with the 
pressure conditions in the pressure evaluation chart shown in the following 
illustration. Once the condition is corrected, take additional pressure 
readings while meeting the conditional requirements for the pressure tests to 
make sure the condition has been corrected.

The evaporator service access gauge port valve is located on the inlet 
connector of the suction accumulator. The high-pressure service access gauge 
port valve is located on the compressor discharge line near the compressor. 
This service port is the quick connect/disconnect type and requires Quick 
Disconnect Test Adapter T77L-19703-A to connect a manifold gauge set or a 
charging station to the service port. The quick connect/disconnect adapter 
should seal the hose when the adapter is disconnected from the service access 
gauge port valve to eliminate accidental discharge of refrigerant from the 
service hose.

 System Performance 

The pressures developed on the high-pressure (discharge) and 
low-pressure (suction) side of the compressor indicate whether or not the 
system is operating properly.

Attach the manifold gauge set but not the refrigerant tank. Set both 
manifold gauge valves at the maximum clockwise, or closed, position.

Check the system pressures with the engine running at 1500 rpm, all 
controls set for maximum cooling, blower speed set at low/medium, and the 
front of the vehicle at least 1.6 m (5 feet) from any wall.

The actual pressures indicated on the gauges will depend on the 
temperature of the surrounding air and the humidity. Higher air temperatures, 
along with high humidity, will give higher system pressures.

At idle speed and with a surrounding air temperature of 38-43°C 
(100-110°F), the high pressure can go as high as 2068 kPa (300 psi) or 
more. If necessary to operate the air conditioner under these conditions, keep 
the high pressure down with a fan directed at the condenser and radiator.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

A/C Evaporator Core/A/C Condenser Core

 On-Vehicle Leak Test 

Verify Rotunda R-134a Manifold Gauge Set 176-R032A or equivalent is 
capable of holding vacuum:

Connect the red and blue hoses together using a 1/4-inch flare coupling.

Connect the gauge set yellow hose to a known good Vacuum Pump 176-R0034 
or equivalent.

Turn the vacuum pump ON and open both gauge set valves.

Operate the vacuum pump for one minute and close both gauge set valves. 
The low side gauge should indicate approximately 30 inches of vacuum.

Allow the gauge set, with vacuum applied, to set for at least one-half 
hour.

If the gauge reading drops during that time, the gauge set hose 
connections, gauges, or valves are leaking and must be serviced before 
proceeding with the leak test.

Discharge the A/C system. Refer to System Evacuating in the Service 
Procedures portion of this section.

Disconnect the liquid line and suction accumulator from the evaporator 
core tubes. DO NOT leak test an evaporator core with the suction accumulator 
attached to the core tubes. Refrigerant outgassing from oil and desiccant in 
the accumulator will indicate a false leak condition.

Clean the evaporator core tube fittings.

For threaded connections wipe any dirt or debris from sealing surfaces 
with a clean, lint-free rag.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

A/C Compressor

 A/C Manifold and Tube Leak Test 

Tighten the manifold retaining bolt to 18-23 Nm (13-17 lb-ft). 

Add refrigerant to the system if necessary. 

Leak test the manifold O-ring seals, using Rotunda Automatic 
Calibration Halogen Leak Detector 023-R1003 or equivalent. 

If no leaks are found, the manifold O-ring seals are good. 

If a leak is found at the manifold and the manifold retaining bolt is 
tightened to 18-23 Nm (13-17 lb-ft), install new manifold O-ring seals 
as outlined. Then, repeat the leak test. 

 Rotating Torque Check 

Check the rotational torque of a used compressor if excessive 
compressor drag is suspected.

Discharge refrigerant system following recommended service procedures. 
Observe all safety precautions.

Remove refrigerant hose and A/C manifold and tube from compressor. Use 
care not to allow dirt to enter compressor.

Remove the compressor from the vehicle. With the A/C clutch disengaged, 
rotate the compressor shaft one complete revolution using a dial-type torque 
wrench and note the torque required to rotate the shaft another complete 
revolution.

If the rotational torque exceeds specification (13.0 Nm/9.6 
lb-ft) replace the compressor assembly.

If the rotational torque is less than specified, excessive drag does 
not exist in the compressor. Install the A/C manifold and tube and leak test, 
evacuate and charge the system.

Check the system for proper operation.
