REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Instrument Cluster

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable.

Disconnect the speedometer connector at the speedometer head. In some 
vehicles, removal may be made easier by first removing the instrument cluster 
retaining screws, tilting the cluster toward the steering column and 
disconnecting the speedometer connector.

On F-Series, remove the finish trim panel.

Remove the screws retaining the instrument cluster assembly to the 
instrument panel and lift the cluster out at the front of the panel.

Disconnect the wiring connector and remove the cluster assembly on 
B-Series. On F-Series, disconnect the brake electric motor and brake warning 
lamps. (Tachometer is powered through the instrument cluster printed circuit.) 
On vehicles with a separate tachometer, or air pressure gauge, disconnect the 
tachometer connector, or electrical connector and air pressure line connections.

 Installation 

Position the instrument cluster assembly to the instrument panel and 
connect the wiring connector. Connect the tachometer, air pressure gauge and 
brake electric motor. Check engine and brake warning lamps, if so equipped.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Instrument Cluster Lenses

 CAUTION: The use of vinyl cleaners and similar other cleaning agents to clean 
the vehicle interior or indicator lamp lens has resulted in damage to the 
indicator lamp lens. The chemical content of these cleaning agents 
(o-dichlorobenzene, ethyl alcohol or cellosolve), has produced fogging, 
spotting, stain, or splotches of the lenses, either through overspray or 
direct use on the lenses. Therefore, extreme caution should be taken during 
interior cleanup to prevent overspray of cleaning agents which contain the 
chemical contents mentioned from contacting the indicator lamp lens. 

The indicator lamp lens should be cleaned with Ultra-Clear Spray Glass 
Cleaner E4AZ-19C507-AA or equivalent commercial cleaning product meeting Ford 
specification ESR-M14P5-A, using a clean, soft, lint-free cloth. The Ford 
Glass Cleaner has been specially formulated for cleaning windows in automotive 
vehicles and is approved for use in cleaning the plastic indicator lamp lens. 
Read and carefully follow the directions on the container for best results.

ADJUSTMENTS

Tachometer Calibration 

On F-Cowl and B-Series, the tachometer is calibrated according to 
engine type, specifically, the number of flywheel teeth. The tachometer can be 
calibrated by setting eight DIP switches on back of the tachometer. The 
switches have the numbers 1 through 8 embossed on the switch. To calibrate the 
tachometer, the switches are set so each switch is either in the ON or OFF 
position, depending on the engine type. A switch is set to the ON position 
when the switch is depressed towards the number on top of the switch. A switch 
is set to the OFF position when the switch is depressed at the bottom, away 
from the switch number. 

 NOTE: The DIP switch settings are shown on the tachometer case identification 
label. 

[FIGURE: K19634A.gif]

On F-Cab with diesel engines, the tachometer can be calibrated by 
setting a four-position rotary switch on back of the tachometer. The switch 
has the numbers 1 through 4 embossed on the case. To calibrate the tachometer, 
simply rotate the switch to the desired number.

PAGE 3537

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

ADJUSTMENTS

Speedometer Calibration

To ensure that the electronic speedometer system operates accurately, 
inspect the vehicle speed sensor (VSS) periodically. Check the VSS for metal 
filings accumulating on the sensor pole face at the following kilometer 
(mileage) intervals: 800 (500), 20,000 (12,500), 40,000 (25,000), 60,000 
(37,500), 80,000 (50,000). Scheduled maintenance beyond 80,000 kilometers 
(50,000 miles) should occur at subsequent 80,000 kilometer (50,000 mile) 
intervals. Metal filings that have developed on the sensor pole face must be 
removed to maintain system integrity. The programmable electronic speedometer 
instrument requires no maintenance.

The bank of switches that are located at the rear of the electronic 
speedometers require setting for proper operation of the speedometer and 
odometer unit. The transmission-mounted speed sensor transmits a signal to the 
speedometer/odometer that is dependent on:

rear axle ratio

tire revolutions per mile (rpm) which is based on tire height

 Rear Axle Ratio Determination 

The axle ratio can be determined by referring to the information 
delivered with the vehicle or finding the metal tag attached to the 
differential. If the vehicle has a two-speed differential (e.g., 4.15/5.72:1), 
use the smaller number (4.15 in this case) in all calculations.

 Tire Revolutions Per Mile Determination 

The revs per mile can be calculated as follows:

Measure the tire height (ground to top of tire) in inches with the 
vehicle on level ground, loaded, with the tires "cold" and inflated to the 
recommended pressure. Measure to the nearest 1/8 inch. Use the following table 
to convert fractions to decimals. (If calculation is done in centimeters, 
divide tire height by 2.54 to convert to inches.)

1/8 — 0.125

1/4 — 0.25

3/8 — 0.375

1/2 — 0.5

5/8 — 0.625

3/4 — 0.75

7/8 — 0.875

(Example: If tire height is 36-1/8 inch, use 36.125 in your revs per 
mile calculation)

Divide 20,168 (constant) by the tire height to get the revs per mile.

(Example: 20,168/36.125 = 558.28)

 Calibration Frequency Determination 

Multiply the axle ratio times the revs per mile times 0.267 (constant)

(Example: 558.28 x 4.10 x 0.267 = 611.49)

Round the 611.49 to the closest whole number, which is 611.

 Determine Speedometer/Odometer Switch Setting 

Determine which type speedometer/odometer you are installing. The 
following procedure applies to both "stand-alone" and gauge "cluster" type 
speedometer/odometer units. (Replacement unit is a 12-switch Beede. The 
10-switch Beede has been discontinued for service.)

There are two speedometer setting charts (Beede 10-position and Beede 
12-position). Using the correct speedometer setting chart on the following 
pages, find the Test Freq in the left-hand column and read the switch settings 
in the next column. A number means that switch is to be placed in the ON or 
closed position and a period "." means that switch is to be placed in the OFF 
or open position (e.g., using the Beede 12-Position chart and the 611 test 
frequency calculated in the example, the chart gives the switch settings as: 
(1.3456.8.0.B). This means that switches 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 are ON and 
switches 2, 7, 9, 11 are OFF. The letters A and B are used to represent 
switches 11 and 12. There are at least three different styles of switches with 
unique switch position labeling. Ignore the switch position labeling. Pushing 
the top of the switch IN turns the switch ON. Pushing the bottom of the switch 
IN turns the switch OFF.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Horn Switch, Steering Wheel-Mounted

The horn switch is mounted in the center of the steering wheel. With 
the horn switch depressed, current flows from Circuit Breaker 12 through the 
horn switch to the low-pitch and high-pitch horns. The horns sound.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Horn Mounting Location

The electric horns are mounted in front of the left-hand fender apron, 
near the windshield washer fluid reservoir (on fixed hood vehicles), and in 
the left front engine compartment hood, on side of hood support (on tilt hood 
vehicles). The air horns are mounted on the roof near the driver side door 
opening.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Horn System

 Inspection and Verification 

Verify the vehicle owner's original concern by operating the horn 
system to duplicate the vehicle owner's concern.

Inspect to determine if one of the following mechanical or electrical 
concerns applies.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Electrical

Verify that horn attaching bolts are tight

Verify that horns are not touching surrounding sheet metal or other
components

Verify that there are no kinks or leaks in air lines of air horn system

Verify that the ground of the horn is good by inspecting connection for
corrosion

Check system fuse

Check wiring for obvious short or opens

Check connectors for obvious damage

If the concern(s) remains after the inspection, determine the 
symptom(s) and proceed to the following symptom chart.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Protection System Components

 NOTE: The engine shutdown option is applicable to F800 and FT900 vehicles 
only. B800 vehicles may have the engine protection system warning lamps and 
audible alarm but not the shutdown system.

The engine protection system (or engine shutdown system) is designed to 
prevent engine damage resulting from operation of the engine during prolonged 
periods of low oil pressure, high coolant temperature or low coolant level.

Switches or sensors direct information to the system's electronic 
engine alarm/shutdown module. When one of the monitored engine systems is not 
functioning properly, a warning lamp in the instrument panel will illuminate. 

The low oil pressure, high coolant temperature, and low coolant level 
warning lamps are accompanied by an audible warning. In vehicles equipped with 
the engine shutdown option, the audible warning will be heard with the warning 
lamp illumination and, after 30-40 seconds, the engine will stop running. The 
30-40 second delay is provided to allow removal of the vehicle from the road. 
After the engine stops running, it can be restarted and operated for 
approximately 30-40 seconds more. There is no limit to how many times the 
shutdown system will allow the engine to be restarted. This feature is only 
provided to allow the vehicle to be driven off the road. Any attempt to use 
this feature to drive the vehicle very far will result in serious engine 
damage. 

The engine warning and shutdown system consists of the following 
components: 

Indicator lamps in the instrument panel for the following warnings: 

low oil pressure

high coolant temperature

low coolant level

Oil pressure switch. 

Coolant temperature switch, located on the rear of the thermostat 
housing. 

Low coolant level sensor, located on the right side of radiator tank. 

Fuel shutoff relay.

Engine alarm/shutdown module.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Audible Warning and Shutdown Activation 

When the engine alarm/shutdown module detects a fault signal at one or 
more of its three inputs, it immediately sounds the audible warning. After 
approximately 30-40 seconds, it opens the circuit which provides battery to 
the fuel shutoff relay. The fuel shutoff relay then cuts the battery supply to 
the hold coil of the fuel shutoff solenoid and the engine is shut down. 

The fuel shutoff solenoid is used to allow the vehicle to run or be 
shut down. This solenoid moves the fuel rack into the fuel on and off 
positions. Power for the solenoid is controlled by the ignition switch and 
relay in the system.

The fuel shutoff solenoid is comprised of two coils within one housing. 
A powerful pull-in coil is used to pull the fuel shutoff lever to the open 
position. The pull-in coil is fed from the switched side of the starter motor 
relay, so it is energized whenever the ignition switch is in the start 
position. At the same time, a much less powerful hold coil is fed from the 
start and run circuits. When the ignition switch is released to the run 
position, the pull-in coil drops out and the hold coil is left energized to 
keep the fuel shutoff lever in the open position.

 CAUTION: The pull-in coil draws a considerable amount of current while it is 
energized. Do not allow it to remain energized for longer than 30 seconds, or 
damage to the coil can result. 

The fuel shutoff electrical system consists primarily of the following 
components:

Fuel shutoff solenoid, located next to the fuel injection pump.

[FIGURE: K19637A.gif]

Fuel shutoff relay, located on right side of instrument panel above 
glove compartment.

Engine alarm/shutdown module, located behind lower right side of 
instrument panel.

 Start 

With the ignition switch in START, the fuel shutoff solenoid pull-in 
coil is energized by Circuit 669 (R/BL) from the starter relay.

The fuel shutoff relay coil is energized by the ignition switch through 
Circuits 16 (R/GN) and 974 (O). This closes the contacts in the fuel shutoff 
relay and the fuel shutoff solenoid hold coil is energized through Circuits 37 
(BK/Y) and 69 (R/GN). The solenoid pulls the shutoff lever to the open 
position to allow fuel flow to the engine.

If the vehicle is equipped with the engine shutdown system, battery 
voltage is supplied from the ignition switch through Circuit 16 (R/GN) and the 
engine alarm/shutdown module to the fuel shutoff relay. The bypass connector 
is not connected.

If the vehicle does not have the engine shutdown system, the bypass 
connector is connected.

 Run 

After starting, the ignition switch returns to RUN. This de-energizes 
the starter relay and the fuel shutoff solenoid pull-in coil. The fuel shutoff 
relay remains energized by the ignition switch through Circuits 16 (R/GN) and 
974 (O). The fuel shutoff solenoid hold coil remains energized by Circuits 37 
(BK/Y) and 69 (R/GN) through the closed contacts of the fuel shutoff relay.

 Shutoff 

When the ignition switch is moved to OFF, current to the fuel shutoff 
relay coil is cut off and the relay contacts open. This de-energizes the fuel 
shutoff solenoid hold coil and the shutoff lever returns to the off position, 
fuel flow is cut off, and the engine stops.

Turning off power to the engine audible warning control resets the 
system and if the engine is restarted, the sequence of events is repeated. 

 Automatic Shutoff with Engine Shutdown System 

If the engine alarm/shutdown module senses low oil pressure, low 
coolant level or high coolant temperature, it will interrupt the run Circuits 
16 (R/GN) and 974 (O) to the fuel shutoff relay after approximately a 30-40 
second delay. This de-energizes the relay, cutting off current to the fuel 
shutoff solenoid hold coil. The shutoff lever moves to the off position and 
the engine stops running.

Turning ignition switch to the engine start position resets the system, 
and if the engine is restarted, the sequence of events is repeated.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Oil Pressure Detection 

The oil pressure switch is normally closed. The presence of adequate 
oil pressure opens the switch, thereby turning off the oil pressure warning 
indicator lamp and the audible warning. When oil pressure is insufficient, the 
oil pressure switch closes, grounding the oil pressure warning indicator lamp 
circuit and the engine alarm/shutdown module. The indicator lamp illuminates 
and the engine alarm/shutdown module sounds a warning signal. If the circuit 
is activated (grounded) for 30-40 seconds, the engine alarm/shutdown module 
opens the battery circuit for the fuel shutoff relay and causes engine 
shutdown (if equipped with engine shutdown).

================================================================================
PAGE 3555
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 13-09A: Engine Protection System

1999 F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

High Coolant Temperature Detection 

The coolant temperature switch is normally open. When the coolant 
temperature is excessive the switch closes, grounding the coolant temperature 
warning indicator lamp circuit and the engine alarm/shutdown module. The 
indicator lamp illuminates and the engine alarm/shutdown module sounds a 
warning signal. If the circuit is activated (grounded) for 30-40 seconds, the 
engine alarm/shutdown module opens the battery circuit for the fuel shutoff 
relay and causes engine shutdown (if equipped with engine shutdown).

================================================================================
PAGE 3556
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 13-09A: Engine Protection System

1999 F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Low Coolant Level Detection 

The engine alarm/shutdown module monitors the resistance through the 
low coolant level sensor. With a sufficient level of well mixed coolant, the 
low coolant level sensor gives a ground short to the engine alarm/shutdown 
module. An alarm or engine shutdown can be caused by one or more of the 
following:

Pure antifreeze is added to the coolant supply tank.

Coolant level drops, exposing the low coolant level sensor.

The engine alarm/shutdown module loses its ground signal and, after 
approximately 7 seconds (to allow for coolant movement), sounds an alarm and 
lights the low coolant level warning lamp.

After 30-40 seconds (if equipped with engine shutdown) the engine 
alarm/shutdown module opens the battery supply through Circuit 974 (O) to the 
fuel shutoff relay.

The fuel shutoff relay opens the battery supply to the fuel shutoff 
solenoid through Circuits 37 (BK/Y) and 69 (R/GN).

The fuel shutoff solenoid hold coil releases and engine fuel is cut off.

 NOTE: Because of its high electrical resistance, pure antifreeze, when added 
to the coolant supply tank, may give a false low-coolant signal to the engine 
alarm/shutdown module. If necessary, the low coolant sensor may have to be 
jumpered to allow the engine to run long enough to mix the coolant.

The warning chime module produces a repetitive chime for the following 
conditions:

Section 13-09B: Gauges/Warning Devices, Chime/Buzzer System

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Headlamp Switch On Warning (Available on Cab Only)

The warning chime sounds when the headlamp switch is in PARK or HEAD 
and the driver door is open. It continues to sound until the headlamp switch 
is moved to OFF or the door is closed. When the headlamp switch is in PARK or 
HEAD, power is supplied through Circuit 285 (BR) to the module. When the 
driver door is open, the driver door lamp switch is closed and power is 
supplied to the module through Circuit 53 (BK/BL).

1999 F and B-Series

Section 13-09C: Engine Protection System, Cummins B5.9 Encore Diesel Engine

1999 F800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Protection System

The Cummins B5.9 Encore (ISB) diesel engine control module (ECM) 
performs self-diagnostic tests and is equipped with an engine protection 
system. The system monitors critical engine temperatures and pressures, and 
will log diagnostic faults when an over or under normal operation condition 
occurs.

The ECM uses the following sensors to provide information on engine 
operating parameters:

engine coolant temperature sensor

engine oil pressure sensor

engine speed/position sensor

intake manifold temperature sensor

low coolant level sensor

water-in-fuel (WIF) sensor

The engine protection system monitors the following parameters:

engine coolant temperature

engine coolant level

engine oil pressure

engine overspeed

fuel temperature

intake manifold temperature

 Engine Warning Lamp 

If an out-of-range condition exists, and engine derate is to be 
initiated, the vehicle operator will be alerted by the ENG WARN lamp. The ENG 
WARN lamp will blink or flash when the out-of-range condition continues to get 
worse. The engine power and speed will gradually reduce, depending on the 
severity of the out-of-range condition.

 Stop Engine Lamp 

 If the out-of range condition reaches the severity where the engine 
needs to be shut down the STOP ENG lamp will illuminate indicating to the 
vehicle operator to stop the vehicle as soon as safely possible and have the 
vehicle serviced. The engine protection system will not shut down the engine 
unless the engine protection shutdown feature has been selected. For 
additional information on this feature, refer to the engine manufacturer's 
service manuals.

 Engine Protection Lamp 

The ENG PROT lamp will illuminate when there is a possible fluid 
out-of-range condition.

 Water In Fuel Lamp 

The WATER IN FUEL lamp will illuminate when the fuel-water separator is 
full and should be drained into a suitable container.

 Diagnostic Switch 

The diagnostic switch is used to check for active electronic fuel 
system and engine protection system fault codes. The diagnostic switch is 
located under the instrument panel on the LH side near the kick panel. For 
additional information on retrieving and translating any active engine 
protection system fault codes, refer to the engine manufacturer's service 
manuals.

 Idle Speed Adjust Switch 

The IDLE SPEED ADJUST switch can be used to step through the entire 
active fault code sequence. For additional information, refer to the engine 
manufacturers service manuals.

 Low Coolant Sensor 

 NOTE: The resistance value of pure antifreeze (without water mix) is high and 
the low coolant level sensor can indicate a low level if it is submerged in 
pure antifreeze. During an engine cooling system refill, mix the antifreeze 
with water in the proper ratio before adding it to the coolant reservoir.

The low coolant sensor is the only Ford supplied sensor that is part of 
the engine protection system. The ECM monitors the resistance between the tip 
of the low coolant sensor and the threaded base of the sensor. If the coolant 
level drops far enough so that the sensor is no longer submerged in the 
coolant mixture, the ECM registers the increase in resistance (air has a much 
higher resistance than coolant). After a short delay, the ECM will illuminate 
the ENG PROT lamp. If the low coolant level sensor remains at a high 
resistance, the ENG WARN lamp will illuminate.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Warning Indicators, Dual Brake

The direct air pressure indication systems consist of a dual air 
pressure gauge with dual pointers mounted in the instrument cluster, a double 
check valve and air tubes connected at the pressure pickup point on the 
vehicle. As the system's air pressure increases, the Bourdon tubes in the dual 
air gauge deflect, causing the pointers to move. The two air pressure 
indicating systems measure the air reservoir's pressure (standard) and the 
application air pressures (RPO).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The generator charging system is a negative ground system that consists 
of a generator, regulator, charge indicator, storage battery and associated 
wiring. Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for 
electrical schematics and locations of wiring harnesses.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Battery and Charging System

 Inspection and Verification 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES AND CLOTHING. SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN OR EYES, FLUSH IMMEDIATELY WITH 
WATER FOR A MINIMUM OF 15 MINUTES AND GET PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION. IF ACID IS 
SWALLOWED, CALL A PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY. 

 WARNING: BATTERIES NORMALLY PRODUCE EXPLOSIVE GASES THAT CAN CAUSE PERSONAL 
INJURY. DO NOT ALLOW FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED SUBSTANCES TO COME NEAR THE 
BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR WORKING NEAR A BATTERY, ALWAYS SHIELD YOUR FACE AND 
PROTECT YOUR EYES. ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION. 

Verify the vehicle owner's original concern by operating the engine to 
duplicate the concern.

Inspect to determine if one of the following mechanical or electrical 
concerns apply.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Mechanical

Electrical

Before attempting to test a battery. Give it a thorough examination to
determine if it has been damaged.

Batteries are tested to determine the state of charge and ability to
crank an engine. The result of these tests is to show that the battery is
either good, needs recharging, or must be replaced.

Preliminary checks to the charging system should be made regardless of
the fault condition. These checks include:

Check the fuses/fuse links to the generator to make sure that they are
not burned or damaged. This condition, resulting in an open circuit or high
resistance, can cause erratic or intermittent charging system concerns.

Check battery posts and cable terminals for clean and tight
connections. Clean the posts and the cables to ensure good electrical contact.

Check for secure connections at the generator output, generator
regulator and engine ground. Also check the connection at the load
distribution point.

Check the generator drive belt to ensure proper tension and no slip
between the generator pulley and the drive belt. Refer to Section 03A-05 ,
 Section 03B-05 , Section 03C-05 or Section 03D-05 .

Check battery for full charge as outlined.

Before performing charging system tests on the vehicle, note conditions
such as: slow cranking, discharged battery, charge indicator lamp stays ON
with engine running, charge indicator lamp does not illuminate with ignition
switch in RUN and engine not running, etc. This information will aid in
isolating the part of the system causing the symptom.

When a relatively new battery is discharged, test for current drain.
The following are some of the most common current drain concerns:

Glove compartment lamp stays on with the door closed.

Engine compartment lamp stays on constantly.

License plate lamp or interior lamp stays on constantly.

Other electronic component damage.

Battery, starting system, and lighting system concerns can be caused by 
poor charging system performance. The charging system can also cause an 
overload in other areas of the electrical system. 

To correctly identify the area where the difficulty lies, isolate the 
battery, the charging system, and the electrical circuits. Check the battery 
before any electrical system diagnosis, to see if it has the ability to accept 
and hold a charge. Refer to Section 14-01 . If the battery is good, check the 
charging system to see if it can keep the battery charged. 

If the battery cannot meet specifications, it must be replaced. 

If the battery meets the required specifications, it must be fully 
charged before proceeding with the diagnosis of other electrical system 
components. 

Before testing any of the individual charging system components, 
perform general component tests in this section. The component tests will 
determine which components require servicing.

Perform Pinpoint Test A using Rotunda Inductive Dwell-Tach-Volts Ohms 
Tester 164-R0254 or equivalent. Be careful when using the ohmmeter near hot 
circuits. The component to be checked should be disconnected from the circuit 
or the battery terminals should be disconnected. Use Rotunda Charging/Starting 
Analyzer 164-R0251 or equivalent for testing the charging system. Test 
instructions are provided with the analyzer. 

 CAUTION: Damage to the component being checked can occur during testing if it is 
not disconnected from the circuit, or if the battery terminals are not 
disconnected. 

Continue through the Diagnosis and Testing until service has been 
completed. Test the system again to see if the service has corrected the 
system.

 Component Tests 

Perform the following tests using Rotunda Inductive Dwell-Tach-Volts 
Ohms Tester 164-R0254 or equivalent, a jumper wire and a test lamp (12 volt). 
The meters should be calibrated once a year and the date of calibration 
stamped on the meter face. It is recommended that this practice be followed by 
all technicians to maintain their meters at acceptable accuracy. 

Troubleshooting or diagnosis is required before performing electrical 
system service. Even where an obvious fault makes the replacement of a unit 
necessary, find out why the unit failed. If a concern is diagnosed correctly, 
unnecessary service is prevented, the time the vehicle is out of operation 
will be decreased, and the service performed will be permanent. 

 Battery Voltage Test 

Before performing charging system tests on the vehicle, verify the 
concern, such as slow cranking, battery dead, ammeter shows excessive charge 
at all times or no charge, generator warning lamp does not come on or never 
goes out or the voltmeter shows above or below normal voltage. This 
information will aid in isolating the part of the system causing the symptom. 
The Rotunda Alternator, Regulator, Battery and Starter Tester (ARBST) 
010-00725 or equivalent will simplify on-vehicle testing. Refer to Section 14-01 for battery warnings and cautions. 

Connect the test block to the generator as shown in the following 
illustration.

With all accessories and carbon pile turned off, increase engine speed 
as required to obtain maximum voltage reading.

service.

Make sure that accessories have not been left on for extended periods. 

Check the drive belt for proper tension.

tightness and cleanliness, including the cable clamps and battery posts.

integral charging system to ground. A zero reading indicates an open between 
voltmeter connection and battery.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Battery

 Removal 

Remove hex nuts and battery cables from battery terminals (negative 
first). 

Clean cable terminals with an acid neutralizing solution and terminal 
cleaning brush. 

Remove hold-down clamps. 

Test battery and determine if it should be: 

placed back in service

recharged before being placed back in service

replaced with a Motorcraft or equivalent battery

 WARNING: WHEN LIFTING A PLASTIC-CASED BATTERY, AVOID PUTTING EXCESSIVE PRESSURE 
ON THE END WALLS, WHICH CAN CAUSE ACID TO SPEW THROUGH THE VENT CAPS, CAUSING 
PERSONAL INJURY OR DAMAGE TO THE VEHICLE OR BATTERY. LIFT WITH A BATTERY 
CARRIER OR WITH YOUR HANDS ON OPPOSITE CORNERS. 

Remove battery using a suitable battery carrier. 

 Installation 

Clean cable terminals and hold-down clamps with a wire brush. Replace 
all cables or parts that are worn or frayed. 

[FIGURE: J6320A.gif]

Clean battery tray with a wire brush and scraper. 

Place battery in tray with positive and negative terminals in the 
original positions. 

Install battery cable hex nuts and bolts. 

Assemble and tighten hold-down clamps so battery is secure. Do not 
overtighten.

Secure cables (positive first) to proper terminals. Do not overtighten. 
Apply a small quantity of Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent 
meeting Ford specification ESA-M1C75-B to terminals.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Battery Charging 

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES. BATTERY CHARGING CAN BE DANGEROUS. WHILE BEING 
CHARGED, THE BATTERY PRODUCES A POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE MIXTURE OF HYDROGEN AND 
OXYGEN GASES. KEEP SPARKS, FLAMES AND LIGHTED CIGARETTES AWAY FROM BATTERIES. 
REMEMBER, IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH LARGE AMOUNTS OF WATER. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION. 

 WARNING: BATTERIES NORMALLY PRODUCE EXPLOSIVE GASES THAT CAN CAUSE PERSONAL 
INJURY, THEREFORE, DO NOT ALLOW FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED TOBACCO TO COME NEAR 
THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR WORKING NEAR A BATTERY, ALWAYS SHIELD YOUR FACE 
AND PROTECT YOUR EYES. ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION. 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES, OR CLOTHING. SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IF ACID CONTACTS SKIN OR EYES, FLUSH IMMEDIATELY WITH WATER FOR A 
MINIMUM OF FIFTEEN MINUTES AND GET PROMPT MEDICAL ATTENTION. CALL A PHYSICIAN 
IMMEDIATELY. 

 NOTE: Perform battery tests to determine battery state of charge and capacity 
or ability to crank an engine. The ultimate result of these tests is to 
determine if the battery is good, needs recharging or must be replaced. 

Before attempting to test a battery, it is important to give it a 
thorough examination to determine if it has been damaged. 

 NOTE: Recommended discharge rate at 27°C (81°F): one-half the cold 
cranking amperage.

Voltage readings at 15 seconds for a good battery are shown on the 
following chart.

Approximate Battery Temperature

Minimum Load Voltage

27°C (81°F) and above

9.6

21°C (70°F)

9.6

16°C (61°F)

9.5

10°C (50°F)

9.4

4°C (39°F)

9.3

-1°C (30°F)

9.1

-7°C (20°F)

8.9

-12°C (10°F)

8.7

-18°C (10°F)

8.5

Wait 2 minutes and check the open circuit voltage (OCV). Measure OCV 
with a digital voltmeter capable of reading 1/100 volt.

Battery is OK if minimum load voltage and OCV measure above 12.40. If 
battery measures below 12.40, charge for 20 minutes at 35 amp. Repeat battery 
capacity test. If battery OCV measures above 12.40, but failed minimum load 
voltage, replace worn battery.

Before recharging a discharged battery, inspect and service the 
following conditions, if they exist: 

loose generator belt

pinched or grounded generator or voltage regulator wiring harness

loose harness connections at the generator or voltage regulator

loose or corroded connections at battery, starter relay or engine ground 

excessive battery drain due to hood, glove compartment and courtesy 
lamps remaining on (damaged or misadjusted switch, glove compartment left 
open, etc.)

The state of charge for Motorcraft Heavy-Duty batteries is determined 
by comparing the measured battery terminal voltage with the Voltage/State of 
Charge Table. 

 VOLTAGE/STATE OF CHARGE

Measured Voltage

State of Charge

Specific Gravity

12.60

100%

1.265

12.45

75%

1.230

12.30

50%

1.200

12.15

25%

1.170

Cold batteries will not readily accept a charge. Therefore, batteries 
should be allowed to warm up to approximately 5°C (41°F) before 
charging. This may require 4 to 8 hours at room temperature depending on the 
initial temperature and battery size. 

A battery that has been completely discharged may be slow to accept a 
charge at the normal charger setting. When batteries are in this condition, 
charging can be started by using the dead battery switch on chargers so 
equipped. 

To determine whether a battery is accepting a charge, follow charger 
manufacturer's instructions for use of dead battery switch. If switch is the 
spring-loaded type, it should be held in the ON position for up to 3 minutes.

After releasing switch, and with charger still on, measure battery 
voltage. If it shows 12 volts or higher, the battery is accepting a charge and 
is capable of being recharged. However, it may require up to two hours of 
charging with batteries colder than 5°C (41°F) before the charge rate 
is high enough to show on the charger ammeter. It has been found that all 
non-damaged batteries can be charged by this procedure. If a battery cannot be 
charged by this procedure, it must be replaced.

 Procedure to Charge a Known Good Battery 

 WARNING: WEAR SAFETY GLASSES. BATTERY CHARGING CAN BE DANGEROUS. WHILE BEING 
CHARGED, THE BATTERY PRODUCES A POTENTIALLY EXPLOSIVE MIXTURE OF HYDROGEN AND 
OXYGEN GASES. KEEP SPARKS, FLAMES AND LIGHTED CIGARETTES AWAY FROM BATTERIES. 
REMEMBER, IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH LARGE QUANTITIES OF WATER. GET MEDICAL ATTENTION. 

 NOTE: If excessive gassing or electrolyte spewing occurs during the charge, 
discontinue charging. The battery has reached serviceable charge. If the 
battery will not accept at least 5A after 20 minutes of charging, replace the 
battery.

A rapid recharge procedure has been developed for recharging batteries 
that have passed the preceding capacity test and only need a recharge.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Battery Cleaning 

Keeping the battery top clean and dry reduces the need for service and 
extends battery life. Make certain the cable clamps are tightly fastened to 
the battery posts. If corrosion is found, disconnect the cables and clean 
clamps and posts with a wire brush. Neutralize the corrosion with a solution 
of baking soda and water. After installing cables, apply a small quantity of 
Premium Long-Life Grease XG-1-C or -K or equivalent meeting Ford specification 
ESA-M1C75-B to each battery post to help prevent corrosion. 

[FIGURE: J6321A.gif]

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Tools 

Using properly designed tools can prevent damage to the battery, 
battery cables and hold-down bracketry. They can also reduce potential hazards 
to both technician and vehicle being serviced. 

Tools and equipment manufactured for servicing batteries have parts 
insulated to help prevent arcing. This feature can reduce potential component 
damage and fire hazards if a tool is dropped and shorts the battery terminals. 

 Pliers 

Battery pliers have jaws specifically designed to grip cable clamp 
bolts securely. Exercise care when removing or replacing the cable clamp bolts 
to make sure that the battery terminal is not subjected to any excessive 
lateral or twisting forces. Such forces can cause major damage to the internal 
components of the battery, and result in leakage at the terminals. 

 Clamp Puller 

Use a clamp puller to remove a cable clamp from the battery terminal. 
The jaws exert a force on the top of the battery post to remove the clamp. 
Proper use of this tool prevents the damaging lateral or twisting forces that 
result when using a pry bar or plier. 

[FIGURE: J3889A.gif]

 Clamp Spreader 

The spreader is used to expand the cable clamp after it has been 
removed from the terminal. The cable clamp can then be easily placed in its 
correct position on the terminal. 

[FIGURE: J3890A.gif]

 Terminal Cleaning Brush 

The terminal cleaning brush is designed to clean both the threaded 
battery terminal and the mating surface of the cable connector. 

[FIGURE: J6320A.gif]

 Carrier 

Use a suitable battery carrier for lifting and transporting the 
battery. The illustration shows a clamp-type carrier used to grip the 
sidewalls of the container just below the lip of the cover. The carrier is 
used on the sidewalls, rather than the end walls, since the sidewalls have 
additional strength from the inner cell partitions. This is particularly 
important with polypropylene-cased batteries that have flexible end walls. 

[FIGURE: J43371A.gif]

Section 14-02A: Generator, 95 and 115 Ampere Integral Rear Mount Regulator, Internal Fan Type

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The electrical charging system is a negative ground system consisting 
of a voltage regulator, charge indicator, storage battery and the necessary 
wiring and cables. Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual 
for schematics and locations of the components and wiring. 

With the ignition key in the RUN position, voltage is applied through 
the charge indicator lamp I circuit to the voltage regulator. This turns the 
voltage regulator on allowing current to flow from the battery sense A circuit 
to the generator field coil. When the engine is started, the generator begins 
to generate alternating current (AC) which is converted to direct current (DC) 
by the rectifier assembly internal to the generator. This current is then 
supplied to the vehicle's electrical system through the output stud located on 
the rear of the generator. 

Once the generator begins generating current, a voltage signal is taken 
from the generator stator and fed back to the voltage regulator S circuit, 
turning off the charge indicator. 

With the system functioning normally, the generator output current is 
determined by the voltage at the A circuit (battery sense voltage). The A 
circuit voltage is compared to a set voltage internal to the voltage 
regulator, and the voltage regulator controls the generator field current to 
maintain proper generator output. 

The set voltage will vary with temperature and is typically higher in 
the winter than in the summer, allowing for better battery recharge in the 
winter and reducing the chance of overcharging the battery in the summer.

[FIGURE: J4757B.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Generator Circuit 

 Battery Positive Voltage (B+) Output 

The generator output is supplied through the B+ output connection 
to the battery and electrical system. 

 I Circuit 

The I circuit, or ignition circuit, is used to turn on the voltage 
regulator. This circuit is powered up with the ignition key in the RUN 
position. This circuit is also used to turn the indicator lamp on if there is 
a concern in the charging system operation or associated wiring circuits.

 A Circuit 

The A circuit, or battery sense circuit, is used to sense the battery 
voltage. This voltage is used by the voltage regulator to determine the 
generator output. This circuit is also used to supply power to the generator 
field coil. This circuit is connected back to the load distribution point and 
is a protected circuit. 

 S Circuit 

The S circuit, or stator circuit, is used to feed back a voltage signal 
from the generator to the voltage regulator. This voltage, typically one-half 
battery voltage, is used by the voltage regulator to turn off the indicator 
lamp.

Section 14-02B: Generator, 100 and 115 Ampere Delco

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The electrical charging system is a negative ground system consisting 
of a generator, voltage regulator, charge indicator lamp (optional), storage 
battery, wiring and cables. Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting 
Manual for schematics and locations of components and wiring.

[FIGURE: J6211B.gif]

Item

Part Number

Slip Ring End (SRE) Housing

(Part of 10346)

5

10A310

Pulley

7

—

Mounting Lugs
(Part of 10346)

The only difference between the 100 and 115 ampere generators is the 
drive pulleys installed on each. The 100 and 115 ampere generators are 
one-wire systems (the minimum number of lead wire connections necessary at the 
generator for proper operation). With a one-wire system, there is residual 
magnetism in the rotor at start-up. As the generator rotor begins turning, the 
residual fields around the rotor induce voltages in the stator windings. The 
faster the rotor turns, the higher the voltage induced in the stator windings 

Once the speed and output are up to specification, the voltage 
available at the diode trio becomes sufficient to supply field current for 
normal operations. If an indicator light is connected in series with the I 
terminal, the light will be on while the generator comes up to speed. The 
indicator lamp will light due to a voltage imbalance between the battery 
voltage on one side of the light and system voltage coming from the diode trio 
on the other side of the light. Once the generator output voltage equals the 
battery voltage, the voltages are balanced on both sides of the indicator 
light. With no difference in potential, the light turns off.

Once the system voltage exceeds 14 volts, the voltage regulator will 
turn off the field current to prevent the voltage from rising any higher. This 
causes the magnetic field around the rotor to collapse, which reduces the 
generator output voltage. As the voltage falls below the battery voltage, the 
voltage regulator turns the field current back on, which allows the magnetic 
field to build up again. This cycle is repeated many times a second, so 
quickly that the output voltage is steady for all practical purposes and the 
indicator light cannot turn on and off fast enough to keep pace and so stays 
off unless a prolonged voltage imbalance should occur. The system voltage is 
used to control the output, which eliminates the need for extra sense wiring.

[FIGURE: J6212A.gif]

The 21-SI series Delcotron® generator is a high-output integral

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Voltage Regulator

The voltage regulator is a solid-state integrated circuit-type with a 
nominal regulated voltage setting of 14.0 volts. In addition, the voltage 
regulator features flat temperature compensation, low parasitic draw and low 
turn-on speed with improved radio frequency interference (RFI) suppression 
capability and load dump protection from voltage spikes. The voltage regulator 
limits system voltage by switching the ground circuit for the rotor field on 
and off.

Section 14-02B: Generator, 100 and 115 Ampere Delco

1999 F-800, FT-900, B-800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Generator Circuit

 Circuit Description 

The generator output or B+ terminal is connected to the battery 
positive terminal. The ground path is through the generator housing and 
mounting back to the battery negative terminal. When the voltage regulator 
switches the ground circuit on, the battery voltage passes through the 
rectifier bridge and into a diode trio, which passes the voltage to the rotor 
through a brush and slip ring assembly located on the rotor shaft. This will 
cause a magnetic field to build up around the rotor windings. The voltage 
regulator also receives battery voltage that it uses to compare with the 
voltage produced by the generator. When the generator voltage exceeds 14 
volts, the voltage regulator switches off the ground circuit going to the 
rotor, which collapses its field and reduces the output momentarily.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charging System

The electrical charging system is a negative ground system consisting 
of a generator, voltage regulator, storage battery, wiring and cables. Refer

The 130-ampere generator is a one-wire system (the minimum number of

generator output voltage. As the voltage falls below the voltage regulator 
setting, the voltage regulator turns the field current back on, which allows

1999 F and B-Series

Section 14-02C: Generator, 130 Ampere Prestolite

1999 F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Generator

The Prestolite 130-ampere generator is a self-current limiting unit 
with a fully adjustable voltage regulator. 

The generator features sealed ball bearings with rotor slip rings and 
generator brush and terminal holders that are in a sealed housing mounted on 
the slip ring end housing. Six generator diodes mounted in heat sinks convert 
alternating current from the delta wound stator into direct current. A radio 
voltage regulator capacitor connected between the heat sinks assists in 
suppressing transient voltage spikes that can damage the generator diodes.

[FIGURE: J5694A.gif]

The generator brush and terminal holders and voltage regulator are 
located in a waterproof housing that can be removed for replacement or 
inspection without disassembling the generator.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Generator

 WARNING: HYDROGEN AND OXYGEN GASES ARE PRODUCED DURING NORMAL BATTERY OPERATION. 
THIS GAS MIXTURE CAN EXPLODE IF FLAMES, SPARKS OR LIGHTED SUBSTANCES ARE 
BROUGHT NEAR THE BATTERY. WHEN CHARGING OR USING A BATTERY IN AN ENCLOSED 
SPACE, ALWAYS PROVIDE VENTILATION AND SHIELD YOUR EYES. 

 WARNING: KEEP BATTERIES OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN. BATTERIES CONTAIN SULFURIC 
ACID. AVOID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING. ALSO, SHIELD YOUR EYES WHEN 
WORKING NEAR THE BATTERY TO PROTECT AGAINST POSSIBLE SPLASHING OF THE ACID 
SOLUTION. IN CASE OF ACID CONTACT WITH SKIN, EYES OR CLOTHING, FLUSH 
IMMEDIATELY WITH WATER FOR A MINIMUM OF FIFTEEN MINUTES. IF ACID IS SWALLOWED, 
DRINK LARGE QUANTITIES OF MILK OR WATER, FOLLOWED BY MILK OF MAGNESIA, A 
BEATEN EGG, OR VEGETABLE OIL. CALL A PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Voltage Regulator 

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery ground cable.

Remove the lead from the voltage regulator terminal. 

Remove the three screws retaining the voltage regulator to the generator.

Slowly pull the voltage regulator from the holder and remove the 
voltage regulator. 

Check generator brush and terminal holders. Replace generator brush and 
terminal holders or voltage regulator if necessary. 

Replace generator brush and terminal holders less than 4.76 mm (0.188 
inch) in length.

[FIGURE: J43461A.gif]

 Installation 

Before installing the voltage regulator, insert the outer generator 
brush and terminal holder into the housing and compress the generator brush 
spring using a small screwdriver or similar tool. 

 NOTE: A suitable pin can be made using drill rod or a 1/32-inch diameter 
drill. 

While holding the generator brush spring compressed, insert a pin 
through the top hole in the rear of the housing so the generator brush spring 
is held in a compressed position. 

Install and compress remaining generator brush and terminal holder in a 
similar manner. 

Hold the generator brush springs in a compressed position by pushing 
the pin farther into the brush housing.

[FIGURE: J43471A.gif]

Slowly push the voltage regulator into the brush housing making sure 
the respective screws go through the positive and negative jumpers. 

Install the voltage regulator mounting screws and hand-tighten. 

 CAUTION: Do not tighten nuts with brush pin in place; damage to the voltage 
regulator will result. 

Remove brush pin; tighten the nuts to 1.1-1.4 Nm (10-12 lb-in).

Install the lead to the voltage regulator terminal.

Connect the battery ground cable.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Generator 

 Disassembly 

Hold generator pulley with a strap wrench and remove shaft nut with an 
impact gun. Remove generator pulley, generator fan, Woodruff key, and 
generator fan/pulley spacer.

Remove the 5/16-18 and 1/4-20 nuts from the positive and negative 
generator output terminals. 

 NOTE: Due to the application of Loctite® to the four brush housing 
screws, heat might need to be applied to assist in removing the screws. Use a 
large soldering iron or gun (300 to 500 watts). Hold the iron on each screw 
head for 40-50 seconds (a drop of solder on the iron's tip will help heat 
transfer). After applying heat to the screw head, remove immediately with a 
screwdriver. 

Remove the four 8-32 screws holding the generator brush holder in 
place. Remove assembly. 

Remove three self-locking nuts and through-bolts. 

 NOTE: If drive end housing binds on stator and coil, loosen by tapping gently 
on mounting ear with fiber hammer. Make sure drive end housing separates from 
stator and coil, and that stator and coil remains attached to slip ring end 
housing to avoid damage to stator leads. 

Remove generator rotor and drive end housing from stator and coil and 
slip ring end housing. 

Remove three nuts securing stator leads to terminals and remove stator 
and coil.

Remove nuts from positive and negative output terminal bolts. Remove 
bolts.

Remove hex screws. 

Remove radio voltage regulator capacitor connected between the heat 
sinks. 

Remove two screws, lockwashers, guard washers and insulating washers 
retaining lower end of heat sinks. 

Noting location of insulating washers and bushings, remove heat sinks. 

 NOTE: There are two bushings in each terminal hole. 

Remove terminal stud insulating washers from housing.

 Slip Ring Bearing Replacement 

With a soldering iron, remove the wire connecting the generator rotor 
to the outside rotor slip ring.

Bend unsoldered wire so it is parallel to the shaft. 

Unsolder the wire from the inside rotor slip ring.

With a gear puller or an arbor press, pull off the rotor slip ring and 
the insulation washer. 

 NOTE: While replacing the bearing keep the new rotor slip ring in a warm 
place so it will press on easily without cracking. 

Remove the bearing using a gear puller; an arbor press can also be used 
with fixture plates behind the bearing. 

Install the new bearing using a pipe or tube to press on the inner race 
of bearing. 

After the new bearing has been pressed on the rotor shaft, press on the 
new rotor slip rings, making sure the slot lines up with the slot in the 
shaft. 

Press new rotor slip rings on the shaft. Apply enough pressure to 
prevent the insulation washer from turning all the way to the shoulder. 

Solder the leads of the generator rotor to new rotor slip rings.

 NOTE: Concentricity of the rotor slip ring with the bearing surfaces of the 
shaft should be held to within 0.05 mm (0.002 inch) total indicator reading. 

Put the generator rotor in a lathe. Take a light cut from the 
circumference of rotor slip rings so they are concentric with the shaft. 

 Assembly

slip rings are not damaged. 

Press the rear housing on rotor shaft. Use a sleeve or pipe so pressure 
is applied on rear bearing inner race only. 

Place positive and negative rectifiers in the slip ring end housing and 
install the lower mounting screws. Do not tighten screws at this time.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Generator

Clean the generator housing with particular care around the vents. Use 
care not to push dirt or debris into the generator through the air vents. Do 
not use solvents unless the generator is disassembled. Solvent runoff may 
carry dirt into the generator.

Inspect the generator for broken or cracked mounting lugs. Inspect for 
loose mounting bolts, loose wires and cracked or burned insulation. Service or 
replace as necessary.

 Generator Components 

The internal parts of the generator may be cleaned with a mild solvent 
and wiped with a soft cloth. Inspect for broken or cracked parts, cracked, 
broken or missing insulation. Service or replace as necessary.

Do not submerge the generator bearings in solvent. The solvent may 
dissolve the lubricant and cause damage if the bearings are installed.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Voltage Regulator

Clean the voltage regulator with a soft brush or cloth. If removed from 
the generator, the voltage regulator may be cleaned with a mild solvent and 
dried completely. Inspect for broken or cracked parts or broken, cracked or 
missing insulation. Service or replace as necessary.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Radio Reception

 Antenna Position 

The AM and FM stereo antenna has a range of about 32 km (20 miles) 
before interference noises are heard. This means that in areas with tall 
buildings or hills, it is necessary to select the strongest possible station. 
The electronic radio automatically tunes to the center of any given station, 
eliminating the need for manual fine tuning.

 Antennas and Mobility 

Although an automotive radio antenna will give outstanding mobile 
reception, it cannot provide the continuous reception of home audio 
components. The home receiver is not limited by the vehicle operating 
characteristics and certain geographical effects as is the mobile unit. For 
example, for the best FM reception, the automotive antenna should be designed 
like a TV antenna and pointed in the direction of the station. The best AM 
antenna is a long piece of wire; the higher the wire, the better the 
reception. However, because of design necessity, the automotive antenna is 
restricted in size, height and direction and must receive both AM and FM 
stations. This means that a limited amount of the station's signal reaches the 
vehicle radio.

 Tuning 

Fine tuning is not required for the radio chassis. The electronic radio 
chassis automatically tunes the radio chassis to the center of the station 
where it will obtain minimum noise and best possible reception.

 Tone Control 

Favoring the rear radio speakers in noisy areas will help to reduce 
noise.

 FM Flutter 

Flutter can best be described as repeated pops and hissing bursts heard 
in the radio speaker, during an otherwise good broadcast. Usually this 
condition exists while traveling in the fringe area of the station. Flutter 
will become more severe beyond approximately 40 km (25 miles) of the station. 
The signal loss becomes greater away from the station, until finally noise 
takes over and reception becomes impossible. Flutter can also be noticed near 
the station because of the line-of-sight characteristics of FM radio waves. 
This condition can occur when a building or large structure is between the 
radio receiver and the station being received. Some of the FM signal bends 
around the building, but certain spots have almost no signal. Some of these 
signal losses are only a few inches wide and if the vehicle is parked in one 
of these dead spots, you will only hear noise from the radio speaker. After 
moving out of the shadow of the structure, the station will return to normal. 
Flutter will not occur on AM because the AM radio waves are much longer than 
FM waves.

 FM Multi-Path Cancellation 

Another effect caused by the line-of-sight characteristics is called 
cancellation. This condition exists when the radio waves are reflected from 
objects or structures. The noise produced by cancellation is similar to 
flutter, with the addition of distortion in the program. A more familiar 
description of cancellation is its similarity to the multiple ghosts and 
picture jumping that occurs on television when a low flying plane passes. The 
same condition exists in the vehicle, except that the vehicle is moving and 
the reflecting structure is stationary. The reflected signal cancels the 
normal signal, causing the antenna to pick up noise and distortion. 
Cancellation effects are most prominent in metropolitan areas, but can also 
become quite severe in hilly terrain and low-lying roadways.

 FM Strong Signal Capture and AM Overloading 

FM capture is an unusual condition that occurs when traveling in the 
vicinity of a broadcast tower. If listening to a weak FM station when passing 
the broadcast tower, a stronger station can interfere without changing the 
tuning control. When passing the tower, the station may switch back and forth 
a few times before returning to the station originally tuned. When several 
broadcast towers are present (common in metropolitan areas) several stations 
can overload the receiver resulting in considerable station changing, mixing 
and distortion. Fortunately, this condition is localized and it will not harm 
the receiver. Some overloading can also be noticed on AM, but usually to a 
lesser degree.

 Receiving FM Stereo 

Because more data is carried in the FM stereo waves than in the 
monaural FM broadcasts, flutter, cancellation and capture are even more 
noticeable. The FM stereo noise-free broadcast range is approximately 8 km (5 
miles) less than that received with the monaural FM radio. The AM/FM stereo 
radio might never encounter any of these troublesome conditions, as they are 
more prominent in metropolitan areas, hilly terrain and low-lying roadways. 
However, when diagnosing FM stereo concerns, it is recommended to tune to the 
strongest FM stereo station.

 Radio Tests 

Internal diagnostic examination of the radio chassis should be left to 
the authorized radio service center. However, the automotive technician should 
be able to analyze and isolate radio chassis reception conditions to the 
proper area or component causing the condition. All radio chassis conditions 
can be isolated to one of four general areas:

antenna system

radio chassis

speaker system

radio noise suppression equipment

 Interfering Noises 

The vehicle ignition system is a possible source of radio interference. 
This high-voltage switching system produces a radio frequency electromagnetic 
field that radiates at AM, FM and CB frequencies. Although components have 
been designed into the vehicle to minimize this concern, the noise is more 
noticeable if the radio is tuned slightly off-channel for FM programs. Vehicle 
electrical accessories and owner add-on accessories can also contribute to 
radio interference. Furthermore, there are many noise sources that are 
external to the vehicle. These include power lines, communication systems, 
ignition systems of other vehicles, neon signs, etc.

Noise or static can result from many causes. Three of the most common 
sources of radio noise are the following.

 Ignition Noise 

The most effective method of evaluating ignition noise is to compare 
the radio performance with the engine on, versus engine off. If ignition noise 
is present with engine running, check the following:

Make sure the spark plug wires are the suppressor type and that the 
spark plugs are the correct resistor type.

If so equipped, make sure that the carbon center insert in distributor 
cap is secure.

If so equipped, check distributor cap and rotor electrodes for silicone 
grease. This can cause ignition noise on FM. This noise is characterized by a 
"motor boat" type sound on weak-to-moderate strength stations. The noise can 
only be eliminated by replacing the distributor cap and rotor with a cap and 
rotor that does not have grease.

 Missing or Poor Grounds 

Check bond strap grounding effectiveness by wedging a large file 
between metal parts, such as between the tail pipe and body, or between the 
fender and frame, to ensure proper ground, while the radio chassis is playing 
and the engine is running. Listen for a decrease in the objectionable radio 
noise. If a reduction in radio noise is noted, first try tightening body and 
exhaust system clamps and brackets. Then, if necessary, install a new bond 
strap between the two metal parts to ensure proper ground.

 Missing or Damaged Noise Suppression Components 

Refer to the description for Missing or Poor Grounds.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Audio System Service

 Inspection and Verification 

 Poor Reception 

 NOTE: Many customers do not understand the limitations of FM reception. Refer 
the customer to the owner guide for information about the limitations of FM 
radio performance.

If AM reception is extremely poor and FM reception drifts or appears to 
have trouble holding stations, make sure the antenna and antenna connectors 
are properly mated. If the antenna connectors are properly mated but the 
reception is still poor, refer to Radio Antenna under Component Tests in the 
Diagnosis and Testing portion of this section.

If only FM reception is poor, it is unlikely that the antenna is at 
fault. Remove the radio chassis for service.

 Tape Player Will Not Accept Cartridge, Eats Tape, Plays Too Fast or 
Too Slow, Etc. (AM and FM Operating Properly) 

Check operation of the tape player by using a known good 
cassette/cartridge. 

If the condition is not corrected by the substitution of a known good 
cassette/cartridge, the radio chassis must be removed and sent to an 
authorized service facility for service.

 Removal 

Remove the four mounting bracket screws. 

Insert Radio Removing Tool T87P-19061-A, one on each side of the radio, 
into the access holes in bezel until a click is heard. Apply an outward 
pressure on the sides to release the locking tangs and slide the radio from 
the dash. 

Disconnect the radio power lead, antenna lead-in cable and the speaker 
lead wires from the radio. 

Remove the support bracket from the back of the radio. 

To disengage radio removing tools press the locking tangs on side of 
the radio while applying slight inward pressure on the tools, and pull tools 
out of access holes. 

 Installation 

Position the radio to the mounting bracket. 

Install the support bracket on the back of the radio. 

Connect the radio power lead, radio speaker wires and the antenna 
lead-in cable to the radio. 

Position radio and mounting bracket to instrument panel. Align locating 
pins on mounting bracket and secure with four screws. 

Slide radio into dash opening until retaining tangs lock. 

Check radio operation.

Headlamps

 Light Switch Rheostat Resistor

[FIGURE: K1451G.gif]

1999 F and B-Series

Section 17-01: Lighting, Exterior

1999 P800, F700, F800, FT900 and B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Stoplight Switch, Vehicles with Hydraulic Brakes 

Vehicles with hydraulic brakes have a plunger stoplight switch mounted 
to the brake pedal arm. 

The mechanical stoplight switch assembly, installed on the pin of the 
brake pedal arm, straddles the master cylinder push rod, but is not attached 
directly to the push rod. The switch assembly moves with the pedal arm when 
the brake pedal is depressed.

The switch actuating pin is held by spring pressure against the rear 
end of the push rod. Because of the slight clearance between the eye of the 
master cylinder push rod and the brake pedal arm pin, the pin and the switch 
move forward slightly before the push rod moves when the pedal is depressed. 
This relative movement between the switch and the end of the push rod moves 
the actuating pin rearward in the switch, closing the switch contacts and 
completing the circuit to the stoplamps.

When the brake pedal is released, the switch moves rearward in relation 
to the push rod. The spring in the switch returns the actuating pin to its 
normal position, opening the switch contacts and interrupting the circuit to 
the stoplamps.

================================================================================
PAGE 3648
================================================================================

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Stoplight Switch, Vehicles with Air Brakes 

F700-800, FT900 vehicles and B-Series vehicles with air brakes have an 
air pressure sensing stoplight switch. The switch is mounted to the air brake 
control valve on the suspended brake pedal support. 

On F800 tractor-trailer air brake systems, an air pressure sensing 
stoplight switch is mounted on a tee-fitting at the double check valve port 
for the tractor protection valve service line.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Hazard Warning Flasher Switch

The flasher switch is located on the steering column. Push the switch 
inward to start the flashers; pull the switch out to stop the flashing action. 
It can be used with the ignition lock cylinder in the RUN or OFF position. 
Make sure the turn signal lever is in the OFF (center) position before turning 
on the hazard warning flasher system.

[FIGURE: K42131A.gif]

 Indicator Flasher 

F-Series vehicles use a combination turn signal/hazard warning flasher 
mounted in the fuse panel. 

B-Series vehicles use a combination turn signal/hazard warning flasher 
that is mounted on the brake and clutch pedal support. 

Flasher will not operate with brake pedal depressed.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Lighting, Exterior

 Inspection and Verification, General 

Common point diagnosis should be used to isolate concerns in a 
multi-load circuit (a circuit with more than one operating component) without 
making any tests. If one system functions properly but another does not, the 
concern must be in the part of the circuit unique to the inoperative system. 

If more than one circuit does not operate, check for blown fuses. 

Before performing any lighting system tests, make sure the battery is 
in a fully charged condition and all battery cable connections are clean and 
tight. 

A visual inspection is an important part of the lighting system test. 
Check for wires with frayed or damaged insulation, loose connections and 
proper harness routing. Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting 
Manual (EVTM). 

Correct any concerns found by the visual inspection before performing 
further tests of the lighting system. For example, a loose ground strap 
between the engine and body dash panel can cause an intermittent operation of 
the lamps and gauges. Inspect and tighten (if necessary) the ground strap 
retaining screws at the back of the engine and the body dash panel. 

If a No. 10 screw is required, use Part No. 42367-S36 hex washer head 
tapping screw. 

Any screws or bolts used for attaching the engine-to-body ground strap 
must have an S36 finish (zinc plate plus dichromate dip).

ADJUSTMENTS

Headlamp

Headlamp aim adjustment should be made with the Rotunda Headlamp Aiming 
Kit 196-00001 or equivalent. Use the latest instructions. The kit equipment 
can be calibrated to accommodate a slight slope in the floor.

The high beam is automatically adjusted when the low beam is adjusted.

Before making any headlamp adjustments, perform the following 
preparatory steps.

Remove ice or mud from underhood assembly fender area (or wheel 
housing). 

Make sure all tires are inflated to recommended pressures. 

Check springs for sag or broken leaves. 

Take into consideration incorrect wheel alignment or improper tracking 
of the rear axle. 

Make sure there is no load in the vehicle other than the fuel tank 
one-half full. 

Check hood for correct locked down position and make sure hood latches 
are secure. 

Clean lenses and aiming pads. 

Check for bulb burnout and proper beam switching. 

Make sure light output is close to normal new lamp value. 

 NOTE: Always bring each beam into final position by turning adjusting screws 
clockwise so that headlamp will be held against the tension springs when the 
operation is completed. 

When setup requirements are satisfied, perform the following steps for 
headlamp adjustment.

Right headlamp: cover left headlamp and turn headlamps on in low beam 
position. 

Horizontal adjustment: turn adjustment screw (B) at left of sealed beam 
retainer ring. Clockwise moves the beam to the right. Counterclockwise moves 
the beam to the left. 

[FIGURE: K90631A.gif]

Vertical adjustment: turn adjustment screw (A) at top of sealed beam 
retainer ring. Clockwise moves the beam upward. Counterclockwise moves the 
beam downward.

Remove left headlamp cover. Turn off headlamps, allow lamps to cool. 

Left headlamps: cover the right headlamp and turn headlamps on in low 
beam position. 

Horizontal adjustment: turn adjustment screw (C) at right of sealed 
beam retainer ring. Clockwise moves the beam to the left. Counterclockwise 
moves the beam to the right. 

[FIGURE: K90641A.gif]

Vertical adjustment: turn adjustment screw (A) at top of sealed beam 
retainer ring. Clockwise moves the beam upward. Counterclockwise moves the 
beam downward. 

Remove right headlamp cover. Turn off headlamps, allow lamps to cool.

 Inspection and Verification

lamps.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Electrical

Open fuses

Fuse panel Fuse 11 (15A)

Loose connectors

symptom(s) and proceed to the following symptom chart.

 Symptom Chart — Lighting, Interior 

 LIGHTING, INTERIOR 

Condition

Possible Source

Action

Interior Lamp(s) Does Not Turn On When One Door Is Opened, OK When 
Other Doors Are Opened

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Switch, Courtesy Lamp 

 Removal 

Unscrew the hex sleeve nut from the pillar.

Extract switch and pull the wiring connector off the switch. 

[FIGURE: K16603B.gif]

Retention of dome lamp switch to the wiring connector is by one of 
three tabs positioned 120 degrees apart on the switch. If the engaged locking 
tab breaks off when the switch is disconnected from the wiring connector, the 
switch must be rotated 120 degrees to engage a new tab. When all three tabs 
have been broken, the switch must be replaced. 

 Installation 

Pull wiring connector and wiring through the switch mounting hole in 
the pillar and connect switch to the connector.

Twist the wiring and switch six turns counterclockwise, push the wiring 
and connector back through the mounting hole and screw the switch into the 
pillar until it is seated. 

Close and open the door to ensure that the courtesy lamp is operating 
properly.

Section 17-04: Lamps, Daytime Running

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Canadian Daytime Running Lamp (DRL) System

The Canadian daytime running lamp (DRL) system is designed to turn the 
high beam headlamps on, with a reduced light output, and without illuminating 
the high beam indicator lamp in the instrument panel when the following 
conditions are met: 

The ignition switch lock cylinder is in the RUN position. 

The parking brake is fully released. 

The headlamp switch is in the OFF or PARK position. 

The daytime running lamps (DRL) control module is grounded through the 
low beam input when the DRL system is active.

 NOTE: When the DRL system is active, the pulsed voltage on the high beam 
circuit cannot be measured accurately. If the low beam headlamps are 
inoperative, refer to Section 17-01 .

================================================================================
PAGE 3682
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 17-04: Lamps, Daytime Running

1999 F700, F800, FT900, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

U.S. Daytime Running Lamp System

The U.S. daytime running lamp (DRL) system is designed to turn the low 
beam headlamps on at a reduced light intensity when the following conditions 
are met:

The ignition switch lock cylinder is in the RUN position.

The parking brake is fully released.

The headlamp switch is in the OFF or PARK position.

 NOTE: When the DRL system is active, the pulsed voltage on the low beam 
circuit cannot be measured accurately. If the high beam headlamps are 
inoperative, refer to Section 17-01 .

The daytime running lamps (DRL) control module is grounded through the 
high beam input when the DRL system is active.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Daytime Running Lamp (DRL) System

 Inspection and Verification 

Before performing any lighting systems tests, check that the battery is 
fully charged, battery connections are clean and tight, and burned out fuses 
and bulbs have been replaced. The DRL system also requires the parking brake 
switch lamp to function correctly.

Verify the original concern by operating the daytime running lamps to 
duplicate the owner's concern.

Inspect to determine if one of the following electrical concerns applies.

 VISUAL INSPECTION CHART

Electrical

Open instrument panel fuses:

Fuse 1, 10A

Fuse 4, 10A

Corroded connectors

Loose connectors

If the concern remains after the inspection, determine the symptoms and 
proceed to the following symptom chart.

 Symptom Chart — Daytime Running Lamps 

Refer to the Electrical and Vacuum Troubleshooting Manual for the 
connector numbers in the pinpoint tests.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Identification

For engine identification and adjustment information, a label, or 
dataplate, is attached to the side of the front gear housing in front of the 
fuel pump. Always refer to the label when replacement parts are required or 
when checking engine calibrations. Some engine parts may vary with engine 
application and vehicle type. The identification codes will ensure that the 
proper parts are obtained. The codes contain all pertinent information 
relating to dates, optional equipment and revisions. The Ford Master Parts 
Catalog contains a complete listing of the codes and their application. In 
addition, there is an engine serial number located on a pad at the lower right 
side of the block.
