Section 03A-01: Engine, Cummins B5.9 Diesel

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Engine 

 Removal 

Remove hood and front bumper, and disconnect battery ground cable. 

Drain engine oil and coolant. 

Release air system pressure, if so equipped. 

Remove air cleaner assembly, turbocharger air supply tube and 
turbo-to-charge air cooler tube. 

Position drain pan and disconnect power steering pump supply hose at 
pump. 

Disconnect power steering pump pressure hose at pump. 

Disconnect brake air compressor air supply hose at compressor, if so 
equipped. 

Remove fan shroud retaining bolts and hang shroud over fan. 

Disconnect the radiator upper and lower hoses. 

Disconnect coolant purge and supply hoses at coolant reservoir. 

Disconnect low coolant sensor at reservoir. 

Remove the two radiator coolant recovery reservoir-to-mounting bracket 
retaining bolts and remove reservoir. 

Disconnect the overflow hose at the radiator. 

Remove the radiator retaining bolts and remove the radiator and charge 
air cooler as an assembly. 

Remove shroud and remove fan blade-to-hub retaining bolts. Remove fan. 

Disconnect brake compressor pressure hose or hydraulic brake lines, if 
so equipped. 

Mark brake compressor governor hoses, if so equipped, prior to 
removing. Disconnect hoses. 

Remove hose retainers at engine block. 

Position hoses away from engine. 

Disconnect oil cooler line at cooler and position out of way. 

Disconnect exhaust pipe at turbocharger. 

Remove air hose from air charge cooler to intake manifold. 

Disconnect heater hoses from tubes at top of thermostat housing. 

Disconnect throttle cable, hand throttle cable and transmission 
kickdown cable (automatic transmission only) and position aside. 

Cut tie wraps and disconnect generator electrical harness. 

Disconnect wiring to coolant temperature senders on thermostat housing. 

Disconnect wiring from starter motor. 

Disconnect speed sensor at flywheel housing. 

Remove cable clamp retaining nut at flywheel housing. 

Remove fuel lines-to-flywheel housing retaining bolts. 

Disconnect two fuel lines at rear of fuel block and cap all openings. 

Remove ground wire retaining bolt at flywheel housing. 

Disconnect electrical connector at fuel shutoff solenoid. 

Loosen clamps and remove oil fill hose. 

Disconnect lower radiator hose at engine. 

Remove radiator lower hose strap retaining bolt and remove hose. 

Remove exhaust pipe clamp retaining nut. Remove exhaust pipe. 

Remove transmission. Refer to appropriate transmission section in 
Group 07 for procedure. 

 NOTE: Lift engine only by front and rear lifting eyes attached to cylinder 
head. 

Install Engine Lifting Brackets T70P-6000.

Remove the rear engine mount retaining bolts. 

Remove the front mount-to-crossmember retaining bolts. 

Position lifting equipment and remove engine assembly from the vehicle. 

Mount engine on a suitable engine stand and move to work area. 

 Installation 

 NOTE: For fastener torque values, refer to Torque Specifications chart in 
the Specifications portion of this section.

Install Engine Lifting Brackets T70P-6000 on engine.

Lift and position engine in vehicle.

Attach front mount-to-crossmember retaining bolts.

Attach rear engine mount retaining bolts.

Install clutch. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Position clutch slave cylinder and attach retaining bolts. Connect 
hydraulic fitting. Refer to Section 08-02 for linkage assembly and hydraulic 
system bleeding.

Install transmission. Refer to Group 07.

Install exhaust pipe and clamp retaining nut.

Connect lower radiator hose and hose strap retaining bolt.

Install oil fill hose and clamps.

Connect fuel shutoff solenoid connector.

Attach ground wire retaining bolt to flywheel housing.

Remove protective caps from two fuel lines and attach to rear of fuel 
block.

Attach fuel lines-to-flywheel housing retaining bolts.

Attach cable clamp retaining nut at flywheel housing.

Connect speed sensor at flywheel housing.

Connect wiring for starter motor.

Connect wiring to coolant temperature senders on thermostat housing.

Connect generator electrical harness.

Connect throttle cable, hand throttle cable and transmission kickdown 
cable.

Connect heater hoses at top of thermostat housing.

Connect exhaust pipe at turbocharger.

Connect air hose from intake manifold to charge air cooler.

Connect oil cooler line to oil cooler.

Connect brake compressor governor hoses, if so equipped, and attach 
hose retainers to engine block.

Connect brake compressor hose or hydraulic brake lines, if so equipped.

Attach fan to hub and install shroud.

Install radiator and charge air cooler.

Attach overflow hose to radiator.

Assemble coolant reservoir.

Connect low coolant sensor at coolant reservoir.

Connect radiator upper and lower hoses.

Connect the brake air compressor air supply hose to compressor, if so 
equipped.

Connect the power steering pump pressure hose to the pump.

Connect the turbocharger-to-charge air cooler, turbocharger air supply 
tube and air cleaner assembly.

Add engine oil and coolant.

Install hood and front bumper.

Connect battery ground cable.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling System

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CONDITIONS WHILE THE ENGINE IS 
OPERATING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THESE INSTRUCTIONS CAN RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AND DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE. 

TO AVOID HAVING SCALDING HOT COOLANT OR STEAM BLOW OUT OF THE RADIATOR, 
 USE EXTREME CARE WHEN REMOVING THE CAP FROM A HOT RADIATOR. IF POSSIBLE, WAIT 
UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, THEN WRAP A THICK CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP 
AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK WHILE THE PRESSURE IS RELEASED 
FROM THE COOLING SYSTEM. WHEN YOU ARE SURE ALL THE PRESSURE HAS BEEN RELEASED, 
PRESS DOWN ON THE CAP (STILL USING A CLOTH), TURN AND REMOVE IT. 

Refer to Section 03-03 .

================================================================================
PAGE 3996
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-03: Engine Cooling, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F700, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Block Heater

The engine block heater consists of an electrical heating element 
installed in one of the core plug openings in the engine block and an 
electrical cable which plugs into a standard 110 volt AC electrical outlet. It 
is designed to keep the engine coolant warm during cold weather to aid in cold 
starting.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator Hose, Upper

 Removal 

Disconnect the battery negative cables.

Drain the engine coolant. Refer to Section 03-03 .

Remove the air cleaner assembly.

Disconnect the air duct assembly at the turbocharger inlet.

Remove the generator drive belt. Refer to Section 03A-05 .

Remove bolt retaining generator to upper bracket.

Loosen generator pivot bolts. Rotate generator downward away from 
upper radiator hose.

Loosen clamp retaining rubber extension hose to upper radiator hose 
neck.

Loosen clamp retaining rubber extension hose to thermostat housing. 
Remove upper radiator hose from vehicle.

Loosen clamps retaining rubber extension hoses to upper radiator hose 
tube. Replace upper radiator hose components as needed.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten generator pivot bolts to 55-67 Nm (41-49 lb-in).

Tighten clamps to 9-11 Nm (80-97 lb-in).

Tighten generator support strap retaining bolts to 30-40 Nm 
(22-30 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator

 Removal 

 NOTE: When removing the radiator, the tilt hood (if so equipped) must be

Drain cooling system. Refer to Section 03-03 .

Disconnect the spring-loaded hood support cables (tilt hood).

bulkhead. Remove support braces.

Attach lifting equipment to radiator. Remove six retaining bolts from 
radiator.

With an assistant, lift and remove radiator from vehicle.

Remove six screws and shroud from radiator.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten radiator mounting bolts and nuts to 75-102 Nm (55-75 
lb-ft).

Tighten radiator hose clamps to 9-11 Nm (80-97 lb-in).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator Coolant Recovery Reservoir

 WARNING: DO NOT STAND IN LINE WITH OR NEAR RADIATOR COOLING FAN WHEN REVVING 
ENGINE. 

 Removal 

Drain the radiator until the coolant is out of the supply tank. 
Disconnect the radiator draw down hose at the supply tank. Disconnect the 
radiator vent tube at the supply tank, if so equipped. 

Remove the overflow tube from the supply tank. Remove the supply tank 
bracket retaining bolt(s) and remove the supply tank. 

 Installation 

Position the supply tank in the chassis and install the bracket 
retaining bolt(s). 

Connect the radiator draw down hose, overflow tube and vent tube, if so 
equipped, to the supply tank. 

Fill and bleed the cooling system. Refer to Section 03-03 . Check for 
coolant leaks and proper coolant level after the engine reaches normal 
operating temperatures.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fittings, Automatic Transmission 

Use a waterproof sealer such as Pipe Sealant with Teflon® 
D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-A2 and 
ESR-M18P7-A when assembling fittings such as the drain cock to the radiator.

When installing a new radiator in a vehicle equipped with automatic 
transmission, transfer the oil cooler line fittings from the old radiator and 
install them in the new radiator, using oil-resistant sealer.

When installation of the radiator is complete, check the oil cooler 
line connections for leaks. Check the transmission fluid level and fill, if 
necessary.

Section 03A-05: Drive Belts, Accessory, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drive Belts, Accessory 

P800, F800, B800 vehicles are equipped with two types of accessory 
drive belts. The drive belt type is selected for each engine based on 
performance requirements. To ensure maximum life, replacement belts must be of 
the same type as originally installed. These belts must be properly adjusted 
at all times. Loose belt(s) will result in slippage, which can cause a noise 
complaint or improper accessory operation (generator will not charge, etc.). 
Overly tight belts will place severe loads on accessory bearings. 

The poly-V (serpentine) drive belt tension is maintained by an 
automatic belt tensioner. Regular inspection is required to check belt 
condition to ensure that excessive belt stretch does not occur. The vee drive 
belt is not automatically tensioned and requires periodic inspection for 
proper belt tension.

[FIGURE: Q1690E.gif]

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fan and Clutch, Engine Operated

The fan and clutch assembly is used to cool the engine. The fan is 
driven through the use of drive belts and pulleys.

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Drive Belts, Accessory

 Inspection and Verification 

 Drive Belt Cracking/Chunking/Wear 

Under severe operating conditions (high temperatures, low humidity), 
drive belt rib cracking can occur at less than 96,000 km (60,000 miles). Drive 
belt rib cracking perpendicular to the belt ribs is not a reason for concern 
and has no detrimental effect on belt performance. Cracks parallel to ribs are 
not acceptable.

Drive belt "chunking" is the condition in which the rubber material 
actually chunks out between the cracks. The drive belt must be replaced if 
chunks are missing on two adjacent ribs or a chunked-out section is 13 mm (0.5 
inch) or longer in length.

[FIGURE: Q4077C.gif]

 Drive Belt Noise 

Drive belt chirp is a regularly occurring chirping noise that occurs 
due to pulley misalignment or excessive pulley runout. It can be a result of a 
damaged pulley or an improperly replaced pulley that was not properly aligned.

To correct, determine the area the noise comes from. Then check each of 
the pulleys in that area with a straightedge to the crankshaft pulley and look 
for the accessory pulleys to be out of position in the fore/aft direction or 
at an angle to the straightedge.

Belt squeal is an intermittent noise that occurs when the drive belt 
slips on a pulley during certain conditions, such as engine start-up, rapid 
engine acceleration or A/C clutch engagement.

Drive belt squeal can occur under the following conditions:

A/C discharge pressure goes above 2895 kPa (420 psi). This can occur if:

the A/C system is overcharged

the A/C condenser core airflow is blocked

the engine fan blade is not engaging fully at idle

A/C OFF equalized pressure (the common discharge and suction pressure 
that occurs after several minutes) exceeds 965 kPa (140 psi), which is a rare 
occurrence at high ambient temperatures with a hot engine. Turn A/C off for a 
few seconds and then back on after fan blade begins to cool A/C condenser core.

Any of the accessories are damaged, or have a worn or damaged bearing 
or internal torsional resistance above normal for any reason. All of the 
accessories should be able to be rotated by hand in the unloaded condition. If 
any are not, inspect the accessory.

Fluid gets on the drive belt. These include power steering fluid, 
engine coolant, engine oil or air conditioning system lubricant.

If fluid does get on the drive belt during service, the best policy is 
to clean the drive belt with soap and water and thoroughly rinse with clean 
water. The drive belt does not have to be replaced if no apparent damage has 
occurred.

Drive belt is too long. A drive belt that is too long will allow the 
drive belt tensioner arm to go all the way to drive belt tensioner arm travel 
stop under certain load conditions, which will untension the drive belt. If 
the drive belt tensioner is resting on the stop, replace the drive belt.

If the drive belt tensioner is worn or damaged. The drive belt 
tensioner arm should rotate freely without binding.

 Component Tests 

 Drive Belt Tension 

Check drive belt tension. Refer to Drive Belt Tension Adjustment in the 
Adjustments portion of this section. If tension is not within specification, 
check drive belt tensioner. Service components as required.

 Drive Belt Tensioner, Automatic 

The drive belt tensioner will maintain correct belt tension if the 
correct length drive belt is on the engine. Check drive belt tensioner as 
follows:

With the engine running, observe drive belt tensioner movement. The 
drive belt tensioner should move (respond) when the A/C compressor cycles or 
when the engine is accelerated rapidly. If the drive belt tensioner movement 
is constant and excessive, a pulley or shaft is probably bent or a pulley is 
out of round. In rare cases, excessive belt rideout (uneven depth of grooves 
in belt) can cause excessive drive belt tensioner movement. This condition can 
be checked by replacing the suspect drive belt with a known good original 
equipment drive belt and repeating the observation.

With engine off, check for proper drive belt routing. Refer to the 
illustrations under Removal and Installation in this section. Service as 
required.

Visually inspect the condition of the drive belt. Replace the drive 
belt as required.

Rotate the drive belt tensioner and check for a binding or frozen 
condition. Replace components as required.

 Drive Belt Misalignment 

 CAUTION: Incorrect drive belt installation will cause excessive drive belt wear 
and can cause the drive belt to come off the drive pulleys. 

 NOTE: Original equipment drive belts are made of a special cord construction 
and are subjected to special testing before approval for use.

 NOTE: Replacement drive belts, other than O.E.M., may track 
differently/improperly. If a replacement drive belt tracks improperly, the 
drive belt must be replaced with an O.E.M. drive belt to avoid performance 
failure or loss of drive belt during cold operation.

With the engine running, check drive belt tracking (the position of the 
drive belt on the drive belt tensioner. If the edge of the drive belt rides 
beyond the edge of the drive bent tensioner, this can cause noise and 
premature wear. 

If a drive belt tracking condition exists, visually check the drive 
belt tensioner for damage, especially the mounting pad surface. If the drive 
belt tensioner is not installed correctly with the locating pins in the 
locating holes, the mounting surface pad will be out of position. This will 
result in drive belt tension and chirp and squeal noises.

If the above procedures do not correct the drive belt noise, try 
replacing the drive belt with a known good original equipment drive belt. 
However, the drive belt noise may return again (with mileage) if one of the 
above conditions still exists uncorrected.

With engine running, visually observe the grooves in the pulleys (not 
the pulley flanges) for excessive wobble. Replace components as required.

Check all accessories, mounting brackets and drive belt tensioner for 
any interference that prevents the component from mounting properly. Correct 
any interference condition and recheck belt tracking.

Tighten all accessories mounting brackets and drive belt tensioner 
retaining hardware to specification. Recheck drive belt tracking.

Check drive belt tension. Refer to Drive Belt Tension Adjustment in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drive Belt Replacement 

Conditions requiring drive belt replacement are rib chunk out, 
excessive wear, severe glazing and frayed cords. Replace any drive belt 
exhibiting any of these conditions. Perpendicular cracks in the ribbed side of 
V-grooved portion of the drive belt are considered acceptable.

 Drive Belt, Serpentine (Poly-V)

 Installation

hand and activate the tensioner pulley outboard until the belt can be slipped 
over the water pump pulley. 

When belt is over the water pump pulley, carefully release the 
tensioner to tighten belt. Check again to make sure the belt is seated 
properly in all pulleys. 

Install Hydro-Max pump assembly vee drive belt, if so equipped.

Start engine and check for proper operation.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drive Belt Tensioner, Automatic

 Removal 

Rotate automatic belt tensioner to release drive belt tension.

With tension released, remove poly-V (serpentine) drive belt from 
tensioner pulley.

Allow drive belt tensioner to slowly rotate to the relaxed position. Do 
not allow tensioner to snap back after the drive belt is removed or damage to 
the tensioner can occur.

Remove drive belt tensioner retainer belt and tensioner.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order. 

Tighten drive belt tensioner bolt to 83 Nm (61 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Starter Motor 

 Removal 

Open battery box and disconnect battery ground cable.

Remove starter motor upper mounting bolt.

Disconnect starter and starter solenoid wires. Tag wires to facilitate 
connection at proper terminals during starter installation.

Remove two remaining starter motor mounting bolts. Remove starter.

 Installation 

Position starter on engine. Install three bolts. Tighten to 150-200 
Nm (110-148 lb-ft).

Connect solenoid wire to starter S-terminal. Tighten nut to 1.8 
Nm (16 lb-in).

Connect remaining starter wires to starter B-terminal and tighten nut 
to 18 Nm (13 lb-ft).

Connect battery ground cable and close battery box. Check operation of 
starter.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Starter Motor 

 Disassembly 

Thoroughly clean outside of starter.

Scribe a mark on starter motor frame, drive end housing and lever 
housing for assembly.

Disconnect starter motor lead on frame from starter solenoid 
M-terminal. Reinstall nut on solenoid terminal.

Remove the two through-bolts.

Remove the four brush plate screws.

Remove the commutator end frame and O-ring.

 NOTE: Use care not to lose the small dowel pin installed between frame, field 
and brush holder assembly, and gear reduction and drive assembly. Dowel pin is 
required for reassembly and must be saved. If dowel pin is lost, replace with 
2-mm (0.079-inch) diameter x 10-mm (0.394-inch) long pin.

Remove the frame, field and brush holder assembly, dowel pin and frame 
seal.

 NOTE: Armature assembly might come off with frame, field and brush holder 
assembly or might be retained by gear reduction and drive assembly.

Remove armature assembly with ball bearings. Do not remove ball 
bearings from armature assembly unless replacement is required.

Remove the solenoid retaining screws.

Remove the solenoid assembly. Pivot inside end of solenoid assembly out 
of engagement with shift lever in gear reduction and drive assembly and 
withdraw solenoid assembly.

 Assembly 

Support gear reduction and drive assembly with pinion gear end down and

Position starter solenoid mounting flange and install solenoid mounting

drive assembly. Make sure gear teeth are aligned, then seat ball bearing on 
armature shaft fully into drive housing recess.

Place dowel pin in hole in armature support bracket of gear reduction 
and drive assembly.

Position frame, field and brush holder assembly over armature assembly. 
Align hole for dowel pin and marks made prior to disassembly and seat in gear 
reduction and drive group.

Twist brush springs away from brushes. Slide brushes in to contact 
commutator on armature and release brush springs to contact ends of brushes.

 NOTE: O-ring can easily be damaged during installation of the commutator end 
frame. To prevent such damage, install O-ring as described.

Install O-ring on frame, field and brush holder assembly so that it is 
against the shoulder on the frame and field assembly that will abut the 
commutator end frame when installed. This is the normal installed position for 
the O-ring.

Carefully roll the O-ring out of its normal installed position up onto 
the major OD of the field frame. Allow O-ring to remain in this position until 
commutator end frame is partially installed.

Align marks on commutator end frame and frame and field assembly made 
prior to disassembly. Start commutator end frame onto frame and field 
assembly, leaving a gap just slightly larger than the thickness of O-ring.

Install brush plate screws. Use a scribe or similar tool to align 
tapped holes in brush holder assembly with screw holes in commutator end 
frame. Tighten screws to 2.8 Nm (25 lb-in).

Install through-bolts and tighten by hand but do not close gap between 
commutator end frame and frame and field assembly where O-ring goes.

Roll O-ring back down into its installed position between commutator 
end frame and frame and field assembly.

Align timing ribs on edge of commutator end frame with timing spots on 
frame and field assembly to ensure proper brush alignment. Marks are located 
in two places on motor but will only match one way. Tighten through-bolts to 
8.5 Nm (75 lb-in).

Remove nut from M-terminal on solenoid. Install starter motor lead 
terminal and reinstall nut. Tighten nut to 11 Nm (100 lb-in).

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Starter Drive Replacement

 Disassembly 

Disassemble starter motor.

Remove the drive housing bolts.

Remove the armature support bracket. Washers might stick to armature 
support bracket or to output shaft and clutch assembly as armature support 
bracket is removed. In either case, note the position and number of each of 
these washers.

Remove washers. The same washers will be installed in the same position 
and number at assembly.

Remove drive housing plug and plate. Pry out drive housing plug using a 
large screwdriver.

Remove shift lever nut, washer and screw.

Remove shift lever and output shaft and clutch assembly from drive 
housing together, then separate. Do not remove bushing plug or bushing from 
drive housing unless replacement is required.

Position driveshaft and clutch assembly on workbench with internal gear 
end down.

Using open tube slightly larger than shaft, drive pinion stop toward 
clutch drive assembly until it clears stop rings.

[FIGURE: J6435A.gif]

Using care not to scratch driveshaft, pry stop rings out of shaft 
groove and slide off end of shaft.

Inspect edges of shaft groove for burrs that might have been formed 
through repeated cranking cycles. Such burrs make removal of pinion stop and 
clutch drive assembly difficult. If burrs are found, use a suitable file to 
carefully remove burrs only — not base metal. Thoroughly clean away 
metal filings.

Slide pinion stop off driveshaft. Discard pinion stop and stop rings. 
New parts must be used at assembly.

Remove clutch drive assembly from driveshaft.

Remove driveshaft support from driveshaft.

Do not remove bearing from driveshaft unless replacement is required.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Induction System

Air is pulled into the engine through an air filter. Clean air is very 
important to the life of the engine. Ingested dust and dirt can damage the 
cylinders very quickly. 

On turbocharged and aftercooled engines, the intake airflow is from the 
air cleaner to the turbocharger. It is then routed to the charge air cooler 
located in front of the radiator. Air leaves the charge air cooler and is 
routed to the intake manifold where it is forced into the cylinders and used 
for combustion. The charge air cooler reduces the temperature of the intake 
air, which lowers combustion chamber temperatures, which in turn reduces NOx 
emissions. Also, cooling the intake air makes it more dense, allowing more 
fuel to be injected into the engine to increase the power-to-weight ratio. 

 Typical Intake Air System, Turbocharged Engine

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Cleaner Element

 CAUTION: If the air cleaner element, air cleaner housing or turbocharger inlet 
tube is removed, use a clean shop rag to prevent contaminants from entering 
the engine. 

A dry-type air cleaner is standard equipment. Air is filtered through a 
pleated, chemically treated paper air cleaner element to remove contaminants 
before entering the engine air induction system. 

Because the air cleaner used with the Cummins B5.9 engine is vertically 
mounted, it also includes a secondary element located inside the primary 
element. Its purpose is to prevent contaminants from falling into the turbo 
inlet hose when the primary filter element is being changed. This secondary 
element should be left in place and should remain undisturbed during routine 
air cleaner servicing. After several normal air cleaner service cycles, the 
secondary element should also be replaced.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Restriction Indicator

All B5.9 engines above 160 HP are equipped with an air restriction 
indicator that indicates red when the air cleaner needs servicing. When the 
gauge reads 6.2 kPa (25 inches of water) vacuum, the air cleaner needs 
servicing. 

[FIGURE: DV0675A.gif]

PAGE 4041
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Charge Air Cooler (Turbocharged Engines Only)

A turbocharger system uses the energy in the flow of exhaust gases to 
increase engine power and efficiency. These increases occur when the 
turbocharger converts the exhaust flow into a pressurized airflow on the 
intake side of the engine. Because more air is available to support 
combustion, additional fuel can be injected into the cylinders. It is the 
combination of additional fuel and a more complete scavenging of exhaust gases 
from the cylinders that produces the increased engine horsepower.

As air in the turbocharger is compressed, it is also heated. To remove 
the heat, the air is routed through the charge air cooler. The charge air 
cooler is an air-to-air heat exchanger similar in construction and function to 
a radiator. By lowering the temperature of the air, it is made denser. The 
increased density of the air delivered to the engine cylinders permits a 
corresponding increase in the weight of fuel that can be injected into the 
cylinders, while maintaining the air/fuel ratio required for proper 
combustion. Since engine power output is a function of the weight of fuel 
burned, the increase in the weight of fuel introduced as a result of 
turbocharger operation results in an increase in engine power output.

[FIGURE: A24462A.gif]

Engine Air Cleaner Intake Duct and Tube, Tilt Hood

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Air Cleaner Element 

 Removal 

 CAUTION: To prevent contaminants from entering the turbocharger inlet tube, 
unless it is being changed, leave the secondary element in place and 
undisturbed during routine air cleaner servicing. 

Remove the fasteners that retain the air cleaner housing cover and 
remove the cover.

 CAUTION: If the air cleaner element, air cleaner housing or turbocharger inlet 
tube is removed, use a clean shop rag to prevent contaminants from entering 
the engine. 

Release the seal gently. The air cleaner element fits tightly over the 
outlet tube, creating the critical seal on the inside diameter of the element 
end cap. Remove the air cleaner element gently to reduce the amount of dust 
dislodged. There will be some initial resistance, similar to breaking the seal 
on a jar. Gently move the end of the air cleaner element up and down and side 
to side or twist to break the seal. 

[FIGURE: V8451A.gif]

Avoid dislodging dust from the air cleaner element. Gently pull the air 
cleaner element off the outlet tube and out of the air cleaner housing. Avoid 
knocking the air cleaner element against the housing. 

[FIGURE: V8452A.gif]

 CAUTION: To minimize air leaks, use care to avoid damage to the air cleaner 
housing outlet tube. 

With a clean shop cloth, carefully clean the outlet tube where it 
extends into the housing. Inspect for possible air leaks in housing, inlet or 
outlet pipes.

[FIGURE: V8453A.gif]

Clean the inside of the outlet tube carefully. Dirt accidentally 
transferred to the inside of the outlet tube will reach the engine and cause 
wear. Use care not to damage the air cleaner element sealing area on the tube. 

[FIGURE: V8454A.gif]

Check the old air cleaner element. Inspect for foreign material on the 
sealing surface that is causing leakage. A streak of dust on the clean air 
side of the air cleaner element seal is the tell-tale sign. If dust exists, 
make sure the cause is removed before installing a new air cleaner element. 

 Installation 

Inspect the new air cleaner element for damage. Always look for 
possible shipping or handling damage. Pay particular attention to the inside 
of the open end (the sealing area). Check for cuts, etc. Do not use a damaged 
air cleaner element.

Insert the new air cleaner element properly. The radial seal area is on 
the inside of the open end of the air cleaner element. This critical sealing 
area will stretch slightly, adjust itself and distribute the sealing pressure 
evenly as the air cleaner element is forced onto the outlet tube. Apply firm 
pressure to complete a tight seal. Apply pressure at the outer rim of the air 
cleaner element, not the flexible center. Cover pressure is not necessary to 
make the air cleaner element seal. 

[FIGURE: V8457A.gif]

Position the cover assembly on the air cleaner housing and install the 
fasteners that retain the cover assembly. Cover pressure is not necessary to 
make the air cleaner element seal.

Press air restriction indicator reset button, located on the air 
restriction indicator (if so equipped).

[FIGURE: DV0675A.gif]

Check connections and ducts for air-tight fit. Make sure all clamps, 
flange connections and cleaner mounting bolts are tight. Seal any leaks in the 
clean air ducting before returning to service — they permit dirt to 
enter the engine directly. All connections and seals, from air cleaner to 
engine, must be tight.

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Air Inlet Restriction Check 

The best method for determining dry-type air cleaner maintenance 
periods is by checking the air restriction indicator, if so equipped. A visual 
inspection of the air cleaner element will not ascertain the need for service. 
The air cleaner should be serviced at regular scheduled maintenance intervals. 
Overservicing is not recommended.

Resetting the air restriction indicator each time the indicator is 
checked is recommended to verify the correct air restriction reading at the 
next check.

================================================================================
PAGE 4053
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Air Cleaner Element

 CAUTION: If the air cleaner element, air cleaner housing or turbocharger inlet 
tube is removed, use a clean shop rag to prevent contaminants from entering 
the engine. 

Inspect the air cleaner element for indications of air leaks that could 
allow unfiltered air to enter the engine. Check for dust streaks that may 
indicate a poor seal with the air cleaner housing. Always replace a restricted 
air cleaner element. Do not attempt to clean air cleaner element.

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Engine Air Cleaner Housing

 CAUTION: If the air cleaner element, air cleaner housing or the turbocharger 
inlet tube is removed, use a clean shop rag to prevent contaminants from 
entering the engine. 

Clean the air cleaner housing and the cover with a mild detergent or 
compressed air. Wipe the air cleaner housing and cover dry. Inspect the air 
cleaner housing and cover for distortion or damage at the air cleaner element 
and cover gasket mating surfaces. Replace cover or housing if damaged beyond 
service.

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

CLEANING AND INSPECTION

Charge Air Cooler Leak Checks

Loss of engine power, low turbocharger boost pressure and higher than 
normal exhaust temperature can be caused by a leaking charge air cooler.

Look for two types of cracks: tube cracks and tank weld cracks. Tube 
cracks will usually occur first in the corners of the core and will be seen 
where the tube goes into the tank. Visual inspection will usually suffice to 
find most tube cracks. A better way to locate cracks is to pressurize the 
cooler to 276 kPa (40 psi). Apply a liquid soap film to all the tank joints. 
If bubbles form, there is a tube crack present.

If tube cracks are found, replace the cooler. Refer to the Master Parts 
Catalog for proper application.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Charge Air Cooler, Aluminum

Listed in the following chart are the components of the air cooler 
system and the types of damage that occur. Some types of damage can be 
repaired while other types cannot. The corrective action is shown for each 
type of damage. In some cases, the cooler should be replaced not repaired.

 ALUMINUM CHARGE AIR COOLER SERVICE PROCEDURES

Condition

Action to Take

 · Tubes torn or cracked.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tubes dented, kinked or bent resulting in a round edge (radius less than 1
mm [1/32 in.]).

 · Weld or epoxy. Refer to Welding Repairs or Epoxy Repairs in the Service
Procedures portion of this section.

 · Tubes dented, kinked or bent resulting in a round edge (radius greater
than 1 mm [1/32 in.]).

 · No repair required.

 · Holes in tubes less than 1 mm (1/32 in.) in all directions on tube surface.

 · Weld or epoxy to fill. Refer to Welding Repairs or Epoxy Repairs in the
Service Procedures portion of this section.

 · External fins crushed or bent; no more than 1 mm (1/32 in.) height
reduction per fin row and the sidemember-to-sidemember dimension is within
specification (687 mm [26-3/4 in.]).

 · No repair required.

 · External fins pushed in with no tearing.

 · Straighten fins. Refer to Straightening in the Service Procedures portion
of this section.

 · External fins pushed in with tearing less than 10 mm (3/8 in.) deep from
core face. Also tearing is less than 20% of a given fin row and less than 5%
of the total fin rows.

 · Remove loose fin material and straighten. Refer to Straightening in the
Service Procedures portion of this section.

 · External fins pushed in with tearing of more than 10 mm (3/8 in.) from
face core or more than 20% of a given row or more than 5% of the total fin row.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Sidemembers bent or dented.

 · Straighten sidemember to original form. If tubes are dented or fins
crushed, refer to Straightening in the Service Procedures portion of this
section.

 · Sidemember surface cracked or broken through.

 · Weld sidemember. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures
portion of this section.

 · Headers bent or dented resulting in three or fewer tube or tube-to-header
leaks, and cracks are less than 2 mm (1/16 in.).

 · Weld header. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 Note: If crack is less than 1 mm (1/32 in.) repair can be
made with epoxy.

 · Headers bent or dented with more than three tube or tube-to-header leaks
or a crack width greater than 2 mm (1/16 in.).

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Headers cracked.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tank walls dented but not cracked or broken through and fit and function
of cooler is not affected.

 · No repair required.

 · Tanks cracked. Crack is no more than 2 mm (1/16 in.) wide and 20 mm (3/4
in.) long.

 · Weld tanks. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 · Tanks cracked. Crack is more than 2 mm (1/16 in.) wide or 20 mm (3/4 in.)
long.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tanks punctured. Hole is no more than 5 mm (3/16 in.) in all directions on
tank surface.

 · Weld tanks. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of
this section.

 · Tanks punctured. Hole is more than 5 mm (3/16 in.) in any direction on
tank surface.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Tank-to-header welds cracked or porous.

 · Weld. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of this
section.

 Caution: Repair welds must not start or stop where 
a production weld ends. 

 · Threads stripped in tapped holes.

 · Drill out stripped threads and tap to accept proper helicoil insert of
same diameter and thread pitch of original hole.

 · Bosses and mounting brackets cracked or broken off, but crack or fractured
surface does not go into tank wall.

 · Weld. Refer to Welding Repairs in the Service Procedures portion of this
section.

 · Bosses or mounting brackets cracked or broken off, and crack goes into
tank wall.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

 · Mounting pins or other hardware cracked, broken or otherwise damaged, and
repair will not affect fit, function or durability.

 · Repair to original condition.

 · Mounting pins or other hardware cracked, broken or otherwise damaged, and
repairs will affect fit, function or durability.

 · Replace cooler. Refer to Charge Air Cooler in the Removal and Installation
portion of this section.

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Straightening

 Straightening Fins 

Use a pointed object no more than 0.5 mm in diameter at the tip that 
will allow access to the apex of the fin. Straighten fins, taking care not to 
damage louvers or distort louver angle.

 Straightening Sidemembers 

Using pliers, vise-grips or similar tool, straighten sidemember from 
sides only. Never pry against tubes or header. Care must be taken not to 
damage fins, tubes or headers when straightening sidemembers.

================================================================================
PAGE 4058
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Welding Repairs

 Surface Preparation 

All surfaces to be welded must be free of all paint, oil, grease, water 
and other foreign matter in the area so the weld repair will adhere to the 
bare aluminum and will not be contaminated.

 Welding Tanks 

Prepare surfaces. Heat crack to chase ends until they stop. MIG weld to 
fill crack and continue bead past ends of crack approximately 25 mm (1 in.). 
Wire brush and grind excess weld material to blend with tank surface.

 Welding Sidemembers 

Prepare surface. Cut a V-shaped groove along the length of the crack to 
a depth equal to the member thickness. MIG weld to fill the groove and grind 
excess material away to provide a flat surface.

 Welding Mounting Brackets 

Tack brackets in place so bracket will retain its correct orientation. 
MIG weld in place. Allow to air cool. Check alignment.

 Welding Tubes or Tube Header Joints 

 CAUTION: Take care not to melt fins of tube-to-header braze joint. If welding 
near core, shield core with large steel plate. This protects it from sparks 
and weld splatter and will act as a heat sink. 

TIG weld using aluminum wire designated Alcan MIG Electrode Wire, 
1.20-mm (3/16-in.) diameter, 4043 aluminum alloy or equivalent.

================================================================================
PAGE 4059
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Epoxy Repairs

 Surface Preparation 

Remove all paint, oil, grease, water and other foreign matter in area 
of the epoxy repair so epoxy will adhere to the bare aluminum.

 Epoxying Tubes or Headers 

Use only high-temperature epoxy. The recommended epoxy is a resin (CIBA 
GEIGY ARALDITE AV 138M) and a hardener (CIBA GEIGY HV 998) or equivalent. Mix 
and cure instructions on product label must be strictly adhered to.

 Cleaning After Weld or Epoxy Repairs 

The cooler must be flushed after either a weld or an epoxy repair to 
remove all debris that may have dropped into the cooler during the repair.

The recommended procedure for cleaning is to power flush the cooler 
with water at a rate of 1.5 mm (5 in.)/sec. for three minutes. To ensure that 
debris exits the cooler, orient the cooler so the tank containing the repair, 
or closest to the repair point, is at the bottom. The flushing water is to be 
introduced into the opposite tank at the top. When complete, invert the cooler 
and power flush in opposite direction.

If power flushing is not possible, flush cooler by hand. Lay cooler 
flat with inlet and outlet ports pointing up. Fill cooler to 40 percent of its 
volume with water, seal off both ports and agitate by hand so water flushes 
all internal surfaces at least ten times. Empty cooler and repeat flushing 
process until no debris is found in the flushing water.

After flushing (either power or by hand) drain cooler of all water and 
allow to air dry. Leak test cooler to check all repairs prior to painting or 
installing cooler into vehicle.

================================================================================
PAGE 4060
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03A-12: Air Intake System, Cummins B5.9 Diesel Engine

1999 P800, F800, B800 Workshop Manual

SERVICE PROCEDURES

Leak Testing Cooler After Repairs

 NOTE: To ensure proper performance, repaired cooler must be leak-tested and 
pressure-checked prior to reinstalling it into vehicle.

Connect an air pressure gauge in one port of cooler and a stop/air 
supply in other port. Apply 345 kPa (50 psi) air pressure to cooler. Reduce 
pressure to 200 kPa (29 psi) and plug cooler to hold pressure. Let cooler 
stand a few minutes and note any loss of air pressure. Loss of air pressure 
should not exceed 10 kPa (1.5 psi) per minute. If leakage exceeds this limit, 
check cooler and make any necessary repairs. Leak test cooler again and 
continue until cooler will hold pressure as stated.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Identification

For exact engine identification and adjustment information, two decal 
labels are located on the valve cover above cylinder No. 1. The engine 
information decal contains pertinent information about the engine and 
adjustments. The identification decal contains information concerning the 
basic engine component group, engine displacement, design level, build date 
and engine calibration code. Always refer to these labels when replacement 
parts are required or when checking engine calibrations. Some engine parts may 
vary with engine application and vehicle type. The identification codes will 
ensure that the proper parts are obtained. The codes contain all pertinent 
information relating to dates, optional equipment and revisions. The Ford 
Master Parts Catalog contains a complete listing of the codes and their 
application. In addition, there is an engine serial number located on a pad at 
the lower right side of the block.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Engine

 Removal 

Disconnect battery ground cable(s).

Remove hood and front bumper.

Drain engine oil and coolant.

Release air system pressure, if so equipped.

Remove air cleaner assembly, turbocharger air supply tube and 
turbocharger-to-charge air cooler tube.

Position drain pan and disconnect power steering pump supply hose at 
pump.

Disconnect power steering pump pressure hose at pump.

Disconnect brake air compressor air supply hose at compressor, if so 
equipped.

Disconnect air conditioner compressor electrical connectors, if so 
equipped.

Remove the air conditioner compressor mounting bolts and position air 
conditioner compressor to the side, if so equipped.

Remove the air conditioner condenser-to-charge air cooler retaining 
bolt and move condenser forward, out of the way, if so equipped.

Remove fan shroud retaining bolts and hang shroud over fan.

Disconnect the radiator upper and lower hoses.

Disconnect coolant purge and supply hoses at coolant recovery reservoir.

Disconnect low coolant sensor at reservoir.

Remove the two reservoir-to-bracket retaining bolts and remove reservoir.

Disconnect the overflow hose at the radiator.

Remove the radiator retaining bolts and remove the radiator and charge 
air cooler as an assembly.

Remove shroud and remove fan-to-hub retaining bolts. Remove fan.

Disconnect brake compressor pressure hose or hydraulic brake lines, if 
so equipped.

Mark brake compressor governor hoses, if so equipped, prior to 
removing. Disconnect hoses.

Remove hose retainers at engine block.

Position hoses away from engine.

Disconnect oil cooler line at cooler and position out of way.

Disconnect exhaust pipe at turbocharger.

Remove air hose from air charge cooler to intake manifold.

Disconnect heater hoses from tubes at top of thermostat housing.

Disconnect throttle cable, hand throttle cable and transmission 
kickdown cable (automatic transmission only) and position aside.

Cut tie wraps and disconnect generator electrical harness.

Disconnect wiring to coolant temperature senders on thermostat housing.

Disconnect wiring from starter motor.

Disconnect speed sensor at flywheel housing.

Remove cable clamp retaining nut at flywheel housing.

Remove fuel lines-to-flywheel housing retaining bolts.

Disconnect two fuel lines at rear of fuel block and cap all openings.

Remove ground wire retaining bolt at flywheel housing.

Disconnect electrical connector at fuel shutoff solenoid.

Loosen clamps and remove oil fill hose.

Disconnect lower radiator hose at engine.

Remove lower hose strap retaining bolt and remove hose.

Remove exhaust pipe clamp retaining nut. Remove exhaust pipe.

Disconnect clutch slave cylinder at cross-shaft.

Remove clutch slave cylinder retaining bolts and remove cylinder.

Remove transmission. Refer to appropriate transmission section in 
Group 07.

 NOTE: Lift engine only by front and rear lifting eyes attached to cylinder 
head.

Install Engine Lifting Brackets T70P-6000 on engine.

Remove the rear engine mount retaining bolts.

Remove the front mount-to-crossmember retaining bolts.

Position lifting equipment and remove engine assembly from the vehicle.

Mount engine on engine stand and move to work area.

 Installation 

 NOTE: For fastener torque values, refer to Torque Specifications chart in 
the Specifications portion of this section.

Install Engine Lifting Brackets T70P-6000 on engine.

Lift and position engine in truck.

Attach front mount-to-crossmember retaining bolts.

Attach rear engine mounting retaining bolts.

If removed, install clutch. Refer to Section 08-01 .

Position clutch slave cylinder and attach retaining bolts. Connect 
hydraulic fitting. Refer to Section 08-02 for linkage assembly and hydraulic 
system bleeding.

Install transmission. Refer to the appropriate transmission section in 
Group 07.

Install exhaust pipe and clamp retaining nut.

Connect lower radiator hose and hose strap retaining bolt.

Install oil fill hose and clamps.

Connect fuel shutoff solenoid connector.

Attach ground wire retaining bolt to flywheel housing.

Remove protective caps from two fuel lines and attach to rear of fuel 
block.

Attach fuel lines-to-flywheel housing retaining bolts.

Attach cable clamp retaining nut at flywheel housing.

Connect speed sensor at flywheel housing.

Connect wiring for starter motor.

Connect wiring to coolant temperature senders on thermostat housing.

Connect generator electrical harness.

Connect throttle cable, hand throttle cable and transmission kickdown 
cable.

Connect heater hoses at top of thermostat housing.

Connect exhaust pipe at turbocharger.

Connect air hose from intake manifold to charge air cooler.

Connect oil cooler line to oil cooler.

Connect brake compressor governor hoses, if so equipped, and attach 
hose retainers to engine block.

Connect brake compressor hose or hydraulic brake lines, if so equipped.

Attach fan to hub and install shroud.

Install radiator and charge air cooler.

Attach overflow hose to radiator.

Assemble coolant reservoir.

Connect low coolant sensor at coolant reservoir.

Connect radiator upper and lower hoses.

Connect the air conditioner compressor and mounting bolts, if so 
equipped.

Connect the air conditioner compressor electrical connectors, if so 
equipped.

Connect the brake air compressor air supply hose to compressor, if so 
equipped.

Connect the power steering pump pressure hose to the pump.

Connect the turbocharger-to-charge air cooler, turbocharger air supply 
tube, and air cleaner assembly.

Add engine oil and coolant.

Install hood and front bumper (tilt hood), or entire front clip 
(alligator hood).

Connect battery ground cable(s).

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Cooling System

 WARNING: NEVER REMOVE THE RADIATOR CAP UNDER ANY CONDITIONS WHILE THE ENGINE IS 
OPERATING. FAILURE TO FOLLOW THESE INSTRUCTIONS CAN RESULT IN PERSONAL INJURY 
AND DAMAGE TO THE COOLING SYSTEM AND ENGINE.

TO AVOID HAVING SCALDING HOT COOLANT OR STEAM BLOW OUT OF THE RADIATOR, 
 USE EXTREME CARE WHEN REMOVING THE CAP FROM A HOT RADIATOR. IF POSSIBLE, WAIT 
UNTIL THE ENGINE HAS COOLED, THEN WRAP A THICK CLOTH AROUND THE RADIATOR CAP 
AND TURN IT SLOWLY TO THE FIRST STOP. STEP BACK WHILE THE PRESSURE IS RELEASED 
FROM THE COOLING SYSTEM. WHEN YOU ARE SURE ALL THE PRESSURE HAS BEEN RELEASED, 
PRESS DOWN ON THE CAP (STILL USING A CLOTH), TURN AND REMOVE IT. 

Refer to Section 03-03 .

1999 F and B-Series

Section 03B-03: Engine Cooling, Cummins C8.3 Diesel Engine

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Engine Block Heater

The engine block heater consists of an electrical heating element 
installed in one of the core plug openings in the engine block and an 
electrical cable that plugs into a standard 110 volt AC electrical outlet. It 
is designed to keep the engine coolant warm during cold weather to aid in cold 
starting.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Radiator Coolant Recovery Reservoir 

 Removal 

Drain the radiator until the coolant is out of the radiator coolant 
recovery reservoir. Disconnect the radiator draw down hose at the radiator 
coolant recovery reservoir. Disconnect the radiator vent tube, if so equipped, 
at the radiator coolant recovery reservoir. 

Remove the overflow tube from the recovery reservoir. Remove the 
recovery reservoir bracket retaining bolt(s) and remove the recovery 
reservoir. 

 Installation 

Position the recovery reservoir in the chassis and install the bracket 
retaining bolt(s). 

Connect the radiator draw down hose, overflow tube and vent tube, if so 
equipped, to the recovery reservoir. 

Fill and bleed the cooling system. Refer to Section 03-03 . Check for 
coolant leaks and proper coolant level after the engine reaches normal 
operating temperatures.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Fittings, Automatic Transmission

Use a waterproof sealer such as Pipe Sealant with Teflon® 
D8AZ-19554-A or equivalent meeting Ford specifications WSK-M2G350-A2 and 
ESR-M18P7-A when assembling fittings such as the drain cock to the radiator.

When installing a new radiator in a vehicle equipped with automatic 
transmission, transfer the oil cooler line fittings from the old radiator and 
install them in the new radiator, using oil-resistant sealer.

When installation of the radiator is complete, check the oil cooler 
line connections for leaks. Check the transmission fluid level and fill, if 
necessary.

Section 03B-05: Drive Belts, Accessory, Cummins C8.3 Diesel Engine

1999 F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Drive Belts, Accessory 

F800 and FT900 vehicles are equipped with two types of accessory drive 
belts. The drive belt type is selected for each engine based on performance 
requirements. To ensure maximum life, replacement belts must be of the same 
type as originally installed. These belts must be properly adjusted at all 
times. Loose belt(s) will result in slippage, which can cause a noise 
complaint or improper accessory operation (generator will not charge, etc.). 
Overly tight belts will place severe loads on accessory bearings. 

The poly-V (serpentine) drive belt tension is maintained by an 
automatic belt tensioner. Regular belt inspection is required to ensure that 
excessive belt stretch does not occur. The vee drive belt is not automatically 
tensioned and requires periodic inspection for proper belt tension.

[FIGURE: Q1690E.gif]

================================================================================
PAGE 4095
================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03B-05: Drive Belts, Accessory, Cummins C8.3 Diesel Engine

1999 F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Fan and Clutch, Engine Operated

The fan and clutch assembly is used to cool the engine. The fan is 
driven by the engine through the poly-V belt.

================================================================================
1999 F and B-Series

Section 03B-05: Drive Belts, Accessory, Cummins C8.3 Diesel Engine

1999 F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DIAGNOSIS AND TESTING

Drive Belts, Accessory

 Inspection and Verification 

 Drive Belt Cracking/Chunking/Wear 

Under severe operating conditions (high temperatures, low humidity), 
drive belt rib cracking can occur at less than 96,000 km (60,000 miles). Drive 
belt rib cracking perpendicular to the belt ribs is not a reason for concern 
and has no detrimental effect on belt performance. Cracks parallel to ribs are 
not acceptable.

Drive belt "chunking" is the condition in which the rubber material 
actually chunks out between the cracks. The drive belt must be replaced if 
chunks are missing on two adjacent ribs or a chunked-out section is 13 mm (0.5 
inch) or longer.

[FIGURE: Q4077C.gif]

 Drive Belt Noise 

Drive belt chirp is a regularly occurring chirping noise that occurs 
due to pulley misalignment or excessive pulley runout. It can be a result of a 
damaged pulley or an improperly replaced pulley that was not properly aligned.

To correct, determine the area the noise comes from. Then check each of 
the pulleys in that area with a straightedge to the crankshaft pulley and look 
for the accessory pulleys to be out of position in the fore/aft direction or 
at an angle to the straightedge.

Belt squeal is an intermittent noise that occurs when the drive belt 
slips on a pulley during certain conditions such as: engine start-up, rapid 
engine acceleration or A/C clutch engagement.

Drive belt squeal can occur under the following conditions:

A/C discharge pressure goes above 2895 kPa (420 psi). This can occur if:

the A/C system is overcharged

the A/C condenser core airflow is blocked

the engine fan blade is not engaging fully at idle

A/C OFF equalized pressure (the common discharge and suction pressure 
that occurs after several minutes) exceeds 965 kPa (140 psi), which is a rare 
occurrence at high ambient temperatures with a hot engine. Turn A/C off for a 
few seconds and then back on after fan blade begins to cool A/C condenser core.

Any of the accessories are damaged, or have a worn or damaged bearing 
or internal torsional resistance above normal for any reason. All of the 
accessories should be able to be rotated by hand in the unloaded condition. If 
any are not, inspect the accessory.

Fluid gets on the drive belt. These include power steering fluid, 
engine coolant, engine oil or air conditioning system lubricant.

If fluid does get on the drive belt during service, the best policy is 
to clean the drive belt with soap and water and thoroughly rinse with clean 
water. The drive belt does not have to be replaced if no apparent damage has 
occurred.

Drive belt is too long. A drive belt that is too long will allow the 
drive belt tensioner arm to go all the way to drive belt tensioner arm travel 
stop under certain load conditions, which will untension the drive belt. If 
the drive belt tensioner is resting on the stop, replace the drive belt.

If the drive belt tensioner is worn or damaged. The drive belt 
tensioner arm should rotate freely without binding.

 Symptom Chart — Accessory Drive Belt Diagnosis 

 ACCESSORY DRIVE BELT DIAGNOSIS

 Component Tests 

 Drive Belt Tension 

Check drive belt tension. Refer to Drive Belt Tension Adjustment in the 
Adjustments portion of this section. If tension is not within specification, 
check drive belt tensioner. Service components as required.

 Drive Belt Tensioner, Automatic 

The drive belt tensioner will maintain correct belt tension if the 
correct length drive belt is on the engine. Check drive belt tensioner as 
follows:

With the engine running, observe drive belt tensioner movement. The 
drive belt tensioner should move (respond) when the A/C compressor cycles or 
when the engine is accelerated rapidly. If the drive belt tensioner movement 
is constant and excessive, a pulley or shaft is probably bent or a pulley is 
out of round. In rare cases, excessive belt rideout (uneven depth of grooves 
in belt) can cause excessive drive belt tensioner movement. This condition can 
be checked by replacing the suspect drive belt with a known good original 
equipment drive belt and repeating the observation.

With engine off, check for proper drive belt routing. Refer to the 
illustrations under Removal and Installation. Service as required.

Visually inspect the condition of the drive belt. Replace the drive 
belt as required.

Rotate the drive belt tensioner and check for a binding or frozen 
condition. Replace components as required.

 Drive Belt Misalignment 

 CAUTION: Incorrect drive belt installation will cause excessive drive belt wear 
and can cause the drive belt to come off the drive pulleys. 

 NOTE: Original equipment drive belts are made of a special cord construction 
and are subjected to special testing before approval for use.

 NOTE: Replacement drive belts, other than O.E.M., may track 
differently/improperly. If a replacement drive belt tracks improperly, the 
drive belt must be replaced with an O.E.M. drive belt to avoid performance 
failure or loss of drive belt during cold operation.

With the engine running, check drive belt tracking (the position of the 
drive belt on the drive belt tensioner). If the edge of the drive belt rides 
beyond the edge of the drive bent tensioner, this can cause noise and 
premature wear.

If a drive belt tracking condition exists, visually check the drive 
belt tensioner for damage, especially the mounting pad surface. If the drive 
belt tensioner is not installed correctly with the locating pins in the 
locating holes, the mounting surface pad will be out of position. This will 
result in drive belt tension and chirp and squeal noises.

If the above procedures do not correct the drive belt noise, try 
replacing the drive belt with a known good original equipment drive belt. 
However, the drive belt noise may return again (with mileage) if one of the 
above conditions still exists uncorrected.

With engine running, visually observe the grooves in the pulleys (not 
the pulley flanges) for excessive wobble. Replace components as required.

Check all accessories, mounting brackets and drive belt tensioner for 
any interference that prevents the component from mounting properly. Correct 
any interference condition and recheck belt tracking.

Tighten all accessories, mounting brackets and drive belt tensioner 
retaining hardware to specification. Recheck drive belt tracking.

Check drive belt tension. Refer to Drive Belt Tension Adjustment in the 
Adjustments portion of this section.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drive Belt Replacement 

Conditions requiring drive belt replacement are rib chunk out, 
excessive wear, severe glazing and frayed cords. Replace any drive belt 
exhibiting any of these conditions. Perpendicular cracks in the ribbed side of 
V-grooved portion of the drive belt are considered acceptable.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Drive Belt Tensioner, Automatic

 Removal 

Rotate automatic belt tensioner to release drive belt tension.

With tension released, remove drive belt from tensioner pulley.

Allow drive belt tensioner to rotate slowly to the relaxed position. Do 
not allow tensioner to snap back after the drive belt is removed, otherwise 
damage to the tensioner can occur.

Remove drive belt tensioner retainer bolt and tensioner. 

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Tighten drive belt tensioner bolt to 83 Nm (61 lb-ft).

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Starter Motor

 Removal 

Open battery box and disconnect battery ground cable. 

Remove starter motor upper mounting bolt. 

Disconnect starter motor and starter solenoid wires. Tag wires to 
facilitate connection at proper terminals during starter motor installation. 

Remove two remaining starter motor mounting bolts. Remove starter motor. 

 Installation 

Position starter motor on engine. Install three bolts. Tighten to 
150-200 Nm (110-148 lb-ft). 

Connect starter solenoid wire to starter terminal. 

Connect remaining starter motor wires to starter terminals. 

Connect battery ground cable and close battery box. Check starter motor 
operation.

fuel solenoid to bracket screws: 9 Nm (80 lb-in)

bracket to intake cover: 9 Nm (80 lb-in)

fuel supply lines: 10 Nm (89 lb-in)

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Glow Plug, Air Intake Heater

 Removal 

 CAUTION: The glow plug heater can be damaged by excessive torque at the 
electrical connector terminal. Do not exceed 4 Nm (36 lb-in) torque 
when removing or installing the connector retaining nut. 

Pull back the protective boot and remove the electrical connector 
retaining nut.

 CAUTION: The glow plug contains a fine mesh filter and a small fuel metering 
orifice. Use care to prevent entry of contaminants. 

Disconnect and cap fuel line.

Loosen jam nut and remove glow plug.

 Installation 

Thread glow plug into intake cover until it bottoms. Back plug out two 
turns and align with pointer on cover.

Connect fuel line. Tighten nut to 10 Nm (89 lb-in).

Tighten glow plug jam nut to 25 Nm (18 lb-ft).

Install wiring connector. Tighten retaining nut to 4 Nm (35 
lb-in). Overtightening retaining nut can destroy heater element.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Starter Motor 

 Disassembly 

Thoroughly clean outside of starter motor.

Scribe an alignment mark on starter frame, lever housing and drive end 
housing for assembly reference.

Remove motor terminal retaining screw at solenoid.

Remove retaining screws and drive end housing. Tap housing with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from lever housing, if necessary.

Tap snap ring retainer toward drive pinion using a hammer and socket.

Remove snap ring from armature shaft and discard.

Remove snap ring retainer.

Remove lever housing retaining screws.

 NOTE: Use care when removing assembly to prevent damage to armature shaft lip 
seal located at front of lever housing.

Remove lever housing, drive pinion and solenoid as an assembly. Tap 
housing with plastic-tipped hammer to remove assembly from frame, if necessary.

Remove thrust washer from armature shaft.

Remove brush end plate retaining screws. Tap edge of end plate with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from starter frame.

Remove thrust washer from armature shaft.

Remove screws attaching brush terminals to brush holder.

Pry brush springs upward using screwdriver and remove brushes.

Remove armature.

Remove screws attaching field terminals to brush holder.

Remove retaining screws and brush holder.

Remove drive assembly from lever housing.

Remove lever housing plug.

Remove pinion depth adjusting screw from end of solenoid plunger shaft.

Remove retaining screws and solenoid.

Remove solenoid plunger and protective boot.

Remove snap ring and shift lever pin.

Remove shift lever from housing. Note direction of installation before 
removing.

Remove screws attaching pole shoes to frame using a pole shoe 
screwdriver and arbor press.

Remove field coils and pole shoes from frame.

Clean and inspect parts. Refer to Section 03-06 .

 Assembly 

Follow disassembly procedure in reverse order.

Inspect O-ring seals on shift lever pin drive end housing, frame and 
lever housing. Replace seals if cut or otherwise damaged.

Lightly coat armature shaft seal and thrust washers with a 
multi-purpose lubricant.

Check pinion depth adjustment. Refer to Starter Drive Pinion Depth 
Adjustment in the Adjustments portion of this section.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Starter Drive

 Removal 

Thoroughly clean outside of starter motor.

Scribe alignment marks on drive end housing, lever housing and frame 
for assembly reference.

Remove motor terminal retaining screw at solenoid.

Remove retaining screws and drive end housing. Tap housing with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from lever housing, if necessary.

Tap snap ring retainer toward drive assembly using hammer and socket.

Remove snap ring from armature shaft and discard.

Remove snap ring retainer.

Remove lever housing retaining screws.

Remove lever housing, drive pinion and solenoid as an assembly. Tap 
housing with plastic-tipped hammer to remove assembly from frame, if necessary.

Use care when removing assembly to prevent damage to armature shaft lip 
seal located at front of lever housing. Also, note thrust washer installed on 
armature shaft.

Disengage drive assembly from shift lever and remove.

Inspect O-ring seals on drive end housing and lever housing. Replace 
seal if cut or otherwise damaged.

Inspect armature shaft lip seal in lever housing. Replace seal if worn, 
cut or otherwise damaged.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Shift lever is under solenoid spring pressure. Pry lever away from 
housing to provide clearance needed to install drive assembly.

Coat armature shaft seal with a light application of multi-purpose 
lubricant.

Make sure thrust washer is in position on armature shaft before 
installing lever housing.

Check drive pinion depth adjustment. Refer to Starter Drive Pinon Depth 
Adjustment in the Adjustments portion of this section.

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Solenoid

 Removal 

Remove retaining screws and brush end plate. If necessary, tap edge of 
end plate with plastic-tipped hammer to remove from starter frame. Note thrust 
washer installed on armature shaft.

Remove screw attaching motor terminal to solenoid.

Pull solenoid away from lever housing and maneuver as necessary to 
clear motor terminal. Carefully pulling forward on motor terminal can provide 
additional clearance.

Inspect end plate O-ring seal on frame and solenoid O-ring seal on 
lever housing. Replace seals if cut or otherwise damaged.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Make sure thrust washer is installed on armature shaft before 
installing brush end plate.

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Brush

 Removal 

Thoroughly clean outside of starter.

Remove brush end plate retaining screws. Tap edge of end plate with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from starter frame. Note thrust washer 
installed on end of armature shaft.

Remove screws attaching brush terminals to brush holder.

Pry brush springs upward using screwdriver and remove brushes.

Inspect O-ring seal on starter frame. Replace seal if cut or otherwise 
damaged.

Inspect armature commutator.

If commutator is contaminated, remove brush holder and clean using 00 
grade sandpaper. If commutator is excessively worn or scored, it should be 
replaced.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Make sure thrust washer is installed on end of armature shaft before 
installing brush end plate.

1999 F700, F800, FT900 Workshop Manual

DISASSEMBLY AND ASSEMBLY

Armature

 Removal 

Thoroughly clean outside of starter motor.

Scribe an alignment mark on starter frame, lever housing and drive end 
housing for assembly reference.

Remove motor terminal retaining screw at solenoid.

Remove retaining screws and drive end housing. Tap housing with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from lever housing, if necessary.

Tap snap ring retainer toward drive pinion using hammer and socket.

Remove snap ring from armature shaft and discard.

Remove snap ring retainer.

Remove lever housing retaining screws.

 NOTE: Use care when removing assembly to prevent damage to armature shaft 
seal located at front of lever housing.

Remove lever housing, drive pinion and solenoid as an assembly. Tap 
housing with plastic-tipped hammer to remove assembly from frame, if necessary.

Remove thrust washer from armature shaft.

Remove brush end plate retaining screws. Tap edge of end plate with 
plastic-tipped hammer to remove from starter frame.

Remove thrust washer from armature shaft.

Pry brush springs upward using screwdriver and pull brushes out of 
holder until spring can be released against side of brush, holding it away 
from armature.

Remove armature.

 Installation 

Follow removal procedure in reverse order.

Inspect O-ring seal on drive end housing and frame. Replace if cut or 
otherwise damaged.

Inspect armature shaft lip seal in lever housing. Replace if worn, cut 
or otherwise damaged.

Coat armature shaft seal with a light application of multi-purpose 
lubricant.

Make sure thrust washers are installed on armature shaft before 
installing brush end plate and lever housing.

Check drive pinion depth adjustment. Refer to Starter Drive Pinion 
Depth Adjustment in the Adjustments portion of this section.

ADJUSTMENTS

Starter Drive Pinion Depth Adjustment

Remove M-terminal retaining screw. To prevent contact between 
M-terminal and solenoid, carefully bend M-terminal away from solenoid using 
needle nose pliers.

Place an insulating material between M-terminal and solenoid.

Connect battery to S-terminal and to a clean metal ground on solenoid 
case.

[FIGURE: J35651A.gif]

 CAUTION: Keep fingers and tools away from opening in drive end housing while 
making electrical connections. The strong shifting action of the solenoid can 
cause personal injury or damage as the drive pinion moves into cranking 
position. 

Momentarily flash a jumper lead from ground to terminal M. The drive 
will now shift into cranking position and remain so until battery is 
disconnected. 

Press on overrunning clutch just enough to take up any drive assembly 
free travel.

Measure distance between pinion and snap ring retainer.

If clearance is not within specifications, adjust by removing access 
plug and turning solenoid plunger shaft nut. If shaft turns, remove solenoid 
so the shaft can be held.

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Induction System 

Air is pulled into the engine through an air filter. Clean air is very 
important to the life of the engine. Ingested dust and dirt can damage the 
cylinders very quickly. 

On turbocharged and aftercooled engines, the intake airflow is from the 
air cleaner to the turbocharger. It is then routed to the charge air cooler 
located in front of the radiator. Air leaves the charge air cooler and is 
routed to the intake manifold where it is forced into the cylinders and used 
for combustion. The charge air cooler reduces the temperature of the intake 
air, which lowers combustion chamber temperatures, which in turn reduces NOx 
emissions. Also, cooling the intake air makes it more dense, allowing more 
fuel to be injected into the engine to increase the power-to-weight ratio. 

 Typical Intake Air System, Turbocharged Engine

DESCRIPTION AND OPERATION

Air Restriction Indicator

All Cummins C8.3 engine air cleaners are equipped with an air 
restriction indicator that indicates when the air cleaner needs servicing. 
When the indicator reads 6.2 kPa (25 inches of water) vacuum, the air cleaner 
needs servicing.

REMOVAL AND INSTALLATION

Engine Air Cleaner Intake Duct and Tube, Tilt Hood

 Removal 

Remove the band clamps from the air cleaner intake tube and flex tube
